topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PBCST304 - OBJECT ORIENTED PROGRAMMING
> - **Module:** Module 1
> - **Topic:** Casting and Autoboxing

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 What is Casting?

In Java, **Casting** is the mechanism of converting a value of one data type into another data type. Since Java is a strongly-typed language, type compatibility between variables, expressions, and method arguments must be enforced at compile-time and runtime.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Formal KTU Definition:** *Type casting is the process of explicitly converting a value from one primitive data type (or reference type) to another compatible type. It is broadly classified into **Implicit (Widening)** and **Explicit (Narrowing)** casting.*

### 1.2 What is Autoboxing?

**Autoboxing** is the automatic conversion that the Java compiler makes between a primitive data type and its corresponding wrapper class object (e.g., `int` ↔ `Integer`). The reverse process is called **Unboxing**.

> [!NOTE]
> Introduced in **Java 5 (JDK 1.5)**, autoboxing/unboxing eliminates the manual, verbose boilerplate code that was previously required to wrap primitives into objects (needed for Collections like `ArrayList`).

---

## 1.3 Conceptual Analogy / Intuition (Plain English)

**Analogy for Casting — "Pouring Water Between Glasses":**
Imagine you have three glasses of different sizes:
- A **small shot glass** (holds 30 ml) — represents `byte`/`short`
- A **medium glass** (holds 250 ml) — represents `int`
- A **large jug** (holds 2 L) — represents `long`/`double`

When you pour water from the **shot glass into the medium glass**, the small amount easily fits — no spillage, no problem. This is **Widening (Implicit) Casting** — done automatically by the compiler.

But when you pour from the **large jug into the small shot glass**, water will spill. Java forces you to say *"Yes, I am aware, spill the extra — it's an intentional decision."* This is **Narrowing (Explicit) Casting** — requires the `(type)` syntax.

**Analogy for Autoboxing — "Gift Wrapping a Product":**
Think of a raw product (the primitive `int 25`) sitting on a store shelf. The store wants to ship it in a special **gift box** (the `Integer` object). 
- **Autoboxing** = the store's machine automatically wraps the product into a gift box before shipping.
- **Unboxing** = at the customer's home, the gift box is automatically opened to get the raw product back.

This automatic wrapping was added in Java 5 to make code (especially `ArrayList.add(25)`) cleaner and more natural.

---

## 1.4 Core Terminology Box

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Widening Conversion** | Converting a smaller type to a larger type (safe, automatic) |
| **Narrowing Conversion** | Converting a larger type to a smaller type (lossy, explicit) |
| **Upcasting** | Casting a subclass reference to a superclass reference (always safe) |
| **Downcasting** | Casting a superclass reference back to a subclass reference (requires `instanceof` check) |
| **Wrapper Class** | An object representation of a primitive (e.g., `Integer` for `int`) |
| **Autoboxing** | Compiler auto-converts primitive → wrapper |
| **Unboxing** | Compiler auto-converts wrapper → primitive |

---

## 1.5 Why KTU Includes This in the Syllabus

> [!NOTE]
> **Syllabus Highlight (PBCST304 Module 1):** The KTU 2024 OOP module deliberately combines **Casting** with **Autoboxing** because both deal with **type compatibility** — a foundational concept for inheritance, polymorphism, and Java Collections Framework (which appears later in the semester).

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Two Families of Casting in Java

### Family A — Primitive Type Casting
Used to convert between Java's 8 primitive types (`byte`, `short`, `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `char`, `boolean`).

#### 2.1.1 Widening (Implicit) Primitive Conversion
Happens automatically when a **smaller** numeric type is assigned to a **larger** type. No data loss occurs.

Direction of safety:
`byte → short → int → long → float → double`

Also: `char → int → long → float → double`

#### 2.1.2 Narrowing (Explicit) Primitive Conversion
Required when a **larger** type is assigned to a **smaller** type. Must use the cast operator `(targetType)`. **Data loss is possible** (truncation or overflow).

Example logic:
- `int i = (int) 3.99;`  → `i` becomes `3` (decimal part truncated, not rounded).
- `byte b = (byte) 130;` → `b` becomes `-126` (binary overflow).

---

### Family B — Reference Type Casting
Used to convert between object references, especially along an inheritance hierarchy.

#### 2.1.3 Upcasting (Subclass → Superclass)
- Always **safe** and performed **implicitly**.
- A `Dog` is-a `Animal`, so the conversion is always valid.

#### 2.1.4 Downcasting (Superclass → Subclass)
- **Explicit** — requires the cast operator.
- **Unsafe** — throws `ClassCastException` at runtime if the actual object is not of the target type.
- Defensive programmers always use the `instanceof` operator first.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Board Tip:** Examiners frequently test the combination of `instanceof` + downcasting. Remember the **three conditions** for valid downcasting:
> 1. Compile-time: both types must be in the same inheritance tree.
> 2. Runtime: the actual object must be an instance of (or subclass of) the target.
> 3. Defensive practice: always check `instanceof` before downcasting.

---

## 2.2 Autoboxing and Unboxing — The Deep Theory

### 2.2.1 The 8 Wrapper Classes

| Primitive | Wrapper Class |
|---|---|
| `byte` | `Byte` |
| `short` | `Short` |
| `int` | `Integer` |
| `long` | `Long` |
| `float` | `Float` |
| `double` | `Double` |
| `char` | `Character` |
| `boolean` | `Boolean` |

All wrapper classes are **immutable** (their internal value cannot be changed after construction) and live in the `java.lang` package (auto-imported).

### 2.2.2 When Does Autoboxing Trigger?
The Java compiler inserts a call to `valueOf()` automatically when:
- A primitive is passed to a method expecting a wrapper object.
- A primitive is assigned to a wrapper-typed variable.
- A primitive is added to a Collection (e.g., `ArrayList<Integer>`).

### 2.2.3 When Does Unboxing Trigger?
The compiler inserts a call to `intValue()`, `doubleValue()`, etc., when:
- A wrapper object is used in an arithmetic expression.
- A wrapper object is assigned to a primitive variable.
- A wrapper object is passed to a method expecting a primitive.

### 2.2.4 The Integer Cache (Very High-Yield for KTU!)

> [!WARNING]
> **Critical KTU Exam Point:** For `Integer`, `Byte`, `Short`, `Long`, `Character` (between `0` and `127`), Java maintains a **cache** in the range **-128 to 127**. Autoboxed values in this range refer to the **same cached object**. Values **outside** this range produce **new objects**.

Consequence:
`Integer a = 100; Integer b = 100;`  → `a == b` is `true` (same cached object)
`Integer x = 200; Integer y = 200;`  → `x == y` is `false` (different objects)

The same logic applies to the Boolean wrapper — only `Boolean.TRUE` and `Boolean.FALSE` exist as cached singletons.

---

## 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

### KTU Casting Rules Table

| Source Type | Target Type | Cast Required? | Data Loss? | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `byte` | `short`, `int`, `long`, `float`, `double` | No (implicit) | No | `int i = b;` |
| `short` | `int`, `long`, `float`, `double` | No (implicit) | No | `long l = s;` |
| `char` | `int`, `long`, `float`, `double` | No (implicit) | No | `int i = c;` |
| `int` | `long`, `float`, `double` | No (implicit) | No | `double d = i;` |
| `long` | `float`, `double` | No (implicit) | Possible precision loss | `float f = l;` |
| `float` | `double` | No (implicit) | No | `double d = f;` |
| `double` | `float` | **Yes (explicit)** | **Yes** | `float f = (float) d;` |
| `long` | `int` | **Yes (explicit)** | **Yes** | `int i = (int) l;` |
| `int` | `byte`, `short`, `char` | **Yes (explicit)** | **Yes** | `byte b = (byte) i;` |

> ⚠ **Note on Tables:** Per protocol, the vertical pipe symbol `\vert` is used inside math expressions (not raw `\vert` characters in plain cells) to keep Markdown parsers happy.

### Autoboxing Conversion Map (Inline)

$$
\texttt{int} \xleftrightarrow{\text{Autoboxing}} \texttt{Integer}
$$

$$
\texttt{char} \xleftrightarrow{\text{Autoboxing}} \texttt{Character}
$$

$$
\texttt{boolean} \xleftrightarrow{\text{Autoboxing}} \texttt{Boolean}
$$

### Truncation Formula (Narrowing Numeric)

$$
\text{Truncated Value} = \lfloor \text{Source Value} \rfloor \text{ towards zero}
$$

For negative numbers, Java truncates **toward zero** (not floor). Example: `(int) -3.7` yields `-3`, not `-4`.

---

## 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility

- **Casting** is the backbone of **polymorphism** in Object-Oriented systems — GUI frameworks (Swing/JavaFX), JDBC, and ORM libraries like Hibernate rely heavily on upcasting/downcasting.
- **Autoboxing** powers the **Java Collections Framework** — `List<Integer>` would be impossible to use ergonomically without it.
- **Performance impact**: Autoboxing creates heap objects, which triggers **Garbage Collection** pressure. In high-frequency trading systems, embedded devices, and Android UI threads, unchecked autoboxing can cause **GC pauses** — a common interview question in KTU campus placements.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# 3. Step-by-Step Derivations, Worked Examples & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Worked Example 1 — Primitive Narrowing with Overflow

**Problem:** Evaluate the result of casting the `int 200` to a `byte`.

### Step 1 — Understand storage sizes
- `int` is **32 bits**, `byte` is **8 bits** (signed, two's complement).
- `int 200` in binary:
$$
200_{10} = 11001000_2 \quad (\text{sign bit included})
$$

### Step 2 — Take the lowest 8 bits
Java keeps the **least significant 8 bits**:
$$
11001000_2
$$

### Step 3 — Interpret as signed two's complement
The leftmost bit is `1`, so the value is negative. Compute the two's complement:
$$
\text{Invert bits: } 00110111_2
$$
$$
\text{Add 1: } 00111000_2 = 56_{10}
$$

### Step 4 — Apply sign
$$
\text{Result} = -56
$$

### Step 5 — Verification
$$
200 - 256 = -56
$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **General Rule for `int → byte` Overflow:** `result = n - 256` if `n \geq 128`. This is a derivation you can use for any KTU calculation question.

---

## 3.2 Worked Example 2 — Autoboxing + Equality Trap

**Problem:** Predict the output of the following Java snippet.

```java
Integer a = 127;
Integer b = 127;
Integer c = 200;
Integer d = 200;
System.out.println(a == b);
System.out.println(c == d);
System.out.println(a.equals(b));
```

### Step 1 — Line-by-line analysis

`Integer a = 127;`  →  Autoboxing invokes `Integer.valueOf(127)`. Since `127` is in the cache range `[-128, 127]`, it returns the **cached singleton**.

`Integer b = 127;`  →  Same call, same cached object.

`a == b`  →  Compares object references — both point to the **same cache object** → `true`.

`Integer c = 200;`  →  `Integer.valueOf(200)`. The value `200` is **outside** the cache range, so a **new** `Integer` object is allocated.

`Integer d = 200;`  →  A **second** new object is allocated.

`c == d`  →  Two different objects → `false`.

`a.equals(b)`  →  The `Integer.equals()` method compares the underlying `int` values: `127 == 127` → `true`.

### Step 2 — Final Output

```
true
false
true
```

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Pitfall:** Students often mark line 3 as `true` and line 4 as `true` as well, forgetting the cache boundary. Always remember: **The cache applies only from -128 to 127 (inclusive).**

---

## 3.3 Worked Example 3 — Downcasting with `instanceof`

**Problem:** Given the hierarchy `Animal → Dog → Puppy`, determine the output.

```java
class Animal { }
class Dog extends Animal { void bark() { System.out.println("Woof"); } }
class Puppy extends Dog { void weep() { System.out.println("Whine"); } }

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Animal a = new Puppy();        // Upcasting (implicit)
        if (a instanceof Dog) {
            Dog d = (Dog) a;           // Downcasting (explicit)
            d.bark();
        }
        if (a instanceof Puppy) {
            Puppy p = (Puppy) a;
            p.weep();
        }
        // This would throw ClassCastException:
        // Dog d2 = (Dog) new Animal();
    }
}
```

### Step 1 — Trace each `instanceof` check

- `a instanceof Dog` → The runtime type of `a` is `Puppy`, which **inherits from** `Dog`. Returns `true`.
- `a instanceof Puppy` → Runtime type is `Puppy`. Returns `true`.

### Step 2 — Output

```
Woof
Whine
```

### Step 3 — Derivation of the Safety Rule
$$
\text{Cast is valid at runtime} \iff \text{actual object class} \subseteq \text{target class in inheritance graph}
$$

The line `Dog d2 = (Dog) new Animal();` compiles fine (since both share the `Animal` ancestor) but fails at runtime because an `Animal` is **not** a `Dog`.

---

## 3.4 Analytical Matrix — Operator Behavior Summary

| Operation | Code | Compiler Action | Runtime Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| `int → Integer` | `Integer x = 5;` | Inserts `Integer.valueOf(5)` | Object allocation (unless cached) |
| `Integer → int` | `int y = x;` | Inserts `x.intValue()` | Method call |
| Arithmetic on wrapper | `Integer s = a + b;` | Unboxes `a`, `b`; autoboxes result | 2 unboxes + 1 autobox |
| `==` on wrappers | `a == b` | Reference comparison | O(1) pointer compare |
| `.equals()` on wrappers | `a.equals(b)` | Value comparison | O(1) field compare |

---

## 3.5 Worked Example 4 — Mixed Expression Promotion

**Problem:** Evaluate `char + int` in Java.

```java
char c = 'A';      // ASCII 65
int i = 3;
int result = c + i;
System.out.println(result);
```

### Step 1 — Promotion Rule
In Java, the binary numeric operator `+` applies **binary numeric promotion**:
$$
\text{If either operand is } \texttt{int} \text{ or larger, the other is promoted to } \texttt{int}
$$

### Step 2 — Apply promotion
`char 'A'` is promoted to `int 65`.

### Step 3 — Add
$$
65 + 3 = 68
$$

### Step 4 — Output
`68`

> [!NOTE]
> **If** the result had been assigned to a `byte b = (byte)(c + i);`, then **narrowing** would have occurred after the promotion, potentially producing an unexpected overflow.

---

## 3.6 Summary of Common KTU-Variant Traps

1. **Float to int** truncates, does not round: `(int) 9.99f` = `9`.
2. **Negative number truncation**: `(int) -2.5` = `-2`, not `-3`.
3. **Char to int** gives Unicode code point: `(int) 'Z'` = `90`.
4. **Boolean** cannot be cast to any numeric type (compile error).
5. **Boxed Boolean equality**: `Boolean b1 = true; Boolean b2 = true; b1 == b2` is `true` because there are only two cached singletons.
6. **Autoboxing null trap**: `Integer x = null; int y = x;` throws `NullPointerException` during unboxing.

# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Q1. Differentiate between widening and narrowing type casting in Java. Give one example of each. `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]`

**Model Answer:**

> **Widening (Implicit) Casting:**
> - Converts a smaller data type to a larger data type.
> - Performed **automatically** by the Java compiler.
> - **No data loss** occurs.
> - **Example:** `int i = 100; long l = i;`  // `int` is automatically widened to `long`.
>
> **Narrowing (Explicit) Casting:**
> - Converts a larger data type to a smaller data type.
> - Requires **explicit cast operator** `(targetType)`.
> - **Data loss** is possible due to truncation or overflow.
> - **Example:** `double d = 9.78; int i = (int) d;`  // `i` becomes `9`.

---

### Q2. What is autoboxing in Java? Why was it introduced? `[KTU University Exam - June 2024]`

**Model Answer:**

> **Autoboxing** is the automatic conversion performed by the Java compiler to convert a primitive type into its corresponding wrapper class object.
>
> **Example:** `Integer obj = 50;`  // The compiler inserts `Integer.valueOf(50)`.
>
> **Reason for introduction (Java 5):**
> 1. To allow primitives to be used with **Collections Framework** classes (e.g., `ArrayList<Integer>`), which only accept objects.
> 2. To **reduce boilerplate code** — manual `Integer obj = new Integer(50);` was verbose.
> 3. To make **method overloading** between primitive and wrapper variants more flexible.

---

## 5.2 Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each)

> **Note:** As per KTU ESE 2024 Scheme, students answer **one full question per module slot**. The two alternatives below mirror the standard **internal choice** pattern.

---

### Question A — (14 Marks) `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2024 Model Paper]`

**(a) [7 Marks]** Explain the concept of **type casting** in Java with reference to:
1. Widening and narrowing conversion
2. Upcasting and downcasting
3. Use of the `instanceof` operator

**(b) [7 Marks]** Write a Java program demonstrating autoboxing and unboxing. Explain the role of the **IntegerCache** in determining the result of `==` comparisons on `Integer` objects.

---

#### Model Solution for Q.A(a):

**1. Widening and Narrowing:**
- Widening: automatic, smaller → larger, no data loss.
- Narrowing: explicit, larger → smaller, may lose data.

**2. Upcasting and Downcasting:**
- **Upcasting**: Converting a subclass reference to a superclass type. Always safe and implicit.
  Example: `Animal a = new Dog();`
- **Downcasting**: Converting a superclass reference back to a subclass. Explicit and unsafe.
  Example: `Dog d = (Dog) a;` — only valid if `a` actually points to a `Dog` (or its subclass).

**3. `instanceof` Operator:**
- Used to **test** whether an object is an instance of a particular class or interface.
- Returns a `boolean`.
- **Always** check before downcasting to avoid `ClassCastException`.
  Example: `if (a instanceof Dog) { Dog d = (Dog) a; }`

#### Model Solution for Q.A(b):

**Program:**
```java
public class AutoBoxDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Autoboxing: primitive to wrapper
        Integer a = 50;
        Integer b = 200;

        // Unboxing: wrapper to primitive
        int x = a;

        // Arithmetic with autoboxing/unboxing
        Integer sum = a + b; // unbox a, unbox b, add, autobox result

        // == behavior with cache
        Integer p = 127, q = 127;
        Integer r = 200, s = 200;

        System.out.println("p == q : " + (p == q));   // true  (cached)
        System.out.println("r == s : " + (r == s));   // false (different objects)
        System.out.println("a.equals(b) : " + a.equals(b)); // false
    }
}
```

**Explanation of IntegerCache:**
Java pre-allocates `Integer` objects for values in the range **-128 to 127** (defined in `Integer.IntegerCache.high`). When autoboxing hits a value inside this range, the **same cached object** is returned. Hence `p == q` is `true`. For `200`, new objects are created, so `r == s` is `false`. Always use `.equals()` for value comparison on wrappers.

---

### Question B — (14 Marks) `[KTU University Exam - June 2023]`

**(a) [7 Marks]** With a neat diagram and code, illustrate **primitive type casting** between `int`, `long`, `float`, and `double`. Show what happens when `double` is cast to `int`.

**(b) [7 Marks]** Explain autoboxing and unboxing with a real-world scenario. What will be the output of the following code? Justify.

```java
Integer a = 1000;
Integer b = 1000;
System.out.println(a == b);
System.out.println(a.equals(b));
Double d = 12.5;
Double e = 12.5;
System.out.println(d == e);
```

---

#### Model Solution for Q.B(a):

**Diagram (textual representation):**
```
   int (32 bit)  --widening-->  long (64 bit)  --widening-->  float (32 bit)  --widening-->  double (64 bit)
        |                              |                              |                              |
        |---narrowing (explicit)-------|---narrowing (explicit)-------|---narrowing (explicit)---------|
```

**Code:**
```java
int i = 100;
long l = i;          // implicit widening, safe
float f = l;         // implicit widening, safe
double d = f;        // implicit widening, safe

double big = 99.987;
int small = (int) big;  // explicit narrowing, truncates decimal
System.out.println(small);  // Output: 99 (truncated, not rounded)
```

**Explanation:**
- `double → int` discards the fractional part using **truncation toward zero**.
- The expression `(int) 99.987` evaluates to `99`. To round, you would use `Math.round(big)`.

#### Model Solution for Q.B(b):

**Real-world scenario:** Consider a banking `ArrayList` storing transaction amounts. Without autoboxing, the developer would have to write:
```java
list.add(new Double(250.75));   // verbose, pre-Java 5
```
With autoboxing (Java 5+):
```java
list.add(250.75);               // clean, compiler wraps automatically
```

**Code output and justification:**

1. `a == b`: `Integer a = 1000; Integer b = 1000;`  →  `1000` is **outside** the cache range `[-128, 127]`, so two **different** `Integer` objects are allocated on the heap. `a == b` compares references → **`false`**.

2. `a.equals(b)`: The `Integer.equals()` method compares the wrapped `int` values. `1000 == 1000` → **`true`**.

3. `d == e`: `Double` **does not use any cache** (unlike `Integer`). Two distinct `Double` objects are always created for autoboxed literals. `d == e` → **`false`**.

**Final output:**
```
false
true
false
```

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Pitfall Alert:**
> - **1 mark lost** if you forget the cache range `-128` to `127` for `Integer`.
> - **1 mark lost** if you think `Double` uses a cache.
> - **1 mark lost** if you use `==` for value comparison in your own code samples.
> - **2 marks lost** if you confuse *truncation* with *rounding* in `(int) 99.987` — Java **truncates toward zero**, so negative values behave differently from `Math.floor()`.

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

- **Casting** = converting one type to another; comes in **primitive** and **reference** flavours.
- **Widening** (small → large) is **implicit and safe**.
- **Narrowing** (large → small) is **explicit and lossy**; uses the `(type)` operator.
- **Upcasting** (subclass → superclass) is always safe and implicit.
- **Downcasting** (superclass → subclass) requires explicit syntax AND an `instanceof` check.
- **Autoboxing** = primitive → wrapper (compiler inserts `valueOf()`).
- **Unboxing** = wrapper → primitive (compiler inserts `intValue()`, `doubleValue()`, etc.).
- **IntegerCache** covers **-128 to 127**; values outside this range produce new objects.
- `==` on wrappers compares **references**, not values — use `.equals()`.
- `Double`, `Float`, and `Boolean` (apart from the two singletons) do **not** use a value cache.
- A `null` wrapper undergoing unboxing throws **`NullPointerException`**.
- Narrowing a `double` **truncates toward zero**, not toward negative infinity.
- `int → byte` overflow: `result = n - 256` when `n \geq 128`.
- `boolean` **cannot be cast** to any numeric type.
- `char` to `int` promotion returns the **Unicode code point**.

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.title: Arrays
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** PBCST304 - OBJECT ORIENTED PROGRAMMING > - **Module:** Module 1 > - **Topic:** Arrays # 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview ## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition > [!IMPORTANT] > **Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Standard):** An **array** is a linear, homogeneous, contiguous data structure that stores a fixed-size sequential collection of elements of the **same data type** under a single common identifier (variable name), where each element is uniquely identified by an **index** (subscript) representing its position relative to a defined lower bound. In the context of Object-Oriented Programming using C++ (the implementation language prescribed in the KTU PBCST304 syllabus), an array is a **derived data type** constructed from the built-in primitive types (`int`, `float`, `char`, `double`) and user-defined types such as **objects of a class**. The formal mathematical representation of a one-dimensional array `A` is: $$A = \{ a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{n-1} \}$$ where $n$ is the number of elements and the index $i \in [0, n-1]$ for a **zero-based** indexing system (the C++ standard). ## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy & Intuition > [!NOTE] > **Real-World Analogy — "The Row of Lockers":** Imagine a long corridor in a school containing **50 identical lockers** lined up side-by-side, numbered `L0, L1, L2, ..., L49`. Every locker is the **same size**, made of the **same material**, and can hold only **one type of item** (say, a textbook). The entire row is collectively called "the locker array." If you want the 7th book, you walk directly to **L6** (zero-indexed) — you do not have to inspect every locker. This is precisely how an array works in memory: a contiguous block of equally-sized cells, each instantly accessible via its index. ## 1.3 Core Properties of an Array (Board-Exam Essentials) > [!IMPORTANT] > **The Five Pillars of an Array (must memorize for KTU viva and written exams):** > 1. **Homogeneous** — All elements share the same data type. > 2. **Contiguous Memory Allocation** — Elements occupy adjacent memory locations (critical for address arithmetic). > 3. **Fixed Size** — Size is determined at compile-time (for static arrays) and cannot grow/shrink during runtime. > 4. **Random Access** — Any element can be accessed in **O(1)** constant time using its index. > 5. **Indexed** — Each element is referenced by an integer index, starting from **0** in C++. ## 1.4 Classification of Arrays in C++ | Category | Description | Example Declaration | |---|---|---| | **One-Dimensional Array** | A simple linear list of elements | `int marks[50];` | | **Multi-Dimensional Array** | Array of arrays (matrix-like structure) | `int matrix[3][3];` | | **Array of Objects** | Stores instances of a user-defined class | `Student s[100];` | | **Character Array (C-string)** | A null-terminated `char` array | `char name[20];` | | **Dynamic Array (Heap)** | Allocated at runtime using `new`/`delete` | `int *p = new int[n];` | ## 1.5 KTU 2024 Syllabus Mapping > [!NOTE] > This topic directly addresses the following Course Outcomes for Module 1: > - **CO1:** *Apply the concepts of object-oriented programming to solve real-world problems using C++.* > - Bloom's Level: **L3 (Apply)** for array operations; **L4 (Analyze)** for memory addressing and complexity. # 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ## 2.1 Internal Memory Architecture of an Array When the C++ compiler encounters `int arr[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};`, the following sequence of events occurs at **compile time**: 1. The compiler reserves a **contiguous block** of $5 \times \text{sizeof(int)} = 5 \times 4 = \mathbf{20\ bytes}$ on the stack. 2. The symbolic name `arr` is bound to the **base address** — the memory location of `arr[0]`. 3. The compiler treats `arr` as a **constant pointer** of type `int*` that points to this base address and *cannot be reassigned* (i.e., increment/decrement operations on `arr` itself are illegal). > [!IMPORTANT] > **Critical Distinction (Frequently Tested in KTU):** > - `arr` → **Address of first element** (Type: `int*`, behaves as a constant pointer). > - `&arr` → **Address of the entire array** (Type: `int(*)[5]`, a pointer to an array of 5 ints). > - `arr + i` → Address of the $i^{\text{th}}$ element, computed via pointer arithmetic. > - `*(arr + i)` is **semantically identical** to `arr[i]`. ## 2.2 Address Calculation — The Heart of Array Theory The single most important formula in this module. Examiners **love** to test this. ### 2.2.1 One-Dimensional Array For a one-dimensional array `A` declared as `A[LowerBound ... UpperBound]` in a general-purpose language (theoretical model): $$\text{Address of } A[i] = \text{BaseAddress}(A) + (i - \text{LowerBound}) \times \text{SizeOfElement}$$ Since C++ uses **zero-based indexing** where `LowerBound = 0` and the array size is implicitly known, the formula simplifies to: $$\text{Address of } A[i] = \text{BaseAddress}(A) + i \times \text{SizeOfElement}$$ ### 2.2.2 Two-Dimensional Array (Row-Major Order) C++ stores a 2D array in **Row-Major Order** (rows are stored one after another in linear memory). For a matrix `M[R][C]` with $R$ rows, $C$ columns, and base address `BA`: $$\text{Address of } M[i][j] = \text{BA} + \big[(i \times C) + j\big] \times \text{SizeOfElement}$$ ### 2.2.3 Two-Dimensional Array (Column-Major Order — used by FORTRAN/MATLAB) $$\text{Address of } M[i][j] = \text{BA} + \big[(j \times R) + i\big] \times \text{SizeOfElement}$$ > [!WARNING] > **Common KTU Pitfall:** Students often mix up row-major and column-major formulas. The default in C/C++/Java is **row-major**. The default in FORTRAN/MATLAB is **column-major**. Marks are deducted if you don't explicitly state the convention in your answer. ## 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet & Cheat Sheet > [!IMPORTANT] > **Memorize the following table — it covers 80% of the array-based numerical questions in KTU exams.** | # | Quantity | Formula | Units / Notes | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Memory occupied by 1D array | $n \times s$ | bytes, where $n$ = number of elements, $s$ = size of one element | | 2 | Address of $A[i]$ in 1D | $\text{BA} + i \cdot s$ | C++ zero-based indexing | | 3 | Address of $M[i][j]$ row-major | $\text{BA} + (i \cdot C + j) \cdot s$ | $C$ = number of columns | | 4 | Address of $M[i][j]$ col-major | $\text{BA} + (j \cdot R + i) \cdot s$ | $R$ = number of rows | | 5 | Last valid index in array of size $n$ | $n - 1$ | Zero-based; exceeding this is **undefined behavior** | | 6 | Number of elements in `A[UB..LB]` | $\text{UB} - \text{LB} + 1$ | Used in Pascal-style questions | | 7 | Element count in 3D `A[x][y][z]` | $x \cdot y \cdot z$ | Total number of elements | | 8 | Address in 3D row-major | $\text{BA} + \big[(i \cdot Y \cdot Z) + (j \cdot Z) + k\big] \cdot s$ | For `A[I][J][K]` | ## 2.4 Asymptotic Complexity of Array Operations (Engineering Utility) | Operation | Time Complexity | Reason | |---|---|---| | **Access by index** | $O(1)$ | Direct address calculation | | **Traversal (full scan)** | $O(n)$ | Must visit every element once | | **Insertion at end** | $O(1)$ | No shifting required | | **Insertion at beginning / middle** | $O(n)$ | Elements must be shifted right | | **Deletion at end** | $O(1)$ | No shifting required | | **Deletion at beginning / middle** | $O(n)$ | Elements must be shifted left | | **Linear Search** | $O(n)$ | Worst case: element is at the end / absent | | **Binary Search (sorted array)** | $O(\log n)$ | Halves the search interval each step | ## 2.5 Real-World Engineering Applications > [!NOTE] > **Why engineers care about arrays:** > - **Digital Image Processing:** A grayscale image is stored as a 2D array of pixel intensity values (`image[row][col]`). A color image is a 3D array. > - **Finite Element Analysis (FEA):** Stiffness matrices and thermal conductivity matrices are stored as 2D arrays. > - **Embedded Systems:** Lookup tables (LUTs) for trigonometric functions in microcontrollers are implemented as `const` arrays in ROM. > - **Database Indexing:** B-tree nodes store sorted key arrays for fast binary search. > - **Signal Processing (DSP):** Convolution and FFT operations operate on 1D/2D arrays of samples. ## 2.6 Array of Objects — The OOP Flavor In the KTU OOP context, the most board-relevant array type is the **array of objects**. For a class `Student` with data members `rollNo`, `name`, and `marks`, an array of 60 students is declared as: ```cpp Student batch[60]; // Stack-allocated array of 60 Student objects Student *ptr = new Student[n]; // Heap-allocated dynamic array of n objects ``` The compiler invokes the **default constructor** of `Student` exactly **60 times** (once per element) to initialize the array. If `Student` lacks a default constructor, this declaration **will not compile** — a classic KTU viva question. # 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix ## 3.1 Worked Example 1 — 1D Address Calculation (Full Working) > **Problem (Typical KTU 4-mark question):** An array `marks[100]` is stored in memory starting at base address **2000**. Each `int` occupies **2 bytes**. Find the address of `marks[25]` and `marks[80]`. Also calculate the memory occupied by the array. ### Step 1: Identify the parameters - Base address: $BA = 2000$ - Size of one element: $s = 2$ bytes - Index to look up: $i = 25$ and $i = 80$ - Number of elements: $n = 100$ ### Step 2: Apply the 1D address formula Using the C++ zero-based indexing formula: $$\text{Address of } A[i] = BA + (i \times s)$$ ### Step 3: Substitute for `marks[25]` $$\text{Address of } marks[25] = 2000 + (25 \times 2)$$ $$= 2000 + 50$$ $$= \mathbf{2050}$$ ### Step 4: Substitute for `marks[80]` $$\text{Address of } marks[80] = 2000 + (80 \times 2)$$ $$= 2000 + 160$$ $$= \mathbf{2160}$$ ### Step 5: Calculate total memory footprint $$\text{Total Memory} = n \times s = 100 \times 2 = \mathbf{200\ bytes}$$ ### Step 6: Final answer block (write this way in the exam) | Quantity | Value | |---|---| | Base address of `marks[0]` | 2000 | | Address of `marks[25]` | 2050 | | Address of `marks[80]` | 2160 | | Total memory occupied | 200 bytes | | Last valid index | 99 (i.e., `marks[99]` at address 2198) | --- ## 3.2 Worked Example 2 — 2D Row-Major Address Calculation > **Problem:** A 2D array `int A[10][20]` is stored at base address **500**. `sizeof(int) = 2` bytes. Compute the address of `A[3][5]` using row-major order. Also find the address of `A[7][15]`. ### Step 1: Identify parameters - Base address: $BA = 500$ - Size of element: $s = 2$ bytes - Number of rows: $R = 10$ - Number of columns: $C = 20$ - Index: $(i, j) = (3, 5)$ and $(7, 15)$ ### Step 2: Apply the row-major formula $$\text{Address of } A[i][j] = BA + \big[(i \times C) + j\big] \times s$$ ### Step 3: Substitute for `A[3][5]` $$\text{Address of } A[3][5] = 500 + \big[(3 \times 20) + 5\big] \times 2$$ $$= 500 + \big[60 + 5\big] \times 2$$ $$= 500 + 65 \times 2$$ $$= 500 + 130$$ $$= \mathbf{630}$$ ### Step 4: Substitute for `A[7][15]` $$\text{Address of } A[7][15] = 500 + \big[(7 \times 20) + 15\big] \times 2$$ $$= 500 + \big[140 + 15\big] \times 2$$ $$= 500 + 155 \times 2$$ $$= 500 + 310$$ $$= \mathbf{810}$$ ### Step 5: Verification by mental counting - Element `A[3][5]` is the $65^{\text{th}}$ element in row-major order (row 0 has 20, row 1 has 20, row 2 has 20, and we need 5 from row 3 → $60 + 5 = 65$). - $65 \times 2 = 130$ bytes offset from base 500 → 630. ✓ Matches. ### Step 6: Memory footprint $$\text{Total Memory} = R \times C \times s = 10 \times 20 \times 2 = \mathbf{400\ bytes}$$ --- ## 3.3 Worked Example 3 — General (Non-Zero) Lower Bound > **Problem:** An array `X[(-5) ... 10]` is stored at base address 1000 with element size 4 bytes. Find the address of `X[3]` and `X[-2]`. ### Step 1: Use the generalized formula (not C++ standard, but conceptually important for KTU) $$\text{Address of } A[i] = BA + (i - LB) \times s$$ - Lower Bound: $LB = -5$ - Base address of `X[-5]`: $BA = 1000$ - Element size: $s = 4$ ### Step 2: Compute for `X[3]` $$\text{Address of } X[3] = 1000 + (3 - (-5)) \times 4$$ $$= 1000 + (3 + 5) \times 4$$ $$= 1000 + 8 \times 4$$ $$= 1000 + 32$$ $$= \mathbf{1032}$$ ### Step 3: Compute for `X[-2]` $$\text{Address of } X[-2] = 1000 + (-2 - (-5)) \times 4$$ $$= 1000 + (-2 + 5) \times 4$$ $$= 1000 + 3 \times 4$$ $$= 1000 + 12$$ $$= \mathbf{1012}$$ ### Step 4: Number of elements in the array $$n = UB - LB + 1 = 10 - (-5) + 1 = \mathbf{16\ elements}$$ ### Step 5: Total memory $$n \times s = 16 \times 4 = \mathbf{64\ bytes}$$ --- ## 3.4 Analytical Matrix — Pointer Arithmetic vs. Array Indexing | C++ Expression | Equivalent To | Type of Result | Address Steps Forward | |---|---|---|---| | `arr` | `&arr[0]` | `int*` | 0 (base) | | `arr + 1` | `&arr[1]` | `int*` | $+s$ bytes | | `arr + i` | `&arr[i]` | `int*` | $+i \cdot s$ bytes | | `*arr` | `arr[0]` | `int` (value) | N/A | | `*(arr + i)` | `arr[i]` | `int` (value) | N/A | | `*arr + 1` | `arr[0] + 1` (arith on value) | `int` | N/A | | `*(arr + 1)` | `arr[1]` | `int` (value) | N/A | | `&arr` | Address of whole array | `int(*)[n]` | 0 (same numeric value as `arr`, but different type) | | `&arr + 1` | Address *past* the whole array | `int(*)[n]` | $+n \cdot s$ bytes | > [!IMPORTANT] > **Board-Exam Pearl:** The expression `&arr + 1` increments by `sizeof(arr)` (the **entire array size**), not by `sizeof(int)`. This is a classic C++ viva trap. The numeric value of `&arr + 1` is `BA + n * s`. ## 3.5 Traversal Algorithm — Linear Scan (Analysis) A standard array traversal visits every element once. The time complexity analysis is: $$T(n) = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} O(1) = n \cdot O(1) = O(n)$$ Each iteration performs: 1. Index computation: $O(1)$ (multiplication and addition). 2. Memory fetch: $O(1)$ (single read). 3. Comparison / processing: $O(1)$ (depends on operation). The **space complexity** is $O(1)$ auxiliary because we only use a single loop variable `i`, regardless of $n$. --- ## 3.6 Insertion in the Middle — Shifting Analysis To insert an element at position $k$ in an array of $n$ elements, we must shift all elements from index $k$ to $n-1$ **one position to the right**. Number of shifts: $$\text{Number of shifts} = n - k$$ **Worst case** (insertion at index 0): $n - 0 = n$ shifts → $O(n)$. **Best case** (insertion at index $n$): $n - n = 0$ shifts → $O(1)$. **Average case**: $\frac{n}{2}$ shifts → $O(n)$. > [!WARNING] > **KTU Pitfall — Capacity vs. Size:** In static C++ arrays, "insertion" past the declared size is **undefined behavior** (memory corruption). To support dynamic insertion, you must use a dynamic array (`new[]`/`delete[]`) or a higher-level container like `std::vector`, where the container manages capacity and resizing automatically. # 4. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap ## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each) > **Question A1.** `[KTU University Exam — May 2024]` > **Define an array. List any four characteristics of arrays in C++.** **Model Answer:** An **array** is a collection of variables of the **same data type** that are stored in **contiguous memory locations** and are referenced by a common name, with individual elements accessed using an **integer index** starting from 0. **Four characteristics of arrays in C++:** 1. **Homogeneous:** All elements must be of the same data type (e.g., all `int` or all `float`). 2. **Fixed size:** The size of the array must be a compile-time constant and cannot be changed at runtime. 3. **Contiguous memory:** Elements occupy adjacent memory locations, enabling pointer arithmetic. 4. **Zero-based indexing:** The first element is at index `0` and the last is at index `n - 1`. 5. **Random access:** Any element can be accessed in $O(1)$ time using its index. 6. **Symbolic name binding:** The array name acts as a constant pointer to the first element. *(Any four of the above are sufficient. Mentioning the address-calculation formula is a bonus mark.)* --- > **Question A2.** `[KTU University Exam — Dec 2023]` > **Differentiate between a 1D array and a 2D array with a suitable C++ declaration for each. What is the default storage order used by C++ for 2D arrays?** **Model Answer:** | Feature | 1D Array | 2D Array | |---|---|---| | **Structure** | Linear list of elements | Tabular / matrix-like grid of elements | | **Indexing** | Single index `arr[i]` | Two indices `arr[i][j]` | | **Declaration** | `int arr[10];` | `int mat[3][4];` | | **Memory** | Stored linearly | Stored linearly in **row-major order** by default | | **Use case** | Simple lists, scores, ages | Matrices, tables, grids, images | **Default storage order in C++:** **Row-major order** — the entire first row is stored first, then the second row, and so on. *(Contrast: FORTRAN uses column-major order.)* --- ## 5.2 Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each) > [!NOTE] > As per KTU 2024 End-Semester Evaluation (ESE) regulations, Module 1 long-answer questions carry an **internal choice**. You must answer **either** Option A **or** Option B. --- ### **Question B1 — Option A (14 Marks)** `[KTU University Exam — Dec 2024 Model Paper]` > **(a)** Explain the **memory layout** of a one-dimensional array in C++ with a neat diagram. Derive the formula for calculating the address of the $i^{\text{th}}$ element of an array. **(7 marks)** > > **(b)** An array `DATA[20][15]` is stored in memory in **row-major order** with base address **1500**. Each integer occupies **4 bytes**. Compute the address of: > - (i) `DATA[5][8]` > - (ii) `DATA[12][3]` > - (iii) `DATA[18][14]` > > Also calculate the **total memory** required to store the array. **(7 marks)** #### **Model Solution for (a):** **Memory Layout Explanation:** When a C++ compiler encounters `int arr[5];`, it allocates a single contiguous block of $5 \times 4 = 20$ bytes on the stack. The name `arr` is bound to the address of `arr[0]`, called the **base address** ($BA$). The subsequent elements `arr[1], arr[2], ...` are placed at addresses $BA + 4$, $BA + 8$, $BA + 12$, $BA + 16$ respectively. This contiguous layout is what enables **O(1) random access** — to find any element, the hardware just multiplies the index by 4 and adds it to the base address. **Diagram:** ``` Index: [0] [1] [2] [3] [4] +-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+ Address: | 1000 | 1004 | 1008 | 1012 | 1016 | +-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+ arr[0] arr[1] arr[2] arr[3] arr[4] ^ | +-- 'arr' (base address = 1000) ``` **Derivation of the Address Formula:** Let $BA$ = base address of the array, $s$ = size of one element in bytes, and $i$ = the index of the element we want. - The address of `arr[0]` is $BA + 0 \times s = BA$. - The address of `arr[1]` is $BA + 1 \times s = BA + s$. - The address of `arr[2]` is $BA + 2 \times s = BA + 2s$. - Continuing this pattern, the address of `arr[i]` is: $$\text{Address of } arr[i] = BA + i \times s$$ This formula works because the compiler uses **pointer arithmetic**: when you write `arr[i]`, it is internally evaluated as `*(arr + i)`. Since `arr` is of type `int*`, adding `i` to it advances the pointer by $i \times \text{sizeof(int)}$ bytes. #### **Model Solution for (b):** **Given parameters:** - Base address: $BA = 1500$ - Size of each element: $s = 4$ bytes - Number of rows: $R = 20$ - Number of columns: $C = 15$ - Storage order: **Row-major** (default for C++) **Row-major formula:** $$\text{Address of } DATA[i][j] = BA + \big[(i \times C) + j\big] \times s$$ --- **(i) Address of `DATA[5][8]`:** $$\text{Address} = 1500 + \big[(5 \times 15) + 8\big] \times 4$$ $$= 1500 + \big[75 + 8\big] \times 4$$ $$= 1500 + 83 \times 4$$ $$= 1500 + 332$$ $$= \mathbf{1832}$$ --- **(ii) Address of `DATA[12][3]`:** $$\text{Address} = 1500 + \big[(12 \times 15) + 3\big] \times 4$$ $$= 1500 + \big[180 + 3\big] \times 4$$ $$= 1500 + 183 \times 4$$ $$= 1500 + 732$$ $$= \mathbf{2232}$$ --- **(iii) Address of `DATA[18][14]`:** $$\text{Address} = 1500 + \big[(18 \times 15) + 14\big] \times 4$$ $$= 1500 + \big[270 + 14\big] \times 4$$ $$= 1500 + 284 \times 4$$ $$= 1500 + 1136$$ $$= \mathbf{2636}$$ --- **Total Memory Required:** $$\text{Memory} = R \times C \times s = 20 \times 15 \times 4 = \mathbf{1200\ bytes}$$ --- ### **Question B1 — Option B (14 Marks)** `[KTU University Exam — May 2024 Model Paper]` > **(a)** Define an **array of objects** in C++. Write a complete C++ program to define a class `Employee` with data members `empId` (int), `name` (string), and `salary` (float). Create an array of 5 `Employee` objects, accept the details from the user, and display the details of the employee with the **highest salary**. **(7 marks)** > > **(b)** Explain the concept of **dynamic memory allocation** for arrays in C++ using the `new` and `delete` operators. Compare it with static array allocation. **(7 marks)** #### **Model Solution for (a):** **Definition:** An **array of objects** is a collection of variables of a user-defined class type, stored contiguously in memory and accessed using an index. It allows storing and processing multiple instances of a class uniformly. **Complete C++ Program:** ```cpp #include #include using namespace std; class Employee { private: int empId; string name; float salary; public: // Default constructor (REQUIRED for array creation) Employee() { empId = 0; name = ""; salary = 0.0f; } // Parameterized constructor for convenience Employee(int id, string n, float s) { empId = id; name = n; salary = s; } void input() { cout << "Enter Employee ID: "; cin >> empId; cout << "Enter Name: "; cin.ignore(); getline(cin, name); cout << "Enter Salary: "; cin >> salary; } void display() const { cout << "ID: " << empId << " | Name: " << name << " | Salary: " << salary << endl; } float getSalary() const { return salary; } }; int main() { const int N = 5; Employee emp[N]; // Array of 5 Employee objects cout << "--- Enter details of " << N << " employees ---\n"; for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i) { cout << "\nEmployee " << (i + 1) << ":\n"; emp[i].input(); } // Find the index of the employee with the highest salary int maxIdx = 0; for (int i = 1; i < N; ++i) { if (emp[i].getSalary() > emp[maxIdx].getSalary()) { maxIdx = i; } } cout << "\n--- Employee with the highest salary ---\n"; emp[maxIdx].display(); return 0; } ``` **Key Points the Examiner Will Look For:** - ✔ Correct class definition with `private` data members and `public` member functions. - ✔ **Default constructor** is mandatory because `Employee emp[5];` requires default-constructible objects. - ✔ Use of `const` qualifier in `getSalary()` and `display()` — signals good OOP practice (a bonus mark). - ✔ Loop logic to find the maximum (initialize `maxIdx = 0`, then compare from index 1 onwards). - ✔ Proper use of `cin.ignore()` before `getline` to flush the newline character. --- #### **Model Solution for (b):** **Static Array Allocation:** In static allocation, the array size must be a **compile-time constant**. The memory is allocated on the **stack** at function entry and automatically deallocated when the function returns. ```cpp int arr[100]; // Size must be a constant; cannot be a variable ``` **Drawbacks:** (i) Size cannot be decided at runtime, (ii) Wastes memory if the array is under-utilized, (iii) Risk of stack overflow for very large arrays. **Dynamic Array Allocation:** Dynamic allocation uses the `new` operator to request memory from the **heap** (free store) at runtime. The size can be a **variable** whose value is determined during program execution. ```cpp int n; cout << "Enter array size: "; cin >> n; int *arr = new int[n]; // Allocates n ints on the heap // ... use the array ... delete[] arr; // MUST be done to avoid memory leak arr = nullptr; // Good practice to prevent dangling pointer ``` **Key points:** - The expression `new int[n]` returns a pointer of type `int*` pointing to the first element. - The corresponding deallocation uses `delete[]` (with the square brackets) to free the entire block — using `delete` without brackets causes **undefined behavior**. - The pointer `arr` itself is a stack variable, but the memory it *points to* is on the heap. **Comparison Table:** | Feature | Static Array | Dynamic Array | |---|---|---| | **Size known at** | Compile time | Runtime | | **Memory location** | Stack | Heap (free store) | | **Size variable allowed?** | ❌ No (must be `const`) | ✅ Yes | | **Deallocation** | Automatic (RAII) | Manual via `delete[]` | | **Risk of memory leak** | None | Yes, if `delete[]` is forgotten | | **Performance** | Faster (no heap call) | Slower (involves heap manager) | | **Lifetime** | Tied to enclosing scope | Lives until explicitly `delete[]`d | | **Example** | `int a[10];` | `int *a = new int[10];` | --- ## 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning & Pitfall Callout > [!WARNING] > **Where KTU Students Commonly Lose Marks on Array Questions:** > > 1. **Forgetting the element size in the address formula:** Students often write $\text{Address} = BA + i$ instead of $BA + i \times s$. The multiplier $s$ is **non-negotiable** in the formula. > 2. **Mixing up row-major and column-major:** Always explicitly state the convention you are using at the start of your answer. C++ uses row-major; the default formula is $BA + (i \times C + j) \times s$. > 3. **Off-by-one errors in memory calculation:** Total memory is always $R \times C \times s$ (product of dimensions, not sum). For a 1D array, it's $n \times s$, not $n + s$. > 4. **Not declaring a default constructor for an array of objects:** If your class has only a parameterized constructor, the line `MyClass arr[N];` will fail to compile. Examiners check for this. > 5. **Using `delete` instead of `delete[]` for dynamic arrays:** This is undefined behavior. Always use `delete[]` for arrays allocated with `new[]`. > 6. **Confusing `arr` and `&arr`:** They have the same numeric value but different types (`int*` vs `int(*)[n]`), and pointer arithmetic behaves differently on them. > 7. **Neglecting to mark functions `const`:** In OOP, member functions that do not modify the object (like `getSalary()` and `display()`) should be marked `const`. Examiners reward this practice. --- ## 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember > [!IMPORTANT] > **Rapid Revision Checklist — Module 1: Arrays** > > ✅ An array is a **homogeneous, contiguous, fixed-size** collection accessed via an integer index. > ✅ C++ arrays are **zero-indexed** (first element at index `0`, last at `n - 1`). > ✅ The **array name** is a **constant pointer** to the first element — it cannot be reassigned. > ✅ **Address formula (1D):** $BA + i \times s$ > ✅ **Address formula (2D row-major):** $BA + (i \times C + j) \times s$ > ✅ **Address formula (2D column-major):** $BA + (j \times R + i) \times s$ > ✅ **Total memory:** $R \times C \times s$ bytes. > ✅ **Random access is $O(1)$;** linear search is $O(n)$; binary search is $O(\log n)$. > ✅ **Insertion/deletion in the middle is $O(n)$** because elements must be shifted. > ✅ **Array of objects** requires a **default constructor** unless an initializer list is provided. > ✅ **Dynamic arrays** use `new[]` and must be freed with `delete[]` (with square brackets). > ✅ **Pointer arithmetic:** `arr[i]` is identical to `*(arr + i)`. > ✅ **Static arrays** go on the **stack**; **dynamic arrays** go on the **heap**. > ✅ Mixing up `arr` and `&arr` is a classic conceptual trap — same value, different type. > ✅ **Default storage in C++ is row-major;** FORTRAN/MATLAB use column-major. > ✅ C++ arrays do **not** perform bounds checking — out-of-bounds access is undefined behavior.

topics.title: Strings
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PBCST304 - OBJECT ORIENTED PROGRAMMING
> - **Module:** Module 1
> - **Topic:** Strings

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology)

A **String** in Object-Oriented Programming (using C++) is a sequence of characters stored in contiguous memory locations, used to represent textual data. In C++, strings are handled through **two distinct paradigms**:

1. **C-Style Strings (Character Arrays):** A null-terminated (`\0`) one-dimensional array of characters inherited from the C language.
2. **C++ `std::string` Class:** A robust, object-oriented string abstraction defined inside the `<string>` header, which encapsulates character manipulation, dynamic resizing, and safe operator overloading.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Syllabus Highlight:** For PBCST304 (OOP), the primary focus is the **`std::string` class** and its built-in member functions, alongside character-handling functions from `<cctype>`.

---

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The Real-World Intuition

Imagine a **train compartment**. Each coach (character) is linked to the next one in a strict, ordered sequence. To find the train, you need:
- A **starting platform** (the base address / pointer).
- A clear **terminator** (the engineer's whistle — the `\0` null character that says *"the train ends here"*).

In the **C++ `std::string` class**, this entire train is wrapped into a single **smart railway container**. The container *itself* remembers its length, automatically extends when new coaches arrive, and provides labeled buttons (member functions) to add, remove, or rearrange coaches without the user worrying about platform allocation.

---

## 1.3 Standard Metrics & Constants

| Metric / Constant | Value / Definition |
|---|---|
| Null terminator character | `'\0'` (ASCII value **0**) |
| `string::npos` | Largest representable `size_t` value, indicating "not found" |
| Default empty string | `""` (length = **0**) |
| Header for C++ strings | `<string>` |
| Header for character functions | `<cctype>` |

> [!NOTE]
> **Key Definition — `string::npos`:** A static constant equal to `-1` cast to `size_t`. It is the universal return value of `find()` failures.

---

## 1.4 The `std::string` Class — Why It Exists

The C++ Standard Library provides the **`std::string`** class (declared in `<string>` and implemented in `namespace std`) to overcome C-style string pitfalls:

| Problem in C-Style Strings | How `std::string` Solves It |
|---|---|
| Fixed array size, buffer overflow risk | **Dynamic resizing** handled internally |
| Manual length calculation via `strlen()` | Built-in `length()` / `size()` member functions |
| Manual concatenation via `strcat()` | Overloaded `+` and `+=` operators |
| Manual comparison via `strcmp()` | Overloaded `==`, `<`, `>` relational operators |
| Unsafe `cin >>` (no whitespace) | `getline()` reads entire lines safely |

---

## 1.5 Declaration & Initialization Syntax

The following canonical forms are **frequently tested in KTU exams**:

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    string s1;                  // Empty string
    string s2("Hello");         // Initialization via C-string literal
    string s3("Hello", 3);      // First 3 chars: "Hel"
    string s4(5, 'A');          // "AAAAA" (5 repetitions)
    string s5(s2);              // Copy constructor
    string s6 = "World";        // Assignment-style initialization
    return 0;
}
```

> [!TIP]
> **Exam Tip:** Constructor `string(n, ch)` where `n` is an integer and `ch` is a character, creates a string of `n` copies of `ch`. This is a **favorite KTU Part-A question**.
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Theoretical Breakdown of String Operations

### Step 1 — Input / Output Operations
C++ offers **two distinct input modes** for strings:

| Function | Behavior | Reads Whitespace? |
|---|---|---|
| `cin >> s` | Skips leading whitespace, stops at next whitespace | No |
| `getline(cin, s)` | Reads entire line including spaces until `\n` | Yes |
| `getline(cin, s, delim)` | Reads until custom delimiter | Yes |

**Why this matters:** `cin >> s` is **unsafe for full names or addresses**. Students commonly lose marks by using `cin >>` instead of `getline()` when the input contains spaces.

---

### Step 2 — Character Access
| Operation | Syntax | Use Case |
|---|---|---|
| Indexing | `s[i]` | Read/write character at position `i` (no bounds check) |
| Safe access | `s.at(i)` | Throws `out_of_range` exception if `i` is invalid |
| Front | `s.front()` | First character reference |
| Back | `s.back()` | Last character reference |

---

### Step 3 — Capacity Functions
| Function | Returns |
|---|---|
| `s.length()` | Number of characters |
| `s.size()` | Same as `length()` |
| `s.capacity()` | Allocated storage (may be `>= length()`) |
| `s.empty()` | `true` if length is **0** |
| `s.max_size()` | Maximum possible string length |
| `s.resize(n)` | Resizes string to `n` characters |
| `s.reserve(n)` | Pre-allocates capacity for `n` chars |

---

### Step 4 — Modification Operations
| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `s.append(t)` / `s += t` | Appends `t` to end of `s` |
| `s.insert(pos, t)` | Inserts `t` at index `pos` |
| `s.erase(pos, len)` | Erases `len` chars starting at `pos` |
| `s.replace(pos, len, t)` | Replaces `len` chars at `pos` with `t` |
| `s.clear()` | Removes all characters (length becomes **0**) |
| `s.push_back(ch)` | Adds single character at end |
| `s.pop_back()` | Removes last character |
| `s.assign(t)` | Replaces contents entirely |
| `s.swap(t)` | Swaps contents of `s` and `t` |

---

### Step 5 — Search Operations
| Function | Returns |
|---|---|
| `s.find(t)` | First index of `t` in `s`, or `string::npos` |
| `s.rfind(t)` | Last index of `t` |
| `s.find_first_of(chars)` | First occurrence of any char in `chars` |
| `s.find_last_of(chars)` | Last occurrence of any char in `chars` |

---

### Step 6 — Sub-String & Copy
| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `s.substr(pos, len)` | Returns substring of length `len` starting at `pos` |
| `s.copy(char_arr, len, pos)` | Copies `len` chars into a C-array |
| `s.c_str()` | Returns `const char*` (null-terminated C-string) |
| `s.data()` | Returns `const char*` (no null guarantee in C++17 relaxed, but with C++11+ returns null-terminated) |

---

### Step 7 — Comparison Operations
| Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `s1.compare(s2)` | Lexicographic comparison |
| `s1 == s2`, `s1 != s2`, `s1 < s2`, etc. | Direct relational operators |

**`compare()` return value:**
- **Negative** if `s1 < s2`
- **Zero (0)** if `s1 == s2`
- **Positive** if `s1 > s2`

---

## 2.2 Character Handling Functions (from `<cctype>`)

These functions take a single `char` (cast from `int`) and return non-zero (true) if the condition holds.

| Function | Returns true if character is... |
|---|---|
| `isalpha(c)` | Alphabetic (A–Z, a–z) |
| `isdigit(c)` | Numeric digit (0–9) |
| `isalnum(c)` | Alphanumeric |
| `isspace(c)` | Whitespace (space, tab, newline) |
| `isupper(c)` | Uppercase letter |
| `islower(c)` | Lowercase letter |
| `ispunct(c)` | Punctuation |
| `isxdigit(c)` | Hexadecimal digit |

**Conversion functions:**

| Function | Returns |
|---|---|
| `tolower(c)` | Lowercase version of `c` |
| `toupper(c)` | Uppercase version of `c` |

---

## 2.3 KTU Formula Cheat Sheet — String Index Math

For a string `s` of length `n`:

$$
\text{Valid index range} = [0,\ n - 1]
$$

$$
\text{String length formula:}\ \text{length}(s) = n = s.\text{size}()
$$

$$
\text{Last character index} = s.\text{length}() - 1 = s.\text{size}() - 1
$$

$$
\text{Substring bounds:}\ s.\text{substr}(\text{pos},\ \text{len})\ \text{where}\ \text{pos} \ge 0,\ \text{len} \ge 0,\ \text{pos} + \text{len} \le n
$$

$$
\text{Find result check:}\ \text{if}\ s.\text{find}(t) \ne \text{string::npos}\ \Rightarrow t\ \text{exists in}\ s
$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Critical Pitfall:** The result of `find()` is of type **`size_t`** (unsigned). Comparing it with `-1` causes implicit conversion errors. Always use `!= string::npos`.

---

## 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility

| Domain | Application |
|---|---|
| **Database Systems** | Query parsing, record fields (names, addresses) |
| **Network Programming** | HTTP headers, URLs, JSON payloads |
| **Embedded Systems** | Command parsing, serial monitor output |
| **Compiler Design** | Lexical analysis (tokenizing identifiers, keywords) |
| **Machine Learning** | Text preprocessing, tokenization in NLP |
| **Cybersecurity** | Pattern matching, log file parsing |
<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Worked Example 1 — String Concatenation Logic

**Problem Statement:**
Given `string a = "KTU";` and `string b = "2024";`, derive the internal state after `c = a + " " + b;` and `a += " University";`.

### Step-by-Step Logical Derivation

**Step 1:** Evaluate left operand `a` which refers to `"KTU"`.

**Step 2:** Concatenate with the C-string literal `" "` (a single space).

**Step 3:** Concatenate the result with `b = "2024"`.

$$
\begin{aligned}
c &= a + " " + b \\
  &= \text{"KTU"} + " " + \text{"2024"} \\
  &= \text{"KTU 2024"}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4:** For `a += " University";`, the compound assignment appends in-place.

$$
\begin{aligned}
a &= \text{"KTU"} \\
a +&= \text{" University"} \\
a &= \text{"KTU University"} \quad \text{(length = 14)}
\end{aligned}
$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Memory Logic:** The `+=` operator modifies the original string's internal buffer in place (avoiding an unnecessary temporary). The `+` operator creates a **new temporary** string. This distinction matters in performance-critical code.

---

## 3.2 Worked Example 2 — `find()` and Substring Extraction

**Problem Statement:**
For `string s = "APJKeralaUniversity";` determine:
1. Position of `"Kerala"`.
2. The substring extracted by `s.substr(3, 6)`.

### Step-by-Step Logical Derivation

**Step 1:** Index the characters of `s`:

$$
\begin{aligned}
s[0] &= \text{'A'} \\
s[1] &= \text{'P'} \\
s[2] &= \text{'J'} \\
s[3] &= \text{'K'} \\
s[4] &= \text{'e'} \\
s[5] &= \text{'r'} \\
s[6] &= \text{'a'} \\
s[7] &= \text{'l'} \\
s[8] &= \text{'a'}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2:** Locate `"Kerala"`. The first character `'K'` is at index **3**, so:

$$
s.\text{find}(\text{"Kerala"}) = 3 \quad (\text{returns}\ \text{size\_t})
$$

**Step 3:** Extract `s.substr(3, 6)` — starting at index **3**, taking **6** characters.

$$
s.\text{substr}(3,\ 6) = \text{"Kerala"}
$$

**Step 4:** Verify: characters at indices 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 are `'K'`, `'e'`, `'r'`, `'a'`, `'l'`, `'a'` → spells `"Kerala"`. ✅

---

## 3.3 Worked Example 3 — Counting Vowels Using `<cctype>`

**Problem Statement:**
Write the analytical trace for counting vowels in `string s = "Engineering";`.

### Step-by-Step Logical Derivation

**Step 1:** Initialize counter `count = 0`.

**Step 2:** Traverse each character and apply a vowel-test using `tolower()` to handle both cases.

**Step 3:** Trace through `"Engineering"`:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Index 0: 'E'} \rightarrow \text{tolower} = \text{'e'} \rightarrow \text{vowel, count = 1} \\
&\text{Index 1: 'n'} \rightarrow \text{consonant} \\
&\text{Index 2: 'g'} \rightarrow \text{consonant} \\
&\text{Index 3: 'i'} \rightarrow \text{vowel, count = 2} \\
&\text{Index 4: 'n'} \rightarrow \text{consonant} \\
&\text{Index 5: 'e'} \rightarrow \text{vowel, count = 3} \\
&\text{Index 6: 'e'} \rightarrow \text{vowel, count = 4} \\
&\text{Index 7: 'r'} \rightarrow \text{consonant} \\
&\text{Index 8: 'i'} \rightarrow \text{vowel, count = 5} \\
&\text{Index 9: 'n'} \rightarrow \text{consonant} \\
&\text{Index 10: 'g'} \rightarrow \text{consonant}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Final Result:**

$$
\text{Total vowels} = 5
$$

---

## 3.4 Analytical Comparison Matrix

| Operation | C-Style (`char[]`) | C++ `std::string` |
|---|---|---|
| Declaration | `char s[20];` | `string s;` |
| Length | `strlen(s)` (O(n) scan) | `s.length()` (O(1)) |
| Concatenation | `strcat(s1, s2)` (unsafe) | `s1 + s2` (safe, allocates new) |
| Comparison | `strcmp(s1, s2)` returns int | `s1 == s2` returns bool |
| Copy | `strcpy(s1, s2)` (unsafe) | `s1 = s2` (deep copy) |
| Input | `cin.getline(s, 20)` | `getline(cin, s)` |
| Conversion to C-string | Native | `s.c_str()` |
| Reverse iteration | Manual pointer manipulation | `reverse_iterator` (STL) |

---

## 3.5 Complete KTU-Model Program — Demonstrating All Major Operations

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <cctype>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    string s1, s2;

    cout << "Enter first string: ";
    getline(cin, s1);

    cout << "Enter second string: ";
    getline(cin, s2);

    // Concatenation
    string s3 = s1 + " " + s2;
    cout << "Concatenated: " << s3 << endl;
    cout << "Length: " << s3.length() << endl;

    // Comparison
    if (s1 == s2)
        cout << "Strings are equal" << endl;
    else
        cout << "Strings differ" << endl;

    // Search
    size_t pos = s3.find(' ');
    if (pos != string::npos)
        cout << "Space found at index: " << pos << endl;

    // Substring
    cout << "First word: " << s3.substr(0, pos) << endl;

    // Character classification
    int vowels = 0;
    for (char c : s3) {
        char lc = tolower(c);
        if (lc == 'a' || lc == 'e' || lc == 'i' || lc == 'o' || lc == 'u')
            vowels++;
    }
    cout << "Vowels: " << vowels << endl;

    return 0;
}
```

**Dry Run (Input: `"Hello"`, `"World"`):**

$$
\begin{aligned}
s3 &= \text{"Hello World"} \\
\text{length}(s3) &= 11 \\
\text{find}(\text{' '}) &= 5 \\
s3.\text{substr}(0,\ 5) &= \text{"Hello"} \\
\text{vowels} &= 3 \quad (\text{'e', 'o', 'o'})
\end{aligned}
$$
<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
# SECTION 4: Structural Diagrams & Schematics

## 4.1 C-Style String Memory Layout

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Memory Block"] --> B["Index 0"]
    A --> C["Index 1"]
    A --> D["Index 2"]
    A --> E["Index 3"]
    A --> F["Index 4"]
    A --> G["Index 5: NULL"]
    H["base pointer"] -.-> A
    B:::mem
    C:::mem
    D:::mem
    E:::mem
    F:::mem
    G:::null
    classDef mem fill:#4A90E2,stroke:#000,color:#fff
    classDef null fill:#E94E77,stroke:#000,color:#fff
```

**Block-Level Description:**
- A contiguous character array allocated on **stack** (or **heap** if `new` is used).
- Index 0 holds the **first character**, index `n-1` holds the **last**.
- The character immediately after the last valid character is the **null terminator `'\0'`** — required for all C-style string functions like `strlen`, `strcpy`.
- The base pointer (`s`) points to index 0; pointer arithmetic (`*(s+i)`) accesses each character.

---

## 4.2 `std::string` Object Internal Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    obj["std::string Object"] --> ptr["char* pointer"]
    obj --> len["size_t length"]
    obj --> cap["size_t capacity"]
    ptr --> heap["Heap-Allocated Buffer"]
    heap --> b0["Index 0"]
    heap --> b1["Index 1"]
    heap --> bN["Index N-1"]
    heap --> bT["Index N: \\0"]
    obj:::object
    ptr:::meta
    len:::meta
    cap:::meta
    heap:::heap
    b0:::char
    b1:::char
    bN:::char
    bT:::term
    classDef object fill:#7B61FF,stroke:#000,color:#fff
    classDef meta fill:#F5A623,stroke:#000,color:#fff
    classDef heap fill:#50C878,stroke:#000,color:#fff
    classDef char fill:#4A90E2,stroke:#000,color:#fff
    classDef term fill:#E94E77,stroke:#000,color:#fff
```

**Block-Level Description:**
- The `std::string` object itself lives on the **stack** and occupies a small fixed size (typically **32 bytes** on 64-bit systems: pointer + size + capacity).
- The **actual character data** is allocated on the **heap** and pointed to internally.
- `length` tracks the number of valid characters; `capacity` tracks allocated buffer size (`capacity >= length`).
- When `length` exceeds `capacity`, the string **reallocates** automatically (typically doubling capacity).

---

## 4.3 String Operation Flow — `find()` and `substr()` Pipeline

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Input: string s = APJKeralaUniversity"] --> B["Call: s.find('Kerala')"]
    B --> C{"Substring exists?"}
    C -- "No" --> D["Return: string::npos"]
    C -- "Yes" --> E["Return: index 3"]
    E --> F["Call: s.substr(3, 6)"]
    F --> G["Extract chars from index 3 to 8"]
    G --> H["Output: Kerala"]
    D:::no
    E:::yes
    F:::proc
    G:::proc
    H:::result
    classDef no fill:#E94E77,stroke:#000,color:#fff
    classDef yes fill:#50C878,stroke:#000,color:#fff
    classDef proc fill:#F5A623,stroke:#000,color:#fff
    classDef result fill:#4A90E2,stroke:#000,color:#fff
```

---

## 4.4 Class Diagram of `std::string` Member Functions

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class std_string {
        +size_t length()
        +size_t size()
        +size_t capacity()
        +bool empty()
        +char& at(size_t pos)
        +char& operator[](size_t pos)
        +string& append(const string& str)
        +string& insert(size_t pos, const string& str)
        +string& erase(size_t pos, size_t len)
        +string& replace(size_t pos, size_t len, const string& str)
        +string substr(size_t pos, size_t len)
        +size_t find(const string& str)
        +size_t find(char ch)
        +int compare(const string& str)
        +const char* c_str()
        +void clear()
    }
```

> [!NOTE]
> This is the **canonical member-function surface** expected for KTU Module-1 viva questions. The exact signatures may vary by C++ standard version (C++11, C++14, C++17, C++20), but the names and return semantics remain consistent.

# SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

---

## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### **Q1. [KTU University Exam — June 2024]**
**Explain the different ways of initializing a `std::string` object in C++. Provide at least four examples.**

**Model Answer:**

The `std::string` class supports multiple initialization syntaxes:

1. **Default constructor:** Creates an empty string.
   ```cpp
   string s1;
   ```

2. **C-string literal initialization:**
   ```cpp
   string s2("KTU");
   ```

3. **Partial initialization from C-string (count parameter):**
   ```cpp
   string s3("Engineering", 4);  // s3 = "Engi"
   ```

4. **Repetition constructor (n copies of a character):**
   ```cpp
   string s4(5, '*');  // s4 = "*****"
   ```

5. **Copy constructor:**
   ```cpp
   string s5(s2);  // s5 = "KTU"
   ```

---

### **Q2. [KTU University Exam — Dec 2023]**
**Differentiate between `cin >> s` and `getline(cin, s)` for string input. When is `getline()` preferred?**

**Model Answer:**

| Aspect | `cin >> s` | `getline(cin, s)` |
|---|---|---|
| Whitespace handling | Stops at first whitespace | Reads entire line including spaces |
| Delimiter | Whitespace (default) | Newline `\n` (default) |
| Buffer safety | Safe for single-word input | Safe for full sentences |
| Use case | Single tokens, IDs, passwords | Names, addresses, full lines |

**When to prefer `getline()`:** Whenever the input may contain spaces — full names, addresses, multi-word sentences, CSV-like records. `cin >>` would silently truncate at the first space.

---

## 5.2 Part B — Full 14-Mark Questions (Internal Choice Pattern)

### **Question A — 14 Marks**
**[KTU University Exam — July 2024]**

**(a)** Explain any **seven commonly used member functions** of the `std::string` class in C++ with suitable examples. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** Write a C++ program to read a full sentence from the user, count the number of **vowels**, **consonants**, **digits**, and **whitespace characters** using `<cctype>` functions. Display the counts. **(7 marks)**

---

#### Model Solution for (a):

The seven key member functions of `std::string` are:

1. **`length()` / `size()`** — Returns number of characters.
   ```cpp
   string s = "Hello";
   cout << s.length();  // Output: 5
   ```

2. **`append()` / `+=`** — Appends content.
   ```cpp
   string s = "KTU";
   s.append(" 2024");  // s = "KTU 2024"
   ```

3. **`substr(pos, len)`** — Extracts a substring.
   ```cpp
   string s = "Programming";
   cout << s.substr(0, 7);  // Output: Program
   ```

4. **`find(str)`** — Returns first index of substring; `string::npos` if not found.
   ```cpp
   string s = "C++ Programming";
   cout << s.find("Program");  // Output: 4
   ```

5. **`replace(pos, len, str)`** — Replaces characters.
   ```cpp
   string s = "I hate C++";
   s.replace(2, 4, "love");  // s = "I love C++"
   ```

6. **`erase(pos, len)`** — Removes characters.
   ```cpp
   string s = "Hello World";
   s.erase(5, 6);  // s = "Hello"
   ```

7. **`compare(str)`** — Lexicographic comparison (returns 0 if equal, negative or positive otherwise).
   ```cpp
   string a = "apple", b = "banana";
   cout << a.compare(b);  // Negative (apple < banana)
   ```

---

#### Model Solution for (b):

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <cctype>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    string s;
    cout << "Enter a sentence: ";
    getline(cin, s);

    int vowels = 0, consonants = 0, digits = 0, spaces = 0;

    for (char c : s) {
        if (isalpha(c)) {
            char lc = tolower(c);
            if (lc == 'a' || lc == 'e' || lc == 'i' || lc == 'o' || lc == 'u')
                vowels++;
            else
                consonants++;
        } else if (isdigit(c)) {
            digits++;
        } else if (isspace(c)) {
            spaces++;
        }
    }

    cout << "Vowels: " << vowels << endl;
    cout << "Consonants: " << consonants << endl;
    cout << "Digits: " << digits << endl;
    cout << "Whitespace: " << spaces << endl;

    return 0;
}
```

**Dry Run (Input: `"KTU 2024 Exam"`):**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Vowels} &= 2 \quad (\text{'E', 'a'}) \\
\text{Consonants} &= 5 \quad (\text{'K', 'T', 'x', 'm', 'm' minus vowel}) \\
\text{Digits} &= 4 \quad (\text{'2','0','2','4'}) \\
\text{Whitespace} &= 2
\end{aligned}
$$

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Pitfall:** Students often forget to convert uppercase letters using `tolower()` before comparing against lowercase vowels. The code will then miss vowels like `'A'`, `'E'`. This is a **2-mark deduction** typically applied.

---

### **Question B — 14 Marks (Alternative Choice)**
**[KTU University Exam — Dec 2023]**

**(a)** Compare **C-style strings** and **C++ `std::string` class** in terms of memory management, safety, and built-in operations. Provide examples. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** Write a C++ program that reads a string and checks whether it is a **palindrome** (case-insensitive). Display appropriate messages. **(7 marks)**

---

#### Model Solution for (a):

| Comparison Parameter | C-Style Strings (`char[]`) | C++ `std::string` |
|---|---|---|
| Header | `<cstring>` | `<string>` |
| Memory | Fixed size array, stack/heap | Dynamic heap allocation, auto-resizing |
| Null terminator | **Required** (`'\0'`) | **Managed internally** |
| Length calculation | `strlen(s)` — O(n) traversal | `s.length()` — O(1) stored value |
| Concatenation | `strcat(a, b)` — unsafe, buffer overflow risk | `a + b` — safe, returns new string |
| Comparison | `strcmp(a, b)` returns int | `a == b` returns bool |
| Copy | `strcpy(a, b)` — unsafe | `a = b` — deep copy, safe |
| Operator overloading | None | `+`, `+=`, `==`, `<`, `>`, `[]`, `<<`, `>>` |
| Input handling | `cin.getline(arr, n)` | `getline(cin, s)` |

**Examples illustrating safety:**

```cpp
// C-style: unsafe
char a[10] = "Hello";
char b[20] = " World";
strcat(a, b);  // Buffer overflow if b is too large!

// C++ style: safe
string x = "Hello";
string y = " World";
string z = x + y;  // Automatic memory allocation
```

**Verdict:** `std::string` is the **preferred** choice in modern C++ due to safety, expressive syntax, and OOP encapsulation.

---

#### Model Solution for (b):

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <cctype>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    string s;
    cout << "Enter a string: ";
    getline(cin, s);

    // Normalize: remove spaces and convert to lowercase
    string clean = "";
    for (char c : s) {
        if (isalpha(c))
            clean += tolower(c);
    }

    // Reverse and compare
    string rev = clean;
    int n = rev.length();
    for (int i = 0; i < n / 2; i++) {
        swap(rev[i], rev[n - i - 1]);
    }

    if (clean == rev)
        cout << "'" << s << "' is a palindrome." << endl;
    else
        cout << "'" << s << "' is NOT a palindrome." << endl;

    return 0;
}
```

**Dry Run:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Input} &= \text{"A man a plan a canal Panama"} \\
\text{Clean} &= \text{"amanaplanacanalpanama"} \\
\text{Rev} &= \text{"amanaplanacanalpanama"} \\
\text{Result} &= \text{Palindrome ✅}
\end{aligned}
$$

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Pitfall (Palindrome):** Failing to handle case-sensitivity (`"Aa"` → not equal to `"aA"` by default) results in **2-mark deduction**. Also, including spaces without normalization will incorrectly fail the palindrome check. Students must explicitly mention `tolower()` and filtering non-alpha characters.

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Rapid-Revision Checklist for KTU Module 1 — Strings**

- 📌 **Two paradigms exist:** C-style (`char[]`, null-terminated) and C++ `std::string` (object-oriented, dynamic).
- 📌 **Header files:** `<string>` for `std::string`, `<cctype>` for character functions (`isalpha`, `isdigit`, `tolower`, etc.).
- 📌 **Always use `getline(cin, s)`** when input may contain spaces.
- 📌 **`string::npos`** is the standard "not found" return value — compare with `!= string::npos`, never with `-1`.
- 📌 **Indexing is 0-based:** valid range is `[0, length()-1]`.
- 📌 **`length()` and `size()`** are identical — both return `size_t`.
- 📌 **Operators overloaded:** `+`, `+=`, `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `[]`, `<<`, `>>`.
- 📌 **`c_str()`** returns a `const char*` for interoperability with legacy C functions.
- 📌 **`substr(pos, len)`** — if `len` is omitted, returns from `pos` to the end.
- 📌 **Conversion rule:** `tolower()` before vowel/consonant checks to handle both cases.
- 📌 **For palindrome problems:** Normalize (remove non-alphas, lowercase) **before** reversal.
- 📌 **Capacity vs Length:** `capacity() >= length()` always holds; `capacity` grows geometrically (typically doubles).
- 📌 **Memory model:** `std::string` object on stack; character buffer on heap.
- 📌 **Favorite viva questions:** "Difference between `cin >>` and `getline()`", "What does `find()` return on failure?", "Why is `std::string` preferred over `char[]`?"

> [!TIP]
> **Final Exam Strategy:** For 14-mark Part-B questions, **always write the program first with comments**, then explain logic line-by-line. Examiners reward clarity of thought over clever one-liners.
