Mention a scenario where using `&&` is preferred over `&`.* **Model Answer (3 Marks):** > | Aspect | Bitwise `&` | Logical `&&` | > | :--- | :--- | :--- | > | **Operands** | Works on integer types bit-by-bit | Works only on `boolean` operands | > | **Result type** | Returns an `int` (or other integer type) | Returns a `boolean` | > | **Evaluation** | Always evaluates **both** operands (eager) | **Short-circuits** — skips RHS if LHS is `false` | > | **Use case** | Masking bits, low-level flag manipulation | Boolean logic in `if`/`while` conditions | > > **Preferred scenario for `&&`:** When the RHS is an *expensive or unsafe* operation, e.g., `if (denominator != 0 && numerator / denominator > 1)`. Here, `&&` prevents the division by zero. --- **Q2. `[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]`** *What is the difference between `>>` and `>>>` shift operators in Java? Illustrate with an example.* **Model Answer (3 Marks):** > Both operators perform a right shift, but they differ in how they fill the **vacated leftmost bits**: > - **`>>` (Signed/Arithmetic Right Shift):** Fills the left side with the **sign bit** (preserves sign). > - **`>>>` (Unsigned/Logical Right Shift):** Always fills the left side with **`0`**. > > **Example:** For `-8 >> 2` we get `-2`; for `-8 >>> 2` we get `1073741822` (a large positive number) because the sign bit is replaced by 0. --- ### 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks Each — Internal Choice) > **ESE Module Question Pattern (KTU 2024 Scheme):** Part B questions carry 14 marks, typically split as Part (a) 7 marks + Part (b) 7 marks. **Two full alternative questions are provided below.** --- #### **Question A (14 Marks)** `[KTU University Exam – Model Paper]` **(a)** Explain the different categories of operators available in Java. List the arithmetic, relational, and logical operators with their symbols and an example for each. **(7 Marks)** **Model Solution:** Java operators are classified based on the operation they perform. The major categories are: 1. **Arithmetic Operators** — perform mathematical operations on numeric operands. | Operator | Meaning | Example (a=10, b=3) | Result | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `+` | Addition | `a + b` | 13 | | `-` | Subtraction | `a - b` | 7 | | `*` | Multiplication | `a * b` | 30 | | `/` | Division | `a / b` | 3 | | `%` | Modulus | `a % b` | 1 | | `++` | Increment | `a++` | 11 | | `--` | Decrement | `--b` | 2 | 2. **Relational Operators** — compare two values and return a boolean. | Operator | Meaning | Example | Result | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `==` | Equal to | `a == b` | `false` | | `!=` | Not equal to | `a != b` | `true` | | `>` | Greater than | `a > b` | `true` | | `<` | Less than | `a < b` | `false` | | `>=` | Greater than or equal | `a >= 10` | `true` | | `<=` | Less than or equal | `b <= 3` | `true` | 3. **Logical (Boolean) Operators** — combine boolean expressions. | Operator | Meaning | Example | Result | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `&&` | Logical AND | `(a > b) && (b > 0)` | `true` | | `\|\|` | Logical OR | `(a < b) \|\| (b < 0)` | `false` | | `!` | Logical NOT | `!(a == b)` | `true` | These operators form the backbone of expressions, control flow, and decision-making in Java. --- **(b)** Write a Java program to demonstrate the use of bitwise operators (`&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `<<`, `>>`, `>>>`). Show the output for inputs `a = 45`, `b = 25`. **(7 Marks)** **Model Solution:** ```java public class BitwiseDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { int a = 45; // binary: 0000...0010 1101 int b = 25; // binary: 0000...0001 1001 System.out.println("a & b = " + (a & b)); // 9 System.out.println("a | b = " + (a | b)); // 61 System.out.println("a ^ b = " + (a ^ b)); // 52 System.out.println("~a = " + (~a)); // -46 System.out.println("a << 2 = " + (a << 2)); // 180 System.out.println("a >> 2 = " + (a >> 2)); // 11 System.out.println("a >>> 2 = " + (a >>> 2)); // 11 System.out.println("-16 >> 2 = " + (-16 >> 2)); // -4 System.out.println("-16 >>> 2 = " + (-16 >>> 2)); // 1073741820 } } ``` **Step-by-step trace for the bitwise operators:** 1. `a & b` = `0001 1001` = `9` (only common `1` bits retained) 2. `a | b` = `0011 1101` = `32+16+8+4+1 = 61` 3. `a ^ b` = `0011 0100` = `32+16+4 = 52` 4. `~a` = `~45` = `-(45+1) = -46` (using the identity `~x = -x-1`) 5. `a << 2` = `45 × 2² = 180` 6. `a >> 2` = `45 / 2² = 11` (integer truncation) 7. `a >>> 2` for a positive number = same as `a >> 2` = `11` 8. `-16 >> 2` = `floor(-16/4) = -4` (sign preserved) 9. `-16 >>> 2` = `1073741820` (sign bit replaced by 0) --- #### **Question B (14 Marks)** `[KTU University Exam – Model Paper]` **(a)** Explain the conditional (ternary) operator in Java with its syntax. Write an expression to find the maximum of three numbers using the ternary operator. **(7 Marks)** **Model Solution:** The **conditional (ternary) operator** `? :` is the only operator in Java that takes three operands. It provides a concise way to express simple `if-else` logic that produces a value. > **Syntax:** `condition ? expressionIfTrue : expressionIfFalse` - First, the `condition` (a boolean expression) is evaluated. - If `true`, the entire expression evaluates to `expressionIfTrue`. - If `false`, it evaluates to `expressionIfFalse`. - The two branch expressions undergo **type promotion** to a common compatible type. **Example — Maximum of three numbers `a`, `b`, `c`:** ```java int a = 25, b = 78, c = 42; int max = (a > b) ? ((a > c) ? a : c) : ((b > c) ? b : c); System.out.println("Maximum = " + max); // Maximum = 78 ``` **Trace:** - Outer condition: `a > b` → `25 > 78` → `false` - Evaluate false-branch: `(b > c) ? b : c` → `78 > 42` → `true` → returns `b = 78` - Final: `max = 78` This is equivalent to the following `if-else` ladder: ```java int max; if (a > b) { max = (a > c) ? a : c; } else { max = (b > c) ? b : c; } ``` The ternary form is more compact and produces a value that can be directly used in further expressions. --- **(b)** Explain compound assignment operators in Java. Illustrate with an example showing how `x += 5` differs from `x = x + 5` when `x` is of type `byte`. **(7 Marks)** **Model Solution:** Compound assignment operators combine a binary operation with an assignment in a single, concise token. The general form is: > `variable op= expression;` which is equivalent to `variable = (TypeOfVariable)(variable op expression);` The **critical nuance** is the *implicit type cast* performed by the compound operator on the result before assignment. **Comparison for `byte x`:** ```java byte x = 50; // Case 1: Plain assignment x = x + 5; // COMPILE-TIME ERROR! // "incompatible types: possible lossy conversion from int to byte" // Because byte + int promotes to int, and int cannot be implicitly narrowed to byte. // Case 2: Compound assignment x += 5; // COMPILES SUCCESSFULLY // Equivalent to: x = (byte)(x + 5); // The result (55) is implicitly cast back to byte. ``` **Another subtle example with overflow:** ```java byte x = 100; x += 200; // x = (byte)(100 + 200) = (byte)300 // 300 in binary = 0001 0010 1100 // Truncated to 8 bits = 0010 1100 = 44 // But 0010 1100 as signed byte = +44 // Wait, recalculation: 300 = 100101100, lower 8 bits = 00101100 = 44. // So x = 44. (No silent sign issue in this case, but in negative cases it occurs.) ``` **List of common compound assignment operators:** | Operator | Meaning | Equivalent Expression | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `+=` | Add and assign | `a = a + b` | | `-=` | Subtract and assign | `a = a - b` | | `*=` | Multiply and assign | `a = a * b` | | `/=` | Divide and assign | `a = a / b` | | `%=` | Modulus and assign | `a = a % b` | | `&=` | Bitwise AND and assign | `a = a & b` | | `\|=` | Bitwise OR and assign | `a = a \| b` | | `^=` | Bitwise XOR and assign | `a = a ^ b` | | `<<=` | Left shift and assign | `a = a << b` | | `>>=` | Signed right shift and assign | `a = a >> b` | | `>>>=` | Unsigned right shift and assign | `a = a >>> b` | --- ### 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout > [!WARNING] > **Where students lose marks in Operator Questions (KTU 2024 Scheme):** > 1. **Confusing `=` with `==`:** `=` is assignment, `==` is comparison. Mark deduction: 1 mark. > 2. **Ignoring short-circuit behavior:** Not predicting whether side effects (e.g., `++y`) occur. Mark deduction: 1–2 marks. > 3. **Integer division vs. modulus sign:** Forgetting that `-7 % 3 = -1` (sign of numerator). Mark deduction: 1 mark. > 4. **Pre vs. post increment in expressions:** Writing `int b = a++;` and answering `b = a + 1` (wrong). Mark deduction: 2 marks. > 5. **Bitwise vs. Logical operator mix-up:** Using `&&` on integers. Mark deduction: 1 mark. > 6. **Shift overflow / sign issues:** Not tracing `>>` vs. `>>>` on negative numbers. Mark deduction: 2 marks. > 7. **Compound assignment cast subtlety:** Forgetting that `x += 1.5` on an `int` truncates. Mark deduction: 2 marks. > 8. **Operator precedence in nested ternaries:** Forgetting that ternary is right-associative. Mark deduction: 1 mark. ### 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember > [!IMPORTANT] > **Rapid-Revision Checklist — Operators in Java (PBCST304 Module 1)** - [ ] Java has **6 major operator families**: Arithmetic, Bitwise, Relational, Logical, Assignment, Ternary. - [ ] **Arithmetic `/`** on two integers performs **truncation toward zero** (not floor division). - [ ] **Pre-increment (`++a`)** changes value first, then uses it. **Post-increment (`a++`)** uses value first, then changes it. - [ ] **Modulus `%`** result takes the sign of the **left operand**. - [ ] **Bitwise operators** (`&`, `|`, `^`, `~`) act on integer **bits**; **Logical operators** (`&&`, `||`, `!`) act on **booleans**. - [ ] **`&&` and `||` are short-circuit**; `&` and `|` (when used as boolean) are **not** — both sides are always evaluated. - [ ] **`x << n`** = $x \cdot 2^n$; **`x >> n`** = $\lfloor x / 2^n \rfloor$ (sign-preserving); **`x >>> n`** is the unsigned variant (always fills with 0). - [ ] **`~x = -x - 1`** (two's complement identity). - [ ] **`==` compares values**; use `.equals()` for object content comparison. - [ ] **Compound assignment `x op= y`** implicitly casts the result to the type of `x` (e.g., `byte b; b += 200;` *compiles*, but `b = b + 200;` *does not*). - [ ] **Ternary operator** `cond ? A : B` returns a value; both `A` and `B` undergo **type promotion** to a common type. - [ ] **Operator precedence** determines evaluation order; use **parentheses** to override and improve readability. - [ ] Java does **not support** user-defined operator overloading (except `+` for `String` concatenation) — a key safety feature over C++. - [ ] **Postfix** (`expr++`, `expr--`) has **highest** precedence; **assignment** operators have the **lowest** precedence. - [ ] Ternary is **right-associative**, meaning nested ternaries are evaluated from right to left.

topics.title: Operator Precedence
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PBCST304 - OBJECT ORIENTED PROGRAMMING
> - **Module:** Module 1
> - **Topic:** Operator Precedence

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus)

In the context of the C++ programming language (the implementation vehicle for Object Oriented Programming in the KTU 2024 B.Tech CSE/IT curriculum), **Operator Precedence** is formally defined as a set of deterministic, language-defined rules that govern the **order in which individual operators are bound to their operands** within a single, complex expression. Every operator in C++ is assigned a fixed **precedence level** (also called a hierarchy rank) — an integer-like priority value that the compiler uses to resolve ambiguity in unparenthesized expressions.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Board Definition (Verbatim Style):**
> *"Operator precedence determines the grouping of terms in an expression and essentially decides which operation is performed first in the absence of parentheses. It is a compile-time binding property of the language grammar."*

The companion concept is **Operator Associativity**, which determines the **direction of evaluation** (left-to-right or right-to-left) when two operators of **the same precedence level** appear adjacent to each other in an expression.

### 1.2 Intuitive Real-World Analogy

Imagine you are a **head chef in a busy kitchen** with multiple assistants. The kitchen receives a complex order:

> *"Chop the onions, boil the rice, and fry the paneer."*

Even without explicit numbering, there is an **inherent priority** in the kitchen:
1. **Boiling the rice** (longest cooking time → done first)
2. **Frying the paneer** (medium time → done second)
3. **Chopping the onions** (quickest task → done last, just before plating)

This **built-in priority system** is exactly what **operator precedence** does for a C++ compiler. The compiler does not read an expression from left to right like a story; instead, it scans the expression and binds the **highest-priority operators first**, then moves down the precedence ladder — just like the chef handling time-consuming tasks first.

> [!NOTE]
> **Key Takeaway for KTU Exam:** If a student writes `5 + 3 * 2` and expects the answer to be 16 (left-to-right evaluation), they are **WRONG**. The compiler, following precedence, evaluates `3 * 2 = 6` first, and then `5 + 6 = 11`. This is the most common source of marks lost in KTU Board examinations.

### 1.3 The Three-Way Relationship

Operator precedence never works in isolation. It always forms a **trinity** with:

| Concept | Question it Answers | Evaluated At |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Precedence** | *Which* operator binds tighter? | Compile time |
| **Associativity** | In *what direction* (L→R or R→L)? | Compile time |
| **Order of Evaluation** | *When* is each operand's value actually computed? | Run time |

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner Trap:** Many students confuse **precedence** with **order of evaluation**. Precedence decides which operator is applied first; order of evaluation decides which operand is fetched first. For example, in `f() + g()`, the function `f()` may be called before `g()`, or vice-versa — precedence is irrelevant here.

---

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 The Theoretical Foundation

The C++ operator precedence table is defined in the **ISO C++ Standard (ISO/IEC 14882)** and is implemented in the compiler's **parser** as part of the language grammar. When the parser encounters an expression, it performs the following structured logic:

1. **Tokenization (Lexical Analysis Phase):** The source code is broken into tokens: identifiers, literals, operators, and punctuation.
2. **Grammar Rule Application (Syntax Analysis Phase):** The parser consults the precedence table (a numerical priority matrix) to decide the **parse tree structure**. Higher precedence operators become **deeper nodes** in the tree, meaning they are evaluated first.
3. **Tree Traversal (Semantic Phase):** A post-order traversal of the parse tree produces the **evaluation order**, which is finally executed.

### 2.2 The KTU High-Yield Precedence Table (Top to Bottom = Highest to Lowest)

Below is the **comprehensive operator precedence table** that KTU examiners typically expect students to reproduce. The table is ordered from **highest precedence (Level 1 — binds tightest)** to **lowest precedence (Level 17 — binds loosest)**.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Memory Trick for KTU Exams:** Memorize the acronym **"UARSMA-LCR-FLSCAMA"** (Unnamed, Array, Resolution, Scope, Member, Arithmetic, Logical, Conditional, Relational, Function, Left, Scope, Comma, Assignment, Member, Address) — a useful mnemonic to recall the broad categories.

| Level | Category | Operators | Associativity | Example of Binding |
| :---: | :--- | :--- | :---: | :--- |
| **1** | Scope Resolution | `::` | L→R | `std::cout` |
| **2** | Post-Increment / Decrement | `++`, `--` | L→R | `a++` |
| **2** | Function Call | `()` | L→R | `foo(x)` |
| **2** | Array Subscript | `[]` | L→R | `arr[5]` |
| **2** | Member Access (Dot/Arrow) | `.`, `->` | L→R | `obj.member` |
| **3** | Pre-Increment / Decrement | `++`, `--` | R→L | `++a` |
| **3** | Unary (Plus, Minus, NOT, Bitwise NOT) | `+`, `-`, `!`, `~` | R→L | `-x` |
| **3** | Address-of / Dereference | `&`, `*` | R→L | `&var` |
| **3** | Sizeof / new / delete | `sizeof`, `new`, `delete` | R→L | `new int` |
| **4** | Pointer-to-Member | `.*`, `->*` | L→R | `ptr->*member` |
| **5** | Multiplicative | `*`, `/`, `%` | L→R | `a * b` |
| **6** | Additive | `+`, `-` | L→R | `a + b` |
| **7** | Shift | `<<`, `>>` | L→R | `x << 2` |
| **8** | Three-Way Comparison (C++20) | `<=>` | L→R | `a <=> b` |
| **9** | Relational | `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` | L→R | `a < b` |
| **10** | Equality | `==`, `!=` | L→R | `a == b` |
| **11** | Bitwise AND | `&` | L→R | `a & b` |
| **12** | Bitwise XOR | `^` | L→R | `a ^ b` |
| **13** | Bitwise OR | $\vert$ | L→R | `a \vert b` |
| **14** | Logical AND | `&&` | L→R | `a && b` |
| **15** | Logical OR | $\vert\vert$ | L→R | `a \vert\vert b` |
| **16** | Conditional (Ternary) | `? :` | R→L | `a ? b : c` |
| **17** | Assignment (and compound) | `=`, `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=` etc. | R→L | `a = 5` |
| **18** | Comma | `,` | L→R | `a, b` |

> [!NOTE]
> **Critical KTU Distinction:** Note that Level 1 (`::`) is the **HIGHEST** precedence. This is why `std::cout` works — the scope resolution binds tighter than anything else. Conversely, the **comma operator (Level 18)** is the **LOWEST** precedence, which is why it is used to separate multiple expressions in a `for` loop header.

### 2.3 The Associativity Rule Explained

When two operators of **equal precedence** appear next to each other, the compiler uses **associativity** as the tie-breaker. There are only **two possible directions**:

- **Left-to-Right (L→R):** The operator on the **left** is applied first. Example: `10 - 5 - 2` = `(10 - 5) - 2` = `3` (NOT `10 - (5 - 2)` = `7`).
- **Right-to-Left (R→L):** The operator on the **right** is applied first. Example: `a = b = 5` is parsed as `a = (b = 5)`, because assignment is **right-associative**.

### 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility

Operator precedence is not merely an academic exercise. It is critical in:

- **Embedded Systems Programming:** Engineers writing bit-manipulation code for microcontrollers (e.g., `PORTA = (1 << 3) \vert 0x0F;`) rely heavily on shift and bitwise precedence to control hardware registers.
- **Compiler Construction:** The YACC/Bison parser-generator tools use precedence declarations to resolve shift-reduce conflicts.
- **Numerical Computing:** In scientific simulations, incorrect precedence in floating-point expressions can lead to **catastrophic cancellation** errors.
- **Cybersecurity:** Buffer overflow exploits and shellcode construction depend on precise understanding of how `++`, `*`, and `[]` interact.

---

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Exhaustive Step-by-Step Expression Evaluation

The following section provides **fully worked-out expression evaluations** — the exact type of analytical problem KTU examiners set in 14-mark questions. Every step is shown explicitly.

---

### **Worked Example 1: Mixed Arithmetic Expression**

**Problem:** Evaluate the C++ expression:
$$
\text{result} = 10 + 2 \times 3 - 8 \div 4 + 5 \% 3
$$

**Step 1 — Identify all operators and their precedence levels:**

The expression contains the following operators, ordered by the precedence table:

| Operator | Symbol | Precedence Level | Associativity |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Multiplication | `*` | **5** | L→R |
| Division | `/` | **5** | L→R |
| Modulus | `%` | **5** | L→R |
| Addition | `+` | **6** | L→R |
| Subtraction | `-` | **6** | L→R |
| Assignment | `=` | **17** | R→L |

**Step 2 — Apply highest precedence first (Levels 5: `*`, `/`, `%`):**

The compiler first scans for all `*`, `/`, and `%` operators. These are the only Level 5 operators in the expression, so they all bind tighter than the `+` and `-` operators at Level 6.

The expression gets partitioned by parenthesization (invisibly inserted by the compiler):

$$
\text{result} = 10 + (2 \times 3) - (8 \div 4) + (5 \% 3)
$$

**Step 3 — Compute each Level 5 sub-expression (left to right, as associativity dictates):**

$$
2 \times 3 = 6
$$

$$
8 \div 4 = 2
$$

$$
5 \% 3 = 2 \quad \text{(since } 5 = 1 \times 3 + 2 \text{)}
$$

**Step 4 — Substitute the computed values back into the expression:**

$$
\text{result} = 10 + 6 - 2 + 2
$$

**Step 5 — Apply next precedence level (Level 6: `+`, `-`):**

All remaining operators (`+` and `-`) share the same precedence level (6) and are **left-associative**, so we scan strictly from left to right:

$$
10 + 6 = 16
$$

$$
16 - 2 = 14
$$

$$
14 + 2 = 16
$$

**Step 6 — Apply the final assignment (Level 17, right-associative):**

$$
\text{result} = 16
$$

**Final Answer:** `result` is assigned the value **16**.

---

### **Worked Example 2: Relational and Logical Operators**

**Problem:** Determine the Boolean value of:
$$
(5 + 3 > 7) \ \&\&\ (10 \leq 10) \ \vert\vert\ (2 == 3)
$$

**Step 1 — Map all operators to their precedence levels:**

| Operator | Precedence Level | Associativity |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| `+` | 6 | L→R |
| `>` | 9 | L→R |
| `<=` | 9 | L→R |
| `==` | 10 | L→R |
| `&&` | 14 | L→R |
| $\vert\vert$ | 15 | L→R |

**Step 2 — Evaluate Level 6 (Addition) first:**

$$
5 + 3 = 8
$$

The expression becomes:
$$
(8 > 7) \ \&\&\ (10 \leq 10) \ \vert\vert\ (2 == 3)
$$

**Step 3 — Evaluate Level 9 (Relational operators):**

$$
8 > 7 \implies \text{true} \equiv 1
$$

$$
10 \leq 10 \implies \text{true} \equiv 1
$$

The expression becomes:
$$
1 \ \&\&\ 1 \ \vert\vert\ (2 == 3)
$$

**Step 4 — Evaluate Level 10 (Equality):**

$$
2 == 3 \implies \text{false} \equiv 0
$$

The expression becomes:
$$
1 \ \&\&\ 1 \ \vert\vert\ 0
$$

**Step 5 — Apply Level 14 (`&&`):** `&&` has higher precedence than `||`, so it binds tighter.

$$
1 \ \&\&\ 1 = 1
$$

The expression becomes:
$$
1 \ \vert\vert\ 0
$$

**Step 6 — Apply Level 15 (`||`):**

$$
1 \ \vert\vert\ 0 = 1
$$

**Final Answer:** The expression evaluates to **1 (true)**.

---

### **Worked Example 3: Assignment Right-Associativity**

**Problem:** Evaluate the chain assignment and determine final values of all variables:
$$
a = b = c = 5 + 3 \times 2
$$

**Step 1 — Identify operators:**

| Operator | Precedence Level | Associativity |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| `*` | 5 | L→R |
| `+` | 6 | L→R |
| `=` | 17 | R→L |

**Step 2 — Apply Level 5 (multiplication) first:**

$$
3 \times 2 = 6
$$

**Step 3 — Apply Level 6 (addition):**

$$
5 + 6 = 11
$$

**Step 4 — Apply Level 17 (assignment, right-to-left):**

Since assignment is **right-associative**, the compiler binds the **rightmost `=` first**:

$$
a = (b = (c = 11))
$$

Evaluating from the **innermost parenthesis outward**:

- `c = 11` → `c` becomes 11, sub-expression evaluates to 11.
- `b = 11` → `b` becomes 11, sub-expression evaluates to 11.
- `a = 11` → `a` becomes 11, sub-expression evaluates to 11.

**Final Answer:** `a = 11`, `b = 11`, `c = 11`.

---

### **Worked Example 4: The Famous Unary vs Binary Pitfall**

**Problem:** Evaluate:
$$
-x^{2} \quad \text{in C++}
$$

> [!WARNING]
> **The Trap:** Mathematics students instinctively read this as `-(x²)`. **In C++, this is WRONG!**

**Step 1 — C++ has no exponentiation operator `^`.** The `^` symbol denotes **bitwise XOR** (Level 12). So this expression, if literally typed in C++, would be `(2) ^ x`, which is not what was intended. Even if we assume the user meant `x * x`, the **unary minus** is the issue.

**Step 2 — Corrected Problem:** Evaluate `-x * x` where `x = 4`.

**Step 3 — Identify operators:**

| Operator | Precedence Level | Associativity |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| `-` (unary) | **3** | R→L |
| `*` (binary) | **5** | L→R |

**Step 4 — Unary minus (Level 3) binds TIGHTER than multiplication (Level 5):**

The compiler parenthesizes this as:
$$
(-x) \times x
$$

**Step 5 — Evaluate:**

$$
(-4) \times 4 = -16
$$

**Final Answer:** `-16` (NOT `-(4 \times 4) = -16` which coincidentally matches, but `-x * y` would be `(-x) * y`, not `-(x*y)`. This is a famous KTU board question trap.)

---

### 3.2 The Analytical Decision Matrix

Use this matrix to **mechanically determine the binding** of any C++ expression:

$$
\text{Binding Order} = \begin{cases} \text{Higher Level} & \text{if precedence levels differ} \\ \text{Use Associativity} & \text{if precedence levels are equal} \\ \text{Use Parentheses} & \text{if explicitly written} \end{cases}
$$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Golden Rule of KTU 2024 Board Exams:** When in doubt, **use parentheses**. The KTU 2024 scheme specifically rewards clarity. A correctly parenthesized expression, even if redundant, demonstrates mastery and guarantees full marks. The official KTU Board instructions state that students should "use parentheses to clarify expressions wherever precedence might be ambiguous."

---

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
## 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

### 4.1 Mermaid Diagram: The Complete Precedence Flow

The following diagram visualizes the **logical flow the C++ compiler follows** when resolving an expression's parse tree. It maps the high-level decision process the parser uses to apply operator precedence.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Start: Raw Expression Tokens] --> B[Lexical Analysis: Tokenize into Operators and Operands]
    B --> C[Syntax Analysis: Apply Grammar Rules]
    C --> D[Step 1: Identify Highest Precedence Operator in Expression]
    D --> E{More Operators Remaining?}
    E -->|Yes| F[Bind That Operator to Its Operands]
    F --> G[Create Parse Tree Node]
    G --> H[Recurse on Sub-Expressions]
    H --> E
    E -->|No| I[Step 2: Apply Associativity for Equal-Precedence Operators]
    I --> J[Post-Order Traversal of Parse Tree]
    J --> K[Step 3: Generate Intermediate Code]
    K --> L[Final: Machine Code Emission]
    L --> M[End: Expression Ready for Execution]
```

### 4.2 Mermaid Diagram: Precedence Level Hierarchy Block

The following block-level diagram maps the **17 precedence levels** as a top-down cascade, showing how an expression's parse tree is built from the highest level (tightest binding at the root) to the lowest level (loosest binding at the leaves).

```mermaid
graph TD
    L1["Level 1: Scope Resolution and Highest Precedence"] --> L2["Level 2: Postfix Operators Plus Function Call"]
    L2 --> L3["Level 3: Unary Operators and Pre-Increment"]
    L3 --> L4["Level 4: Pointer to Member Access"]
    L4 --> L5["Level 5: Multiplicative: Star Slash Modulus"]
    L5 --> L6["Level 6: Additive: Plus Minus"]
    L6 --> L7["Level 7: Shift Left and Shift Right"]
    L7 --> L8["Level 8: Three Way Comparison Spaceship"]
    L8 --> L9["Level 9: Relational: Less Greater LessEqual GreaterEqual"]
    L9 --> L10["Level 10: Equality: DoubleEqual NotEqual"]
    L10 --> L11["Level 11: Bitwise AND"]
    L11 --> L12["Level 12: Bitwise XOR"]
    L12 --> L13["Level 13: Bitwise OR"]
    L13 --> L14["Level 14: Logical AND"]
    L14 --> L15["Level 15: Logical OR"]
    L15 --> L16["Level 16: Conditional Ternary"]
    L16 --> L17["Level 17: Assignment and Compound Assignment"]
    L17 --> L18["Level 18: Comma Operator and Lowest Precedence"]
```

### 4.3 Mermaid Diagram: Parse Tree Construction for `a + b * c`

This diagram illustrates how the C++ compiler constructs a **parse tree** for the expression `a + b * c`. Notice that `*` (Level 5) becomes a **deeper node** than `+` (Level 6), confirming it is evaluated first.

```mermaid
graph TD
    root["Expression Root"] --> plusNode["+  Addition Operator Level 6"]
    plusNode --> operandA["a"]
    plusNode --> subExpr["Sub-Expression Group"]
    subExpr --> mulNode["*  Multiplication Operator Level 5"]
    mulNode --> operandB["b"]
    mulNode --> operandC["c"]
```

### 4.4 Mermaid Diagram: Associativity Direction Map

This diagram clarifies when **left-to-right** vs **right-to-left** associativity applies, which is essential for the 14-mark KTU question type.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph LAR["Left to Right Associative Operators"]
        LA1["Arithmetic: Star Slash Modulus Plus Minus"]
        LA2["Relational: Less Greater Equal NotEqual"]
        LA3["Bitwise: AND XOR OR"]
        LA4["Logical: AND OR"]
        LA5["Comma Operator"]
    end
    subgraph RAR["Right to Left Associative Operators"]
        RA1["Unary: Negative Not BitwiseNot PreIncrement"]
        RA2["Conditional Ternary: QuestionMark Colon"]
        RA3["Assignment: Equal PlusEqual MinusEqual etc"]
        RA4["Scope Resolution: ColonColon"]
    end
    LAR --> NoteLeft["Bind Leftmost Operator First"]
    RAR --> NoteRight["Bind Rightmost Operator First"]
```

---

<!-- SECTION_4_END -->

<!-- SECTION_5_START -->
## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### 5.1 Part A: Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

---

**Q1. [KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]**

**Define operator precedence and operator associativity. Explain why they are essential in C++ expression evaluation.**

**Model Answer:**

**Operator Precedence** is the set of rules in C++ that determine the **order in which different operators are applied** in an expression when parentheses are not present. Each operator is assigned a priority level — higher precedence operators bind to their operands before lower precedence operators.

**Operator Associativity** is the rule that determines the **direction of evaluation** (left-to-right or right-to-left) when two operators of the **same precedence level** appear adjacent in an expression.

**Why they are essential:**

1. **Ambiguity Resolution:** Without precedence, the expression `5 + 3 * 2` would be ambiguous. Precedence unambiguously mandates evaluation as `5 + (3 * 2) = 11`.
2. **Deterministic Compilation:** The compiler produces identical object code regardless of platform, ensuring cross-platform consistency.
3. **Code Readability:** Programmers can write concise expressions without explicitly parenthesizing every operation, relying on standard rules.
4. **Parse Tree Construction:** Precedence and associativity guide the compiler's parser to build a unique, unambiguous syntax tree.

> [!NOTE]
> **3-Mark Distribution Tip:** KTU 2024 examiners allot 1 mark for each definition and 2 marks for the "why essential" elaboration. Use bullet points for clarity.

---

**Q2. [KTU University Exam - May 2024]**

**List the precedence of the following operators in C++ from highest to lowest: `*`, `++`, `&&`, `=`, `,`, `::`, `()`, `==`.**

**Model Answer:**

The operators, ordered from **highest to lowest** precedence, are:

1. `::` — Scope Resolution (Level 1)
2. `()` — Function Call (Level 2)
3. `++` — Pre/Post Increment (Levels 2 and 3, treating `++` as a single category)
4. `*` — Multiplication (Level 5)
5. `==` — Equality (Level 10)
6. `&&` — Logical AND (Level 14)
7. `=` — Assignment (Level 17)
8. `,` — Comma (Level 18)

**Order:** `::` > `()` > `++` > `*` > `==` > `&&` > `=` > `,`

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Mistake:** Students often place `++` and `*` in the wrong order, forgetting that `++` (as a unary operator at Level 3) binds tighter than the binary `*` (at Level 5). Also, the comma `,` is the **lowest** — this surprises many students.

---

### 5.2 Part B: Full 14-Mark Questions (ESE Module Internal Choice)

---

### **Question A (14 Marks)**

**Q3(A). [KTU University Exam - Dec 2024 Model Paper]**

**(a)** With the help of a complete C++ operator precedence table, explain the concept of precedence and associativity. Identify the precedence and associativity of at least 8 operators from the table. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** Evaluate the following C++ expressions step-by-step, showing parenthesization due to precedence: **(7 marks)**

   (i) `8 + 12 / 4 * 2 - 5 % 3`
   (ii) `(4 > 2) && (3 != 5) || (6 <= 6) == 1`

**Model Answer for (a):**

**Concept of Precedence:**
Operator precedence in C++ is a compile-time rule that assigns each operator a priority level. Operators with **higher precedence** bind to their operands **first**, before operators with lower precedence. This is essential because complex expressions often contain multiple operators; without precedence rules, the compiler could not determine the order of operations.

**Concept of Associativity:**
When an expression contains two or more operators of the **same precedence**, associativity determines the **direction of binding**. There are two types:
- **Left-to-Right (L→R):** Left operator is applied first.
- **Right-to-Left (R→L):** Right operator is applied first.

**Identification of 8 Operators (Table excerpt):**

| Operator | Symbol | Precedence Level | Associativity |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Scope Resolution | `::` | 1 | L→R |
| Function Call | `()` | 2 | L→R |
| Pre-Increment | `++` | 3 | R→L |
| Multiplication | `*` | 5 | L→R |
| Modulus | `%` | 5 | L→R |
| Addition | `+` | 6 | L→R |
| Equality | `==` | 10 | L→R |
| Logical AND | `&&` | 14 | L→R |
| Assignment | `=` | 17 | R→L |
| Comma | `,` | 18 | L→R |

**Model Answer for (b)(i):**

**Expression:** `8 + 12 / 4 * 2 - 5 % 3`

**Step 1:** Identify operators and their levels:
- `/`, `*`, `%` are all at **Level 5** (highest among those present).
- `+`, `-` are at **Level 6**.

**Step 2:** Apply Level 5 first (left-to-right associativity for equal precedence):
$$
8 + (12 \div 4) \times 2 - (5 \% 3)
$$

**Step 3:** Compute each sub-expression:
$$
12 \div 4 = 3
$$

$$
5 \% 3 = 2
$$

**Step 4:** Substitute:
$$
8 + 3 \times 2 - 2
$$

**Step 5:** Continue Level 5 (multiplication remaining):
$$
8 + (3 \times 2) - 2 = 8 + 6 - 2
$$

**Step 6:** Apply Level 6 (left-to-right):
$$
8 + 6 = 14
$$

$$
14 - 2 = 12
$$

**Final Answer (i):** **12**

**Model Answer for (b)(ii):**

**Expression:** `(4 > 2) && (3 != 5) || (6 <= 6) == 1`

**Step 1:** Note that parentheses are explicitly given, so the expressions inside are evaluated first.

**Step 2:** Evaluate innermost relational and equality operators (Levels 9 and 10):
- `4 > 2` → true → `1`
- `3 != 5` → true → `1`
- `6 <= 6` → true → `1`

**Step 3:** Substitute:
$$
1 \ \&\&\ 1 \ \vert\vert\ 1 == 1
$$

**Step 4:** Apply Level 10 (`==` is higher than `&&` and `||`):
$$
1 \ \&\&\ 1 \ \vert\vert\ (1 == 1)
$$

**Step 5:** Evaluate equality:
$$
1 == 1 \implies 1
$$

**Step 6:** Substitute:
$$
1 \ \&\&\ 1 \ \vert\vert\ 1
$$

**Step 7:** Apply Level 14 (`&&` higher than `||`):
$$
(1 \ \&\&\ 1) \ \vert\vert\ 1
$$

**Step 8:** Evaluate `&&`:
$$
1 \ \&\&\ 1 = 1
$$

**Step 9:** Apply Level 15 (`||`):
$$
1 \ \vert\vert\ 1 = 1
$$

**Final Answer (ii):** **1 (true)**

---

### **Question B (14 Marks) — Alternative Choice**

**Q3(B). [KTU University Exam - May 2024]**

**(a)** Differentiate between operator precedence and order of evaluation. Why is the comma operator given the lowest precedence in C++? Justify with an example. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** Without using a compiler, predict and justify the output of the following C++ code snippet: **(7 marks)**

```cpp
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;
int main() {
    int a = 5, b = 10, c = 15;
    int result = a++ + ++b * c-- - --a + b;
    cout << "a = " << a << ", b = " << b << ", c = " << c;
    cout << ", result = " << result;
    return 0;
}
```

**Model Answer for (a):**

**Difference between Precedence and Order of Evaluation:**

| Aspect | Operator Precedence | Order of Evaluation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Decides** | Which operator binds first | Which operand is computed first |
| **Time** | Compile time | Run time |
| **Property** | Syntactic (grammar-driven) | Semantic (implementation-defined for some cases) |
| **Example** | In `a + b * c`, `*` binds first | In `f() + g()`, the order of `f()` and `g()` calls is unspecified in C++17 |

**Why Comma Has the Lowest Precedence:**

The comma operator `,` is intentionally assigned the **lowest precedence** (Level 18) in C++ so that it can be used as a **separator** in contexts like:
- `for` loop headers: `for (int i = 0, j = 10; i < j; i++, j--)`
- Function argument lists: `printf("%d %d", a, b);`
- Variable declarations: `int a, b, c;`

If comma had high precedence, the `for` loop header would be parsed incorrectly. For example, the comma in `i++, j--` must evaluate both increment expressions sequentially, but if comma had higher precedence than `<` or `;`, the parse tree would be malformed.

**Justification Example:**

```cpp
int x = (1, 2, 3);   // x becomes 3 (last value wins)
int y = 1, 2, 3;     // Error: comma treated as separator, not operator
```

The second line shows the **separator** usage (legal declaration), while the first shows the **operator** usage (parenthesized to force operator behavior).

**Model Answer for (b):**

**Initial values:** `a = 5`, `b = 10`, `c = 15`

**Expression:** `a++ + ++b * c-- - --a + b`

**Step 1 — Identify all operators and precedence levels:**

| Operator | Precedence | Associativity |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| `++` (postfix, `a++`, `c--`) | 2 | L→R |
| `++` (prefix, `++b`), `--` (prefix, `--a`) | 3 | R→L |
| `*` | 5 | L→R |
| `+`, `-` | 6 | L→R |

**Step 2 — Apply prefix unary operators (Level 3) first:**

- `++b` → `b` becomes `11`, value used is `11`.
- `--a` → `a` becomes `4` (after first being used as `a++` below), value used is `4`.

**Step 3 — Apply postfix operators (Level 2):**

- `a++` → value used is `5`, then `a` becomes `6`.
- `c--` → value used is `15`, then `c` becomes `14`.

**Step 4 — Substitute the values into the expression:**

The expression is now (using **values from the snapshot** at each position):

$$
5 + 11 \times 15 - 4 + 11
$$

**Step 5 — Apply Level 5 (multiplication):**

$$
5 + 165 - 4 + 11
$$

**Step 6 — Apply Level 6 (additive, left-to-right):**

$$
5 + 165 = 170
$$

$$
170 - 4 = 166
$$

$$
166 + 11 = 177
$$

**Step 7 — Determine final values of variables after all side effects:**

- `a`: was `5`, `a++` made it `6`, then `--a` made it `5`. **Final `a = 5`**
- `b`: was `10`, `++b` made it `11`. **Final `b = 11`**
- `c`: was `15`, `c--` made it `14`. **Final `c = 14`**
- `result = 177`

**Predicted Output:**

```
a = 5, b = 11, c = 14, result = 177
```

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Pitfall Warning:** This question is a **classic 14-mark trap** designed to test whether students understand the **order of side effects**. The most common error is to assume `a` becomes `4` before `a++` uses it (wrong), or to forget that `c--` returns `15` but decrements `c` to `14` for the final print. **Marks are lost for not tracking each variable's value carefully across all three side-effect operators.**

---

### 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **High-Density Rapid Revision Checklist (Read this 5 minutes before the exam):**

- [x] **Precedence** decides *which* operator binds first; **Associativity** decides the *direction* when levels are equal.
- [x] C++ has **17 to 18 distinct precedence levels** (depending on whether `<=>` is counted, introduced in C++20).
- [x] **Highest precedence:** `::` (Scope Resolution). **Lowest precedence:** `,` (Comma).
- [x] **Arithmetic** (`*`, `/`, `%`, `+`, `-`) binds tighter than **Relational** (`<`, `>`, `==`), which binds tighter than **Logical** (`&&`, `||`).
- [x] **Assignment** is **right-associative** — `a = b = 5` means `a = (b = 5)`.
- [x] **Unary operators** (`-`, `++`, `!`, `&`) are Level 3 and bind **tighter** than binary arithmetic.
- [x] The expression `-x * y` evaluates as `(-x) * y`, **not** `-(x * y)`.
- [x] **Order of evaluation** of operands (e.g., in `f() + g()`) is **unspecified** in C++ — precedence does not dictate this.
- [x] When in doubt, **use parentheses**. KTU 2024 examiners reward explicit clarity.
- [x] The **ternary operator** `? :` is **right-associative** — `a ? b : c ? d : e` parses as `a ? b : (c ? d : e)`.
- [x] **Short-circuit evaluation:** `&&` and `||` do **not** evaluate the right operand if the left operand determines the result.
- [x] **Comma operator** (lowest precedence) returns the value of its rightmost operand: `(1, 2, 3)` evaluates to `3`.
- [x] **Post-increment** (`a++`) returns the old value then increments; **Pre-increment** (`++a`) increments first then returns the new value.
- [x] The `^` symbol in C++ is **bitwise XOR**, **not exponentiation** (mathematical `$x^y$`).
- [x] The `<<` operator is **left-shift** in arithmetic contexts but **insertion** (overloaded) in `cout` contexts — a famous duality in OOP using C++.

---

**End of Module 1 — Operator Precedence Notes**

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.title: Control Statements: Selection Statements, Iteration Statements, and Jump Statements
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PBCST304 - OBJECT ORIENTED PROGRAMMING
> - **Module:** Module Module 1
> - **Topic:** Control Statements - Selection Statements, Iteration Statements and Jump Statements

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Control Statements** are programming language constructs used to alter the sequential flow of execution of a program. They govern the order in which individual statements, instructions, or function calls are executed, enabling **decision-making**, **repetition**, and **unconditional branching** within a program.

In the context of **Object Oriented Programming (OOP)** using Java (the standard KTU 2024 reference language for PBCST304), control statements are broadly classified into three categories as per the KTU 2024 Scheme syllabus for Module 1:

1. **Selection Statements (Decision-Making Statements):** `if`, `if-else`, `nested if`, `if-else-if ladder`, `switch-case`, and the **ternary operator (`? :`)**.
2. **Iteration Statements (Looping Statements):** `while`, `do-while`, `for`, and the **enhanced for-each loop** (introduced in Java 5).
3. **Jump Statements (Branching Statements):** `break`, `continue`, `return`, and (in C/C++) `goto`. Java deliberately omits `goto` as a structured programming best practice.

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU Syllabus Highlight:** The Module 1 outcomes (CO1: Apply Object Oriented Programming concepts) require students to write programs demonstrating **decision making using selection statements** and **iteration using looping constructs**. Jump statements are essential for early termination and skipping iterations.

---

### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Intuition (Plain English for Freshers)

Imagine you are **driving a car from Kochi to Trivandrum on NH-66**:

- **Selection Statement** = A **road intersection with signboards**. At each junction, the driver (the program) checks a condition: *“Is the signboard pointing to Trivandrum?”* If **YES**, take the right road. If **NO**, keep going straight. This is the essence of `if-else`.

- **Iteration Statement** = A **repeating round trip on a circular metro line**. The metro keeps circling the same loop **while** the number of trips is not complete. The passenger boards → travels → alights → boards again. This is the essence of a `for` or `while` loop.

- **Jump Statement** = An **emergency exit in a metro station**. If there is a fire (a special condition), passengers `break` out of the loop immediately (emergency exit). If a passenger simply wants to **skip one station** (perhaps a closed station), they `continue` to the next iteration without exiting the loop.

> [!TIP]
> **Key Takeaway:** Without control statements, a program would execute **linearly from top to bottom** with no intelligence. Control statements are what make a program "smart" and capable of solving real-world problems involving **logic, repetition, and exception handling**.

---

### 1.3 Key Engineering Metrics & Standards

| Metric | Standard Value / Convention | KTU Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Default Fall-Through in `switch`** | Required explicit `break` in each case (C/C++/Java pre-14) | Tested frequently in 3-mark questions |
| **Java 14+ `switch` Expression** | Arrow syntax `case X -> ...` (no fall-through) | Mentioned as advanced update |
| **Infinite Loop Safe Iterations** | Loops must have a **terminating condition** | Common exam pitfall |
| **Enhanced For-Loop** | Iterates over arrays/collections only (read-only) | KTU Module 1 specific |
| **`goto` in Java** | Reserved word but **not implemented** | Conceptual question favorite |

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 Detailed Breakdown of Control Statement Categories

#### 2.1.1 Selection Statements (Decision-Making Constructs)

**A. The `if` Statement (Single-Selection)**
- Tests a single boolean condition.
- Executes a block **only if** the condition evaluates to `true`.
- **Syntax:**
  ```java
  if (condition) {
      // statement(s) executed when condition is TRUE
  }
  ```

**B. The `if-else` Statement (Double-Selection)**
- Provides an **alternate path** when the condition is `false`.
- **Syntax:**
  ```java
  if (condition) {
      // TRUE block
  } else {
      // FALSE block
  }
  ```

**C. The `if-else-if` Ladder (Multi-Selection)**
- Used when there are **multiple mutually exclusive conditions** to be tested in sequence.
- The first condition that evaluates to `true` has its block executed; the rest are skipped.
- A trailing `else` is optional and acts as a **default catch-all**.

**D. The `switch-case` Statement (Multi-Way Branching)**
- Tests a single variable/expression against a list of **discrete constant values**.
- Highly efficient replacement for long `if-else-if` ladders.
- Supports `byte`, `short`, `char`, `int`, **wrapper classes** (Java 5+), **Strings** (Java 7+), and **enums**.
- **Critical Rule:** Every `case` **must end with a `break`** (or `return`/`throw`) to prevent **fall-through**, unless intentional.

**E. The Ternary Operator (`? :`)**
- Compact single-line replacement for simple `if-else`.
- **Syntax:** `result = (condition) ? value_if_true : value_if_false;`
- **KTU Warning:** Excessive nesting of ternaries reduces readability and is discouraged.

---

#### 2.1.2 Iteration Statements (Looping Constructs)

**A. The `while` Loop (Entry-Controlled)**
- Condition is checked **before** entering the loop body.
- If the condition is initially `false`, the loop body **never executes** (zero or more iterations).
- Best for **indefinite iteration** where the number of repetitions is unknown in advance.

**B. The `do-while` Loop (Exit-Controlled)**
- Loop body executes **at least once** before the condition is checked.
- The terminating semicolon after `while(condition);` is **mandatory**.
- Best for **menu-driven programs** where at least one iteration is guaranteed.

**C. The `for` Loop (Counter-Controlled)**
- The most compact loop, integrating **initialization, condition, and update** in one line.
- **Syntax:** `for (initialization; condition; update) { // body }`
- Best for **definite iteration** with a known count.

**D. The Enhanced `for-each` Loop (Java 5+)**
- Introduced specifically for **iterating over arrays and collections**.
- **Syntax:** `for (Type variable : arrayOrCollection) { // body }`
- **Limitation:** The loop variable is **read-only**; it cannot be used to modify the original array elements, nor can it be used to traverse in reverse order.

---

#### 2.1.3 Jump Statements (Branching Constructs)

**A. `break` Statement**
- **Two uses:** (1) Terminates a `switch` case. (2) Terminates the **innermost enclosing loop** (`for`, `while`, `do-while`) prematurely.
- **Labeled `break` (Java):** Used to break out of a **nested outer loop** by referring to a label.

**B. `continue` Statement**
- Skips the **remaining statements** of the current iteration and proceeds to the **next iteration** of the loop.
- Does **not** terminate the loop entirely (unlike `break`).
- **Labeled `continue`:** Skips to the next iteration of a **labeled outer loop**.

**C. `return` Statement**
- Exits from the **current method**, optionally returning a value to the caller.
- Two forms: `return;` (for `void` methods) and `return value;` (for value-returning methods).

**D. `goto` Statement**
- A reserved keyword in Java but **not implemented** (a deliberate design choice to enforce structured programming).
- In C/C++, `goto` performs unconditional jump to a labeled statement; its use is strongly discouraged.

---

### 2.2 KTU High-Yield Formula / Syntax Sheet

> [!NOTE]
> The following table is your **rapid-revision cheat sheet** for KTU university exam questions on control statements. All syntax is in **Java** (KTU 2024 default).

| Construct | Syntax Template | Loop Type | Termination Condition | Fall-Through? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `if` | `if (cond) { ... }` | N/A (Selection) | N/A | N/A |
| `if-else` | `if (cond) { ... } else { ... }` | N/A (Selection) | N/A | N/A |
| `if-else-if` | `if (c1) {...} else if (c2) {...} else {...}` | N/A (Selection) | N/A | N/A |
| `switch` | `switch(expr) { case v1: ...; break; ... }` | N/A (Selection) | `break` or `default` | Yes, if no `break` |
| `while` | `while (cond) { ... }` | Entry-controlled | When `cond == false` | No |
| `do-while` | `do { ... } while (cond);` | Exit-controlled | When `cond == false` | No |
| `for` | `for (init; cond; update) { ... }` | Entry-controlled | When `cond == false` | No |
| `for-each` | `for (T x : arr) { ... }` | Entry-controlled | End of array | No |
| `break` | `break;` or `break label;` | N/A (Jump) | Exits loop/switch | N/A |
| `continue` | `continue;` or `continue label;` | N/A (Jump) | Skips to next iteration | N/A |
| `return` | `return;` or `return value;` | N/A (Jump) | Exits method | N/A |

---

### 2.3 Real-World Engineering Applications

- **Selection Statements:** ATM cash withdrawal logic (`if balance >= amount`), password validation (`if-else`), compiler opcode dispatch (`switch` in JVM).
- **Iteration Statements:** Sensor data sampling loops in IoT devices (`while sensor_active`), array traversal for image processing (`for-each`), packet retransmission in networking (`do-while`).
- **Jump Statements:** Early loop termination on error detection (`break`), skipping noisy sensor readings (`continue`), returning computed results from a function (`return`).
<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations, Analytical Matrix & Trace Tables

> [!IMPORTANT]
> This section provides **exhaustive dry-run trace tables** (a KTU examiner favorite) for every control statement type. Each table walks through a complete sample program with explicit line-by-line execution.

### 3.1 Analytical Trace Matrix: `if-else-if` Ladder

**Sample Problem:** Write a Java program to assign a **grade** based on marks using the `if-else-if` ladder.

```java
int marks = 78;
char grade;
if (marks >= 90)      grade = 'A';
else if (marks >= 80) grade = 'B';
else if (marks >= 70) grade = 'C';
else if (marks >= 60) grade = 'D';
else                  grade = 'F';
System.out.println("Grade = " + grade);
```

**Step-by-Step Dry Run Trace Table:**

| Step | Statement | Condition Evaluated | Result | Action Taken | Variable `grade` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `int marks = 78;` | — | — | Declaration | `undefined` |
| 2 | `if (marks >= 90)` | `78 >= 90` | `false` | Skip, go to next `else if` | `undefined` |
| 3 | `else if (marks >= 80)` | `78 >= 80` | `false` | Skip, go to next `else if` | `undefined` |
| 4 | `else if (marks >= 70)` | `78 >= 70` | **TRUE** | Execute: `grade = 'C';` | `'C'` |
| 5 | All remaining `else if` | — | — | **Skipped** (ladder exits at first TRUE) | `'C'` |
| 6 | `System.out.println(...)` | — | — | Prints `Grade = C` | `'C'` |

**Key Insight:** Only the block corresponding to the **first TRUE** condition executes. All subsequent `else if` blocks are bypassed.

---

### 3.2 Analytical Trace Matrix: `switch-case`

**Sample Problem:** Print the **weekday name** for a given number (1-7) using `switch`.

```java
int day = 4;
String name;
switch (day) {
    case 1: name = "Monday";    break;
    case 2: name = "Tuesday";   break;
    case 3: name = "Wednesday"; break;
    case 4: name = "Thursday";  break;
    case 5: name = "Friday";    break;
    case 6: name = "Saturday";  break;
    case 7: name = "Sunday";    break;
    default: name = "Invalid";
}
System.out.println(name);
```

**Step-by-Step Dry Run Trace Table:**

| Step | Action | Variable `name` | Output So Far |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Declare `day = 4` | — | — |
| 2 | Enter `switch(4)` | — | — |
| 3 | Compare with `case 1` (4==1) → FALSE | — | — |
| 4 | Compare with `case 2` (4==2) → FALSE | — | — |
| 5 | Compare with `case 3` (4==3) → FALSE | — | — |
| 6 | Compare with `case 4` (4==4) → **MATCH** | — | — |
| 7 | Execute: `name = "Thursday";` | `"Thursday"` | — |
| 8 | Execute: `break;` | `"Thursday"` | (Exits switch) |
| 9 | `System.out.println(name);` | `"Thursday"` | `Thursday` |

**Demonstration of Fall-Through (WITHOUT `break`):**
If `break` were missing after `case 4:`, execution would **fall through** and also execute `case 5`, `case 6`, `case 7`, and `default` — printing `ThursdayFridaySundayInvalid`.

---

### 3.3 Analytical Trace Matrix: `for` Loop

**Sample Problem:** Compute the **sum of the first N natural numbers** using a `for` loop.

```java
int N = 5, sum = 0;
for (int i = 1; i <= N; i++) {
    sum = sum + i;
}
System.out.println("Sum = " + sum);
```

**Complete Iteration Trace Table:**

| Iteration | Init `i=1` | Condition `i<=5` | Update `i++` | `sum` Before | `sum + i` | `sum` After |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | i=1 | 1≤5 → TRUE | i becomes 2 | 0 | 0+1 | **1** |
| 2 | — | 2≤5 → TRUE | i becomes 3 | 1 | 1+2 | **3** |
| 3 | — | 3≤5 → TRUE | i becomes 4 | 3 | 3+3 | **6** |
| 4 | — | 4≤5 → TRUE | i becomes 5 | 6 | 6+4 | **10** |
| 5 | — | 5≤5 → TRUE | i becomes 6 | 10 | 10+5 | **15** |
| 6 | — | 6≤5 → FALSE | (loop exits) | 15 | — | **15** |

**Output:** `Sum = 15`

**Mathematical Verification (Analytical Derivation):**

The sum of first N natural numbers is given by the well-known arithmetic series formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_N &= \sum_{i=1}^{N} i \\
&= 1 + 2 + 3 + \dots + N \\
&= \frac{N \cdot (N + 1)}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

For N = 5, this yields:

$$
S_5 = \frac{5 \cdot (5 + 1)}{2} = \frac{5 \cdot 6}{2} = \frac{30}{2} = 15
$$

The program output `15` **matches** the formula — confirming correctness.

---

### 3.4 Analytical Trace Matrix: `while` vs `do-while`

**Sample Program A (while):**
```java
int x = 10;
while (x < 5) {
    System.out.println(x);
    x++;
}
```

**Sample Program B (do-while):**
```java
int x = 10;
do {
    System.out.println(x);
    x++;
} while (x < 5);
```

**Comparative Trace Table:**

| Step | Program A (`while`) | Program B (`do-while`) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `x = 10` | `x = 10` |
| 2 | Check `10 < 5` → **FALSE** | Enter body, print `10`, `x=11` |
| 3 | Loop body **never executes** | Check `11 < 5` → **FALSE** |
| 4 | Output: *(nothing printed)* | Output: `10` |

**Conclusion:** `do-while` guarantees **at least one execution**, while `while` may execute **zero times**. This is the most frequently tested conceptual difference in KTU exams.

---

### 3.5 Analytical Trace Matrix: `break` and `continue` in a Loop

**Sample Program:**
```java
for (int i = 1; i <= 6; i++) {
    if (i == 4) break;
    if (i % 2 == 0) continue;
    System.out.print(i + " ");
}
```

**Step-by-Step Trace:**

| Iteration | `i` | `i == 4`? | `i % 2 == 0`? | Action | Output |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | No | No | Print `1` | `1` |
| 2 | 2 | No | Yes | `continue` → skip print | (skipped) |
| 3 | 3 | No | No | Print `3` | `1 3` |
| 4 | 4 | **Yes** | — | `break` → **exit loop** | (loop terminated) |

**Final Output:** `1 3`

> [!NOTE]
> **Why this matters in KTU exams:** This single program tests understanding of **all three** control categories — `for` (iteration), `if` (selection), and `break`/`continue` (jump). It is a classic 7-mark sub-question pattern.

---

### 3.6 Analytical Trace Matrix: Enhanced `for-each` Loop

**Sample Program:**
```java
int[] arr = {10, 20, 30};
int sum = 0;
for (int val : arr) {
    sum += val;
}
System.out.println("Sum = " + sum);
```

**Step-by-Step Trace:**

| Iteration | `val` (current element) | `sum` Before | `sum` After |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10 | 0 | 10 |
| 2 | 20 | 10 | 30 |
| 3 | 30 | 30 | 60 |

**Output:** `Sum = 60`

**Key Constraint:** `val` is a **local copy** of the array element. Modifying `val` does **not** modify `arr`. The enhanced for-loop is **read-only by design**.

## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

---

**Q1.** `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023, Model QP]`

**Differentiate between `while` and `do-while` loops in Java. Give one example for each.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

| Feature | `while` loop | `do-while` loop |
|---|---|---|
| Type | Entry-controlled loop | Exit-controlled loop |
| Condition Check | Tested **before** body execution | Tested **after** body execution |
| Minimum Executions | **Zero** (body may never execute) | **One** (body executes at least once) |
| Semicolon | Not required after `while(cond)` | **Mandatory** after `while(cond);` |
| Syntax | `while (cond) { body }` | `do { body } while (cond);` |

**Example — `while`:** Prints nothing if initial condition is FALSE.
```java
int i = 10;
while (i < 5) {
    System.out.println(i);
    i++;
}
// Output: (nothing printed)
```

**Example — `do-while`:** Prints `10` even though condition is FALSE.
```java
int i = 10;
do {
    System.out.println(i);
    i++;
} while (i < 5);
// Output: 10
```

---

**Q2.** `[KTU University Exam - June 2024, Model QP]`

**Explain the concept of `fall-through` in a `switch` statement. How can it be prevented?**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

**Fall-through** is the phenomenon in which, after executing a matching `case` block, the program **does not exit the switch** and continues executing all subsequent `case` blocks (including `default`) **regardless of whether their values match**.

**Cause:** Occurs when a `case` block **does not end with a `break` statement** (or `return`/`throw`).

**Prevention Methods:**
1. Add a **`break;`** statement at the end of every `case` block — this is the standard practice.
2. Use the **`return` statement** instead of `break` if the value must be returned from a method.
3. In **Java 14+**, use the **arrow syntax** `case X -> ...` which inherently does not fall through.
4. Group multiple labels for a single block (Java 14+): `case 1, 2, 3 -> System.out.println("Q1");`

**Illustration of fall-through (input day = 2, missing break after case 2):**
```
case 2: System.out.println("Tuesday");
case 3: System.out.println("Wednesday");   // executes unintentionally
default: System.out.println("Invalid");   // also executes
```
**Output for `day=2`:** `Tuesday Wednesday Invalid`

---

### 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks with Internal Choice)

---

### **Question A (14 Marks)** `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023, Model QP]`

**(a) [7 Marks]** Write a Java program to read an integer `N` from the user and print whether it is a **prime number** or not. Use a `for` loop with a `break` statement for early termination.

**(b) [7 Marks]** Explain the differences among the three iteration statements — `while`, `do-while`, and `for` — using a comparative table and one example program for each.

---

#### **Solution for Q-A (a) — Prime Number Check [7 marks]**

```java
import java.util.Scanner;
public class PrimeCheck {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);
        System.out.print("Enter a positive integer: ");
        int n = sc.nextInt();
        boolean isPrime = true;

        // Edge cases: 0, 1, and negative numbers are NOT prime
        if (n <= 1) {
            isPrime = false;
        } else {
            // Check divisibility from 2 to sqrt(n)
            for (int i = 2; i * i <= n; i++) {
                if (n % i == 0) {
                    isPrime = false;
                    break;   // Early termination - divisor found
                }
            }
        }

        if (isPrime)
            System.out.println(n + " is a PRIME number.");
        else
            System.out.println(n + " is NOT a prime number.");

        sc.close();
    }
}
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation (for valuation):**
- [1 mark] Import `Scanner` and read input `n`.
- [1 mark] Handle edge case `n <= 1` as non-prime.
- [1 mark] Use `for` loop from 2 to `sqrt(n)` (efficient optimization).
- [1 mark] Apply `break` to exit the loop once a divisor is found.
- [1 mark] Use boolean flag `isPrime` to track result.
- [1 mark] Print appropriate message.
- [1 mark] Proper indentation, class structure, and `sc.close()`.

**Trace Example for n = 17:**
| i | i*i <= 17 | n % i | isPrime | Action |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 4 ≤ 17 → TRUE | 17%2 = 1 | TRUE | Continue |
| 3 | 9 ≤ 17 → TRUE | 17%3 = 2 | TRUE | Continue |
| 4 | 16 ≤ 17 → TRUE | 17%4 = 1 | TRUE | Continue |
| 5 | 25 ≤ 17 → FALSE | — | TRUE | **Loop ends** |

**Output:** `17 is a PRIME number.`

---

#### **Solution for Q-A (b) — Iteration Comparison [7 marks]**

| Feature | `while` loop | `do-while` loop | `for` loop |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Control Type** | Entry-controlled | Exit-controlled | Entry-controlled |
| **Initialization** | Outside loop | Outside loop | Inside loop header |
| **Condition Check** | Before body | After body | Before body |
| **Update Statement** | Inside body | Inside body | Inside loop header |
| **Min. Executions** | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| **Use Case** | Unknown iterations | Menu-driven (≥1 run) | Known counter |
| **Syntax** | `while(c){...}` | `do{...}while(c);` | `for(i;c;u){...}` |

**Example 1 — `while` (Sum until sentinel):**
```java
int sum = 0, num = 1;
while (num != 0) {
    sum += num;
    num = new Scanner(System.in).nextInt();
}
```

**Example 2 — `do-while` (Menu):**
```java
int choice;
do {
    System.out.println("1. Add  2. Exit");
    choice = sc.nextInt();
} while (choice != 2);
```

**Example 3 — `for` (Factorial):**
```java
int fact = 1;
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    fact *= i;
}
System.out.println("5! = " + fact);  // Output: 5! = 120
```

---

### **Question B (14 Marks)** `[KTU University Exam - June 2024, Model QP]`

**(a) [7 Marks]** Write a Java program using a `switch` statement to design a **simple calculator** that takes two numbers and an operator (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`) as input and displays the result. Handle the case of **division by zero** using `if`.

**(b) [7 Marks]** Explain the enhanced `for-each` loop in Java with its **syntax, advantages, and limitations**. Provide one example program demonstrating its use.

---

#### **Solution for Q-B (a) — Simple Calculator [7 marks]**

```java
import java.util.Scanner;
public class Calculator {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);
        System.out.print("Enter first number: ");
        double a = sc.nextDouble();
        System.out.print("Enter operator (+, -, *, /, %): ");
        char op = sc.next().charAt(0);
        System.out.print("Enter second number: ");
        double b = sc.nextDouble();
        double result = 0;
        boolean valid = true;

        switch (op) {
            case '+': result = a + b; break;
            case '-': result = a - b; break;
            case '*': result = a * b; break;
            case '/':
                if (b != 0) result = a / b;
                else {
                    System.out.println("Error: Division by zero!");
                    valid = false;
                }
                break;
            case '%':
                if (b != 0) result = a % b;
                else {
                    System.out.println("Error: Modulus by zero!");
                    valid = false;
                }
                break;
            default:
                System.out.println("Invalid operator!");
                valid = false;
        }

        if (valid)
            System.out.println("Result: " + a + " " + op + " " + b + " = " + result);

        sc.close();
    }
}
```

**Trace Example: a=10, op=`/`, b=2** → `Result: 10.0 / 2.0 = 5.0`
**Trace Example: a=10, op=`/`, b=0** → `Error: Division by zero!`

**Valuation Breakdown:**
- [1 mark] Variable declarations and input reading.
- [1 mark] Correct `switch` with all 5 cases.
- [1 mark] `break` statement in each case.
- [1 mark] Division-by-zero handling using `if`.
- [1 mark] `default` case for invalid operator.
- [1 mark] Correct output formatting.
- [1 mark] Code structure and `sc.close()`.

---

#### **Solution for Q-B (b) — Enhanced For-Each Loop [7 marks]**

**Definition:** The enhanced `for` loop (also called the **for-each** loop), introduced in **Java 5 (JDK 1.5)**, provides a **simplified syntax** to iterate over arrays and collections (e.g., `ArrayList`, `HashSet`).

**Syntax:**
```java
for (Type variableName : arrayOrCollection) {
    // body using variableName
}
```

**Example Program:**
```java
public class ForEachDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] marks = {85, 90, 78, 92, 88};
        int total = 0;

        // Using enhanced for-each loop
        for (int m : marks) {
            total += m;
        }

        double average = (double) total / marks.length;
        System.out.println("Total = " + total);
        System.out.println("Average = " + average);
    }
}
```

**Output:**
```
Total = 433
Average = 86.6
```

**Advantages (3 marks):**
1. **Concise syntax** — eliminates the need for explicit index management.
2. **No risk of `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`** — bounds are automatically handled.
3. **Readability** — intent is clear: "do something for each element".
4. Works uniformly for both **arrays** and **any object implementing `Iterable`**.

**Limitations (3 marks):**
1. **Read-only iteration** — the loop variable is a **local copy**; modifying it does NOT modify the original array.
2. **No index access** — cannot retrieve the current position/index of the element.
3. **Forward-only traversal** — cannot iterate in reverse.
4. **Cannot skip elements easily** — requires complex `if` conditions, defeating the simplicity.
5. **Not applicable to all data structures** — only works with arrays and `Iterable` collections.

---

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls:**
> 1. **Missing `break` in `switch`:** Forgetting `break` in even ONE case results in **partial marks loss (1-2 marks)**. Examiners specifically scan for this.
> 2. **Semicolon after `while` in `do-while`:** Writing `} while (cond)` instead of `} while (cond);` is a **syntax error** that costs the full 7 marks in a program question.
> 3. **Confusing `break` with `continue`:** Saying "`break` skips to the next iteration" is a **factual error** (2-3 marks deducted in theory).
> 4. **Modifying array in for-each:** Writing `for (int x : arr) x = 0;` and claiming it zeroes the array is a **conceptual error**.
> 5. **Missing `default` in `switch`:** Not handling unmatched values is considered **incomplete design** (1 mark deduction in 7-mark programs).
> 6. **Infinite loops in `while`:** Forgetting to update the loop variable inside the body results in **no output or runtime hang** — examiners deduct 2-3 marks for not catching this.

---

### 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid Revision Checklist)

> [!NOTE]
> **Last-minute revision before KTU University Exam — print or screenshot this section.**

- [x] Control statements alter the **default top-to-bottom sequential flow** of a program.
- [x] **Three categories:** Selection, Iteration, Jump — tested independently and combined in 14-mark questions.
- [x] **`if`** tests one condition; **`if-else`** provides an alternate path; **`if-else-if`** ladder handles multiple mutually exclusive conditions.
- [x] **`switch`** works with `byte`, `short`, `char`, `int`, **wrapper types** (Java 5+), **String** (Java 7+), and **enum**.
- [x] **Fall-through in `switch`** happens when `break` is missing — preventable with `break`, `return`, or Java 14+ arrow syntax.
- [x] **`while`** = entry-controlled, may execute **zero** times.
- [x] **`do-while`** = exit-controlled, executes **at least once**. Semicolon after `while(cond);` is **mandatory**.
- [x] **`for`** integrates init, condition, update in one line — best for known counters.
- [x] **Enhanced `for-each`** is **read-only**, forward-only, no index — works on arrays and `Iterable` collections.
- [x] **`break`** terminates the **innermost loop/switch**; **`break label`** exits a labeled outer loop (Java specific).
- [x] **`continue`** skips remaining statements in the current iteration and proceeds to the next.
- [x] **`return`** exits the current method; can optionally return a value.
- [x] **`goto`** is a **reserved keyword in Java but not implemented** (deliberate design).
- [x] **Infinite loop rule:** Every loop must have a **reachable terminating condition** or a `break` statement.
- [x] **Practice writing trace tables** — they fetch full marks in dry-run questions (often 5-7 marks).
- [x] **KTU favourite combined program:** One program using `if-else` + `for` + `break`/`continue` (e.g., prime check, number search, pattern printing).

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->
