topics.title: Command Line Arguments
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** PBCST304 - OBJECT ORIENTED PROGRAMMING > - **Module:** Module 1 > - **Topic:** Command Line Arguments ## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview ### 1.1 Formal Academic Definition In Java, **Command Line Arguments** are the **String values supplied to a program at the time of execution** from the operating system shell (e.g., `cmd.exe`, `bash`, `PowerShell`). They are received by the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) and delivered to the program through the parameter of the entry-point method: ```java public static void main(String[] args) ``` The parameter `args` is a one-dimensional **String array** that holds every argument typed after the class name on the command line. The JVM automatically populates this array *before* the first line of the program executes, making the technique a form of **runtime parameterization** (a type of runtime configuration where the program's behaviour is altered without modifying or recompiling its source code). > [!NOTE] > **KTU Syllabus Highlight (Module 1, OOP):** Command line arguments are introduced as the simplest form of passing external data into a Java program. Mastering `args` and its related type-conversion utilities is a **frequently tested 3-mark and 14-mark concept** in the End Semester Examination (ESE). > [!IMPORTANT] > **Definitive Properties** (must be memorised verbatim for ESE): > 1. Command line arguments are **always received as `String` objects**, even if the user types a number. > 2. They are stored in the **`String[] args`** parameter of `main`. > 3. They are **space-separated** by default. Multi-word arguments must be enclosed in double quotes (`" "`). > 4. **Indexing starts at `0`**, just like any Java array. > 5. `args.length` returns the **total number of arguments** actually passed (which may be `0`). --- ### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Intuitive Overview > **Real-world Analogy — "The Restaurant Order Slip"** Imagine walking into a restaurant and handing the chef a written order slip **before** the chef begins cooking: | Real World | Java World | |------------|------------| | Restaurant kitchen | Your Java program | | Order slip handed in | Command line arguments typed in the terminal | | Items listed on the slip | Elements of `String[] args` (`args[0]`, `args[1]`, …) | | Number of items on the slip | `args.length` | | Chef starts cooking using the slip | `main` method begins executing with `args` pre-filled | | Chef converting "two tomatoes" into 2 actual tomatoes | Calling `Integer.parseInt(args[0])` to convert a String into an `int` | The order slip (command line) is the **only channel** through which external information reaches the chef (the program) *before* cooking starts. If the slip is empty (`args.length == 0`), the chef simply has no instructions and proceeds with the default behaviour. If the slip says `"abc"` when a number was expected, the chef cannot cook — analogous to a `NumberFormatException`. This analogy makes it immediately clear *why* command line arguments exist: to **feed external data into a program at startup**, without the user having to interact with the program *during* execution. --- ### 1.3 Why Command Line Arguments Matter in OOP > [!IMPORTANT] > Command line arguments are the **first practical exposure** students get to the concept that **a program's behaviour is driven by external data**, not hard-coded values. This idea is foundational to: > - **Object construction with parameters** (covered in later modules). > - The **Strategy and Factory design patterns**. > - Writing **reusable utility classes** (e.g., calculators, file processors). > - **Build automation** (Maven, Gradle, CI/CD pipelines pass arguments like `-Xmx512m` to the JVM). ## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ### 2.1 Operational Breakdown — How Command Line Arguments Travel The journey of a command line argument from the terminal to the program is a **six-stage pipeline**. Understanding each stage is critical for KTU ESE questions that ask "explain the flow" or "what happens when the command is executed". - **Step 1 — User Invocation:** The user types a command such as `java AddNumbers 25 30` in the shell. - **Step 2 — Shell Tokenisation:** The shell (or `java` launcher) splits the line on whitespace, producing a token list: `["java", "AddNumbers", "25", "30"]`. - **Step 3 — JVM Bootstrapping:** The `java` launcher starts the JVM and asks it to load the class `AddNumbers`. - **Step 4 — Argument Packaging:** The launcher packages every token *after* the class name into a fresh `String[]` — in our example: `["25", "30"]`. - **Step 5 — main() Invocation:** The JVM calls the `main` method, passing the array as the `args` parameter. - **Step 6 — Program Execution:** The body of `main` runs with `args[0] = "25"` and `args[1] = "30"`. > [!NOTE] > **Critical Insight:** Notice that even though the user typed the number `25`, Java stores it as the *string* `"25"` (two characters: `'2'` and `'5'`). This is why **explicit conversion is required** before any arithmetic operation. --- ### 2.2 Type-Conversion Utilities (Wrapper Class Methods) Because everything in `args` is a `String`, the programmer must call a **wrapper-class parse method** to obtain primitive types. These methods are part of Java's autoboxing-friendly API and are tested almost every semester in KTU exams. | Purpose | Method Signature | Wrapper Class | Example Call | Resulting Type | |---------|------------------|---------------|--------------|----------------| | String → `int` | `static int parseInt(String s)` | `Integer` | `Integer.parseInt("123")` | `int` | | String → `long` | `static long parseLong(String s)` | `Long` | `Long.parseLong("9999999999")` | `long` | | String → `double` | `static double parseDouble(String s)` | `Double` | `Double.parseDouble("3.14")` | `double` | | String → `float` | `static float parseFloat(String s)` | `Float` | `Float.parseFloat("2.5f")` | `float` | | String → `boolean` | `static boolean parseBoolean(String s)` | `Boolean` | `Boolean.parseBoolean("true")` | `boolean` | | String → `char` (at index i) | `charAt(int i)` on String | `String` (inherent) | `args[0].charAt(0)` | `char` | | Primitives → String | `String.valueOf(x)` | `String` | `String.valueOf(42)` | `String` | > [!IMPORTANT] > All `parseXxx` methods **throw `NumberFormatException`** (a checked subclass of `IllegalArgumentException`) if the supplied string is not a valid representation of the target type. For example, `Integer.parseInt("abc")` will crash the program unless handled. --- ### 2.3 KTU High-Yield Formula / Cheat-Sheet The following compact table is the **minimum recall set** required to answer any KTU question on command line arguments. Memorise the symbols, semantics, and edge cases. | Symbol / Construct | Meaning | Allowed Range / Edge Case | |--------------------|---------|---------------------------| | `String[] args` | The argument array delivered to `main` | May be empty (`args.length == 0`) | | `args.length` | Number of arguments actually typed | Returns `0` if no arguments are passed | | `args[i]` | The *i*-th argument as a `String` | Valid indices: `0` to `args.length - 1` | | `args[0]` | The **first** argument after the class name | Throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` if no argument was passed | | `args[args.length - 1]` | The **last** argument | Safe only when `args.length > 0` | | `Integer.parseInt(args[i])` | Converts `args[i]` to `int` | Throws `NumberFormatException` on invalid input | | `Double.parseDouble(args[i])` | Converts `args[i]` to `double` | Throws `NumberFormatException` on invalid input | | `Boolean.parseBoolean(args[i])` | Converts `args[i]` to `boolean` | Returns `true` only for `"true"` (case-insensitive); everything else → `false` | | Quoted multi-word argument | `"Hello World"` passed as one argument | Unquoted `Hello World` becomes **two** separate arguments | | Direct arithmetic on `args` | `args[0] + args[1]` | Performs **String concatenation**, NOT addition! `"10" + "20"` → `"1020"` | --- ### 2.4 Real-World Utility in Engineering & Software Industry Command line arguments are not an academic curiosity; they underpin the operation of virtually every production-grade tool an engineer will touch: - **Compilers and Build Tools:** `javac -d ./out MyClass.java` — the `-d` flag and its value are command line arguments. - **JVM Tuning:** `java -Xmx2g -Xms512m MyApp` — heap-size arguments critical for performance engineering. - **DevOps & CI/CD:** Docker, Kubernetes, and shell scripts pass container IDs, ports, and credentials as arguments. - **Data Engineering:** Apache Spark jobs: `spark-submit --master yarn --class org.apache.spark.examples.SparkPi /opt/spark/examples/jars/spark-examples.jar 1000` — the final `1000` (number of slices) is a command line argument consumed by `main(String[] args)`. - **Testing Frameworks:** JUnit can be invoked with `-Dtest=MyTest` system properties — a related but distinct mechanism. > [!NOTE] > **Engineering Takeaway:** Mastering `String[] args` early gives a student the conceptual foundation to later understand `ProcessBuilder`, `Runtime.exec`, and shell-script integration — all of which depend on the same argument-passing paradigm. ## 3. Step-by-Step Program Analysis & Analytical Matrix > This section is the **exhaustive analytical walkthrough** of three reference programs. Every line of input, every transition, and every output byte is explained. No step is skipped. --- ### 3.1 Reference Program A — Sum of Two Integers ```java // File: AddNumbers.java public class AddNumbers { public static void main(String[] args) { // STEP 1: Guard clause — verify argument count if (args.length != 2) { System.out.println("Usage: java AddNumbers "); return; } // STEP 2: Type conversion from String to int int num1 = Integer.parseInt(args[0]); int num2 = Integer.parseInt(args[1]); // STEP 3: Arithmetic operation (now safe — operands are int) int sum = num1 + num2; // STEP 4: Output System.out.println("First number = " + num1); System.out.println("Second number = " + num2); System.out.println("Sum = " + sum); } } ``` #### 3.1.1 Compilation Phase The source file is compiled with: ```bash javac AddNumbers.java ``` This produces a bytecode file `AddNumbers.class`. The compiler does **not** validate the use of `args`; it simply allows the program to be compiled as long as the syntax is legal. #### 3.1.2 Execution Phase — Successful Run The user types the following command at the terminal: ```bash java AddNumbers 25 30 ``` **Stage-by-stage execution table:** | Stage | What Happens | Internal State | |-------|--------------|----------------| | 1. Shell parsing | Shell tokenises the line on whitespace. | Token list: `["java", "AddNumbers", "25", "30"]` | | 2. JVM starts | `java` launcher boots JVM and requests the class `AddNumbers`. | Class loader searches for `AddNumbers.class` | | 3. Argument packaging | Tokens after class name packaged into `String[]`. | `args = new String[]{"25", "30"}` | | 4. main() invoked | JVM calls `main(args)`. | `args.length == 2`, `args[0] = "25"`, `args[1] = "30"` | | 5. Guard check | `args.length != 2` is `false`. | Program proceeds past the `if` block | | 6. parseInt(args[0]) | Converts the string `"25"` to integer `25`. | `num1 = 25` | | 7. parseInt(args[1]) | Converts the string `"30"` to integer `30`. | `num2 = 30` | | 8. Addition | `sum = 25 + 30`. | `sum = 55` | | 9. Output | Three `println` calls execute. | See output below | **Terminal Output:** ``` First number = 25 Second number = 30 Sum = 55 ``` #### 3.1.3 Failure Scenario A — Missing Arguments If the user types: ```bash java AddNumbers 25 ``` then `args.length == 1`, the guard clause fires, and the program prints: ``` Usage: java AddNumbers ``` and exits gracefully. This is the **recommended defensive-programming pattern** and is worth full marks in ESE. #### 3.1.4 Failure Scenario B — Non-Numeric Input If the user types: ```bash java AddNumbers ten 30 ``` then `args.length == 2` (guard passes), but `Integer.parseInt("ten")` throws `NumberFormatException` because the literal string `"ten"` is not a valid decimal integer. The JVM prints a stack trace and terminates the program. To prevent this, the conversion lines can be wrapped in a `try-catch` block — see Reference Program C below. > [!IMPORTANT] > **String Concatenation vs Addition Pitfall (KTU Favourite):** > If a student *forgets* to call `parseInt` and writes `int sum = args[0] + args[1];`, the code **will not compile** because the `+` operator is not defined between a `String` and an `int`. However, if a student writes `String result = args[0] + args[1];`, the result is the **concatenated string** `"2530"` — not the integer sum `55`. This is one of the most commonly tested traps in KTU exams. --- ### 3.2 Reference Program B — String Concatenation Without Conversion ```java public class Greet { public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length == 0) { System.out.println("Hello, Stranger!"); } else { System.out.println("Hello, " + args[0] + "!"); } } } ``` **Execution analysis:** | Command | `args` State | Output | |---------|--------------|--------| | `java Greet` | `args.length == 0` | `Hello, Stranger!` | | `java Greet Arun` | `args = ["Arun"]` | `Hello, Arun!` | | `java Greet "John Doe"` | `args = ["John Doe"]` | `Hello, John Doe!` | | `java Greet John Doe` | `args = ["John", "Doe"]` | `Hello, John!` *(only first name used)* | The last row is a **classic KTU trap**: without quotes, the shell splits `John Doe` into two arguments, and the program prints only `args[0]`. --- ### 3.3 Reference Program C — Safe Conversion with try-catch ```java public class SafeAdd { public static void main(String[] args) { try { int a = Integer.parseInt(args[0]); int b = Integer.parseInt(args[1]); System.out.println("Sum = " + (a + b)); } catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) { System.out.println("Error: Please provide two integers."); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { System.out.println("Error: Both arguments must be valid integers."); } } } ``` **Execution analysis matrix:** | Command | Exception Triggered | Output | |---------|--------------------|--------| | `java SafeAdd 5 7` | None | `Sum = 12` | | `java SafeAdd 5` | `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` at `args[1]` | `Error: Please provide two integers.` | | `java SafeAdd five 7` | `NumberFormatException` at `parseInt("five")` | `Error: Both arguments must be valid integers.` | | `java SafeAdd` | `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` at `args[0]` | `Error: Please provide two integers.` | > [!NOTE] > The use of multiple `catch` blocks is preferred over a single generic `catch (Exception e)` because it allows **distinct, user-friendly error messages** for distinct failure modes — a hallmark of professional-grade OOP design. --- ### 3.4 Analytical Summary Matrix — All Reference Programs | # | Program | `args` Length Check | Type Conversion | Exception Handling | Use Case Demonstrated | |---|---------|----------------------|------------------|--------------------|------------------------| | A | `AddNumbers` | `if (args.length != 2)` | `Integer.parseInt` | None (crash on bad input) | Basic addition with guard clause | | B | `Greet` | `if (args.length == 0)` | Not required (String output) | None | Default behaviour + first-name display | | C | `SafeAdd` | Implicit in `catch` | `Integer.parseInt` | `try-catch` with two catches | Production-grade defensive programming | > [!IMPORTANT] > **Cross-Reference to KTU Course Outcomes (COs):** > - **CO1:** *Apply the object-oriented programming concepts to design programs in Java.* — Reference Program A satisfies this. > - **CO2:** *Demonstrate the use of arrays, strings, and exception handling in Java.* — Reference Programs B and C satisfy this. ## 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics ### 4.1 End-to-End Command Line Argument Flow The diagram below traces a command line argument from the moment the user presses **Enter** in the terminal to the moment it appears as a `String` inside `main`. ```mermaid flowchart TD userInput[User Types Command in Terminal]:::stage shellToken[Shell Splits Command on Whitespace]:::stage jvmBoot[JVM Bootstraps and Loads Target Class]:::stage argPack[Java Launcher Builds String Array]:::stage mainCall[JVM Invokes main with args Parameter]:::stage guardChk[Program Checks args.length]:::stage typeConv[Program Converts Strings to Primitives]:::stage logicExec[Program Logic Executes on Typed Data]:::stage output[Result Printed to Standard Output]:::stage userInput --> shellToken shellToken --> jvmBoot jvmBoot --> argPack argPack --> mainCall mainCall --> guardChk guardChk -- Length OK --> typeConv guardChk -- Length Mismatch --> output typeConv --> logicExec logicExec --> output classDef stage fill:#E8F4FD,stroke:#1F77B4,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 ``` **Reading the diagram:** - The **left-side vertical chain** (`userInput` → `shellToken` → `jvmBoot` → `argPack` → `mainCall`) represents the **JVM's responsibility**. - The **right-side horizontal branch** (`guardChk` → `typeConv` → `logicExec` → `output`) represents the **programmer's responsibility**. - The **decision diamond** is implicit in the `guardChk` node, which has two outgoing edges: one for a length match, one for a mismatch. --- ### 4.2 Block-Level Functional Architecture of `main(String[] args)` This block diagram is a **functional decomposition** of what happens *inside* the `main` method once the JVM hands control to the program. Each block represents a logical phase that any robust command line program should implement. ```mermaid flowchart LR argsBlock[args Parameter
String Array]:::input guardBlock[Guard Clause
Validates args.length]:::validate parseBlock[Parse Block
Integer.parseInt et al]:::convert logicBlock[Business Logic Block
Arithmetic or String Ops]:::logic outputBlock[Output Block
System.out.println]:::output errBlock[Error Handler Block
try catch Blocks]:::error argsBlock --> guardBlock guardBlock -- Valid --> parseBlock guardBlock -- Invalid --> errBlock parseBlock -- Success --> logicBlock parseBlock -- Failure --> errBlock logicBlock --> outputBlock errBlock --> outputBlock classDef input fill:#D4EDDA,stroke:#28A745,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef validate fill:#FFF3CD,stroke:#FFC107,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef convert fill:#D1ECF1,stroke:#17A2B8,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef logic fill:#F8D7DA,stroke:#DC3545,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef output fill:#E2E3E5,stroke:#6C757D,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef error fill:#F5C6CB,stroke:#721C24,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 ``` **Reading the diagram:** - The **green input block** is the `args` array, an immutable handoff from the JVM. - The **yellow guard block** is the first programmer-written check; it protects against `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. - The **cyan parse block** performs type conversion; it can throw `NumberFormatException`. - The **red logic block** is where the *real work* of the program happens. - The **grey output block** and **dark-red error block** are the two terminal states — every well-written program ends in one of them. --- ### 4.3 Mermaid State Diagram — Program Lifecycle This diagram shows the *state* of the program with respect to command line arguments, including all valid transitions. ```mermaid stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> NoArgs NoArgs --> ArgsProvided : User supplies arguments NoArgs --> DefaultBehaviour : args.length is zero DefaultBehaviour --> [*] ArgsProvided --> LengthChecked : args.length evaluated LengthChecked --> ParseStage : Length matches expectation LengthChecked --> LengthMismatch : Length does not match LengthMismatch --> ErrorReported ErrorReported --> [*] ParseStage --> Converted : parse methods succeed ParseStage --> NumberFormatThrown : Invalid numeric input NumberFormatThrown --> ErrorReported Converted --> LogicExecuted LogicExecuted --> ResultPrinted ResultPrinted --> [*] ``` **Reading the diagram:** - The diagram has **two entry paths**: with arguments or without. - The **central spine** (`ArgsProvided` → `LengthChecked` → `ParseStage` → `Converted` → `LogicExecuted` → `ResultPrinted`) is the *happy path*. - The two error sinks (`LengthMismatch` and `NumberFormatThrown`) both converge on `ErrorReported`, which then terminates the program. ## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap > All questions below are modelled on the **KTU 2024 Scheme End Semester Examination (ESE)** pattern: Part A is 3 marks each, Part B is 14 marks each with internal choice (Or option). Marks are explicitly distributed across sub-parts. **Model answers are exhaustive** — written in the same detail expected from a top-scoring answer script. --- ### 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each) #### Question 1 `[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]` **Define command line arguments. How are they accessed in a Java program? What is the default data type of command line arguments?** **Model Answer (3 marks):** > Command line arguments are the values supplied to a Java program at the time of execution, typed after the class name in the terminal. They are accessed through the parameter `String[] args` of the `main` method, which the JVM automatically populates before program execution begins. > > **Data Type:** The default data type of every command line argument is **`java.lang.String`**. Even if the user types a numeric value such as `25`, it is stored in `args` as the string `"25"`, and any arithmetic operation requires explicit conversion using wrapper-class methods such as `Integer.parseInt()`. > > *(Distribution: 1 mark for definition, 1 mark for `String[] args`, 1 mark for `String` default type.)* --- #### Question 2 `[KTU University Exam – May 2024]` **What is the role of `args.length` in a Java program? What happens if `args.length` is `0`?** **Model Answer (3 marks):** > The field `args.length` is a **public final `int` instance variable** of the `args` array that returns the total number of arguments actually passed to the program at runtime. It is the **primary defensive check** a programmer uses to validate input before accessing individual elements. > > If `args.length` is `0`, it means **no command line arguments were supplied**. In this state, any attempt to read `args[0]` throws an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` at runtime. Programs that expect arguments should therefore include a guard clause: > > ```java > if (args.length == 0) { > System.out.println("Usage: java MyClass "); > return; > } > ``` > > *(Distribution: 1 mark for role of `args.length`, 1 mark for `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` explanation, 1 mark for guard-clause example.)* --- ### 5.2 Part B — Full-Descriptive Questions (14 Marks Each, Internal Choice) --- #### **Question A (14 Marks)** `[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]` **(a)** Write a Java program that accepts **three command line arguments** — a student's `name` (String), `rollNumber` (int), and `marks` (double) — and prints them in a formatted report card. Include a guard clause to handle missing or invalid input. **(7 marks)** **(b)** Explain the differences between the following pairs of concepts in the context of command line arguments: 1. `args[0]` vs `args.length` 2. `Integer.parseInt(args[0])` vs `Integer.valueOf(args[0])` 3. `args[0] + args[1]` (String) vs `Integer.parseInt(args[0]) + Integer.parseInt(args[1])` (int) **(7 marks)** --- ##### Model Solution for Q.A(a) — 7 Marks ```java public class ReportCard { public static void main(String[] args) { // Guard clause 1: argument count if (args.length != 3) { System.out.println("Usage: java ReportCard "); return; } try { // Type conversions String name = args[0]; int rollNo = Integer.parseInt(args[1]); double marks = Double.parseDouble(args[2]); // Guard clause 2: business validation if (marks < 0 || marks > 100) { System.out.println("Error: Marks must be between 0 and 100."); return; } // Formatted output System.out.println("================ REPORT CARD ================"); System.out.println("Name : " + name); System.out.println("Roll No. : " + rollNo); System.out.println("Marks : " + marks); System.out.println("============================================"); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { System.out.println("Error: rollNumber must be an integer and marks must be a number."); } } } ``` **Sample Run:** ```bash javac ReportCard.java java ReportCard Arun 42 89.5 ``` **Output:** ``` ================ REPORT CARD ================ Name : Arun Roll No. : 42 Marks : 89.5 ============================================ ``` **Mark Distribution for Q.A(a):** | Component | Marks | Justification | |-----------|-------|---------------| | Guard clause on `args.length` | 1 | Demonstrates defensive programming | | Correct use of `args[0]`, `args[1]`, `args[2]` | 1 | Indexing knowledge | | Type conversion using `parseInt` and `parseDouble` | 2 | Core command line concept | | Business validation of marks | 1 | Beyond-syllabus polish, rewarded | | Formatted output with `println` | 1 | Clean I/O | | `try-catch` for `NumberFormatException` | 1 | Exception handling (linked to CO2) | --- ##### Model Solution for Q.A(b) — 7 Marks **1. `args[0]` vs `args.length` (2 marks)** | Aspect | `args[0]` | `args.length` | |--------|------------|---------------| | What it represents | The **first** argument (a `String`) | The **count** of arguments (an `int`) | | Data type | `String` | `int` | | Behaviour when `args` is empty | Throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` | Returns `0` | | Use case | Reading a specific value | Validating the number of inputs | **2. `Integer.parseInt(args[0])` vs `Integer.valueOf(args[0])` (2 marks)** | Aspect | `Integer.parseInt(args[0])` | `Integer.valueOf(args[0])` | |--------|------------------------------|------------------------------| | Return type | Primitive `int` | Wrapper `Integer` object | | Autoboxing? | Not required (already primitive) | Result may be auto-unboxed to `int` | | Memory | Stack allocation (lighter) | Heap allocation (heavier) | | Preferred when | Arithmetic is needed | Object required (e.g., for `Collections`) | **3. `args[0] + args[1]` vs `Integer.parseInt(args[0]) + Integer.parseInt(args[1])` (3 marks)** | Aspect | `args[0] + args[1]` (both `String`) | After `parseInt` (both `int`) | |--------|---------------------------------------|---------------------------------| | Operator semantics | **String concatenation** | **Integer addition** | | Input `args` = `["10", "20"]` | Result: `"1020"` (the string) | Result: `30` (the integer) | | Type of result | `String` | `int` | | Exam trap | Frequently tested — students lose marks by assuming `+` means addition when `args` is involved. | The **only** correct way to perform arithmetic on command line inputs. | --- #### **Question B (14 Marks)** `[KTU University Exam – May 2024]` **(a)** Write a Java program that accepts **two integer command line arguments** and performs **all five basic arithmetic operations** — addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and modulus — on them. Handle the special case of division by zero. **(7 marks)** **(b)** Discuss the **limitations of command line arguments** in Java. Suggest two alternative mechanisms for passing input to a program, with one example each. **(7 marks)** --- ##### Model Solution for Q.B(a) — 7 Marks ```java public class ArithmeticOps { public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length != 2) { System.out.println("Usage: java ArithmeticOps "); return; } try { int a = Integer.parseInt(args[0]); int b = Integer.parseInt(args[1]); System.out.println("Addition : " + (a + b)); System.out.println("Subtraction : " + (a - b)); System.out.println("Multiplication : " + (a * b)); if (b == 0) { System.out.println("Division : Undefined (divide by zero)"); System.out.println("Modulus : Undefined (divide by zero)"); } else { System.out.println("Division : " + (a / b)); System.out.println("Modulus : " + (a % b)); } } catch (NumberFormatException e) { System.out.println("Error: Both arguments must be valid integers."); } } } ``` **Sample Run:** ```bash javac ArithmeticOps.java java ArithmeticOps 20 6 ``` **Output:** ``` Addition : 26 Subtraction : 14 Multiplication : 120 Division : 3 Modulus : 2 ``` **Mark Distribution for Q.B(a):** | Component | Marks | Justification | |-----------|-------|---------------| | Correct parsing with `Integer.parseInt` | 2 | Core concept | | All 5 operations implemented | 3 | 0.6 marks each | | Division-by-zero handling | 1 | Edge case | | `try-catch` for `NumberFormatException` | 1 | Exception handling | --- ##### Model Solution for Q.B(b) — 7 Marks **Limitations of Command Line Arguments (4 marks):** 1. **Limited Interactivity:** Once the program starts, no further input can be accepted from the command line. The arguments are frozen at startup. 2. **No Encryption or Hiding:** Arguments are visible in shell history (`history`), in process lists (`ps`), and in logs — making them unsuitable for **passwords, API keys, or sensitive data**. 3. **All-or-Nothing Input:** Either all required arguments must be passed at once, or the program must implement complex parsing. There is no support for interactive prompts. 4. **String-Only by Default:** Numeric data must be **explicitly converted**; failure to do so leads to silent bugs (e.g., concatenation instead of addition). 5. **Difficult for End-Users:** Casual users are uncomfortable with terminals; command line programs exclude the vast majority of non-technical users. 6. **No Validation in the Shell:** The shell does not check argument types or values; all validation must be coded manually in Java. **Alternative Mechanisms (3 marks):** | Alternative | Description | Example | |-------------|-------------|---------| | **Scanner Class** | Reads interactive input from the keyboard (`System.in`) at runtime. | `Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in); int n = sc.nextInt();` | | **BufferedReader** | Reads input line-by-line from the console; more flexible but slightly verbose. | `BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in));` | | **JOptionPane (Swing)** | Pops up a graphical dialog box to collect input. | `String name = JOptionPane.showInputDialog("Enter your name");` | | **GUI Forms (Swing/JavaFX)** | Full graphical user interface with text fields and buttons. | A login form that reads username and password. | | **Command Line Files / Properties** | Read from a configuration file or `.properties` file at startup. | `Properties prop = new Properties(); prop.load(new FileInputStream("config.properties"));` | --- ### 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout > [!WARNING] > **Where students LOSE marks on Command Line Argument questions — and how to AVOID it:** > > 1. **Forgetting the type conversion** — writing `int sum = args[0] + args[1];` will not even compile, but writing `String s = args[0] + args[1];` silently gives `"1020"`. **Always use `Integer.parseInt`.** > 2. **Skipping the `args.length` check** — accessing `args[0]` without verifying `args.length > 0` results in `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. The examiner will deduct **at least 1 mark** for not handling this. > 3. **Confusing `parseInt` and `valueOf`** — these are not the same. `parseInt` returns `int`, `valueOf` returns `Integer`. Read the question carefully. > 4. **Forgetting that command line arguments are space-separated** — `java MyClass John Doe` is two arguments, not one. Quote multi-word arguments. > 5. **Missing `try-catch` for `NumberFormatException`** — even if the question does not explicitly ask for exception handling, adding `try-catch` blocks earns **bonus marks** and demonstrates mastery of CO2. > 6. **Not including a `Usage` message** — a professional touch that is often expected in 14-mark answers and rewarded accordingly. > 7. **Hard-coding values inside `main`** — defeats the entire purpose of command line arguments. The examiner will look specifically for `args[i]` usage. --- ### 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember > **Rapid-Revision Checklist (Print this and read it the night before the exam):** - ☐ Command line arguments are passed to `main(String[] args)` automatically by the JVM. - ☐ They are **always `String`** — never `int`, `double`, etc., by default. - ☐ `args.length` tells you **how many** arguments were passed; check it **before** accessing any `args[i]`. - ☐ `args[0]` is the **first** argument, not `args[1]` — indexing starts at **`0`**. - ☐ Use `Integer.parseInt(args[i])`, `Double.parseDouble(args[i])`, `Boolean.parseBoolean(args[i])` for type conversion. - ☐ All parse methods throw **`NumberFormatException`** on invalid input; handle with `try-catch`. - ☐ Accessing a missing argument throws **`ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`**; handle with a guard clause. - ☐ The `+` operator on two `String` arguments performs **concatenation**, not addition — `"10" + "20" = "1020"`. - ☐ Multi-word arguments must be enclosed in **double quotes**: `java MyClass "John Doe"`. - ☐ A typical **defensive pattern** is: (1) check `args.length`, (2) parse with `try-catch`, (3) validate business rules, (4) execute logic, (5) print output. - ☐ The `String[] args` parameter can be renamed (e.g., `String[] argv`) — the name is conventional, not mandatory. - ☐ Command line arguments cannot be modified by the program — they are **read-only** at runtime. - ☐ Pass **sensitive data** via environment variables or config files, **never** as command line arguments. - ☐ Common exam traps: string concatenation, missing `args.length` check, confusion between `parseInt` and `valueOf`. - ☐ Always include a **Usage message** in production-grade answers — it is a free mark. - ☐ `main` is the **only** method the JVM calls automatically — `args` is the **only** mechanism the JVM uses to pass data into the program at startup.

topics.title: Variable Length Arguments
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PBCST304 - OBJECT ORIENTED PROGRAMMING
> - **Module:** Module 1
> - **Topic:** Variable Length Arguments

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### Formal Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology)

**Variable Length Arguments** (commonly called **Varargs**) is a Java language feature introduced in **JDK 5.0** that allows a method to accept **zero, one, or multiple arguments of a specified type** without having to overload the method for each possible argument count. It is implemented using the **ellipsis operator (`...`)** placed between the data type and the parameter name.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Definition**: *"A method that takes a variable number of arguments is known as a variable-arity method or simply varargs method. Internally, the compiler converts these arguments into a single-dimensional array of the specified type."*

**Formal Syntax:**
```java
returnType methodName(dataType ... parameterName) {
    // method body
}
```

**Generalized Form:**
```java
static void display(String message, int ... numbers) {
    // 'numbers' behaves as int[]
}
```

### Conceptual Analogy / Intuition

Imagine you walk into a **tea stall in Kerala** and ask the vendor: *"Give me some bananas."* You don't tell him **exactly how many** — you just stretch out your hand. The vendor gives you **one, two, or a bunch** depending on your grip. You never know the count in advance.

> Variable Length Arguments work the **same way**: you tell the method *"give me some values of type int"* by writing `int ... x`, and the Java runtime decides **how many** values were passed at the call site. The method is smart enough to handle **0, 1, 2, or 100** values using the **exact same signature**.

- If you pass **0 arguments** → the array is created with **length 0** (empty, not null).
- If you pass **N arguments** → the array is created with **length N**.
- If you pass **one argument** → a one-element array is created.

> [!NOTE]
> **Key Insight for Examiners**: A method declared with `...` is **not** a different method. It is internally a **method accepting an array** of that type. This means `method(int... x)` and `method(int[] x)` **cannot be overloaded together** — they have the same erased signature!

### Physical Constants / Standard Metrics (Highlighted)

| Metric | Value / Behavior |
|---|---|
| **Maximum varargs parameters per method** | **1 (One only)** |
| **Position of varargs** | **Last parameter (mandatory)** |
| **Minimum arguments to varargs** | **0 (zero arguments allowed)** |
| **Internal JVM representation** | **Single-dimensional array** |
| **Java Version introduced** | **JDK 5.0 (J2SE 5.0 / Tiger Release)** |
| **Autoboxing interaction** | Allowed but separate overloads preferred |

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### Internal Operational Mechanism — Step-by-Step Breakdown

When the Java compiler encounters a method signature containing `...`, it performs the following transformations:

**Step 1 — Source Level**
The programmer writes:
```java
void printNumbers(int ... nums) { ... }
```

**Step 2 — Compiler Transformation (Bytecode Level)**
The compiler converts the ellipsis `...` into a **single-dimensional array parameter**:
```java
void printNumbers(int[] nums) { ... }
```

**Step 3 — Call Site Transformation**
- If arguments are passed individually → compiler wraps them in an array.
- `printNumbers(1, 2, 3)` becomes `printNumbers(new int[]{1, 2, 3})`.
- `printNumbers()` becomes `printNumbers(new int[0])`.

**Step 4 — Runtime Behavior**
Inside the method body, the parameter can be used exactly like an array — accessed via index, used in `for-each` loops, passed to other methods, etc.

### KTU High-Yield Rules (Cheat Sheet)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> These rules are **favourite KTU 2024 question patterns**. Memorize verbatim.

| Rule # | Rule Statement | Why It Matters |
|---|---|---|
| **R1** | Only **ONE** varargs parameter is allowed per method | Two `...` would create ambiguity |
| **R2** | The varargs parameter **MUST be the last parameter** | Otherwise the compiler cannot determine where varargs ends |
| **R3** | You **CAN** mix varargs with normal parameters | `void show(String s, int... x)` is legal |
| **R4** | You **CAN** overload methods using varargs | Resolution depends on argument count and type |
| **R5** | You **CANNOT** overload `m(int... x)` and `m(int[] x)` together | Both erase to the same array signature |
| **R6** | `m(int... x)` and `m(int... x, int y)` are **NOT valid** together | Varargs must always be last |
| **R7** | Calling `m(int... x)` with **zero arguments** is legal | Compiler creates an empty array |

### Method Resolution Priority (Compiler Phase)

When a method call is made and multiple overloaded methods match, the compiler applies this **strict 5-step priority order** (extremely high yield for KTU 2024!):

| Priority | Match Type | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **1 (Highest)** | **Exact match** (primitive/widening) | `m(int)` called with `m(10)` |
| **2** | **Autoboxing / Unboxing** | `m(Integer)` called with `m(10)` |
| **3** | **Varargs match** | `m(int... x)` called with `m(10, 20)` |
| **4** | **Varargs with autoboxing** | `m(Integer... x)` called with `m(10)` |
| **5 (Lowest)** | **Most specific varargs** | Resolved by compiler analysis |

### Real-World Engineering Utility

- **Logging frameworks** (like `Log4j`, `SLF4J`) use varargs to accept any number of message arguments.
- **String formatting** methods (e.g., `String.format`) internally use varargs.
- **Mathematical utilities** like `Math.max` were enhanced in Java to support variable arguments.
- **GUI event handlers** where callback counts cannot be predicted in advance.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### Worked Example 1: Basic Varargs Declaration and Invocation

**Problem:** Demonstrate a method that accepts a variable number of integer arguments and prints their sum.

**Step 1 — Declaration (source code):**
```java
class VarargsDemo {
    static int sum(int ... numbers) {
        int total = 0;
        for (int n : numbers) {
            total += n;
        }
        return total;
    }
}
```

**Step 2 — Compiler interpretation:**
$$
\text{int ... numbers} \;\xrightarrow{\text{compiler}}\; \text{int[] numbers}
$$

The compiler rewrites the method as:
```java
static int sum(int[] numbers) { ... }
```

**Step 3 — Different call sites resolved by the compiler:**

| Call Statement | Compiler-Generated Internal Form | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `sum()` | `sum(new int[0])` | Returns **0** |
| `sum(10)` | `sum(new int[]{10})` | Returns **10** |
| `sum(10, 20)` | `sum(new int[]{10, 20})` | Returns **30** |
| `sum(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)` | `sum(new int[]{1, 2, 3, 4, 5})` | Returns **15** |

**Step 4 — Inside the method, `numbers` behaves as an array:**
$$
\text{numbers.length} = N, \quad \text{numbers}[0], \text{numbers}[1], \ldots, \text{numbers}[N-1]
$$

### Worked Example 2: Varargs Mixed with Normal Parameters

**Problem:** Write a method that accepts a `String` label followed by any number of `double` values.

**Step 1 — Source Code:**
```java
class Report {
    static void printReport(String title, double ... values) {
        System.out.println("Title: " + title);
        for (double v : values) {
            System.out.println("  Value: " + v);
        }
    }
}
```

**Step 2 — Invocation verification:**
- `printReport("Sales", 100.5)` → valid: `title="Sales"`, `values=[100.5]`
- `printReport("Sales", 100.5, 200.75, 300.0)` → valid: array of 3 doubles
- `printReport("Sales")` → valid: `values` becomes an **empty array** (length 0)
- `printReport(100.5, "Sales")` → **COMPILE ERROR** (varargs must be last)

**Step 3 — Mathematical proof of compliance with Rule R2:**

$$
\text{Parameter Order} = \underbrace{String \; title}_{\text{fixed}} \; \to \; \underbrace{double \ldots \; values}_{\text{varargs, last}}
$$

The general order must be:
$$
\text{fixed}_1, \; \text{fixed}_2, \; \ldots, \; \text{fixed}_n, \; \text{varargs}
$$

Any deviation:
$$
\text{fixed}_1, \; \text{varargs}, \; \text{fixed}_2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \textbf{COMPILE-TIME ERROR}
$$

### Worked Example 3: Method Resolution Priority (KTU Favourite)

**Problem:** Predict the output of the following program.

```java
class Test {
    static void show(int a) { System.out.println("int"); }
    static void show(int ... a) { System.out.println("varargs"); }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        show(10);
        show(10, 20);
        show();
    }
}
```

**Step-by-step resolution (apply the priority table from Section 2):**

| Call | Available Matches | Resolution Path | Selected Method | Output |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `show(10)` | `show(int)`, `show(int...)` | Priority 1: exact match | `show(int)` | **`int`** |
| `show(10, 20)` | `show(int)` (1 arg), `show(int...)` | Only varargs accepts 2 args | `show(int...)` | **`varargs`** |
| `show()` | `show(int)` (needs 1 arg), `show(int...)` | Only varargs accepts 0 args | `show(int...)` | **`varargs`** |

**Final Output:**
$$
\boxed{\text{int} \quad \text{varargs} \quad \text{varargs}}
$$

### Worked Example 4: Ambiguity Error (Compile-Time Pitfall)

**Problem:** Why does the following program cause a compile error?

```java
class Ambiguous {
    static void test(int ... a) { System.out.println("int varargs"); }
    static void test(long ... a) { System.out.println("long varargs"); }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        test(10);  // Which one is called?
    }
}
```

**Step-by-step analysis:**

**Step 1 — Identify the call:** `test(10)` passes an `int` literal.

**Step 2 — Check `test(int ... a)`:**
- Priority 1: `int` is **already** an `int` → **exact match**.

**Step 3 — Check `test(long ... a)`:**
- Priority 1: `int` widens to `long` → **wider primitive match**.

**Step 4 — Apply priority rules:**
- Both reach Priority 1 / 2 (no autoboxing needed since `int`/`long` are primitives).
- No single method is **more specific** than the other.

**Step 5 — Compiler conclusion:**
$$
\text{Both methods equally applicable} \;\Rightarrow\; \textbf{Reference to test is ambiguous}
$$

$$
\boxed{\text{COMPILE-TIME ERROR: reference to test is ambiguous}}
$$

### Analytical Summary Matrix

| Concept | Behavior | KTU Question Likelihood |
|---|---|---|
| Empty varargs call | Legal, creates array of length 0 | ★★★★★ |
| Varargs as last parameter | Mandatory rule | ★★★★★ |
| One varargs per method | Mandatory rule | ★★★★ |
| Mixing varargs with normal args | Legal | ★★★★ |
| Overloading `m(int...x)` and `m(int[]x)` | **Compile error** (duplicate) | ★★★★★ |
| Priority over autoboxing | Varargs is **lower** priority | ★★★★★ |
| Cannot pass `int[]` and primitives mixed | `m(1, new int[]{2,3})` is **illegal** | ★★★★ |

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
## 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

### Diagram A: Compiler Transformation Pipeline (Varargs Internals)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Source Code with int dot dot dot x] --> B[Java Compiler javac]
    B --> C[Bytecode int array x]
    C --> D[JVM Loads Method]
    D --> E{Call Site Analysis}
    E -->|Zero args| F[Create int array length 0]
    E -->|N args| G[Create int array length N]
    F --> H[Execute Method Body]
    G --> H
    H --> I[Return Result]
```

### Diagram B: Method Resolution Priority Flow (KTU High-Yield)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start[Method Call Encountered] --> Q1{Is there an exact type match?}
    Q1 -->|Yes| P1[Select Exact Match Method]
    Q1 -->|No| Q2{Is there an autoboxing or unboxing match?}
    Q2 -->|Yes| P2[Select Boxing Match]
    Q2 -->|No| Q3{Is there a varargs match?}
    Q3 -->|Yes| P3[Select Varargs Method]
    Q3 -->|No| Q4{Is there a varargs with boxing match?}
    Q4 -->|Yes| P4[Select Boxing Varargs Method]
    Q4 -->|No| Err[COMPILE TIME ERROR No Method Found]
```

### Diagram C: Parameter Ordering Rules (Block Architecture)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Legal["LEGAL METHOD SIGNATURES"]
        L1[m int dot dot dot x]
        L2[m String s int dot dot dot x]
        L3[m String s int n int dot dot dot x]
    end
    subgraph Illegal["ILLEGAL METHOD SIGNATURES"]
        I1[m int dot dot dot x int y]
        I2[m int dot dot dot x String s]
        I3[m int dot dot dot x int dot dot dot y]
    end
```

### Diagram D: Varargs Call Site Wrapping Logic

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Call[User Writes m of 1 comma 2 comma 3] --> Wrap[Compiler Wraps in Array]
    Wrap --> New1[New int array of 1 comma 2 comma 3]
    Call2[User Writes m of empty] --> Wrap2[Compiler Wraps in Empty Array]
    Wrap2 --> New2[New int array of length 0]
    Call3[User Writes m of int array of 1 comma 2] --> Direct[Pass Array Directly]
```

### Diagram E: Overloading with Varargs — Resolution Tree

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Root[Method Call show of args] --> A{Number of Arguments}
    A -->|0 args| V[Select show int dot dot dot]
    A -->|1 arg| T{Type of Argument}
    T -->|int| E[Select show int Exact Match Wins]
    T -->|long| W[Select show long via Widening]
    A -->|2 or more args| V2[Only show int dot dot dot matches]
```

<!-- SECTION_4_END -->

<!-- SECTION_5_START -->
## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

---

**Q1. [KTU University Exam – May 2024, Model]**
*Define Variable Length Arguments in Java. Write its syntax and state any two rules that must be followed while using varargs.*

**Model Answer:**

**Definition:**
Variable Length Arguments (varargs) is a feature in Java, introduced in JDK 5.0, that allows a method to accept zero or more arguments of the same type. Internally, the compiler treats the varargs parameter as a single-dimensional array.

**Syntax:**
```java
returnType methodName(dataType ... parameterName)
```

**Two Rules:**
1. A method can have **only one** varargs parameter.
2. The varargs parameter must be the **last parameter** in the method signature.
3. (Bonus) Zero or more arguments can be passed to a varargs parameter.

---

**Q2. [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023, Model]**
*What happens internally when a varargs method is called with zero arguments? Explain briefly.*

**Model Answer:**

When a varargs method is called with **zero arguments**, the Java compiler internally creates an **empty array of length 0** (not `null`) and passes it to the method.

**Example:**
```java
void display(int ... x) { System.out.println(x.length); }
display();   // Output: 0
display(5);  // Output: 1
```

The array is initialized with `new int[0]`, so any iteration (`for-each` loop) over `x` simply executes zero times without throwing a `NullPointerException`.

---

### Part B Questions (14 Marks Each — Internal Choice)

---

### **Question A (14 Marks)** — [KTU University Exam – Dec 2024, Model]

**(a)** Explain the concept of Variable Length Arguments in Java with a suitable example. List any **four rules** that must be followed when declaring a varargs method. **(7 Marks)**

**(b)** Consider the following Java program. Predict the output with proper justification for each `printf` call. **(7 Marks)**

```java
class Demo {
    static void test(int x) {
        System.out.println("test(int): " + x);
    }
    static void test(int ... x) {
        System.out.println("test(int...): length=" + x.length);
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        test();
        test(5);
        test(10, 20);
        test(new int[]{1, 2, 3});
    }
}
```

**Model Solution for (a):**

Variable Length Arguments allow a method to accept a variable number of arguments of the same type. It uses the ellipsis `...` operator.

**Example:**
```java
static int total(int ... marks) {
    int sum = 0;
    for (int m : marks) sum += m;
    return sum;
}
```

**Four Rules:**
1. Only **one** varargs parameter is allowed per method.
2. Varargs must be the **last** parameter in the method signature.
3. Zero or more arguments can be passed.
4. Varargs is internally treated as an **array**; hence `m(int...x)` and `m(int[]x)` cannot be overloaded together.

**Model Solution for (b):**

| Call Statement | Argument Count | Resolution | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| `test()` | 0 | Only `test(int...)` matches | `test(int...): length=0` |
| `test(5)` | 1 | `test(int)` is exact match (Priority 1) | `test(int): 5` |
| `test(10, 20)` | 2 | Only `test(int...)` matches | `test(int...): length=2` |
| `test(new int[]{1,2,3})` | Array passed | Compiler treats as `test(int[])` → matches `test(int...)` | `test(int...): length=3` |

**Final Output:**
```
test(int...): length=0
test(int): 5
test(int...): length=2
test(int...): length=3
```

**Justification:** The compiler always prefers an **exact match with fixed parameters** over a varargs match. Hence, when a single `int` argument is provided, `test(int)` wins.

---

### **Question B (14 Marks)** — [KTU University Exam – May 2023, Model]

**(a)** Explain the **method resolution priority** used by the Java compiler when varargs methods are overloaded with other methods. Illustrate with an example. **(7 Marks)**

**(b)** Write a Java program that accepts a course code and a variable number of student marks. Compute and display the **average, highest, and lowest** mark using varargs. Handle the case where **no marks** are passed. **(7 Marks)**

**Model Solution for (a):**

The Java compiler resolves overloaded methods using this strict priority order:

**Priority 1 (Highest):** Exact type match (no widening, no boxing).
**Priority 2:** Widening primitive conversion (`int` → `long`).
**Priority 3:** Autoboxing / Unboxing (`int` ↔ `Integer`).
**Priority 4:** Varargs match.
**Priority 5 (Lowest):** Varargs with autoboxing.

**Illustration:**
```java
class Resolve {
    static void show(int x)         { System.out.println("int"); }
    static void show(Integer x)     { System.out.println("Integer"); }
    static void show(int ... x)     { System.out.println("varargs"); }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        show(10);        // Output: int   (Priority 1)
        show(10L);       // Output: varargs (long → no exact match, varargs widens)
    }
}
```

**Model Solution for (b):**

```java
import java.util.Scanner;

class MarksAnalyzer {
    static void analyze(String courseCode, int ... marks) {
        System.out.println("Course: " + courseCode);
        if (marks.length == 0) {
            System.out.println("No marks provided. Exiting.");
            return;
        }
        int sum = 0, highest = marks[0], lowest = marks[0];
        for (int m : marks) {
            sum += m;
            if (m > highest) highest = m;
            if (m < lowest)  lowest  = m;
        }
        double average = (double) sum / marks.length;
        System.out.println("Average: " + average);
        System.out.println("Highest: " + highest);
        System.out.println("Lowest : " + lowest);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        analyze("PBCST304", 85, 90, 78, 92, 88);
        analyze("PBCST304");
    }
}
```

**Sample Output:**
```
Course: PBCST304
Average: 86.6
Highest: 92
Lowest : 78
Course: PBCST304
No marks provided. Exiting.
```

---

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls**
>
> 1. **Forgetting the "last parameter" rule:** Many students write `void m(int... x, String s)` and lose **2 full marks** in Part B. Always check parameter ordering first.
> 2. **Confusing varargs with method overloading:** Writing both `m(int... x)` and `m(int[] x)` will cause a **duplicate method error**. The compiler treats them as the same method.
> 3. **Assuming `null` for zero arguments:** Zero arguments create an **empty array (`new int[0]`)**, **NOT** `null`. Iterating over it is safe.
> 4. **Incorrect priority reasoning:** Students often claim varargs has the **highest** priority. The correct order is: **exact match → boxing → varargs**.
> 5. **Mixing array and individual arguments in the call site:** `m(1, new int[]{2,3})` is **illegal** because the compiler cannot decide where the varargs list ends.
> 6. **Forgetting to import `Scanner` or use proper I/O in Part B code questions** — KTU deducts marks for non-compilable code.

---

### Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

- ✅ Varargs was introduced in **Java 5.0** (J2SE 5.0).
- ✅ Syntax uses the **ellipsis (`...`)** operator between type and parameter name.
- ✅ Internally, the compiler converts varargs to a **single-dimensional array**.
- ✅ Only **ONE** varargs parameter is permitted per method.
- ✅ Varargs parameter **must be the last** parameter in the signature.
- ✅ **Zero arguments are legal** — creates an empty array of length `0`.
- ✅ Varargs and autoboxing/unboxing are **independent overload-resolution phases**.
- ✅ Priority order: **Exact Match → Widening → Boxing/Unboxing → Varargs → Varargs with Boxing**.
- ✅ Cannot overload `m(int...x)` and `m(int[]x)` together — same erased signature.
- ✅ Cannot mix varargs with array arguments in a single call (e.g., `m(1, new int[]{2,3})` is illegal).
- ✅ `m(int...x)` and `m(int...x, int y)` together are **invalid** — varargs must be last.
- ✅ Varargs is heavily used in **logging frameworks, printf, format strings, and assertion mechanisms**.

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

# 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology)

> [!NOTE]
> **CLASS (Object-Oriented Programming Definition):**
> A **class** is a user-defined, composite, reference data type in C++ that serves as a **blueprint**, **template**, or **prototype** for creating objects. It encapsulates **data members** (attributes/state) and **member functions** (methods/behaviour) into a single, cohesive logical unit, supporting the OOP pillars of **Encapsulation** and **Data Abstraction**.

Mathematically, a class $C$ can be represented as a set of attributes and operations:

$$C = \{A, M, V\}$$

Where:
- $A$ = Set of attributes (data members) $\rightarrow A = \{a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots, a_n\}$
- $M$ = Set of member functions (methods) $\rightarrow M = \{m_1, m_2, m_3, \dots, m_n\}$
- $V$ = Set of visibility/access specifiers $\rightarrow V = \{public, private, protected\}$

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Syllabus Highlight:** A class is **declaration only** — no memory is allocated for data members until an **object (instance)** of that class is created. This is a frequently asked concept in KTU examinations.

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Real-World Intuition

Imagine you are an **architect**:

| Real-World Entity | OOP Counterpart | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Architectural Blueprint | **Class** | Defines structure but is not a building itself |
| Actual Building constructed | **Object** | A real, tangible instance occupying space |
| Rooms, doors, windows | **Data Members** | Properties describing the structure |
| "Open door", "Switch on light" | **Member Functions** | Behaviours/actions the structure can perform |
| Locked vs Open doors | **Access Specifiers** | Control over who/what can access parts |

> [!TIP]
> **Plain English Explanation:** A class is like a *recipe for biriyani*. The recipe (class) lists ingredients and steps, but it is not food. Only when you actually cook using that recipe do you get a *dish* (object) that occupies your plate (memory).

## 1.3 Core Characteristics of a Class

1. **User-defined type** — Programmer creates it (unlike `int`, `float`).
2. **Reference type in C++** — Objects are accessed via references/pointers (unlike structures in C, which are value types by default).
3. **Encapsulation unit** — Bundles data + functions together.
4. **Abstraction enabler** — Hides internal complexity using `private`/`protected`.
5. **Access control granularity** — Three visibility levels: `public`, `private`, `protected`.
6. **No memory on declaration** — Memory is allocated only when an object is instantiated.

## 1.4 Standard Metrics & Boundaries

| Property | Standard Value / Boundary |
|---|---|
| Default access in `class` | **private** |
| Default access in `struct` | **public** |
| Minimum members to form a class | **Zero (empty class is valid, size = 1 byte)** |
| Maximum access specifiers per class | **No hard limit (KTU perspective)** |
| Keyword to define | `class` (C++), `public class` (Java) |

---

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Anatomical Structure of a C++ Class — Operational Breakdown

A class declaration in C++ follows a strict, layered structure. Let us dissect each layer:

### Layer 1 — Class Header
```cpp
class ClassName {
```
This opens the class scope. The keyword `class` is mandatory in C++ (unlike `struct`, where it is optional).

### Layer 2 — Access Specifier Block
```cpp
private:    // visible only inside the class
protected:  // visible inside class + derived classes
public:     // visible everywhere
```

### Layer 3 — Data Members (State)
```cpp
int rollNo;       // attribute
float marks;      // attribute
char name[50];    // attribute
```

### Layer 4 — Member Functions (Behaviour)
```cpp
void setData(int r);   // mutator
int getRollNo();       // accessor
```

### Layer 5 — Scope Resolution Closure
```cpp
};
```

## 2.2 The Three Pillars Encoded in a Class

| Pillar | Class Mechanism | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Encapsulation** | Binding data + functions into one unit (`class`) | Reduces system complexity |
| **Abstraction** | `private`/`protected` hiding implementation | Protects internal state |
| **Modularity** | One class = one logical entity | Improves maintainability |

## 2.3 Access Specifier Decision Matrix

| Access Specifier | Accessible Within Class | Accessible in Derived Class | Accessible Outside Class | Typical Use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `private` | **Yes** | **No** | **No** | Internal data, helper functions |
| `protected` | **Yes** | **Yes** | **No** | Data meant for inheritance |
| `public` | **Yes** | **Yes** | **Yes** | Interface (functions exposed to user) |

## 2.4 Defining Member Functions — Two Methods

### Method 1: Inside the Class (Implicitly Inline)
```cpp
class Student {
    public:
        void display() {   // Inline by default
            cout << "Hello";
        }
};
```

### Method 2: Outside the Class (Using Scope Resolution Operator `::`)
```cpp
class Student {
    public:
        void display();    // Declaration only
};

void Student::display() {  // Definition outside
    cout << "Hello";
}
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU High-Yield Point:** The scope resolution operator `::` tells the compiler that the function `display()` belongs to the class `Student`. Without `Student::`, it becomes a regular global function — a very common mistake leading to *compilation errors* in board exams.

## 2.5 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| # | Concept | Formula / Rule | Application |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Size of empty class | $Size = 1 \text{ byte}$ | To ensure unique address per object |
| 2 | Size with members | $Size = \sum(\text{sizeof each member}) + \text{padding}$ | Memory estimation |
| 3 | Object memory | $Memory(obj) = Size(class)$ | Each object gets independent copy |
| 4 | Static member | Shared across **all** objects (one copy only) | Class-level data |
| 5 | Access default (`class`) | **private** | Without explicit specifier |
| 6 | Access default (`struct`) | **public** | C-compatibility reason |
| 7 | Number of objects possible | $N = \frac{\text{Available Heap Memory}}{Size(Class)}$ | Theoretical limit |
| 8 | Function binding | Early binding (static) by default; `virtual` enables late binding | Polymorphism support |

## 2.6 Real-World Engineering Utility of Classes

| Engineering Domain | Class Use-Case |
|---|---|
| **Embedded Systems** | Class for `Sensor` with `read()`, `calibrate()` methods |
| **Database Systems** | Class for `Connection`, `Query`, `Transaction` |
| **Game Development** | Classes for `Player`, `Enemy`, `Weapon`, `Level` |
| **Automotive (ECU)** | Classes for `EngineControlUnit`, `BrakeSystem` |
| **Networking** | Classes for `Packet`, `Router`, `Socket` |
| **Compiler Design** | Classes for `Token`, `SymbolTable`, `ASTNode` |

---

# 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Derivation: Memory Footprint of a Class Object

Let us rigorously derive how much memory an object occupies given a class definition.

### Step 1 — Class Definition
```cpp
class Box {
    int length;     // 4 bytes
    int width;      // 4 bytes
    int height;     // 4 bytes
};
```

### Step 2 — Sum of Primitive Member Sizes
$$Size_{raw} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \text{sizeof}(member_i)$$

### Step 3 — Substitute Values
$$\begin{aligned}
Size_{raw} &= \text{sizeof}(length) + \text{sizeof}(width) + \text{sizeof}(height) \\
&= 4 + 4 + 4 \\
&= 12 \text{ bytes}
\end{aligned}$$

### Step 4 — Apply Alignment Padding Rule
The compiler aligns members to the size of the largest primitive type. Since all are `int` (4 bytes), no extra padding is required.

$$Size_{object} = Size_{raw} + Padding = 12 + 0 = 12 \text{ bytes}$$

### Step 5 — Validation with Mixed Types
```cpp
class Mixed {
    char c;      // 1 byte
    int i;       // 4 bytes
    double d;    // 8 bytes
};
```

$$\begin{aligned}
Size_{raw} &= 1 + 4 + 8 = 13 \text{ bytes} \\
Largest &= 8 \text{ bytes (alignment boundary)} \\
Size_{aligned} &= 16 \text{ bytes (after padding)}
\end{aligned}$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Derivation Logic:** Raw sum gives 13 bytes. Alignment forces the total to be a multiple of 8 → next multiple ≥ 13 is 16. Hence, 3 bytes of padding are inserted.

## 3.2 Analytical Matrix — Class vs Object vs Structure

| Parameter | Class | Object | Structure |
|---|---|---|---|
| What is it? | Blueprint / Template | Instance of class | C-style user-defined type |
| Memory allocated? | **No** (declaration only) | **Yes** (on instantiation) | **Yes** (on declaration) |
| Default access | `private` | N/A | `public` |
| Can have functions? | **Yes** | Inherits from class | Only in C++ (not in C) |
| Reference type? | **Yes** (in C++) | Yes | No (value type in C) |
| Supports inheritance? | **Yes** | Inherits | Limited |
| Existence | Logical | Physical | Physical |

## 3.3 Derivation: Number of Member Functions Accessible

For a class with $p$ private functions, $q$ protected functions, and $r$ public functions:

$$Total_{functions} = p + q + r$$

Accessible from **outside** the class:
$$Accessible_{outside} = r$$

Accessible from a **derived class**:
$$Accessible_{derived} = q + r$$

Accessible from **within** the class:
$$Accessible_{inside} = p + q + r$$

### Worked Example
Suppose a class has $p = 3$ private, $q = 2$ protected, $r = 5$ public functions.

$$\begin{aligned}
Total &= 3 + 2 + 5 = 10 \\
From\ outside &= 5 \\
From\ derived &= 2 + 5 = 7 \\
From\ inside &= 3 + 2 + 5 = 10
\end{aligned}$$

## 3.4 Derivation: Static vs Non-Static Member Memory

Let $N$ be the number of objects and $S$ be the size of one non-static data member.

**Non-static members** (instance variables):
$$Memory_{non\text{-}static} = N \times S$$

**Static members** (class variables):
$$Memory_{static} = S \quad (\text{shared, only one copy})$$

**Total memory for N objects:**
$$\begin{aligned}
Memory_{total} &= Memory_{non\text{-}static} + Memory_{static} \\
&= N \times S_{non\text{-}static} + S_{static}
\end{aligned}$$

### Example
Class `Counter` has one non-static `int id` (4 bytes) and one static `int count` (4 bytes).

For $N = 100$ objects:
$$Memory_{total} = (100 \times 4) + 4 = 404 \text{ bytes}$$

## 3.5 Complete C++ Class Declaration — Annotated Model

```cpp
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

class Student {                  // Class declaration begins
private:                          // Access specifier 1
    int rollNo;                   // Data member 1
    float marks;                  // Data member 2

protected:                        // Access specifier 2
    char grade;                   // Data member 3 (inheritable)

public:                           // Access specifier 3
    Student();                    // Default constructor declaration
    void setData(int r, float m); // Mutator function declaration
    void display();               // Accessor function declaration
};

Student::Student() {              // Constructor definition
    rollNo = 0;
    marks = 0.0;
    grade = 'F';
}

void Student::setData(int r, float m) {   // Mutator definition
    rollNo = r;
    marks = m;
    if (marks >= 90) grade = 'A';
    else grade = 'B';
}

void Student::display() {                 // Accessor definition
    cout << "Roll: " << rollNo;
    cout << ", Marks: " << marks;
    cout << ", Grade: " << grade;
}

int main() {
    Student s1;        // Object instantiation
    s1.setData(101, 95.5);
    s1.display();
    return 0;
}
```
