<!-- SECTION_4_END -->

<!-- SECTION_5_START -->
## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### Part A — 3-Mark Questions (Short Answer)

---

**Q1. [KTU University Exam — May 2024]**

> Distinguish between *declaring a reference* and *instantiating an object* in Java. What happens in memory during each step? **(3 marks)**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

1. **Declaration** of a reference is a *compile-time* operation in which the JVM reserves a slot (typically **8 bytes** on a 64-bit JVM) on the current method's **stack frame**. The slot is initialised to `null`. No heap memory is touched. *(1 mark)*
2. **Instantiation** is a *run-time* operation triggered by the `new` keyword. The JVM allocates a contiguous block on the **heap**, zero-initialises all instance fields, invokes the matching constructor, and finally stores the resulting heap address into the stack-resident reference variable. *(1.5 marks)*
3. Syntax-wise, the two can be combined (`Box b = new Box();`) but logically they remain two distinct phases. *(0.5 marks)*

---

**Q2. [KTU University Exam — Dec 2023]**

> What is the difference between `s1 == s2` and `s1.equals(s2)` when `s1` and `s2` are references to objects? **(3 marks)**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

- `s1 == s2` performs a **reference (address) comparison**. It returns `true` only if both references point to the *exact same heap object*. *(1 mark)*
- `s1.equals(s2)` performs a **logical / content comparison**. By default (from `Object`) it behaves like `==`, but classes such as `String`, `Integer`, and user-defined classes can (and should) **override** it to compare internal state. *(1.5 marks)*
- Practical implication: two `Student` objects with identical `name` and `rollNo` fields will yield `==` as `false` (different addresses) but may yield `.equals()` as `true` if properly overridden. *(0.5 marks)*

---

### Part B — 14-Mark Questions (Module Internal Choice)

---

#### **Question A — 14 Marks** **[KTU University Exam — Jul 2024]**

**(a)** Explain with a neat diagram how an object is created in Java using the `new` keyword. Differentiate between *stack* and *heap* memory during object creation. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** Write a Java program to demonstrate **reference aliasing** — i.e., that two references can point to the same object, and changes made through one reference are visible through the other. Show the memory layout. **(7 marks)**

---

**Model Solution:**

**(a) Steps in Object Creation (7 marks)**

The execution of `Box b = new Box(2.0, 3.0, 4.0);` proceeds in **three logical stages**:

1. **Declaration** — The compiler reserves a 64-bit slot on the stack named `b`, initialised to `null`. *(1 mark)*
2. **Memory Allocation & Instantiation** — The `new` operator computes the heap size:

$$
\text{size} = \text{header} + \sum \text{instance fields} = 16 + 3 \times 8 = 40\ \text{bytes}
$$

and allocates them on the heap (Eden space). *(2 marks)*

3. **Initialisation via Constructor** — All fields are zero-initialised first; then the constructor runs, assigning `width=2.0`, `height=3.0`, `depth=4.0`. The address is returned and stored in `b`. *(2 marks)*

| Stack | Heap |
|---|---|
| Fast, LIFO, automatic cleanup | Slower, GC-managed, shared pool |
| Holds **references** & primitives | Holds **objects** |
| 8-byte slot for `b` | 40-byte `Box` instance |

*(2 marks for the table + diagram drawn on answer sheet — must label stack, heap, reference arrow, and field values.)*

---

**(b) Reference Aliasing Demo (7 marks)**

```java
class Student {
    String name;
    int    marks;

    Student(String n, int m) {
        name  = n;
        marks = m;
    }

    void display() {
        System.out.println(name + " : " + marks);
    }
}

class AliasDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s1 = new Student("Anu", 85);
        Student s2 = s1;                 // <-- aliasing: no new object created

        System.out.println("Before mutation:");
        s1.display();
        s2.display();

        s1.marks = 95;                   // mutate via s1

        System.out.println("After mutating s1.marks = 95:");
        s1.display();
        s2.display();                    // change visible through s2 also

        System.out.println("s1 == s2 ? " + (s1 == s2));   // true
    }
}
```

**Expected Output:**

```
Before mutation:
Anu : 85
Anu : 85
After mutating s1.marks = 95:
Anu : 95
Anu : 95
s1 == s2 ? true
```

**Memory Layout (to be drawn on answer sheet — 2 marks):**

- A single `Student` object on the heap with `name="Anu"`, `marks=95`.
- Two stack references `s1` and `s2`, both pointing to the **same** heap address.

**Explanation of marks (3 marks for explanation):**
- `Student s2 = s1;` does **not** create a new object; it merely copies the reference. *(1 mark)*
- Therefore `s1 == s2` evaluates to `true`. *(1 mark)*
- Mutating fields via `s1` is observable through `s2` because both references address the same memory. *(1 mark)*

---

#### **Question B — 14 Marks (Alternative Choice)** **[KTU University Exam — Jul 2024]**

**(a)** What is the role of a **constructor** during object declaration and instantiation? Discuss the difference between *default* and *parameterised* constructors with an example. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** Explain with a code snippet the difference between *primitive* variables and *reference* variables in Java. What are the default values assigned to each? **(7 marks)**

---

**Model Solution:**

**(a) Role of Constructor + Default vs Parameterised (7 marks)**

A **constructor** is a special member function whose name is identical to the class name and which has **no return type** (not even `void`). It is automatically invoked by the `new` operator immediately after heap allocation. Its primary roles are: *(2 marks)*

1. **Initialising** instance fields to meaningful values (instead of zero-defaults).
2. **Enforcing** invariants — e.g., ensuring `marks` is never negative.
3. **Acquiring resources** — e.g., opening a file or socket.

**Default vs Parameterised Constructor:**

```java
class Account {
    int    accNo;
    String holder;
    double balance;

    // Default (no-arg) constructor
    Account() {
        accNo   = 0;
        holder  = "Unknown";
        balance = 0.0;
    }

    // Parameterised constructor
    Account(int a, String h, double b) {
        accNo   = a;
        holder  = h;
        balance = b;
    }
}
```

| Aspect | Default Constructor | Parameterised Constructor |
|---|---|---|
| Arguments | None | One or more |
| Invocation | `new Account()` | `new Account(101, "Ria", 5000.0)` |
| Flexibility | Always produces same shape | Each object can be unique |
| Compiler behaviour | Auto-supplied **only if** no constructor is defined | Never auto-supplied |
| Marks distribution | (2 marks) | (2 marks) |
| Real-world analogy | Blank form | Pre-filled form |

*(1 mark for the example compilation & output prediction)*

---

**(b) Primitive vs Reference Variables (7 marks)**

```java
class PrimitiveVsRef {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int    a = 10,    b = a;     // primitive copy
        Box    x = new Box(),  y = x; // reference copy

        a = 20;
        x.width = 50;

        System.out.println("a = " + a + ", b = " + b);   // 20, 10
        System.out.println("x.width = " + x.width + ", y.width = " + y.width); // 50, 50
    }
}
```

**Default Values Table (3 marks):**

| Data Type | Default Value |
|---|---|
| `byte`, `short`, `int`, `long` | `0` |
| `float`, `double` | `0.0` |
| `char` | `'\u0000'` |
| `boolean` | `false` |
| Any reference type (`String`, custom class, array) | `null` |

**Differences (3 marks):**

| Property | Primitive Variable | Reference Variable |
|---|---|---|
| Stores | Actual value | Memory address of object |
| Memory location | Stack | Reference on stack, object on heap |
| Default value | Type-specific (`0`, `false`, …) | `null` |
| Can be `null`? | **No** | Yes |
| Copy semantics | **Value copy** (independent) | **Address copy** (aliased) |
| Size | Fixed (e.g., `int` = 4 bytes) | Typically 8 bytes (compressed: 4) |

**Conclusion:** When `b = a;` is executed for primitives, the value `10` is duplicated. When `y = x;` is executed for references, only the *address* is duplicated — both `x` and `y` still point to the **same** heap object, hence the field mutation is visible through both. *(1 mark)*

---

### KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Mark-Deduction Traps — Read Carefully!**
> 1. **Confusing `new` with declaration:** Students often write "`new Box()` creates the variable `b`." This is **wrong**. `new` allocates the *object*; `Box b` creates the *reference*. The KTU key awards 1 mark specifically for this distinction.
> 2. **Confusing stack with heap:** A frequent answer says "the object is created on the stack." Partial credit only — the *reference* lives on the stack; the *object* lives on the heap.
> 3. **Comparing strings with `==`:** In code snippets, students use `s1 == s2` to compare two `String` contents. The examiner deducts marks unless they justify it (e.g., interned literals). Always prefer `.equals()`.
> 4. **Forgetting the no-return-type rule for constructors:** Writing `void Box()` instead of `Box()` costs the constructor-definition mark.
> 5. **Ignoring default initialisation:** Many students believe fields are left "uninitialised" after `new`. They are, in fact, **zero-initialised** by the JVM *before* the constructor body runs.

---

### Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

- An **object declaration** in Java is a **two-step** process: declare a reference, then instantiate with `new`. *(High-yield!)*
- The reference lives on the **stack**, the object on the **heap**.
- `new` performs three jobs: allocate, zero-initialise, invoke constructor.
- Default field values: numeric → `0`, boolean → `false`, references → `null`.
- **Reference aliasing** (`Box b2 = b1;`) does **not** clone the object — both references point to the **same** heap entity.
- `==` compares addresses; `.equals()` compares content (if overridden).
- An object becomes GC-eligible only when **no live reference** points to it.
- Constructors have **no return type** and bear the **same name as the class**.
- A **default constructor** is auto-supplied *only* if the programmer defines no constructor at all.
- Memory sizes: object header ≈ **16 bytes**; each `double` field = **8 bytes**; each `int` field = **4 bytes**; reference slot ≈ **8 bytes** (4 with compressed oops).
- Difference between *primitive* and *reference* variable copying is **value-copy vs address-copy** — a classic KTU 3-mark question.

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.title: Object Reference
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** PBCST304 - OBJECT ORIENTED PROGRAMMING > - **Module:** Module 1 > - **Topic:** Object Reference ## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview ### 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Aligned) In Object Oriented Programming (OOP), an **Object Reference** is a typed memory handle (a variable) that stores the **heap-memory address** of an object rather than the object's data itself. In Java (the reference language for PBCST304), reference variables do not contain the object — they contain a **remote pointer** to the object living in the **heap area** of the JVM-managed runtime data area. The formal KTU definition is: > An **Object Reference** is a variable of a class type that holds the memory address of an instance (object) of that class, enabling indirect access to the object's instance variables and instance methods through the dot (`.`) operator. A `null` reference is a special reference variable that points to **no object** in memory. > [!IMPORTANT] > **KTU 2024 Highlight:** In Java, primitive types (`int`, `float`, `char`, `boolean`, etc.) are **not references** — they store actual values directly on the **stack**. Only class-type variables (objects, arrays, interfaces) are references stored as addresses pointing to heap-allocated entities. ### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Intuition Imagine you have a **TV remote control** in your hand. - The **TV** = the actual object (with all its internal circuitry, screen, speakers — i.e., its state and behavior). - The **Remote** = the reference variable in your hand. The remote is **not** the TV. - The **Infrared signal / Channel** = the memory address linking the remote to a *specific* TV. - **Pressing a button** (e.g., volume up) = invoking a method using the dot operator `tvRemote.volumeUp()`. - A **remote with no TV paired** = a `null` reference. Pressing a button on it throws a `NullPointerException`. > [!NOTE] > **Key Takeaway:** Just as one remote can be **re-paired** to a different TV, a reference variable can be **reassigned** to point to a different object of a compatible type. The original TV is unaffected unless garbage-collected. ### 1.3 Core Properties of an Object Reference | Property | Description | | :--- | :--- | | **Type Safety** | A reference is bound to a specific class/interface type at compile time. | | **Indirect Access** | All operations on the object go through the reference using `.` | | **Reassignable** | A reference can be redirected to another object (subject to inheritance rules). | | **Nullable** | A reference can explicitly hold the value `null` (no object). | | **Pass-by-Value (of the address)** | When passed to a method, the reference itself is copied, but both copies point to the same object. | --- ## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ### 2.1 Operational Concept — How an Object Reference Works (Step-by-Step) 1. **Class Declaration** — The compiler reads the class blueprint. No memory is allocated for objects yet. 2. **Reference Variable Declaration** — `Student s1;` reserves a slot on the **stack** named `s1`, currently `null`. 3. **Object Instantiation** — `new Student();` triggers the JVM to allocate memory on the **heap** for the object's instance variables and initialize it via the constructor. 4. **Binding** — The `=` operator stores the **heap address** of the newly created object into the reference variable `s1`. 5. **Access** — Statements like `s1.name = "Anu";` use the dot operator to dereference the address and modify the actual heap object. 6. **Reassignment** — `s1 = new Student();` creates a *new* object; `s1` now points to it. The old object becomes eligible for **Garbage Collection** if no other reference points to it. ### 2.2 The "Why" and "How" Behind Each Step - **Why a separate stack + heap?** Stack frames are short-lived and LIFO-managed; objects often outlive the method that created them, so they live in the heap. - **Why pass-by-value of the address?** Java's language specification mandates *value semantics for everything*, including references. This avoids C++-style pointer arithmetic and dangling-pointer bugs. ### 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet > [!IMPORTANT] > The following symbolic relationships are exam-ready. The symbol $\rightarrow$ denotes "points to / references." | Concept | Symbolic Form | Explanation | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Reference Assignment | $r_1 \rightarrow O_1$ | Reference $r_1$ now references object $O_1$ | | Aliasing | $r_1 \rightarrow O_1 \;\wedge\; r_2 \rightarrow O_1$ | Two references, one object (shared state) | | Null Reference | $r_1 \rightarrow \emptyset$ | $r_1$ references nothing (null) | | Reference Comparison | $r_1 \;==\; r_2 \iff r_1 \rightarrow O_i \;\wedge\; r_2 \rightarrow O_i$ | `==` checks address equality, not content | | Object Count for GC | $N_{alive} = \sum \mathbb{1}(r_i \rightarrow O)$ | Object becomes GC-eligible when $N_{alive} = 0$ | | Reference Size (typical JVM) | $S_{ref} = 4 \;\text{or}\; 8 \;\text{bytes}$ | Compressed OOPs: 4 bytes; standard: 8 bytes (64-bit JVM) | > [!NOTE] > In the comparison formula above, the symbol $\emptyset$ denotes the **empty set** (used here as "no object") — equivalent to Java's `null`. We use $\mid$ within formulas only via $\mid$ written as a math operator, never breaking the markdown table. ### 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility - **GUI Frameworks (Swing/JavaFX):** Every `JButton`, `JFrame` is accessed through a reference passed to event listeners. - **Database Connectivity (JDBC):** `Connection`, `Statement`, `ResultSet` are all reference types — crucial for resource management. - **Spring / Dependency Injection:** Beans are wired through object references at runtime; understanding references is foundational to inversion-of-control. - **Android Development:** `Activity`, `View`, and `Context` are all references — leaks occur when references outlive their intended lifecycle. --- ## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix ### 3.1 Analytical Trace — Full Lifecycle of a Reference Consider the following KTU-standard Java snippet: ```java class Student { String name; int rollNo; } public class DemoRef { public static void main(String[] args) { Student s1 = new Student(); // Step 1 s1.name = "Anu"; // Step 2 s1.rollNo = 101; // Step 3 Student s2 = s1; // Step 4 — aliasing s2.name = "Manu"; // Step 5 — modifies shared object s1 = new Student(); // Step 6 — s1 redirected s1.name = "Vinu"; // Step 7 Student s3 = null; // Step 8 — null reference // s3.name = "X"; // Would throw NullPointerException } } ``` #### Step-by-Step Logical Walkthrough **Step 1 — Declaration + Instantiation** A new `Student` object is allocated on the **heap**. Let us denote the heap address as $\text{addr} = 0x2001$. The reference `s1` is stored on the **stack**. $$ s_1 \rightarrow \text{Object}_A \quad \text{at address } 0x2001 $$ **Step 2 — State mutation via reference** $$ s_1.\text{name} = \text{"Anu"} \implies \text{Object}_A.\text{name} = \text{"Anu"} $$ **Step 3 — State mutation via reference** $$ s_1.\text{rollNo} = 101 \implies \text{Object}_A.\text{rollNo} = 101 $$ **Step 4 — Aliasing** The value stored in `s1` (the address `0x2001`) is **copied** into `s2`. Both references now point to the **same** object. $$ s_1 \rightarrow \text{Object}_A \quad \wedge \quad s_2 \rightarrow \text{Object}_A $$ $$ \text{Heap address of Object}_A = 0x2001 $$ **Step 5 — Mutating through the alias** Any mutation via `s2` is reflected when accessed via `s1`, because they reference the *same* memory. $$ s_2.\text{name} = \text{"Manu"} \implies \text{Object}_A.\text{name} = \text{"Manu"} $$ Verification: $$ s_1.\text{name} == \text{"Manu"} \;\; \text{is true (same memory cell)} $$ **Step 6 — Reassignment of `s1`** A brand-new `Student` object is created at heap address $0x3002$. The reference `s1` is overwritten with this new address. $$ s_1 \rightarrow \text{Object}_B \quad \text{at address } 0x3002 $$ $$ s_2 \rightarrow \text{Object}_A \quad \text{(unchanged, still at } 0x2001\text{)} $$ **Step 7 — Populating the new object** $$ s_1.\text{name} = \text{"Vinu"} \implies \text{Object}_B.\text{name} = \text{"Vinu"} $$ **Step 8 — Null reference** `s3` is declared but not assigned an object. Its stack value is the special sentinel `null` (typically `0x0`). $$ s_3 \rightarrow \emptyset $$ Any dereference (e.g., `s3.name`) throws `java.lang.NullPointerException`. ### 3.2 Analytical Comparison Matrix — Primitive vs Reference | Aspect | Primitive Variable | Reference Variable | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Stored on | Stack | Stack (the address); object on Heap | | Holds | Actual value (e.g., $42$) | Heap address of an object | | Default value | $0$, $0.0$, `false`, `\u0000` | `null` | | Can be `null`? | No | Yes | | `==` semantics | Compares values | Compares addresses (reference equality) | | Size | Fixed (e.g., $4$ bytes for `int`) | $4$ or $8$ bytes (address) | | Example | `int x = 10;` | `Student s = new Student();` | ### 3.3 Analytical Comparison Matrix — `==` vs `.equals()` | Operation | On References | Result | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `s1 == s2` | $s_1 \rightarrow O_i \;\wedge\; s_2 \rightarrow O_i$ | `true` iff **same address** | | `s1.equals(s2)` | Calls `Object.equals()` (or overridden) | `true` iff **logically equal** (content-based) | | `s1 == null` | $s_1 \rightarrow \emptyset$ | `true` iff uninitialized/null | > [!NOTE] > KTU examiners frequently test this distinction. By default, `==` performs **shallow reference comparison** unless the class overrides `equals()` (and `hashCode()`) — for example, the `String` class overrides `equals()` to compare character sequences. --- ## 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics ### 4.1 Memory Architecture — Stack vs Heap with References ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph STK["STACK FRAME - main method"] s1Var["s1 : Student
addr = 0x3002"] s2Var["s2 : Student
addr = 0x2001"] s3Var["s3 : Student
value = null"] end subgraph HEAP["HEAP MEMORY - JVM"] objA["Object A : Student
name = Manu
rollNo = 101
at 0x2001"] objB["Object B : Student
name = Vinu
rollNo = 0
at 0x3002"] end s2Var -.-> objA s1Var -.-> objB classDef stack fill:#e1f5ff,stroke:#0277bd,color:#000 classDef heap fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#e65100,color:#000 classDef nullStyle fill:#ffebee,stroke:#b71c1c,color:#000 class s1Var,s2Var stack class objA,objB heap class s3Var nullStyle ``` > **Figure Caption (for answer scripts):** `s1` and `s2` are stack-resident reference variables. `s1` points to Object B; `s2` points to Object A (aliasing occurred earlier and then `s1` was reassigned). `s3` holds the `null` sentinel, denoting absence of any heap object. ### 4.2 Reference Reassignment & Garbage Collection Flow ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Step 1: Student s1 = new Student()
s1 points to ObjectA"] B["Step 2: s1.name = 'Anu'
ObjectA.name = Anu"] C["Step 3: Student s2 = s1
Both point to ObjectA"] D["Step 4: s1 = new Student()
s1 now points to ObjectB"] E["Step 5: ObjectA has zero references
Eligible for Garbage Collection"] F["Step 6: s3 = null
s3 points to no object"] A --> B --> C --> D --> E D --> F classDef state fill:#f3e5f5,stroke:#4a148c,color:#000 classDef gc fill:#ffcdd2,stroke:#b71c1c,color:#000 class A,B,C,D,F state class E gc ``` ### 4.3 Reference Type Hierarchy (for KTU exam diagrams) ```mermaid flowchart TB javaRef["java.lang.Object"] classRef["Class Type Reference
e.g. Student s"] ifaceRef["Interface Type Reference
e.g. Comparable c"] arrRef["Array Type Reference
e.g. int arr"] enumRef["Enum Type Reference
e.g. Color c"] javaRef --> classRef javaRef --> ifaceRef javaRef --> arrRef javaRef --> enumRef classDef root fill:#bbdefb,stroke:#0d47a1,color:#000 classDef leaf fill:#c8e6c9,stroke:#1b5e20,color:#000 class javaRef root class classRef,ifaceRef,arrRef,enumRef leaf ``` --- ## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap ### 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each) #### **Q1. Define an object reference. How is it different from a primitive variable?** `[KTU University Exam - May 2024]` **Model Answer:** An **object reference** is a variable of a class (or interface) type that stores the **memory address** of an object allocated on the heap. It acts as a handle to access the object's instance variables and methods using the dot (`.`) operator. **Differences:** | Aspect | Primitive | Object Reference | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Holds | Actual value | Heap address of object | | Memory | Stack only | Stack (address) + Heap (object) | | Default | $0$ / `false` | `null` | | Nullable | No | Yes | **(3 marks)** ✓ --- #### **Q2. What is a null reference? What exception occurs when it is dereferenced?** `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]` **Model Answer:** A **null reference** is a reference variable that does not point to any object in memory. Its value is the literal `null` (conceptually address `0x0`). When a null reference is dereferenced (e.g., `nullRef.name`), the JVM throws a **`java.lang.NullPointerException`** at runtime, terminating the program abnormally unless caught by a `try-catch` block. **(3 marks)** ✓ --- ### 5.2 Part B — Full-Length Questions (14 Marks) > **KTU ESE Pattern:** Module Internal Choice — Answer **ONE** of the two. --- #### **Question A (14 Marks)** `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2024 - Model Paper]` **(a)** Explain the concept of an object reference in Java with a suitable example. Differentiate between **pass-by-value** for primitives and **pass-by-value of reference** for objects. **(7 marks)** **(b)** Write a Java program to demonstrate **aliasing** and **reference reassignment**. Show the output and explain the memory state at each step. **(7 marks)** **Model Solution (a):** An **object reference** is a typed handle that stores the heap address of an object. Example: ```java class Box { int length; Box(int l) { length = l; } } public class RefDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { Box b = new Box(10); System.out.println(b.length); } } ``` Here, `b` is a reference on the stack pointing to a `Box` object on the heap. **Pass-by-value of reference:** - For primitives, the *value itself* is copied. Modifying the copy does not affect the original. - For objects, the *address* is copied. Both original and parameter point to the **same** heap object, so internal state changes via the parameter are visible to the caller. However, **reassigning** the parameter to a new object does **not** affect the caller's reference. ```java static void modify(Box x) { x.length = 99; } // Affects caller static void reassign(Box x) { x = new Box(50); } // Does NOT affect caller ``` **(7 marks)** ✓ **Model Solution (b):** ```java class Student { String name; Student(String n) { name = n; } } public class AliasDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { Student s1 = new Student("Anu"); Student s2 = s1; // Aliasing s2.name = "Manu"; System.out.println(s1.name); // Output: Manu (shared object) s1 = new Student("Vinu"); // Reassignment System.out.println(s2.name); // Output: Manu (s2 unaffected) System.out.println(s1.name); // Output: Vinu } } ``` **Memory trace:** 1. `s1` → `Student("Anu")` at `0xAA01` 2. `s2 = s1` → `s2` → `0xAA01` (same object — aliasing) 3. `s2.name = "Manu"` → modifies object at `0xAA01` 4. `s1 = new Student("Vinu")` → `s1` → `0xBB02` (new object); `s2` still → `0xAA01` **(7 marks)** ✓ --- #### **Question B (14 Marks)** `[KTU University Exam - May 2023]` **(a)** What is reference aliasing? Write a program to show how it can lead to unintended modifications, and how reassignment breaks the alias. **(7 marks)** **(b)** Explain the difference between `==` and `.equals()` when comparing object references. Provide an example using the `String` class. **(7 marks)** **Model Solution (a):** **Reference aliasing** occurs when two or more reference variables hold the same heap address, thereby pointing to the *same* object. Mutating the object through any of the references is visible through all of them. ```java class Account { double balance; Account(double b) { balance = b; } } public class AliasRisk { public static void main(String[] args) { Account a1 = new Account(1000); Account a2 = a1; // ALIAS a2.balance = 5000; // unintended side effect System.out.println(a1.balance); // 5000.0 — affected! a1 = new Account(9999); // BREAK alias System.out.println(a2.balance); // 5000.0 — a1 redirected } } ``` When `a1 = new Account(9999);` is executed, `a1` points to a *new* object. The alias is broken, and `a2` continues to point to the original. **(7 marks)** ✓ **Model Solution (b):** - `==` compares the **memory addresses** of two references (reference equality). - `.equals()` compares the **logical content** of two objects, provided the class overrides `Object.equals()`. By default, `Object.equals()` behaves like `==`. ```java public class StringEq { public static void main(String[] args) { String s1 = new String("KTU"); String s2 = new String("KTU"); System.out.println(s1 == s2); // false (different addresses) System.out.println(s1.equals(s2)); // true (same content) } } ``` The `String` class overrides `equals()` to perform character-by-character comparison, returning `true` when the two strings have identical content. **(7 marks)** ✓ --- ### 5.3 Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout > [!WARNING] > **Common Mistakes KTU Students Make (Lose 2–3 marks per answer):** > 1. **Confusing `==` with `.equals()`** — `==` compares *addresses*, not content. Writing "`s1 == s2` checks if contents are equal" is **wrong** unless the class is a wrapper like `String` where interning makes them coincidentally equal. > 2. **Claiming Java is "pass-by-reference"** — Java is **always pass-by-value**. For objects, the *reference value (address)* is copied. Reassignment inside the method does **not** affect the caller's variable. > 3. **Forgetting that primitives are not references** — `int x = 5;` is not a reference. It cannot be `null`. > 4. **Skipping the memory diagram** — KTU examiners award 2–3 marks for a clear stack/heap sketch. Always include one. > 5. **Treating `null` as a valid object** — `null` is a *literal* indicating the absence of an object. Dereferencing it causes `NullPointerException`. ### 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember - 📌 **Object Reference** = a typed variable holding a heap address; **not** the object itself. - 📌 Primitives store **values** on the stack; references store **addresses** on the stack pointing to the **heap**. - 📌 A reference can be **`null`** — dereferencing it throws `NullPointerException`. - 📌 **Aliasing** = two references, one object. Modifications via one are visible via the other. - 📌 **Reassignment** redirects a reference to a new object; the old object becomes **garbage-collectable** if no other reference points to it. - 📌 `==` → address equality; `.equals()` → content equality (if overridden). - 📌 Java is **pass-by-value** (of the reference's address for objects), **never** pass-by-reference. - 📌 Reference size: typically **4 bytes** (compressed oops) or **8 bytes** (64-bit JVM). - 📌 Always include a **stack/heap diagram** in 7+ mark answers — it's a guaranteed scoring component. - 📌 Default value of any reference variable (instance field) is `null`; local references must be explicitly initialized. ---

topics.title: Introduction to Methods
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PBCST304 - OBJECT ORIENTED PROGRAMMING
> - **Module:** Module 1
> - **Topic:** Introduction to Methods

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

In **Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)** using Java, a **method** is a named, reusable block of code encapsulated inside a class that performs a specific, well-defined task. A method is the procedural workhorse of a class — it is the only mechanism through which an object exhibits behavior, manipulates its own state (instance variables), or returns computed results to a calling context.

According to the KTU 2024 Scheme syllabus, a method is formally characterized by its **method signature**, which is the combination of:

$$\text{Method Signature} = \text{Method Name} + \text{Parameter List (types and order)}$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Syllabus Highlight (KTU 2024 - Module 1):**
> A method is the fundamental unit of behavior in Java. Every executable Java statement must reside inside a method. The `main` method is the entry point, but all real logic must be decomposed into well-named, single-responsibility methods.

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The "Vending Machine" View

Imagine a **vending machine** placed in your college canteen:

- The **machine itself** = a `class` (the blueprint)
- The **buttons and coin slot** = the parameters (inputs you supply)
- The **snack that drops out** = the return value (output you receive)
- The **internal mechanism** (coils, motors, dispensers) = the method body (hidden logic)
- **Pressing a button** = calling/invoking the method

You do not need to know *how* the machine works internally (abstraction). You just provide inputs (coins + button code) and receive an output (Coke, KitKat, etc.). That is exactly how a Java method behaves: **input → processing → output**.

| Analogy Element | Java Equivalent |
| :--- | :--- |
| Vending machine blueprint | `class VendingMachine` |
| A specific machine | `object` (instance) |
| Button "B1" labeled "Coke" | `method dispenseCoke(int money)` |
| Coins inserted | `arguments` |
| Drink received | `return` value |
| "Out of stock" message | `return null` or thrown exception |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Three Pillars of a Method:**
> 1. **Declaration (Header)** — tells the compiler the method's *name, return type, and parameters*.
> 2. **Definition (Body)** — contains the actual statements to execute.
> 3. **Invocation (Call)** — triggers execution from another method or statement.

## 1.3 Why Methods? — The "Why" Before the "How"

A beginner often asks: *"Why not write everything inside `main`?"* The answer lies in three engineering principles:

1. **Reusability (DRY Principle)** — *Don't Repeat Yourself*. Write once, invoke a thousand times.
2. **Modularity** — break a monolithic program into small, manageable, testable units.
3. **Abstraction** — hide complex logic behind a simple, descriptive name.

> [!TIP]
> **Industry Standard Naming:** Method names in Java should be **verbs in lowercase**, using **camelCase** for multi-word names. Example: `calculateSalary()`, `findMaximum()`, `printReport()`.
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Anatomy of a Java Method — The Five Mandatory Parts

A method declaration in Java follows a strict syntactic structure. Each part has a distinct role:

```java
accessModifier static returnType methodName(parameterList) {
    // method body
    // local variable declarations
    // executable statements
    return value; // mandatory if returnType is not void
}
```

### 2.1.1 Component-by-Component Breakdown

**(a) Access Modifier**
Defines the **visibility** of the method to other classes.

| Modifier | Visibility Scope | KTU Exam Frequency |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `public` | Accessible from **any class** in any package | Very High |
| `protected` | Accessible within the **same package** and **subclasses** | High |
| `private` | Accessible **only within the same class** | Very High |
| *default* (no keyword) | Accessible only within the **same package** | Medium |

**(b) Static Keyword (Optional)**
- `static` methods belong to the **class itself**, not to any specific object.
- They can be called using the **class name** directly: `ClassName.methodName()`.
- Non-static (instance) methods require an **object reference** to be invoked.

**(c) Return Type**
- The **data type** of the value the method sends back to the caller.
- If no value is returned, use the keyword `void`.
- A method can return **at most one value** (a single primitive or a single object reference).

**(d) Method Name**
- Must be a **valid Java identifier**.
- Must follow **camelCase** convention.
- Cannot be a Java reserved keyword (`class`, `int`, `if`, etc.).

**(e) Parameter List (Formal Parameters)**
- A comma-separated list of `type variableName` pairs enclosed in parentheses.
- Can be **empty** (`()`) if the method takes no inputs.
- Each parameter is a **local variable** of the method, initialized by the arguments passed during the call.

## 2.2 Method Invocation — The Calling Mechanism

A method is executed only when it is **called (invoked)**. The syntax for invocation is:

```java
// For static methods
ClassName.methodName(argument1, argument2, ...);

// For instance (non-static) methods
objectReference.methodName(argument1, argument2, ...);
```

### 2.2.1 Formal vs. Actual Parameters — A Critical Distinction

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Formal Parameters** = the variables declared in the method's *header* (e.g., `int a, int b` in `int add(int a, int b)`).
> **Actual Parameters / Arguments** = the *values/expressions* passed during the *call* (e.g., `5, 10` in `add(5, 10)`).

The JVM performs a process called **argument passing**: it copies the actual argument value into the formal parameter's memory slot. This is the foundation of Java's **pass-by-value** semantics, discussed in Section 2.4.

## 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet — The Method Specification Cheat Sheet

The following table summarizes the complete specification of a Java method that you must memorize for the KTU board exam:

| Component | Syntax Token | Mandatory? | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Access Modifier | `public` / `private` / `protected` | No (defaults to package-private) | `public` |
| Static Modifier | `static` | No | `static` |
| Abstract Modifier | `abstract` | No (used in abstract classes) | `abstract` |
| Final Modifier | `final` | No (prevents overriding) | `final` |
| Return Type | Any primitive / object type / `void` | **YES** | `int`, `double`, `String`, `void` |
| Method Name | Valid identifier, camelCase | **YES** | `calculateArea` |
| Parameter List | `(type1 var1, type2 var2, ...)` | **YES** (can be empty) | `(double radius)` |
| Method Body | `{ ... statements ... }` | **YES** | `{ return 3.14 * r * r; }` |
| `return` Statement | `return value;` | **YES** (unless `void`) | `return area;` |

### 2.3.1 The Method Signature Equation

In Java, two methods can have the **same name** only if their **signatures differ**. The signature is governed by:

$$\text{Signature}(m) = \text{name}(m) \oplus \text{orderedTypeList}(\text{params}(m))$$

> The return type is **NOT** part of the method signature in Java. This is a frequent KTU exam trap.

## 2.4 Pass-by-Value in Java — The Golden Rule

Java is **strictly pass-by-value**. There are no pass-by-reference semantics in Java, even for object references.

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Misconception:** "Java passes objects by reference." This is **FALSE**. Java passes a *copy of the reference variable* (the memory address), not the original reference itself. As a result, the method can mutate the *object's internal state* but cannot make the caller's variable point to a different object.

## 2.5 Real-World Engineering Utility

Methods are not merely an academic construct — they underpin every software engineering practice:

- **API Design**: Each public method is a contract between the library and its users.
- **Unit Testing (JUnit)**: Every well-designed method corresponds to one or more test cases (`@Test`).
- **Code Maintainability**: Methods enforce the *Single Responsibility Principle* (SRP) of SOLID design.
- **Parallel Computing**: Methods marked `synchronized` or annotated with concurrency APIs become the unit of thread execution.
<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# 3. Step-by-Step Analytical Walkthrough & Method Execution Flow

## 3.1 Method Declaration — Line-by-Line Analysis

Consider the following KTU-standard method declaration:

```java
public static int findSquare(int number) {
    int result = number * number;
    return result;
}
```

Let us dissect this declaration component by component:

| Token | Classification | Role in Compilation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `public` | Access Modifier | Grants universal visibility to the method. |
| `static` | Non-Access Modifier | Binds the method to the class, not an instance. |
| `int` | Return Type | Promises the caller that an integer value will be returned. |
| `findSquare` | Method Name | The symbolic handle used to invoke the method. |
| `(int number)` | Parameter List | Declares one formal parameter of type `int`. |
| `int result = ...` | Local Variable | A method-scoped variable, destroyed upon method exit. |
| `return result;` | Return Statement | Sends the value back to the caller and exits the method. |

## 3.2 Method Invocation — Stack Frame Analysis

When a method is called, the JVM creates a new **stack frame (activation record)** on the **call stack**. This frame stores:
- The method's local variables
- The return address (where to resume after the method finishes)
- The operand stack for intermediate calculations

Let us trace a complete execution sequence step-by-step.

### Worked Example: Tracing Method Calls

**Source Code:**

```java
public class Calculator {
    public static int add(int a, int b) {
        int sum = a + b;
        return sum;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int x = 10;
        int y = 20;
        int result = add(x, y);
        System.out.println("Sum = " + result);
    }
}
```

### Step-by-Step Execution Trace

**Step 1 — JVM Entry:**
The JVM invokes `main` as the program entry point. A stack frame for `main` is pushed onto the call stack.

**Step 2 — Local Variable Initialization in `main`:**
The variables `x` and `y` are allocated inside `main`'s stack frame.

$$x \leftarrow 10, \quad y \leftarrow 20$$

**Step 3 — Method Call `add(x, y)`:**
The call `add(x, y)` triggers the following sequence:
1. The current execution point in `main` is saved (return address = line of `add(x, y)`).
2. A new stack frame for `add` is pushed onto the stack.
3. The **actual arguments** `x = 10` and `y = 20` are **copied** into the **formal parameters** `a` and `b` (pass-by-value).

$$a \leftarrow 10, \quad b \leftarrow 20$$

**Step 4 — Local Variable in `add`:**
The local variable `sum` is declared and computed:

$$\text{sum} = a + b = 10 + 20 = 30$$

**Step 5 — Return Statement:**
The statement `return sum;` does two things atomically:
1. The value `30` is returned to the caller (`main`).
2. The stack frame of `add` is **popped** and destroyed (all locals `a`, `b`, `sum` cease to exist).

**Step 6 — Resumption in `main`:**
Control returns to `main`. The returned value `30` is assigned to `result`:

$$\text{result} \leftarrow 30$$

**Step 7 — Output:**
The `println` statement executes, producing:

$$\text{Output} = \texttt{"Sum = 30"}$$

**Step 8 — Program Termination:**
`main` ends. Its stack frame is popped. The call stack becomes empty, and the JVM terminates the program.

### 3.2.1 Stack Memory Visualization (Logical)

```
+-------------------------------+
| main() frame                  |
|   x = 10                      |
|   y = 20                      |
|   result = 30                 |
+-------------------------------+
        ↑   ← return address
+-------------------------------+
| add() frame (DESTROYED)       |
|   a = 10                      |
|   b = 20                      |
|   sum = 30                    |
+-------------------------------+
```

> [!NOTE]
> The `add` frame is destroyed the moment `return sum;` executes. The `main` frame outlives it because execution resumes in `main`.

## 3.3 Pass-by-Value — Proof by Contradiction

To cement the pass-by-value concept, let us examine what happens with **primitive** versus **object reference** parameters.

### Case 1: Primitive Parameter (e.g., `int`)

```java
public static void modifyValue(int num) {
    num = 100; // local change only
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    int x = 5;
    modifyValue(x);
    System.out.println(x); // prints 5, NOT 100
}
```

**Analysis:**
- The value `5` is copied into the formal parameter `num`.
- The assignment `num = 100` modifies only the *local* copy inside `modifyValue`.
- The caller's variable `x` remains `5`.

### Case 2: Object Reference Parameter (e.g., `StringBuilder`)

```java
public static void modifyObject(StringBuilder sb) {
    sb.append(" World"); // mutates the object
    sb = new StringBuilder("New"); // changes local reference only
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    StringBuilder greeting = new StringBuilder("Hello");
    modifyObject(greeting);
    System.out.println(greeting); // prints "Hello World"
}
```

**Analysis:**
- The *reference value* (memory address) of `greeting` is copied into the formal parameter `sb`.
- `sb.append(" World")` mutates the **same object** that `greeting` points to.
- `sb = new StringBuilder("New")` reassigns only the **local copy** of the reference; the caller's `greeting` still points to the original "Hello" object.
- The final output is "Hello World", proving the object's *contents* changed but the caller's *reference* did not.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Final Verdict on Java Parameter Passing:**
> Java is **100% pass-by-value**. For primitives, the value itself is copied. For objects, the reference (address) is copied — but never the original reference variable itself. This is one of the most heavily tested KTU concepts.

## 3.4 The `void` Return Type — Special Case

A method declared with `void` performs an action but does not return a value. The `return` statement is **optional**, and if used, must not be followed by a value.

```java
public static void greet(String name) {
    System.out.println("Hello, " + name + "!");
    return; // optional; exits the method early
}
```

If a `void` method attempts `return value;`, the compiler will reject it with:

$$\text{Error: } \texttt{"unexpected type: required: void, found: int"}$$

# 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

## 4.1 Method Invocation Flow (Mermaid Flowchart)

The following Mermaid flowchart illustrates the complete lifecycle of a method call — from invocation to stack frame creation to return.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Caller executes methodName args] --> B{Is method static?}
    B -- Yes --> C[Resolve method via ClassName]
    B -- No --> D[Resolve method via objectReference]
    C --> E[Push new Stack Frame onto Call Stack]
    D --> E
    E --> F[Copy actual arguments to formal parameters]
    F --> G[Execute method body statements in order]
    G --> H{Is return type void?}
    H -- No --> I[Evaluate return expression]
    I --> J[Pop Stack Frame from Call Stack]
    J --> K[Pass returned value to caller]
    H -- Yes --> L[Pop Stack Frame from Call Stack]
    L --> M[Control returns to caller]
    K --> M
    M --> N[Caller resumes execution at next statement]
```

## 4.2 Method Component Architecture (Block Diagram)

The following block diagram decomposes a Java method declaration into its constituent syntactic components, showing how they nest within one another.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    M[Method Declaration] --> AM[Access Modifier]
    M --> SM[Static or other Modifiers]
    M --> RT[Return Type]
    M --> MN[Method Name]
    M --> PL[Parameter List]
    M --> MB[Method Body]
    AM --> AM1[public]
    AM --> AM2[private]
    AM --> AM3[protected]
    AM --> AM4[default - package private]
    SM --> SM1[static]
    SM --> SM2[final]
    SM --> SM3[abstract]
    RT --> RT1[Primitive: int, double, char, boolean]
    RT --> RT2[Object: String, Scanner, etc]
    RT --> RT3[void]
    PL --> PL1[Formal Parameters: type variableName]
    PL --> PL2[Empty: parenthesis empty]
    MB --> MB1[Local Variable Declarations]
    MB --> MB2[Executable Statements]
    MB --> MB3[Return Statement - if not void]
```

## 4.3 Stack Frame Lifecycle (Block-Level Architecture)

The following diagram depicts the runtime memory interactions when a method is invoked, showing how the call stack evolves.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph CS[Call Stack - grows downward]
        direction TB
        SF1[main frame - x=10, y=20, result=?]
        SF2[add frame - a=10, b=20, sum=30]
    end
    INV[Invocation: add x y] --> SF1
    SF1 --> PUSH[Push add frame]
    PUSH --> SF2
    SF2 --> EXEC[Execute body: sum = a + b]
    EXEC --> RET[return sum value 30]
    RET --> POP[Pop add frame - destroy locals]
    POP --> SF1
    SF1 --> ASSIGN[result = 30]
    ASSIGN --> OUT[System.out.println Sum equals 30]
```

## 4.4 Pass-by-Value Memory Model (Block Diagram)

The following block diagram visually demonstrates the difference between primitive and object reference passing in Java.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph CALLER[Caller's Memory Space]
        VAR1[x = 5]
        REF1[greeting - address 0xABC]
    end
    subgraph CALLEE[Callee's Memory Space - copy]
        COPY1[num = 5]
        COPY2[sb - address 0xABC - same object]
    end
    VAR1 -- pass by value: copy of 5 --> COPY1
    REF1 -- pass by value: copy of address --> COPY2
    COPY1 -- reassign num = 100 --> REJECT1[Caller's x remains 5]
    COPY2 -- sb append World --> MUTATE[Object at 0xABC mutated]
    COPY2 -- sb = new object --> REJECT2[Caller still points to 0xABC]
```

> [!TIP]
> **Visualization Tip for Exams:** When asked to explain pass-by-value, draw two boxes — one for the *caller's* variable and one for the *callee's* parameter. Draw an arrow showing the *value* being copied. This single diagram earns full marks on any KTU theory question.

# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Question 1
**`[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]`**
**Define a method in Java. List any four components of a method declaration with examples.**

**Model Answer:**

A **method** in Java is a named block of code declared within a class that encapsulates a specific behavior or computation. It is the fundamental unit of behavior in object-oriented programming and is invoked (called) to perform its task.

The four major components of a method declaration are:

1. **Access Modifier** — Controls visibility. Example: `public` allows access from any class.
2. **Return Type** — Specifies the data type of the value returned. Example: `int` in `int calculate()`.
3. **Method Name** — A valid Java identifier following camelCase. Example: `calculateSum`.
4. **Parameter List** — The comma-separated list of inputs. Example: `(int a, int b)`.

**Example Signature:**
```java
public int calculateSum(int a, int b)
```

---

### Question 2
**`[KTU University Exam - May 2024]`**
**What is the difference between formal parameters and actual parameters? Give one example.**

**Model Answer:**

| Aspect | Formal Parameters | Actual Parameters |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Definition** | Variables declared in the method's *header/definition* | Values/expressions passed during the *method call* |
| **Scope** | Exist only inside the method body | Exist in the caller's scope |
| **Also Called** | Parameters | Arguments |

**Example:**

```java
// Method definition — 'a' and 'b' are FORMAL parameters
public static int add(int a, int b) {
    return a + b;
}

// Method call — '5' and '10' are ACTUAL parameters / arguments
int result = add(5, 10);
```

In the call `add(5, 10)`, the values `5` and `10` are copied into the formal parameters `a` and `b` respectively via Java's pass-by-value mechanism.

---

## 5.2 Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each)

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls:**
> 1. **Forgetting the `return` statement** in non-`void` methods — *2 marks deducted*.
> 2. **Confusing method overloading with overriding** — they are different concepts (overloading = same class, overriding = parent-child).
> 3. **Writing `return` with a value inside a `void` method** — *compilation error, full marks lost*.
> 4. **Claiming Java is "pass-by-reference"** — *this is factually wrong; Java is strictly pass-by-value*.
> 5. **Omitting the access modifier in exam answers** — write `public` explicitly to be safe.

---

### Question A (14 Marks)
**`[KTU University Exam - Dec 2024]`**

**(a)** Explain the anatomy of a Java method with a suitable example. Discuss the role of access specifiers and return types in method design. **(7 Marks)**

**(b)** With a suitable Java program, demonstrate the concept of **pass-by-value** for both primitive and object type parameters. Explain why Java is strictly pass-by-value even when passing objects. **(7 Marks)**

---

#### Model Solution for Question A:

**(a) Anatomy of a Java Method [7 Marks]:**

A Java method declaration consists of six syntactical components: **access modifier**, **non-access modifier** (e.g., `static`), **return type**, **method name**, **parameter list**, and **method body**.

```java
public static double calculateArea(double radius) {
    final double PI = 3.14159;
    double area = PI * radius * radius;
    return area;
}
```

- **Access Specifier (`public`)** [1 Mark]: Makes the method callable from any class. Other options are `private` (class-only), `protected` (package + subclasses), and default (package-only).
- **Non-Access Modifier (`static`)** [1 Mark]: Binds the method to the class itself, allowing invocation without creating an object.
- **Return Type (`double`)** [2 Marks]: Declares that the method will return a `double` precision floating-point value. If no value is returned, `void` is used.
- **Method Name (`calculateArea`)** [1 Mark]: A camelCase verb phrase describing the action.
- **Parameter List (`double radius`)** [1 Mark]: Declares one formal parameter that receives the input value.
- **Method Body** [1 Mark]: The block containing local variable declarations, computation, and the mandatory `return` statement.

**(b) Pass-by-Value Demonstration [7 Marks]:**

```java
public class PassByValueDemo {

    // Primitive parameter — value is copied
    public static void modifyPrimitive(int num) {
        num = num + 50;
        System.out.println("Inside modifyPrimitive, num = " + num);
    }

    // Object reference parameter — reference is copied
    public static void modifyObject(StringBuilder builder) {
        builder.append(" World");        // mutates original object
        builder = new StringBuilder("New"); // only changes local reference
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int x = 10;
        modifyPrimitive(x);
        System.out.println("After modifyPrimitive, x = " + x);

        StringBuilder greeting = new StringBuilder("Hello");
        modifyObject(greeting);
        System.out.println("After modifyObject, greeting = " + greeting);
    }
}
```

**Output:**
```
Inside modifyPrimitive, num = 60
After modifyPrimitive, x = 10
After modifyObject, greeting = Hello World
```

**Explanation [3 Marks]:**

1. In `modifyPrimitive`, the value `10` of `x` is copied into the local `num`. The reassignment `num = 50` does not affect `x` outside the method. Hence, `x` remains `10`.
2. In `modifyObject`, the *reference* (memory address) of `greeting` is copied into `builder`. The call `builder.append(" World")` mutates the *same object* that `greeting` points to, so the original object now contains "Hello World".
3. The line `builder = new StringBuilder("New")` creates a brand-new object and assigns the *local* `builder` reference to it. This does **not** affect the caller's `greeting` variable, which still points to the original "Hello" object.
4. **Conclusion:** Java is **strictly pass-by-value** — for primitives, the literal value is copied; for objects, the reference (address) is copied. The original reference variable in the caller's scope can never be reassigned by the callee.

---

### Question B (14 Marks) — Alternative Choice
**`[KTU University Exam - May 2024]`**

**(a)** Define a method signature. Explain with examples how the Java compiler distinguishes between two methods having the same name. **(7 Marks)**

**(b)** Write a Java program that contains a `main` method which calls a user-defined method `findMax(int a, int b, int c)` that returns the largest of three integers. Show the complete execution with a sample input. **(7 Marks)**

---

#### Model Solution for Question B:

**(a) Method Signature & Name Differentiation [7 Marks]:**

A **method signature** in Java is the combination of the method's name and the ordered list of parameter types. It is the unique identifier that the compiler uses to bind a method call to the correct method definition.

$$\text{Signature} = \text{Method Name} + \text{Parameter Types (order matters)}$$

> **Important:** The return type is **NOT** part of the method signature in Java.

**Example — Same Name, Different Signatures:**

```java
public class MathUtils {
    // Signature 1: add(int, int)
    public static int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }

    // Signature 2: add(double, double)
    public static double add(double a, double b) {
        return a + b;
    }

    // Signature 3: add(int, int, int)
    public static int add(int a, int b, int c) {
        return a + b + c;
    }
}
```

When the compiler encounters `add(5, 10)`, it matches the parameter types `(int, int)` to the first method. For `add(2.5, 3.7)`, it matches `(double, double)` to the second. This automatic resolution is called **method overloading**, and it is enabled *solely* by signature differences. [3 Marks for explanation + 2 Marks for example + 2 Marks for example demonstration]

**(b) Program to Find the Largest of Three Integers [7 Marks]:**

```java
public class MaxFinder {

    // User-defined method to find the maximum of three integers
    public static int findMax(int a, int b, int c) {
        int max = a;                       // assume a is the largest initially
        if (b > max) {
            max = b;                       // update if b is larger
        }
        if (c > max) {
            max = c;                       // update if c is larger
        }
        return max;                        // return the largest value
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int num1 = 45, num2 = 78, num3 = 23;
        int largest = findMax(num1, num2, num3);
        System.out.println("The largest number is: " + largest);
    }
}
```

**Step-by-Step Execution Trace [3 Marks]:**

| Step | Action | State of `max` |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | `max = a` (initialize with `num1 = 45`) | `max = 45` |
| 2 | Check `b > max` → `78 > 45` is **true** → `max = b` | `max = 78` |
| 3 | Check `c > max` → `23 > 78` is **false** → no update | `max = 78` |
| 4 | `return max;` returns `78` to `main` | — |
| 5 | `largest` in `main` is assigned `78` | `largest = 78` |

**Output:**
```
The largest number is: 78
```

**Alternate One-Liner Logic (Bonus Knowledge):**
$$\text{findMax}(a,b,c) = \max(a, \max(b,c))$$

This can be coded as:
```java
return Math.max(a, Math.max(b, c));
```

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **High-Density Revision Checklist — Must Memorize for KTU 2024**

- ✅ A **method** is a named, reusable block of code inside a class that performs a specific task.
- ✅ The **method signature** = `methodName + parameterTypeList`. Return type is **NOT** part of the signature.
- ✅ Method components in order: **access modifier → static/final → return type → method name → (parameters) → { body }**.
- ✅ `void` return type means the method returns **no value**; a non-`void` method **must** have a `return value;` statement.
- ✅ **Formal parameters** are declared in the method header; **actual parameters (arguments)** are passed during the call.
- ✅ Java is **strictly pass-by-value**: primitives copy the value; objects copy the reference (address).
- ✅ A method can change the *internal state* of an object passed to it, but it **cannot reassign the caller's reference** to a different object.
- ✅ Method names must be **camelCase verbs** (e.g., `computeTotal`, not `Compute_Total`).
- ✅ `static` methods belong to the **class**; non-static methods belong to an **object (instance)**.
- ✅ A stack frame is created on the **call stack** when a method is invoked and destroyed when it returns.
- ✅ Two methods in the same class can have the same name **only if their parameter lists differ** (method overloading).
- ✅ Common KTU traps: confusing overloading with overriding; claiming Java is pass-by-reference; omitting `return` in non-`void` methods.
<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

Access Modifiers
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PBCST304 - OBJECT ORIENTED PROGRAMMING
> - **Module:** Module Module 1
> - **Topic:** Access Modifiers

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Formal Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Standard)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Access Modifiers** (also called **Visibility Modifiers** or **Access Specifiers**) in Object-Oriented Programming are reserved keywords that control the **visibility**, **accessibility**, and **scope** of classes, methods, constructors, and data members across different packages, classes, and inheritance hierarchies. They are the cornerstone of the OOP principle of **Encapsulation** and **Data Hiding**.

In Java (the prescribed language for KTU PBCST304), there are exactly **four** access modifiers:

1. `private`
2. `default` (also called *package-private* — no keyword is written)
3. `protected`
4. `public`

There is also a non-access modifier `static`, `final`, `abstract`, etc., but those are **not** access modifiers.

### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The "House Security" Model

Imagine your house has multiple zones:

| Zone | Real-world analogy | Java access modifier |
|---|---|---|
| Your personal diary | Only you can read it | `private` |
| Your bedroom | Family members + you | `protected` |
| Your living room | Family + close friends (same package/family) | `default` |
| Your front lawn | Anyone in society | `public` |

> [!NOTE]
> Think of access modifiers as **locks on doors**. Each modifier decides *who holds the key*: only the owner, the family, the neighborhood, or the entire city.

### 1.3 The Four Pillars of Access Control — At a Glance

```
private   →  strictest, only SAME class
default   →  SAME package (folder)
protected →  SAME package + subclasses (even in other packages)
public    →  accessible EVERYWHERE
```

> [!TIP]
> **KTU 2024 Examiner Tip:** If a question says *"no keyword is used"*, the answer is **default access**, NOT public. This is one of the most common mistakes in board exams.

### 1.4 Why Access Modifiers Exist — Engineering Motivation

- **Security:** Prevent unauthorized manipulation of sensitive data.
- **Maintainability:** Allow internal restructuring without breaking external code.
- **Encapsulation support:** Enforce the OOP rule *"internal details should be hidden from outside world"*.
- **Controlled inheritance:** Let parent classes expose *only* the parts that child classes should inherit.

---

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 The Access Modifier Hierarchy

```
MOST RESTRICTIVE  ←—————————————————→  LEAST RESTRICTIVE
   private   →   default   →   protected   →   public
```

This is a **strict ordering**. Whatever is accessible to `private` is automatically accessible to `default`, `protected`, and `public`. Conversely, `public` gives the maximum freedom.

### 2.2 Detailed Breakdown of Each Modifier

#### (a) `private` Access Modifier
- **Scope:** Only within the **same class**.
- **NOT accessible** in: subclasses (even same package), other classes in same package, or any class in another package.
- **Use case:** Data members of a class that hold sensitive state (e.g., bank balance, password).

#### (b) `default` (Package-Private) Access Modifier
- **Keyword:** *None* — if you write no access modifier, this is what you get.
- **Scope:** Within the **same package**.
- **NOT accessible** in: subclasses in other packages, classes in other packages.
- **Use case:** Helper classes/methods that are meant to be internal to a package.

#### (c) `protected` Access Modifier
- **Scope:** Within the **same package** **PLUS** subclasses in **any package** (via inheritance).
- **NOT accessible** in: non-subclass classes in other packages.
- **Use case:** Methods meant to be overridden by child classes, but still hidden from unrelated classes.

#### (d) `public` Access Modifier
- **Scope:** **Everywhere** — any class in any package.
- **Use case:** API methods, utility functions, constants meant for global use.

### 2.3 KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet — Access Visibility Matrix

The table below is the **single most important table** for KTU board exams. Memorize it.

| Modifier | Same Class | Same Package (non-subclass) | Subclass (same package) | Subclass (different package) | Other Package (non-subclass) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `private`   | ✅ Yes | ❌ No  | ❌ No  | ❌ No  | ❌ No  |
| `default`   | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | ❌ No  | ❌ No  |
| `protected` | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | ❌ No  |
| `public`    | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes |

> [!NOTE]
> **Mnemonic for the matrix — "PDPP":** *Private → Default → Protected → Public* — each step *adds* more accessibility. This is the exact order KTU examiners expect students to write.

### 2.4 Access Modifiers Applicable To What?

| Element | `private` | `default` | `protected` | `public` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Class       | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |
| Variable    | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Method      | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Constructor | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Interface   | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ (implicit) |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Top-level classes** in Java can ONLY be `public` or `default`. You cannot declare a top-level class as `private` or `protected`. This is a guaranteed 1-mark question in KTU Part A.

### 2.5 Real-World Engineering Utility

- **Banking software:** Account balance declared `private`, exposed via `public` getter/setter with validation logic.
- **Android development:** UI components use `public` access for framework callbacks.
- **Library design (e.g., Java's `Collections` framework):** Internal helper classes are `default` (package-private) to keep APIs clean.
- **Microservices & APIs:** Only `public` methods form the API contract; everything else is hidden via `private`/`protected`.

### 2.6 Key Logical Rules (Why & How)

- **Why `protected` allows different-package access only via inheritance?**
  Because the JVM checks accessibility through the **inheritance chain**, not through object reference. A subclass in another package must *extend* the parent to access protected members.

- **How does `default` differ from `protected` in the same package?**
  They behave **identically** inside the same package. The difference appears only when subclasses cross package boundaries.

- **Why is `public` not always best?**
  Exposing too much increases **coupling**, makes refactoring harder, and violates the *Principle of Least Privilege* — a cornerstone of secure software engineering.

---

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Comprehensive Java Program Demonstrating All Four Modifiers

Below is a **single executable program** that shows every access modifier in action, with comments explaining *why* each line compiles or fails.

```java
package university;            // Package "university"

public class Student {        // TOP-LEVEL class — can only be public or default

    private   int rollNo      = 101;        // STEP 1: only Student class can access
                String name   = "Anu";      // STEP 2: default access — university package only
    protected double cgpa    = 8.7;        // STEP 3: university package + all subclasses
    public    String college  = "KTU";      // STEP 4: accessible everywhere

    private void privateMethod() {           // STEP 5
        System.out.println("Private method called");
    }

    void defaultMethod() {                   // STEP 6
        System.out.println("Default method called");
    }

    protected void protectedMethod() {       // STEP 7
        System.out.println("Protected method called");
    }

    public void publicMethod() {             // STEP 8
        System.out.println("Public method called");
    }

    public void displayAll() {
        // INSIDE THE SAME CLASS — all four are accessible.
        System.out.println(rollNo);          // ✅ private OK
        System.out.println(name);            // ✅ default OK
        System.out.println(cgpa);            // ✅ protected OK
        System.out.println(college);         // ✅ public OK
    }
}
```

### 3.2 Step-by-Step Logical Walkthrough

**Step 1 — `private int rollNo`**
   - Logic: Restrict direct read/write to the Student class.
   - Consequence: Even subclasses like `EngineeringStudent` cannot access `rollNo` directly.

**Step 2 — `String name` (default)**
   - Logic: Visible inside the `university` package only.
   - Consequence: A non-student class in the same package (e.g., `UniversityAdmin`) can read it, but classes outside `university` cannot.

**Step 3 — `protected double cgpa`**
   - Logic: Visible inside `university` package + any subclass anywhere.
   - Consequence: An `EngineeringStudent` in another package can read `cgpa`, but a non-related class in another package cannot.

**Step 4 — `public String college`**
   - Logic: Global visibility.
   - Consequence: Any class, anywhere, can read `college`.

**Step 5 to 8 — Method Visibility**
   - Same rules apply to methods. Inside `displayAll()`, all four methods are callable because we are within the same class.

### 3.3 Testing the Access from Different Contexts

#### Context A — Same Class (always ✅)

```java
package university;
public class DemoSameClass {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s = new Student();
        System.out.println(s.rollNo);    // ✅ PRIVATE — accessible because same class context
        System.out.println(s.name);      // ✅ DEFAULT
        System.out.println(s.cgpa);      // ✅ PROTECTED
        System.out.println(s.college);   // ✅ PUBLIC
    }
}
```
> **Logic:** `DemoSameClass` is INSIDE `Student.java`'s perspective — when you access `private` from within the same `.java` file's class body, the JVM allows it. Wait — actually, `DemoSameClass` is a *different* class, so accessing `s.rollNo` would be a **compile-time error**.

#### Context B — Same Package, Different Class (✅ default, protected, public; ❌ private)

```java
package university;
public class SamePackageTest {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s = new Student();
        // System.out.println(s.rollNo);   // ❌ COMPILE ERROR — private
        System.out.println(s.name);        // ✅ default OK
        System.out.println(s.cgpa);        // ✅ protected OK
        System.out.println(s.college);     // ✅ public OK
    }
}
```

#### Context C — Different Package, Subclass (✅ protected, public; ❌ private, default)

```java
package college;                                // DIFFERENT package
import university.Student;
public class EngineeringStudent extends Student {
    void show() {
        // System.out.println(rollNo);         // ❌ private — not accessible
        // System.out.println(name);           // ❌ default — different package
        System.out.println(cgpa);              // ✅ protected — accessible via inheritance
        System.out.println(college);           // ✅ public
    }
}
```

#### Context D — Different Package, Non-Subclass (✅ public only)

```java
package external;
import university.Student;
public class Outsider {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s = new Student();
        // System.out.println(s.rollNo);        // ❌ private
        // System.out.println(s.name);          // ❌ default
        // System.out.println(s.cgpa);          // ❌ protected
        System.out.println(s.college);          // ✅ public
    }
}
```

### 3.4 Analytical Equation — Calculating Effective Accessibility

We can model accessibility as a **logical OR** over allowed contexts:

$$
A_{\text{effective}}(x) \;=\; \bigvee_{i=1}^{n} \text{context}_i \;\land\; \text{modifier permits } \text{context}_i
$$

Where each $\text{context}_i$ is one of the **5 columns** in the visibility matrix (Section 2.3). A member $x$ is accessible in context $C$ **iff** the modifier explicitly permits $C$.

For example, for a `protected` member:

$$
A_{\text{protected}} \;=\; \text{(same class)} \lor \text{(same pkg)} \lor \text{(subclass any pkg)}
$$

Explicitly excluded contexts:

$$
\neg A_{\text{protected}} \;=\; \text{(other-package, non-subclass)}
$$

This equation is the **formal specification** of the matrix. KTU examiners may ask you to *"justify"* the matrix in Part B — use this reasoning.

### 3.5 Comparative Logic Tree

```
                    Is it the SAME CLASS?
                            │
                  ┌─────────┴─────────┐
                 YES                 NO
                  │                   │
              ALL OK ✅        Is it SAME PACKAGE?
                                    │
                          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
                         YES                 NO
                          │                   │
              default, protected,    Is it a SUBCLASS?
                public OK ✅             │
                                  ┌──────┴──────┐
                                 YES           NO
                                  │             │
                          protected,        only
                          public OK ✅    public OK ✅
```

This decision tree mirrors the visibility matrix **exactly** and is the fastest way to answer any KTU short question.
