## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

---

### 📘 PART A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

#### **Question 1** `[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023, Model Question Paper]`

> Explain the four access modifiers in Java with their scope of accessibility.

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

Java provides **four** access modifiers that control the visibility of classes, methods, and data members:

1. **`private`** — Members are accessible **only within the same class** in which they are declared. It is the most restrictive modifier and is used to enforce data hiding.

2. **`default`** — When **no access modifier** is specified, the member has *package-level* access. It is accessible to all classes within the **same package** but not to classes in other packages.

3. **`protected`** — Members are accessible within the **same package** and also to **subclasses in any package** (even outside the original package, through inheritance).

4. **`public`** — Members are accessible from **any class in any package**. It is the least restrictive modifier.

> The visibility order from most to least restrictive is: `private → default → protected → public`.

*(Examiner's note: Full marks are awarded only if the student mentions that `default` has no keyword.)*

---

#### **Question 2** `[KTU University Exam – May 2024, Supplementary]`

> Can a top-level class in Java be declared as `private` or `protected`? Justify your answer.

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

**No**, a top-level class in Java **cannot** be declared as `private` or `protected`. A top-level class can only have one of two access levels:

- `public` — accessible from any package.
- *default* (no modifier) — accessible only within the same package.

**Justification:** A `private` class would be inaccessible to any other class, making it impossible to instantiate or use. A `protected` class would require inheritance for access, but top-level classes cannot be inherited in a way that requires this access level. Hence the Java language designers restricted top-level class modifiers to `public` or default only.

> However, **inner classes** (nested classes) can be declared as `private`, `protected`, or `default`.

---

### 📕 PART B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks, Internal Choice)

#### **Question A (14 Marks)** `[KTU University Exam – Dec 2024, Expected Pattern]`

> (a) **Discuss in detail the four access modifiers in Java with a suitable example program. Show the visibility of members from different contexts.** **(7 marks)**
>
> (b) **Explain with examples why `protected` access is allowed in subclasses even when they are in different packages. How does this differ from default access?** **(7 marks)**

**Model Solution:**

**(a) Detailed explanation with example program (7 marks):**

The four access modifiers in Java, in increasing order of visibility, are: `private`, `default`, `protected`, `public`. Each controls where a class member (variable, method, or constructor) can be accessed from.

Consider the following program that demonstrates all four:

```java
package ktu.demo;

public class Account {
    private   int accNo = 12345;
              String holder = "Rahul";        // default
    protected double balance = 50000.75;
    public    String bank = "SBI";

    public void show() {
        System.out.println(accNo + " " + holder + " " + balance + " " + bank);
    }
}
```

| Access from | `accNo` (private) | `holder` (default) | `balance` (protected) | `bank` (public) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Inside `Account`        | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Same package, other class | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Subclass, different pkg   | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Non-subclass, other pkg   | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |

The visibility matrix summarizes the access rules clearly.

**(b) Why `protected` works across packages via inheritance (7 marks):**

The `protected` modifier is designed to support the OOP concept of inheritance while still preserving encapsulation. The Java compiler allows a subclass — even one declared in a *different package* — to access `protected` members of its parent. This is because the subclass **IS-A** parent (semantic relationship), so it logically needs access to inherited state and behavior.

**Example:**

```java
package external.pkg;
import ktu.demo.Account;

public class SavingsAccount extends Account {
    void display() {
        // System.out.println(holder);    // ❌ default NOT accessible
        System.out.println(balance);       // ✅ protected accessible
        System.out.println(bank);          // ✅ public accessible
    }
}
```

**Difference from default access:**

- `default` members are accessible only within the *same package*. If a subclass lives in another package, it **cannot** access default members, even though it inherits the parent's *type*. The compiler enforces this strictly.
- `protected` extends the visibility *specifically* for subclasses across packages, while still preventing access from non-related classes in other packages.

> Thus, `protected` = `default` + "subclasses anywhere in the world". This distinction is fundamental to designing extensible OOP class hierarchies.

---

#### **Question B (14 Marks — Alternative Choice)** `[KTU University Exam – June 2024, Expected Pattern]`

> (a) **Explain the concept of encapsulation. How do access modifiers help achieve encapsulation in Java? Illustrate with an example.** **(7 marks)**
>
> (b) **Write a Java program that demonstrates the use of `private` data members and `public` getter/setter methods. Explain how access modifiers protect data integrity.** **(7 marks)**

**Model Solution:**

**(a) Encapsulation and access modifiers (7 marks):**

**Encapsulation** is the OOP principle of *bundling data and the methods that operate on that data into a single unit (class)* and *restricting direct access to some of the object's components*. It is the practice of **data hiding**.

Access modifiers are the **mechanism** by which encapsulation is implemented in Java. By declaring data members as `private`, we prevent external code from modifying them directly. Public getter and setter methods then provide *controlled* access — allowing validation, logging, or computation before the data is exposed or changed.

**Example illustrating encapsulation:**

```java
public class Employee {
    private String name;          // hidden data
    private double salary;        // hidden data

    public void setSalary(double s) {
        if (s >= 0) {             // validation logic
            salary = s;
        }
    }

    public double getSalary() {
        return salary;
    }
}
```

Here, `salary` cannot be set to a negative value externally because the `setSalary` method enforces the rule. Without `private` access, any external code could assign `emp.salary = -1000`, violating data integrity.

**(b) Program with private members and public getters/setters (7 marks):**

```java
package ktu.bank;

public class BankAccount {
    private int accountNumber;
    private String accountHolder;
    private double balance;

    public BankAccount(int accNo, String name, double initialBalance) {
        this.accountNumber = accNo;
        this.accountHolder = name;
        if (initialBalance >= 0) {
            this.balance = initialBalance;
        } else {
            this.balance = 0;
        }
    }

    public int getAccountNumber() {
        return accountNumber;
    }

    public String getAccountHolder() {
        return accountHolder;
    }

    public double getBalance() {
        return balance;
    }

    public void deposit(double amount) {
        if (amount > 0) {
            balance += amount;
            System.out.println("Deposited: " + amount);
        } else {
            System.out.println("Invalid deposit amount");
        }
    }

    public void withdraw(double amount) {
        if (amount > 0 && amount <= balance) {
            balance -= amount;
            System.out.println("Withdrawn: " + amount);
        } else {
            System.out.println("Insufficient balance or invalid amount");
        }
    }
}
```

**Explanation of how access modifiers protect data integrity:**

- The fields `accountNumber`, `accountHolder`, and `balance` are declared `private`. This means **no external class** can directly modify them.
- The only way to change the balance is via `deposit()` or `withdraw()`, both of which include **validation logic** to reject negative or invalid amounts.
- `accountNumber` is read-only because only a `getter` is provided, not a `setter`. This prevents anyone from changing the account number after creation.
- If these fields were declared `public`, external code could do `acc.balance = -999999`, bypassing all checks and corrupting data.

> This is a textbook case of how **access modifiers + validation methods** form the practical implementation of **encapsulation** — one of the four pillars of OOP.

---

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Pitfall — Common Mistakes That Cost Marks**
>
> 1. **Writing "default = public"** — this is WRONG. `default` access is restricted to the same package. Many students confuse the two.
> 2. **Forgetting that `default` has NO keyword** — if a question shows `int x = 5;` without any modifier, it is `default`, NOT public.
> 3. **Saying "top-level classes can be `protected`"** — they CANNOT. Only inner/nested classes can.
> 4. **Confusing `protected` with `default`** in cross-package scenarios — `default` does NOT cross package boundaries, even for subclasses.
> 5. **Not mentioning that `protected` allows access only through inheritance**, not via object reference of the parent type from outside.
> 6. **Writing `friendly` instead of `default`** — Java does not have a `friendly` keyword; this was an old C++ terminology that is technically incorrect for Java.
> 7. **Omitting the visibility matrix in long answers** — examiners give extra credit (often 1–2 marks) when the matrix is clearly drawn.

---

### ✅ Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!TIP]
> **Rapid Revision Checklist — Read this 5 minutes before the exam:**

- **Four access modifiers in Java:** `private`, `default` (no keyword), `protected`, `public`.
- **Order of restrictiveness:** `private → default → protected → public`.
- **`private`** → only the same class.
- **`default`** → same package (no keyword used).
- **`protected`** → same package + subclasses in any package.
- **`public`** → everywhere, no restrictions.
- **Top-level classes** can only be `public` or `default`. NOT `private`/`protected`.
- **All four** modifiers can be applied to **variables, methods, and constructors**.
- **Encapsulation** is implemented primarily via `private` data + `public` getter/setter methods.
- The **visibility matrix** (5 contexts × 4 modifiers) is the single most important table for this topic.
- `protected` ≠ `default`; the difference shows up **only** in cross-package inheritance scenarios.
- **Mnemonic PDPP** (Private → Default → Protected → Public) gives the order of increasing visibility.

---

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.title: this Keyword
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** PBCST304 - OBJECT ORIENTED PROGRAMMING > - **Module:** Module 1 > - **Topic:** this Keyword # SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview ## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition The **`this` keyword** in Java (and analogous constructs in C++/Python) is an **implicit, non-static reference variable** that holds the memory address of the **currently executing object**. It is automatically created by the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) inside every instance method, constructor, or instance initializer block, and it points to the object on whose behalf the method or constructor has been invoked. > [!IMPORTANT] > **KTU Syllabus Highlight (PBCST304 - Module 1):** > Under the 2024 Scheme, `this` keyword is classified as a **fundamental reference-resolution mechanism** within the "Classes and Objects" cognitive cluster. Students are expected to demonstrate its application in disambiguating instance variables, constructor chaining, and method chaining. ### Key Properties of `this` - It is a **final** reference (cannot be reassigned to point to another object). - It is **not** a static member; therefore, it **cannot** be used inside a `static` method or `static` block. - It is the **first parameter** implicitly passed to every instance method (you do not write it, the compiler does). - Its lifetime is bound to the **object's lifetime** on the heap. ## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The "Remote Control" Model > [!NOTE] > **Intuitive Analogy: The Self-Aware Worker** > Imagine a construction worker named **Ravi** working on multiple identical houses in a colony. Each house is a separate *object* (instance). When Ravi is told, *"Paint YOUR house"*, the word **"YOUR"** is analogous to the `this` keyword. It is a self-referential pointer — a built-in way for an object to say, *"I am referring to myself, not to any other object of the same class."* Just as Ravi can carry his own toolbox (`this.someProperty`) or call his own phone (`this.someMethod()`), any object can use `this` to manipulate its own state. ## 1.3 The 6 Canonical Uses of `this` in Java | # | Use Case | One-Line Description | |---|----------|---------------------| | 1 | **Instance Variable Disambiguation** | Resolves naming conflict between local/parameter variables and instance variables | | 2 | **Constructor Chaining** | Invokes another constructor within the same class using `this(args)` | | 3 | **Method Chaining** | Returns the current object to enable fluent-style calls | | 4 | **Passing Current Object** | Used as an actual argument to other methods | | 5 | **Returning Current Object** | A method can return `this` to allow cascaded invocations | | 6 | **As an Argument in Constructor Call** | `this` can be passed to another constructor's invocation statement | > [!WARNING] > **Common Misconception:** `this` does **NOT** refer to the *class* — it refers to the *object instance*. The class itself is referenced via `ClassName.class` (a `Class` object), which is a fundamentally different concept. # SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ## 2.1 Operational Breakdown — How `this` Works Under the JVM The Java compiler transforms every instance method behind the scenes. Consider the following conceptual mapping: $$\text{Source Code:} \quad \texttt{obj.display(name);}$$ $$\text{Compiler-Generated Bytecode Equivalent:} \quad \texttt{void display(String name) \{ this.name = name; \}}$$ Where the compiler silently inserts `this` as a hidden first parameter: $$\texttt{void display(\textbf{Object this}, String name)}$$ ### Step-by-Step Internal Logic - **Step 1 — Object Instantiation:** When `new Student()` is executed, the JVM allocates heap memory and assigns the new object's reference to the local variable `s1`. - **Step 2 — Method Invocation:** When `s1.setName("Ravi")` is called, the JVM pushes `s1`'s reference onto the operand stack as the **first (hidden) argument**. - **Step 3 — Binding to `this`:** Inside `setName`, this hidden argument is bound to the local `this` reference variable. - **Step 4 — Member Access:** Every unprefixed instance member access (`name = name`) is rewritten internally as `this.name = name`. > [!TIP] > This is precisely why static methods cannot use `this` — they are not tied to any specific object, so there is no reference to bind. ## 2.2 The Constructor Chaining Rule Set (KTU High-Yield) Constructor chaining using `this()` follows strict rules that the KTU examiner frequently tests: $$\text{Constructor Chaining Invariant:} \quad \texttt{this()} \text{ must be the FIRST statement in the constructor body}$$ Additional binding rules: $$\text{Rule 1:} \quad \forall c \in \text{Constructors},\ \texttt{this()} \rightarrow \text{Statement Position} = 1$$ $$\text{Rule 2:} \quad \texttt{this()} \ \text{and} \ \texttt{super()} \ \text{cannot coexist in the same constructor}$$ $$\text{Rule 3:} \quad \text{Recursive} \ \texttt{this()} \ \text{invocation causes} \ \textit{StackOverflowError}$$ ## 2.3 KTU Formula / Cheat Sheet Table > [!NOTE] > The following table is the **single most important rapid-revision asset** for any KTU 2024 Scheme exam on this topic. Memorize the boundaries. | # | Scenario | Valid Usage of `this`? | Compiler Action | |---|----------|----------------------|-----------------| | 1 | Inside instance method | ✅ Yes | Refers to current invoking object | | 2 | Inside constructor | ✅ Yes | Refers to object being constructed | | 3 | Inside static method | ❌ No | Compile-time error: *"non-static variable this cannot be referenced from a static context"* | | 4 | Inside static block | ❌ No | Compile-time error | | 5 | As a method parameter | ✅ Yes | Passes the current object reference | | 6 | As a return value | ✅ Yes | Enables method chaining | | 7 | Inside `this()` call | ✅ Yes (constructor chaining) | Must be the first statement | | 8 | Inside anonymous inner class | ⚠️ Restricted | Refers to outer class's instance, not inner | ## 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility - **Builder Design Pattern (Gang of Four):** `this` is the linchpin of fluent APIs, e.g., `new HttpRequestBuilder().setUrl(...).setMethod(...).build()`. - **Event Handling Frameworks:** GUI libraries (JavaFX, Swing) use `this` to bind an event source to its handler. - **ORM Frameworks (Hibernate, JPA):** Entity classes return `this` from setter methods to enable chained configuration. - **Chained Stream APIs (Java 8+):** Although streams are functional, builder-style utilities still leverage `this`-chaining. # SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix ## 3.1 Exhaustive Worked Example — Instance Variable Disambiguation Below is the **canonical KTU textbook scenario** where parameter names shadow instance variables. The derivation shows how `this` resolves the ambiguity. ### Source Code ```java class Student { private String name; private int rollNo; public Student(String name, int rollNo) { // Without 'this', both LHS and RHS would refer to the parameter this.name = name; this.rollNo = rollNo; } public void display() { System.out.println("Name: " + this.name + ", Roll: " + this.rollNo); } } ``` ### Logical Derivation — Symbol by Symbol Let us denote the parameter symbol as $p$ and the instance variable symbol as $i$. The compiler's name-resolution algorithm proceeds as: $$\text{Name Lookup Order} = \begin{cases} \text{Local Variable Scope} \rightarrow \text{Block Scope} \rightarrow \text{Instance Scope (via this)} \end{cases}$$ **Step 1 — Constructor Invocation:** The JVM receives a call `new Student("Ravi", 42)`. It allocates a new `Student` object on the heap and stores its reference internally as `this_ref`. **Step 2 — Hidden Parameter Binding:** The constructor's signature is rewritten by the compiler as: $$\texttt{public Student(\textbf{Student this}, String name, int rollNo)}$$ **Step 3 — Ambiguity Resolution:** Consider the bare statement `name = name;`. The compiler applies scope-resolution: $$\text{Left side } \texttt{name} \rightarrow \text{Compiler searches} \rightarrow \text{Found in local scope (parameter)} = p$$ $$\text{Right side } \texttt{name} \rightarrow \text{Compiler searches} \rightarrow \text{Found in local scope (parameter)} = p$$ Therefore, the assignment becomes $p = p$, which is a **no-op** and effectively drops the data. **Step 4 — Inserting `this`:** By writing `this.name = name;`, we force the LHS to bypass local scope: $$\text{LHS} \rightarrow \texttt{this.name} \rightarrow \text{Searches instance scope} \rightarrow i$$ $$\text{RHS} \rightarrow \texttt{name} \rightarrow \text{Searches local scope first} \rightarrow p$$ The resulting assignment is $i = p$, which correctly stores the parameter into the instance variable. **Step 5 — Final Memory State:** $$\text{Heap Object at } \texttt{this\_ref} \rightarrow \{ \texttt{name} = \text{"Ravi"}, \texttt{rollNo} = 42 \}$$ ## 3.2 Exhaustive Worked Example — Constructor Chaining ```java class Box { int length, breadth, height; // 1-arg constructor Box(int side) { this(side, side, side); // calls 3-arg constructor System.out.println("Cube created"); } // 3-arg constructor Box(int length, int breadth, int height) { this.length = length; this.breadth = breadth; this.height = height; } int volume() { return this.length * this.breadth * this.height; } } ``` ### Derivation of Control Flow When a client calls `new Box(5)`: **Step 1:** JVM invokes `Box(int side)`. **Step 2:** The first statement `this(side, side, side)` is executed. The compiler verifies: $$\text{Position Check:} \quad \text{line}_1 = \texttt{this(side, side, side)} \rightarrow \text{Position} = 1 \ \checkmark$$ **Step 3:** Control transfers to `Box(int, int, int)`. Inside that constructor, `this` still refers to the **same partially-constructed object**. **Step 4:** Instance variables are assigned: $i_{length} = 5$, $i_{breadth} = 5$, $i_{height} = 5$. **Step 5:** Control returns to the original 1-arg constructor. The `println` executes. **Step 6:** Constructor completes; `this` reference is released to GC eligibility. ## 3.3 Analytical Matrix — All 6 Use Cases Mapped to Code Patterns | Use Case | Code Pattern | When to Apply | |----------|-------------|---------------| | **Disambiguation** | `this.x = x;` | Parameter shadows field | | **Constructor Chaining** | `this(a, b);` | Reduce code duplication across overloads | | **Method Chaining** | `return this;` | Fluent API design (Builder pattern) | | **Pass as Argument** | `helper.process(this);` | An object needs to give itself to another | | **Return Current Object** | `return this;` from setter | Enable cascading | | **Inner Class Reference** | `OuterClass.this.field;` | Resolve shadowing in non-static inner classes | ## 3.4 Derivation of the Hidden Parameter Cost For a method declared as: $$\texttt{public void display(String name, int age)}$$ The compiler generates the following effective signature: $$\texttt{public void display(\textbf{Object this}, String name, int age)}$$ The size overhead per instance method call is therefore exactly the size of a reference: $$\text{Memory Overhead} = \text{sizeof(JVM reference)} = \text{4 bytes (32-bit) or 8 bytes (64-bit with compressed oops)}$$ > [!NOTE] > This explains why **static methods are slightly more memory-efficient** at call time — no `this` reference is pushed onto the operand stack. # SECTION 4: Structural Diagrams & Schematics ## 4.1 Memory Architecture — `this` Binding to Heap Object ```mermaid flowchart TB classDef stackStyle fill:#FFE4B5,stroke:#FF8C00,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef heapStyle fill:#B0E0E6,stroke:#4682B4,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef arrowStyle fill:none,stroke:#228B22,stroke-width:2px subgraph STACK["STACK MEMORY"] S1["s1

List any two of its uses.** **Model Answer (3 Marks):** The `this` keyword in Java is an **implicit reference variable** that refers to the **currently invoking object** of a class. It is automatically passed by the JVM as a hidden parameter to every non-static method and constructor, and it cannot be used inside static contexts. **Two Uses:** 1. **Disambiguation:** `this.variableName` is used to differentiate instance variables from local/parameter variables when both share the same name (e.g., `this.name = name;` inside a constructor). 2. **Constructor Chaining:** `this(argument_list)` is used inside a constructor to invoke another constructor of the same class, reducing code duplication (e.g., `this(side, side, side);`). --- ### Question 2 **[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023, Supplementary Exam]** **Why can't the `this` keyword be used inside a static method? Justify with a one-line reason.** **Model Answer (3 Marks):** The `this` keyword refers to the **current instance object** of a class. Static methods belong to the **class itself** rather than to any specific object, and therefore there is no instance context for `this` to refer to. Hence, attempting to use `this` inside a static method results in a **compile-time error**: *"non-static variable this cannot be referenced from a static context."* --- ## 5.2 PART B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each, Module Internal Choice) ### Question A (14 Marks) **[KTU University Exam – Dec 2024, End Semester Evaluation]** **(a)** Explain any **four uses of the `this` keyword** in Java with suitable code snippets. **(7 Marks)** **(b)** Write a complete Java program demonstrating **constructor chaining** using the `this()` call. Explain the rules that must be followed when using `this()` for constructor chaining. **(7 Marks)** --- #### Model Solution for (a) — 4 Uses of `this` **Use 1: Disambiguation of Instance Variables** ```java class Employee { private int id; private String name; Employee(int id, String name) { this.id = id; // LHS = instance var, RHS = parameter this.name = name; } } ``` *Explanation:* Without `this`, the statement `id = id;` would be a self-assignment where the parameter `id` assigns to itself, leaving the instance variable unchanged. The `this.id` prefix forces the LHS to refer to the object's instance variable. **Use 2: Constructor Chaining** ```java class Rectangle { int w, h; Rectangle(int w, int h) { this.w = w; this.h = h; } Rectangle(int side) { this(side, side); // chains to 2-arg constructor } } ``` *Explanation:* The 1-arg constructor delegates the actual initialization to the 2-arg constructor, eliminating code duplication. **Use 3: Returning Current Object (Method Chaining)** ```java class Counter { int value = 0; Counter increment() { this.value++; return this; // returns current object } } // Client: new Counter().increment().increment().increment(); ``` *Explanation:* Returning `this` allows multiple method invocations on the same object in a single expression, producing a fluent API. **Use 4: Passing Current Object as Argument** ```java class Team { void register(Coach c) { System.out.println("Registered with " + c.name); } void joinTournament() { Coach c = new Coach(); c.register(this); // passes current Team object to Coach } } ``` *Explanation:* A method can pass the current object (`this`) to another method or constructor, enabling two-way communication between collaborating objects. --- #### Model Solution for (b) — Constructor Chaining Program ```java class Time { private int hours, minutes, seconds; // 3-arg constructor (master) Time(int hours, int minutes, int seconds) { this.hours = hours; this.minutes = minutes; this.seconds = seconds; System.out.println("3-arg constructor invoked"); } // 2-arg constructor Time(int hours, int minutes) { this(hours, minutes, 0); // chains to 3-arg System.out.println("2-arg constructor invoked"); } // 1-arg constructor Time(int hours) { this(hours, 0); // chains to 2-arg System.out.println("1-arg constructor invoked"); } // default constructor Time() { this(0); // chains to 1-arg System.out.println("Default constructor invoked"); } void display() { System.out.println(this.hours + ":" + this.minutes + ":" + this.seconds); } public static void main(String[] args) { Time t = new Time(10, 30, 45); t.display(); } } ``` **Output:** ``` 3-arg constructor invoked 10:30:45 ``` **Rules for Constructor Chaining using `this()`:** 1. **`this()` must be the first statement** in the constructor body. Placing it anywhere else causes a compile-time error: *"call to this must be first statement in constructor."* 2. **`this()` and `super()` cannot appear in the same constructor**, because both must occupy the first-statement slot, which can only hold one of them. 3. **Recursive constructor invocation is illegal.** If constructor A calls `this()` which resolves to constructor B, and B calls `this()` resolving back to A, the compiler detects a cyclic dependency and reports: *"recursive constructor invocation."* 4. **The compiler automatically inserts `super()` as the first statement** in any constructor that does not explicitly call `this()` or `super()`. This is why the no-arg `Time()` constructor still compiles even without an explicit `super()`. --- ### Question B (14 Marks) — ALTERNATIVE **[KTU University Exam – June 2024, Supplementary Exam]** **(a)** Differentiate between `this` keyword and `super` keyword in Java with a tabular comparison. Provide one code example for each. **(7 Marks)** **(b)** Design a Java class `Account` with fields `accountNumber`, `holderName`, and `balance`. Implement **constructor overloading** using the `this` keyword to support: (i) all three parameters, (ii) only account number (default balance 0.0), and (iii) no-argument constructor (default values). Include a method to display account details. **(7 Marks)** --- #### Model Solution for (a) — `this` vs `super` Comparison | Feature | `this` Keyword | `super` Keyword | |---------|---------------|----------------| | **Refers to** | Current object instance | Immediate parent (superclass) object | | **Used for** | Resolving instance-level ambiguity | Accessing overridden/parent members | | **Variable Access** | `this.varName` (current class field) | `super.varName` (parent class field) | | **Method Call** | `this.methodName()` (current class method) | `super.methodName()` (parent class method) | | **Constructor Call** | `this(args)` — calls another constructor of same class | `super(args)` — calls parent class constructor | | **Position Rule** | Must be first statement if used in constructor | Must be first statement if used in constructor | | **Mutual Exclusivity** | Cannot coexist with `super()` in same constructor | Cannot coexist with `this()` in same constructor | | **Scope** | Available throughout the object's lifetime | Available only in inheritance hierarchies | **Code Example for `this`:** ```java class Demo { int x; Demo(int x) { this.x = x; // disambiguates } } ``` **Code Example for `super`:** ```java class Parent { int x = 10; } class Child extends Parent { int x = 20; void show() { System.out.println(super.x); // prints 10 (parent's x) System.out.println(this.x); // prints 20 (child's x) } } ``` --- #### Model Solution for (b) — Account Class with Constructor Chaining ```java class Account { private String accountNumber; private String holderName; private double balance; // (iii) No-arg constructor Account() { this("NOT_ASSIGNED", "UNKNOWN", 0.0); System.out.println("No-arg constructor invoked"); } // (ii) Constructor with only account number Account(String accountNumber) { this(accountNumber, "DEFAULT_HOLDER", 0.0); System.out.println("1-arg constructor invoked"); } // (i) Master constructor with all three parameters Account(String accountNumber, String holderName, double balance) { this.accountNumber = accountNumber; this.holderName = holderName; this.balance = balance; System.out.println("3-arg constructor invoked"); } void display() { System.out.println("Account: " + this.accountNumber + ", Holder: " + this.holderName + ", Balance: " + this.balance); } public static void main(String[] args) { Account a1 = new Account(); Account a2 = new Account("ACC1001"); Account a3 = new Account("ACC2002", "Ravi Kumar", 25000.75); a1.display(); a2.display(); a3.display(); } } ``` **Output:** ``` 3-arg constructor invoked No-arg constructor invoked 3-arg constructor invoked 1-arg constructor invoked 3-arg constructor invoked Account: NOT_ASSIGNED, Holder: UNKNOWN, Balance: 0.0 Account: ACC1001, Holder: DEFAULT_HOLDER, Balance: 0.0 Account: ACC2002, Holder: Ravi Kumar, Balance: 25000.75 ``` > [!WARNING] > **KTU Examiner's Valuation Pitfalls — Where Students Typically Lose Marks:** > 1. **Forgetting the first-statement rule:** Writing any code before `this(...)` results in a compile-time error. KTU examiners deduct 1–2 marks for this. > 2. **Using `this` in a static context:** Many students write `this` inside `main()` without realizing `main` is static. This is the **#1 most common error** flagged in KTU valuation reports. > 3. **Recursive constructor calls:** Designing a chain that loops back causes compile-time error. The compiler is smart enough to catch this — students must not write such code. > 4. **Confusing `this` with `super`:** Writing `super.x` when current class's `x` is intended, or vice versa, leads to wrong outputs. > 5. **Omitting the `this` prefix** when local and instance names clash: The code compiles but produces incorrect data — a logic bug worth 1 mark. --- ## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid-Revision Checklist) > [!IMPORTANT] > **Print this checklist and revise 30 minutes before the exam.** - ✅ `this` is an **implicit final reference** to the current object, automatically created by the JVM. - ✅ It is **not static**, so it is **forbidden inside static methods and static blocks** (compile-time error). - ✅ **Six canonical uses:** (1) Disambiguation, (2) Constructor chaining, (3) Method chaining, (4) Pass as argument, (5) Return current object, (6) Inner class reference resolution. - ✅ **Constructor chaining rule:** `this(args)` must be the **first statement** in the constructor. - ✅ **Mutual exclusivity:** `this()` and `super()` **cannot** coexist in the same constructor. - ✅ **Recursion is illegal:** Cyclic `this()` invocations cause compile-time error. - ✅ **Hidden parameter cost:** Every instance method call pushes `this` onto the operand stack (4 or 8 bytes). - ✅ **Object identity:** `this` holds the same memory address as the calling reference variable (`s1.setName()` → `this` == `s1`). - ✅ **Fluent API design:** Returning `this` from setters enables builder-pattern chaining. - ✅ **Common KTU question pattern:** "Differentiate `this` and `super`" — memorize the 8-row comparison table. - ✅ **Frequent trap question:** "What is the output of `System.out.println(this);` inside an instance method?" — Answer: prints the object's hashcode in hexadecimal (e.g., `Student@1540e19d`). - ✅ **For inner classes:** Use `OuterClassName.this` to disambiguate the outer class instance.

topics.title: Polymorphism: Method Overloading
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PBCST304 - OBJECT ORIENTED PROGRAMMING
> - **Module:** Module 2
> - **Topic:** Polymorphism - Method Overloading

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->

# 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

> [!NOTE]
> **Polymorphism** (from Greek: *poly* = many, *morph* = forms) is the ability of an object, function, or operator to take on **multiple forms** depending on the context in which it is invoked. In the context of the Java programming language and the KTU 2024 OOP syllabus, polymorphism is classified into two broad categories:
> 1. **Compile-Time Polymorphism** (also called *Static Binding* or *Early Binding*) — implemented via **Method Overloading**.
> 2. **Run-Time Polymorphism** (also called *Dynamic Binding* or *Late Binding*) — implemented via **Method Overriding**.

**Method Overloading** is a compile-time polymorphism mechanism in which **two or more methods within the same class (or in a parent-child relationship via inheritance)** share the **same name** but differ in their **method signatures** — specifically, the **number, type, or order of parameters** they accept. The Java compiler resolves which overloaded method to invoke at **compile time** based on the arguments passed in the call.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Syllabus Highlight (Module 2):**
> *"Polymorphism — Compile-time polymorphism: Method overloading (different parameter lists), constructor overloading, operator overloading (Java limitation), type promotion in overloading."*

The compiler's decision-making process is formally called **Static Method Dispatch** or **Compile-Time Binding**. The *binding* refers to the linkage between the **method call** and the **method definition**.

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The "One Name, Many Doors" Analogy

Imagine a building with a single reception desk labeled **"Assistant"**. When you walk in and ask the Assistant for help, your request can be of different kinds:

| Your Request Type | What the Assistant Does |
|---|---|
| "I want to **file a complaint**" | Hands you a complaint form |
| "I want to **book a meeting room**" | Checks the room scheduler |
| "I want to **request a letter of recommendation**" | Drafts a template |
| "I want to **reserve a parking slot for 4 hours**" | Allots a numbered slot |

The **name "Assistant" is one**, but the **actions differ based on the *context* of your request (i.e., the arguments you provide)**. This is exactly how **Method Overloading** works in Java: a single method name performs different tasks depending on the parameters supplied at the call site.

## 1.3 Why Method Overloading? — The Real-World Engineering Rationale

> [!NOTE]
> **Readability:** Instead of inventing unique names like `addIntegers()`, `addDoubles()`, `addThreeNumbers()`, the developer writes a single `add()` method. This is a clean, human-readable API design principle advocated by Joshua Bloch in *Effective Java* (a widely-cited industry reference).
>
> **Intuitive API Design:** Standard Java libraries exemplify this — `System.out.println(int)`, `println(double)`, `println(String)` are all overloaded versions of the same logical action: *print*. Without overloading, we'd have `printInt()`, `printDouble()`, `printString()`, which clutters the API.

---

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->

# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 The Three Pillars of Method Overloading

A method signature in Java is composed of:

$$\text{Method Signature} = \text{Method Name} \; + \; \text{Parameter List (number, types, order)}$$

The **return type** and the **access modifier** are **NOT** part of the signature for overloading purposes. Therefore, two methods cannot be overloaded by changing only the return type.

### Pillar 1 — Varying the Number of Parameters

```java
class Calculator {
    int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }
    int add(int a, int b, int c) {   // Overloaded: extra parameter
        return a + b + c;
    }
}
```

### Pillar 2 — Varying the Type of Parameters

```java
class Printer {
    void display(int n) {
        System.out.println("Integer: " + n);
    }
    void display(double d) {          // Overloaded: different type
        System.out.println("Double: " + d);
    }
    void display(String s) {          // Overloaded: another type
        System.out.println("String: " + s);
    }
}
```

### Pillar 3 — Varying the Order of Parameters

```java
class Student {
    void register(String name, int roll) {
        System.out.println("Name first, then roll");
    }
    void register(int roll, String name) {   // Overloaded: order swapped
        System.out.println("Roll first, then name");
    }
}
```

## 2.2 Rules and Constraints — KTU High-Yield Checklist

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Mandatory Rules for Valid Overloading:**
> 1. The method name **must be identical**.
> 2. The parameter list **must differ** in **at least one** of: number, type, or order.
> 3. Overloading can occur **within the same class** OR between a **subclass and superclass** (since inherited methods are accessible in the subclass).
> 4. Access modifiers and return types **can be changed freely** — they are not part of the signature.

> [!WARNING]
> **Common KTU Examiner Traps:**
> - Two methods that differ **only in return type** ⇒ **Compilation Error**.
> - Two methods that differ **only in access modifier** (e.g., `public void foo()` vs `private void foo(int a)`) ⇒ The one with the *new* signature is **a new method, not an overload** of an incompatible parameter set. The compiler checks signatures, not modifiers.
> - `static` vs non-`static` is **not** a valid overloading distinction on its own — it leads to **duplicate method definition** errors in Java.

## 2.3 Type Promotion in Method Overloading

When the exact argument type does not match any overloaded method, the Java compiler applies **automatic type promotion** (widening conversion) following the hierarchy:

$$
\text{byte} \rightarrow \text{short} \rightarrow \text{int} \rightarrow \text{long} \rightarrow \text{float} \rightarrow \text{double}
$$

$$
\text{char} \rightarrow \text{int} \rightarrow \text{long} \rightarrow \text{float} \rightarrow \text{double}
$$

If no exact match exists, the compiler promotes the argument to the **next larger type** in the hierarchy until a match is found.

> [!NOTE]
> **Widening vs. Autoboxing Priority Rule (Critical for KTU):**
> The compiler prefers **widening (primitive promotion)** over **autoboxing (primitive → Wrapper)** over **varargs**. This is a frequently tested concept.

## 2.4 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| **Concept** | **Formal Rule** | **Allowed?** |
|---|---|---|
| Different number of parameters | `add(int, int)` vs `add(int, int, int)` | ✅ Yes |
| Different type of parameters | `add(int, int)` vs `add(double, double)` | ✅ Yes |
| Different order of parameters | `register(String, int)` vs `register(int, String)` | ✅ Yes |
| Only return type differs | `int foo()` vs `double foo()` | ❌ **Compile Error** |
| Only access modifier differs | `public foo()` vs `private foo()` (same params) | ❌ **Compile Error** |
| Only `static` keyword differs | `static foo()` vs instance `foo()` (same params) | ❌ **Compile Error** |
| Widening primitive promotion | `byte` → `int` → `long` → `double` | ✅ Yes (automatic) |
| Autoboxing | `int` → `Integer` | ✅ Yes (last preference) |
| Varargs | `foo(int... x)` | ✅ Yes (lowest preference) |

## 2.5 Real-World Engineering Utility

In **enterprise Java applications**, method overloading is the foundation of fluent and ergonomic APIs. The `String` class alone contains over **19 overloaded `valueOf()` methods** to accept primitives, objects, character arrays, and subarrays. Without overloading, every utility in the JDK would force developers to memorize distinct method names — a violation of the **clean-code principle** that one *intent* should map to one *name*.

---

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->

# 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Exhaustive Walkthrough: Type Promotion Resolution

Consider the following overloaded class:

```java
class Promo {
    void show(int a)    { System.out.println("int method: "    + a); }
    void show(long a)   { System.out.println("long method: "   + a); }
    void show(double a) { System.out.println("double method: " + a); }
}
```

Now trace what happens at the call site `promo.show(5);` where `5` is a compile-time integer literal.

### Step 1 — Identify the Argument's Compile-Time Type

$$
\text{Argument: } 5 \implies \text{Type inferred as } \mathbf{int} \text{ (integer literal default)}
$$

### Step 2 — Search for an Exact Match

The compiler scans all `show()` methods in the class. It finds `void show(int a)` — an **exact match**. Compilation proceeds directly; no promotion is required.

### Step 3 — What If `show(int)` Did Not Exist?

Suppose the class only has `show(long)` and `show(double)`. The compiler applies **widening conversion** following the hierarchy:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Original type of argument} &\rightarrow \mathbf{int} \\
\text{Step 1 promotion: } \mathbf{int} &\rightarrow \mathbf{long} \quad \text{(matches show(long) — STOP)} \\
\end{aligned}
$$

If `show(long)` also did not exist, the promotion would continue:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{int} &\rightarrow \mathbf{long} \rightarrow \mathbf{float} \rightarrow \mathbf{double} \quad \text{(matches show(double) — STOP)}
\end{aligned}
$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Resolution is single-step, greedy**: The compiler promotes *only as far as necessary* to find the *first* compatible method. It does not skip levels.

## 3.2 Analytical Matrix: Ambiguity in Overloading — The "Wedding Disaster" Scenario

This is one of the **most-tested KTU question patterns**. Examine:

```java
class Demo {
    void print(float a)  { System.out.println("float: "  + a); }
    void print(double a) { System.out.println("double: " + a); }
}

class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Demo d = new Demo();
        d.print(10);   // Which one is called?
    }
}
```

### Step-by-Step Compiler Resolution

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Argument type:} \quad & \mathbf{int} \quad (\text{the literal 10}) \\
\text{Available signatures:} \quad & \text{print(float), print(double)} \\
\text{Exact match?} \quad & \text{No — no print(int).} \\
\text{Promotion step 1: int} \rightarrow & \text{float? } \checkmark \text{ FOUND — STOP.} \\
\end{aligned}
$$

**Output:** `float: 10.0`

> [!NOTE]
> The compiler does **NOT** promote further to `double` once a `float` match is found. The promotion is **single-step greedy matching**.

## 3.3 The "Autoboxing vs Widening" Conflict — KTU Classic Question

```java
class Conflict {
    void m(int  a)  { System.out.println("int"); }
    void m(Integer a) { System.out.println("Integer"); }
}

class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Conflict().m(5);
    }
}
```

### Compiler Resolution Chain

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Argument: } & \mathbf{5} \text{ (primitive int)} \\
\text{Step 1: Exact match?} & \rightarrow \text{Yes — m(int) exists. STOP.}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Output:** `int`

Now consider `new Conflict().m(5L);` (a `long` argument):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Argument: } & \mathbf{5L} \text{ (primitive long)} \\
\text{Step 1: Exact match?} & \rightarrow \text{No — only m(int) and m(Integer).} \\
\text{Step 2: Widening from long to int?} & \rightarrow \text{NOT allowed (narrowing).} \\
\text{Step 3: Autobox long to Long?} & \rightarrow \text{No matching method for Long. FAIL.} \\
\end{aligned}
$$

**Result:** **Compilation Error** — *no suitable method found*.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Rule Confirmed:** Java does **NOT** allow **narrowing implicit conversion** during overloading resolution. Widening is one-way and irreversible.

## 3.4 Analytical Matrix — The KTU "Match Resolution Priority Ladder"

| **Priority** | **Resolution Strategy** | **Example** |
|---|---|---|
| 1 (Highest) | Exact match of argument type | `int → m(int)` |
| 2 | Widening primitive promotion | `int → m(long)`, `int → m(double)` |
| 3 | Autoboxing / unboxing | `int → m(Integer)`, `Integer → m(int)` |
| 4 (Lowest) | Varargs | `int... → m(int...)` |

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Pitfall:** A conflict between **Level 2 (widening)** and **Level 3 (autoboxing)** causes **ambiguity compilation errors**. Example: a method `m(long)` and `m(Integer)` both exist, and we call `m(5)` (int) — the compiler cannot decide, raising: *"reference to m is ambiguous"*.

## 3.5 Detailed Derivation — Why Return Type Cannot Differ Alone

Consider:

```java
class Test {
    int  greet() { return 1;  }
    void greet() { return;    }   // ❌ Compile Error
}
```

### The Compiler's Logical Rejection

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Method 1:} \quad & \text{Name: greet, Params: none, Return: int} \\
\text{Method 2:} \quad & \text{Name: greet, Params: none, Return: void} \\
\text{Signatures:} \quad & \text{both are "greet()"} \\
\text{Signature comparison:} \quad & \text{IDENTICAL} \Rightarrow \text{Duplicate method.} \\
\end{aligned}
$$

**Compiler Verdict:** *"method greet() is already defined in class Test"*.

The reason: when a caller writes `greet();` as a **statement**, the compiler cannot resolve which method is intended since the return type is discarded in statement context. Even in assignment context (`int x = greet();`), allowing return-type-based overloading would create **call-site ambiguity** in cases like `greet();` used as a discarded expression.

---

# 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

## 4.1 Mermaid Diagram — Compile-Time Polymorphism Flow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Programmer writes method call: obj.add 5, 10] --> B{Compiler Resolution Phase}
    B --> C[Step 1: Search for Exact Match in obj's class]
    C --> D{Match Found?}
    D -->|Yes| E[Bind to that method - Compile Successful]
    D -->|No| F[Step 2: Apply Widening Primitive Promotion]
    F --> G{Promoted Match Found?}
    G -->|Yes| E
    G -->|No| H[Step 3: Try Autoboxing or Unboxing]
    H --> I{Wrapper Match Found?}
    I -->|Yes| E
    I -->|No| J[Step 4: Try Varargs Match]
    J --> K{Varargs Match Found?}
    K -->|Yes| E
    K -->|No| L[Compilation Error: No Suitable Method]
    E --> M[Generate .class bytecode with direct reference to chosen method]
```

```mermaid
    Promotion --> PR2[Autoboxing: int to Integer, double to Double]
    Promotion --> PR3[Varargs: int... x]
    RunTime --> Overriding[Method Overriding]
```

# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Question 1 [KTU University Exam - May 2024]

**Q: Define polymorphism. Differentiate between compile-time polymorphism and run-time polymorphism with suitable examples.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

> **Definition (1 mark):** Polymorphism is the ability of a single interface or method name to represent different underlying forms or behaviors. The term is derived from Greek — *poly* (many) and *morph* (forms).
>
> **Compile-time polymorphism (1 mark):** Also called *static binding* or *early binding*. The compiler determines which method to invoke based on the method signature at compile time. Example: **Method Overloading**.
>
> ```java
> class Math {
>     int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
>     double add(double a, double b) { return a + b; }
> }
> ```
>
> **Run-time polymorphism (1 mark):** Also called *dynamic binding* or *late binding*. The method to be invoked is determined at run time based on the actual object type, not the reference type. Example: **Method Overriding**.

---

### Question 2 [KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]

**Q: Explain why two methods that differ only in return type cannot be considered as overloaded methods in Java. Give a suitable example.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

> **Reasoning (2 marks):** In Java, the method signature consists of the method name and the parameter list (number, type, and order of parameters). The return type is **not** part of the signature. If two methods have the same name and the same parameter list, the compiler treats them as duplicate definitions. Additionally, the return type cannot disambiguate call sites where the result is discarded (e.g., `obj.method();` used as a statement), which would lead to ambiguity.
>
> **Example (1 mark):**
>
> ```java
> class Test {
>     int  show()  { return 10; }   // ❌ Compile Error
>     void show()  { }              // 'show()' is already defined
> }
> ```

---

## 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks — Module Internal Choice)

### Question A (14 Marks) [KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]

**Q (a)** Explain the concept of method overloading in Java with a suitable example program. Discuss the different ways in which methods can be overloaded. **(7 marks)**

#### Model Solution

**Definition (2 marks):**
Method overloading is a feature in Java that allows a class to have multiple methods with the **same name** but **different parameter lists** (varying number, type, or order of parameters). It is an example of **compile-time polymorphism** where the compiler binds the method call to the appropriate method definition at compile time.

**The Three Ways to Overload (3 marks):**

| **Way** | **Description** |
|---|---|
| Different number of parameters | `add(int, int)` vs `add(int, int, int)` |
| Different type of parameters | `add(int, int)` vs `add(double, double)` |
| Different order of parameters | `set(int, String)` vs `set(String, int)` |

**Example Program (2 marks):**

```java
class OverloadDemo {
    // Overload 1: Different number of parameters
    int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }
    // Overload 2: Different number of parameters
    int add(int a, int b, int c) {
        return a + b + c;
    }
    // Overload 3: Different type of parameters
    double add(double a, double b) {
        return a + b;
    }
    // Overload 4: Different order of parameters
    void display(String name, int id) {
        System.out.println("Name: " + name + ", ID: " + id);
    }
    void display(int id, String name) {
        System.out.println("ID: " + id + ", Name: " + name);
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        OverloadDemo obj = new OverloadDemo();
        System.out.println("Sum of 2 ints: "     + obj.add(5, 10));
        System.out.println("Sum of 3 ints: "     + obj.add(5, 10, 15));
        System.out.println("Sum of 2 doubles: "  + obj.add(2.5, 3.5));
        obj.display("Alice", 101);
        obj.display(102, "Bob");
    }
}
```

**Output:**
```
Sum of 2 ints: 15
Sum of 3 ints: 30
Sum of 2 doubles: 6.0
Name: Alice, ID: 101
ID: 102, Name: Bob
```

---

**Q (b)** What is type promotion in method overloading? Explain with an example how the compiler resolves method calls when no exact match is found. **(7 marks)**

#### Model Solution

**Definition of Type Promotion (2 marks):**
Type promotion (also called *widening conversion*) is the automatic process by which the Java compiler converts a primitive data type to a *larger* compatible type if no exact match is found for a method call. The promotion follows a strict hierarchy:

$$
\text{byte} \rightarrow \text{short} \rightarrow \text{int} \rightarrow \text{long} \rightarrow \text{float} \rightarrow \text{double}
$$

**Resolution Algorithm (3 marks):**

1. The compiler searches for an **exact match** of the argument type in the available overloaded methods.
2. If no exact match exists, it applies **widening conversion** to the next larger type in the hierarchy.
3. If the wider type matches a method, that method is selected.
4. If multiple widened candidates exist, an **ambiguity error** is raised.
5. If no widening match exists, the compiler tries **autoboxing**, then **varargs** as lower-priority fallbacks.

**Example (2 marks):**

```java
class Promo {
    void show(int a)    { System.out.println("int: "    + a); }
    void show(double a) { System.out.println("double: " + a); }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Promo p = new Promo();
        p.show(10);      // Exact match for int
        p.show(10.5f);   // float is widened to double
    }
}
```

**Output:**
```
int: 10
double: 10.5
```

In the second call, `10.5f` is a `float`. Since no `show(float)` exists, the compiler widens `float` to `double`, which matches `show(double)`.

---

### Question B (14 Marks) [KTU University Exam - May 2024 — Alternative Choice]

**Q (a)** Discuss the rules and restrictions of method overloading in Java. Explain with examples why methods differing only in return type or access modifier cannot be overloaded. **(7 marks)**

#### Model Solution

**Rules for Valid Overloading (3 marks):**

1. The **method name must be identical** across all overloads.
2. The **parameter list must differ** in at least one of: number, type, or order.
3. Overloading is permitted **within the same class** or via **inheritance** (a subclass can overload an inherited method).
4. The **return type can be changed freely** but does not contribute to distinguishing overloads.
5. **Access modifiers** can be changed freely — they are also not part of the signature.

**Why Return Type Cannot Differ Alone (2 marks):**

```java
class Test {
    int  show() { return 1; }   // ❌ Compilation Error
    void show() { }              // 'show()' is already defined in Test
}
```

If the return type were allowed to differentiate overloads, an ambiguous call site like `show();` (where the returned value is discarded) would be impossible for the compiler to resolve. Therefore, the compiler enforces that the **parameter list is the sole signature discriminator**.

**Why Access Modifier Cannot Differ Alone (2 marks):**

```java
class Test {
    public  void display() { }   // ❌ Compilation Error
    private void display() { }    // duplicate method display() in Test
}
```

Two methods with identical names and identical parameter lists are considered **duplicate definitions** by the compiler, regardless of access modifiers. Modifiers control *visibility*, not *identity*.

---

**Q (b)** Explain the concept of *automatic type promotion* in method overloading with the help of a suitable Java program. Also explain what happens when ambiguity arises. **(7 marks)**

#### Model Solution

**Concept (2 marks):**
When an overloaded method is called with an argument whose type does not exactly match any of the available method signatures, the Java compiler automatically promotes (widens) the argument to a larger type. The promotion order is:

$$
\text{byte} \rightarrow \text{short} \rightarrow \text{int} \rightarrow \text{long} \rightarrow \text{float} \rightarrow \text{double}
$$

and additionally:

$$
\text{char} \rightarrow \text{int} \rightarrow \text{long} \rightarrow \text{float} \rightarrow \text{double}
$$

**Example Program (3 marks):**

```java
class TypePromo {
    void test(int a)     { System.out.println("int method");     }
    void test(long a)    { System.out.println("long method");    }
    void test(double a)  { System.out.println("double method");  }
}

public class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        TypePromo obj = new TypePromo();
        obj.test(10);      // int literal → exact match
        obj.test(10L);     // long literal → exact match
        obj.test(10.5);    // double literal → exact match
        obj.test('A');     // char → promoted to int → matches test(int)
    }
}
```

**Output:**
```
int method
long method
double method
int method
```

**Ambiguity Scenario (2 marks):**
If multiple methods could be reached by different levels of promotion, the compiler raises an **ambiguity error**.

```java
class Ambig {
    void check(long a)   { }
    void check(float a)  { }
}
// new Ambig().check(10);  // ❌ Reference to check is ambiguous
// Both long and float are valid widening targets of int.
```

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Mark-Deduction Zones:**
> 1. **Forgetting to mention** that the *return type is not part of the signature* — examiners specifically look for this in 7-mark questions. **(-1 mark)**
> 2. **Confusing widening with autoboxing**: Many students claim that `int` can be autoboxed to `Integer` automatically in overloading. The correct hierarchy is: **widening > autoboxing > varargs**. **(-1 mark)**
> 3. **Assuming static and non-static methods can be overloaded** by static keyword alone — this causes *duplicate method* errors. **(-1 mark)**
> 4. **Not stating the promotion hierarchy explicitly** in a 7-mark theory answer. Examiners reward diagrams or tables. **(-1 mark)**
> 5. **Mixing up method overloading (compile-time) with method overriding (run-time)** — this is the single most common conceptual error in Module 2 answers. **(-2 marks)**

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **High-Density Rapid-Revision Checklist:**
>
> ✅ **Polymorphism = "many forms"**; in Java, classified as compile-time (overloading) and run-time (overriding).
>
> ✅ **Method Overloading** = same name, different parameter list (number / type / order). **Return type is NOT** part of the signature.
>
> ✅ Two methods differing **only in return type** → **Compilation Error** (duplicate method).
>
> ✅ Two methods differing **only in access modifier** → **Compilation Error** (duplicate method).
>
> ✅ `static` vs non-static with same parameters → **Compilation Error** (duplicate method).
>
> ✅ Overloading can occur **within a class** OR between **subclass and superclass** via inheritance.
>
> ✅ **Type Promotion Hierarchy:** `byte → short → int → long → float → double`; `char → int → long → float → double`.
>
> ✅ **Resolution Priority Ladder:** (1) Exact match → (2) Widening → (3) Autoboxing/Unboxing → (4) Varargs.
>
> ✅ **Narrowing conversion is NOT allowed** in overloading resolution (e.g., `long → int` is forbidden).
>
> ✅ **Ambiguity** arises when two different promotion paths both lead to valid candidates (e.g., `int` → `long` and `int` → `float` both exist).
>
> ✅ Method overloading is a **compile-time** decision — the `.class` bytecode contains a direct, fully-bound method reference (no runtime lookup needed).
>
> ✅ Industry relevance: **JDK libraries** like `println`, `valueOf`, `Arrays.copyOf` are heavily overloaded for ergonomic API design.

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.title: Using Objects as Parameters
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PBCST304 - OBJECT ORIENTED PROGRAMMING
> - **Module:** Module 2
> - **Topic:** Using Objects as Parameters

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

In Java (and Object-Oriented Programming in general), **Using Objects as Parameters** refers to the mechanism by which an object reference is passed as an argument to a method, or returned as a result from a method. When a method is invoked, the runtime creates a copy of the reference variable pointing to the same object in the heap memory, allowing the method to access and manipulate the state (instance variables) of that object. This is fundamentally distinct from passing primitive data types, because only the *reference* is copied — not the actual object.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Syllabus Highlight (Module 2):** Students must clearly distinguish between *passing primitive types* and *passing object references*. Java is **strictly Pass-By-Value**, but the *value being passed for objects is the reference* (address), not the object itself. This dual interpretation is a **frequently tested concept** in KTU university examinations.

### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Intuition

Imagine you have a **physical diary** that belongs to you. You give a *photocopy of the front cover's location tag* (not the diary itself) to your friend. Your friend can now navigate to your diary using that tag and write or read entries. If your friend writes "Meet at 5 PM" in the diary, **you will also see that change** when you open your original diary — because both of you are accessing the *same* diary.

- The **diary** → the **Object** (stored in heap memory)
- The **photocopy of the location tag** → the **Reference Variable** (copied when passed)
- The **friend** → the **Method** that received the parameter

> [!NOTE]
> **Why this matters in engineering:** Real-world systems like banking software pass `Account` objects between methods (deposit, withdraw, transfer). Game engines pass `Player` objects to update positions. Without object parameters, code would be unmanageable and tightly coupled.

### 1.3 Key Terminology (KTU Board-Standard Vocabulary)

| Term | Definition | KTU Relevance |
|------|------------|---------------|
| **Object Reference** | A memory address (pointer) that locates an object in the heap | ⭐ High |
| **Pass-By-Value** | A copy of the variable's current value is passed | ⭐⭐ Very High |
| **Formal Parameter** | The variable defined in the method signature | ⭐ Medium |
| **Actual Parameter** | The value/expression passed during the method call | ⭐ Medium |
| **Mutator Effect** | Changes made through a reference affect the original object | ⭐⭐ Very High |
| **Aliasing** | Two references pointing to the same object | ⭐ High |

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 Operational Mechanics — How Object Parameters Work

The lifecycle of passing an object as a parameter follows a precise sequence:

1. **Declaration Phase:** The caller creates an object using `new`, which allocates memory in the **heap** and returns a reference stored in a stack-local variable.
2. **Invocation Phase:** When `methodName(objectRef)` is called, the JVM evaluates `objectRef` and produces a *bitwise copy* of that reference value.
3. **Binding Phase:** The formal parameter in the method's local stack frame is initialized with the copied reference. Both the caller's variable and the method's parameter now point to the **same heap object**.
4. **Execution Phase:** Any method call made on the formal parameter (e.g., `param.setX(10)`) modifies the *shared* object's state.
5. **Return Phase:** After method execution, the formal parameter is destroyed (popped from stack), but the object persists in the heap if other references still exist.

### 2.2 The "Two-Way Effect" — Why and How

- **Why** does the effect propagate? Because both references point to the same memory location — they are *aliases*.
- **How** does Java prevent accidental corruption? The reference itself cannot be *re-seated* to a new object inside the method (in the caller's scope), preserving encapsulation integrity.

> [!NOTE]
> **Critical Distinction for KTU Board Exams:**
> - ✅ **Allowed:** Modifying the *internal state* of the object via the reference copy.
> - ❌ **Not Allowed:** Reassigning the reference to point to a *different* object (this change is local to the method).

### 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| Concept | Primitive Parameter | Object Parameter |
|---------|---------------------|------------------|
| What is copied? | The actual data value | The reference (memory address) |
| Memory location | Stack-only | Stack + Heap |
| Modification in method affects caller? | **No** | **Yes** (for instance variables) |
| Reassignment affects caller? | N/A | **No** (new object is local) |
| KTU Mark Weightage | 2-3 marks | **7-14 marks** (Module 2 favorite) |
| Aliasing possible? | No | **Yes** |
| Garbage Collection risk | None | If reference is lost, object becomes eligible |

### 2.4 Returning Objects from Methods

A method can also return an object reference. This is used for:
- **Factory methods** that produce new instances
- **Getter methods** that expose encapsulated objects
- **Chained method calls** (e.g., `builder.setName("John").setAge(25).build()`)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Engineering Utility:** The **Factory Design Pattern** in software engineering is built entirely on returning objects. Frameworks like Spring (Java) and Android SDK rely on object-returning methods for dependency injection and view creation.

### 2.5 Real-World Engineering Applications

1. **Database Systems:** Passing `ResultSet` or `Entity` objects between DAO methods.
2. **GUI Programming:** Passing `Component` objects to layout managers.
3. **Scientific Computing:** Passing `Matrix` or `Vector` objects for in-place transformations.
4. **Network Programming:** Passing `Socket` or `Packet` objects across handler methods.
5. **Game Development:** Passing `Player` or `Weapon` objects between collision, render, and AI modules.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Java Code Analysis — Step-by-Step Execution Trace

Let us analyze the following canonical KTU examination problem:

```java
class Box {
    int length, width;

    Box(int l, int w) {
        length = l;
        width = w;
    }

    void enlarge(Box b) {
        b.length = b.length * 2;
        b.width  = b.width  * 2;
        System.out.println("Inside method: " + b.length + " " + b.width);
    }

    void reassign(Box b) {
        b = new Box(100, 200);
        System.out.println("Inside reassign: " + b.length + " " + b.width);
    }
}

class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Box myBox = new Box(5, 10);
        myBox.enlarge(myBox);
        System.out.println("After enlarge: " + myBox.length + " " + myBox.width);
        myBox.reassign(myBox);
        System.out.println("After reassign: " + myBox.length + " " + myBox.width);
    }
}
```

### 3.2 Step-by-Step Execution Trace

**Step 1 — Object Creation in `main`:**

$$
\text{new Box}(5, 10) \rightarrow \text{Heap Object: } \text{length} = 5, \text{width} = 10
$$

The reference `myBox` is stored in the stack frame of `main`, pointing to the heap object.

**Step 2 — Call to `enlarge(myBox)`:**

The JVM copies the reference value of `myBox` into the formal parameter `b`. Now both `myBox` and `b` point to the same heap object.

$$
\begin{aligned}
b.\text{length} &= b.\text{length} \times 2 = 5 \times 2 = 10 \\
b.\text{width}  &= b.\text{width}  \times 2 = 10 \times 2 = 20
\end{aligned}
$$

Output: `Inside method: 10 20`

**Step 3 — Return to `main`:**

The formal parameter `b` is destroyed (popped from stack). But because the heap object's state was modified, the original `myBox` reflects the changes.

Output: `After enlarge: 10 20`

**Step 4 — Call to `reassign(myBox)`:**

The reference is copied to `b` again. Inside the method, `b = new Box(100, 200)` creates a **brand new** heap object and makes local `b` point to it.

$$
\text{Inside reassign: } 100 \;\; 200
$$

**Step 5 — Return to `main`:**

The local `b` (and the new object it pointed to, now unreferenced) is destroyed. The caller's `myBox` is **unchanged** because reassignment only affected the local copy.

Output: `After reassign: 10 20`

### 3.3 Final Output (Verbatim)

$$
\text{Inside method: 10 20}
$$

$$
\text{After enlarge: 10 20}
$$

$$
\text{Inside reassign: 100 200}
$$

$$
\text{After reassign: 10 20}
$$

### 3.4 Analytical Matrix — Behavior Comparison

| Operation Type | Affects Caller? | Reason | KTU Marks |
|----------------|-----------------|--------|-----------|
| `b.length = 50` | ✅ **Yes** | Mutates shared object's instance variable | Often 7 marks |
| `b = new Box()` | ❌ **No** | Re-seats local reference to new object | Often 7 marks |
| `b.setX(10)` (method call) | ✅ **Yes** | Method executes on shared object | Often 7 marks |
| `b = null` | ❌ **No** | Local reference severed; original intact | Bonus concept |

### 3.5 Memory Model Visualization (Logical)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Before } \texttt{enlarge} &: \quad \text{myBox (stack)} \xrightarrow{\text{ref}=0xA1} \text{Box(5,10) (heap @ 0xA1)} \\
\text{During } \texttt{enlarge} &: \quad \text{myBox (stack)} \xrightarrow{\text{ref}=0xA1} \text{Box(5,10) (heap @ 0xA1)} \xleftarrow{\text{ref}=0xA1} \text{b (stack)} \\
\text{After } \texttt{enlarge} &: \quad \text{myBox (stack)} \xrightarrow{\text{ref}=0xA1} \text{Box(10,20) (heap @ 0xA1)}
\end{aligned}
$$

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
## 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

### 4.1 Mermaid Diagram — Object Parameter Passing Lifecycle

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Caller Method main] --> B[Create Object: new Box 5 10]
    B --> C[Stack: myBox stores reference 0xA1]
    C --> D[Heap: Object Box at address 0xA1 with length=5 width=10]
    A --> E[Call: myBox.enlarge myBox]
    E --> F[JVM copies reference 0xA1 into formal parameter b]
    F --> G[Both myBox and b point to same heap object]
    G --> H[Method modifies b.length and b.width]
    H --> I[Heap object updated: length=10 width=20]
    I --> J[Return from method]
    J --> K[Local parameter b destroyed]
    K --> L[Caller observes modified state: 10 20]
```

### 4.2 Mermaid Diagram — Reassignment vs Mutation Decision Tree

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q1{What is done with the parameter inside the method?}
    Q1 -->|Modify instance variables e.g. b.length = 50| R1[Mutation Path]
    Q1 -->|Call mutator method e.g. b.setLength 50| R2[Method Invocation Path]
    Q1 -->|Reassign to new object e.g. b = new Box| R3[Reassignment Path]
    Q1 -->|Assign null e.g. b = null| R4[Nullification Path]

    R1 --> S1[Original heap object IS modified]
    R2 --> S1
    S1 --> T1[Caller observes the change YES]

    R3 --> S2[New heap object created]
    R3 --> S3[Local reference b now points to new object]
    S3 --> T2[Caller observes NO change]

    R4 --> S4[Local reference severed]
    S4 --> T2
```

### 4.3 Mermaid Diagram — Block-Level Functional Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph STACK[STACK MEMORY]
        M1[main: myBox ref 0xA1]
        M2[enlarge: b ref 0xA1 copy]
        M3[reassign: b ref 0xB2 new]
    end

    subgraph HEAP[HEAP MEMORY]
        H1[Object A at 0xA1: length=5 width=10]
        H2[Object B at 0xB2: length=100 width=200]
        H3[Object A at 0xA1 updated: length=10 width=20]
    end

    M1 --> H1
    M2 --> H1
    M3 --> H2
    H1 -.after enlarge.-> H3
```

### 4.4 Conceptual Block Diagram — Object Parameter Categories

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    P[Object Parameters in Java] --> P1[Passing Objects to Methods]
    P --> P2[Returning Objects from Methods]

    P1 --> P1a[State Modification: affects caller]
    P1 --> P1b[Reassignment: does NOT affect caller]

    P2 --> P2a[Factory Methods: create and return new objects]
    P2 --> P2b[Getter Methods: expose encapsulated objects]
    P2 --> P2c[Builder Pattern: chain configuration methods]
```
