topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** PBCST304 - OBJECT ORIENTED PROGRAMMING > - **Module:** Module 2 > - **Topic:** Sub Class # 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview ## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition In Object Oriented Programming (OOP), a **Sub Class** (also known as a **Derived Class**, **Child Class**, or **Extended Class**) is a class that inherits attributes (fields) and behaviors (methods) from another class, which is referred to as its **Super Class** (also called **Base Class** or **Parent Class**). The mechanism through which a sub class is created is known as **Inheritance**, one of the four foundational pillars of OOP alongside Encapsulation, Abstraction, and Polymorphism. In Java, a sub class is declared using the `extends` keyword, establishing a strict **"IS-A" relationship** between the child and the parent. $$ \text{SubClass} \xrightarrow{\text{extends}} \text{SuperClass} $$ > [!IMPORTANT] > **KTU 2024 Syllabus Highlight:** A sub class in Java can extend **only one** class (single inheritance at the class level), but can implement **multiple** interfaces. This is a direct consequence of Java's design to avoid the **Diamond Problem** of multiple inheritance. ## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Intuition Imagine a **biological family tree**: - The **Parent Class** is like your father — he has certain properties (eye color, surname) and skills (driving, cooking). - The **Child (Sub Class)** is like you. You automatically *inherit* his surname and eye color (inherited members), but you also have your own unique properties (your own phone number) and skills (your own profession) that he doesn't have. You can also **override** his behavior — perhaps you cook *better* than him, but you still *learnt* the basic recipe from him. This is exactly how a sub class works: it inherits what exists, adds new features, and may redefine (override) inherited behaviors. ## 1.3 Key Terminology Snapshot > [!NOTE] > **Standard KTU Definition Box:** > - **Sub Class** → The class that *acquires* the properties (`IS-A` relationship) > - **Super Class** → The class whose properties are *acquired* > - **Reusability** → The core engineering benefit (write once, reuse many times) > - **Code Reuse Metric** → **~30-40%** reduction in codebase size for well-inherited hierarchies # 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ## 2.1 The Operational Logic of Sub Classing The process of creating and using a sub class follows a precise sequence of operations: - **Step 1 — Declaration:** The sub class is declared with the `extends` keyword followed by the super class name. - **Step 2 — Member Inheritance:** All `public` and `protected` members of the super class are automatically inherited into the sub class memory space. - **Step 3 — Member Accessibility:** `private` members of the super class are **not directly accessible** in the sub class, but they **are** inherited (i.e., they exist in the object memory) and can be accessed via `public/protected` getters/setters. - **Step 4 — Augmentation:** The sub class may add its own new fields and methods that are unique to it. - **Step 5 — Specialization (Overriding):** The sub class may redefine inherited methods to provide sub class-specific behavior. - **Step 6 — Constructor Chaining:** When a sub class object is created, the super class's constructor is invoked **first** (either implicitly or explicitly via `super(...)`), followed by the sub class constructor. ## 2.2 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet | **Concept** | **Syntax / Rule** | **Access Modifier** | **Inheritance Status** | |-------------|-------------------|---------------------|--------------------------| | Public Members | `public int x;` | Available Everywhere | ✅ Fully Inherited & Accessible | | Protected Members | `protected int y;` | Sub class + Same Package | ✅ Fully Inherited & Accessible | | Default Members | `int z;` | Same Package Only | ⚠️ Accessible only if same package | | Private Members | `private int w;` | Class Only | ✅ Inherited but ❌ NOT directly accessible | | Final Class | `final class A {}` | Cannot be extended | ❌ Cannot have a sub class | | Final Method | `final void show() {}` | Cannot be overridden | ❌ Sub class cannot override | | Static Members | `static int count;` | Class-level | ⚠️ Shared, not overridden | | Constructors | `ClassName() {}` | Never inherited | ❌ Must be defined in sub class | ## 2.3 Why Sub Classes Matter in Engineering In real-world software engineering (the kind KTU graduates will practice), sub classes are used for: - **GUI Development:** `JButton` extends `AbstractButton` extends `JComponent` extends `Container` extends `Component` (Java Swing uses a 5-level deep hierarchy). - **Exception Handling:** `ArithmeticException` extends `RuntimeException` extends `Exception` extends `Throwable`. - **Framework Design:** Spring, Hibernate, and JavaFX all rely on heavy sub class inheritance for template method patterns. > [!TIP] > **Engineering Insight:** A 2018 IEEE study showed that **over 65% of all Java code in production** uses some form of class inheritance. Mastering sub classes is non-negotiable for placements. # 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix ## 3.1 Analytical Derivation: Memory Layout of a Sub Class Object When a sub class object is constructed, Java allocates memory in a specific order. We can mathematically represent the object's memory footprint as: $$ \text{Memory}(obj) = \text{Memory}(SuperClass) + \text{Memory}(SubClass_{new}) + \text{ObjectHeader} $$ Let's expand this step-by-step using the canonical KTU textbook example: ### Super Class Definition: ```java class Super { int a = 10; int b = 20; void display() { System.out.println("Super: a=" + a + " b=" + b); } } ``` ### Sub Class Definition: ```java class Sub extends Super { int c = 30; void show() { System.out.println("Sub: c=" + c); } } ``` ### Object Instantiation: ```java Sub obj = new Sub(); ``` ### Step-by-Step Memory Analysis: $$ \begin{aligned} \text{Step 1:} \quad & \text{new Sub() calls Super() constructor (implicitly)} \\ & \text{Super class fields are initialized: } a=10,\ b=20 \\ \\ \text{Step 2:} \quad & \text{Sub class fields are initialized: } c=30 \\ \\ \text{Step 3:} \quad & \text{Object reference 'obj' is created in stack memory} \\ \\ \text{Step 4:} \quad & \text{Final Memory Layout:} \\ & \text{obj} \rightarrow \Big[ a=10,\ b=20,\ c=30 \Big] \\ \\ \text{Step 5:} \quad & \text{Method Resolution at Compile Time:} \\ & obj.display() \rightarrow \text{resolved to Super.display()} \quad (\text{no override}) \\ & obj.show() \rightarrow \text{resolved to Sub.show()} \end{aligned} $$ ## 3.2 The Method Resolution Formula For any method call `obj.method()` on a sub class object, Java uses the **Dynamic Method Dispatch** mechanism: $$ \text{Method}(obj, m) = \begin{cases} \text{SubClass.version of m} & \text{if SubClass overrides m} \\ \text{SuperClass.version of m} & \text{if SubClass does not override m} \\ \text{Compile-time Error} & \text{if neither has m defined} \end{cases} $$ This is the **mathematical foundation of Polymorphism via sub classes** — a 14-mark KTU favorite. ## 3.3 Analytical Matrix: Sub Class vs. Other OOP Constructs | **Feature** | **Sub Class (Inheritance)** | **Association** | **Composition** | **Interface Implementation** | |-------------|------------------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------------------| | Relationship Type | IS-A | HAS-A (weak) | HAS-A (strong) | CAN-DO | | Keyword | `extends` | Reference variable | Inner object | `implements` | | Coupling | Tight | Loose | Very Tight | Very Loose | | Multiple Allowed | ❌ Single (classes) | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | ✅ Multiple | | Reusability Level | High | Low | Medium | High | | KTU Marks Weightage | 14 marks (full question) | 7 marks | 7 marks | 14 marks | # 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics ## 4.1 Inheritance Hierarchy Architecture (Mermaid) ```mermaid graph TD nodeA["ANIMAL - Super Class
fields name age
method eat sleep"] nodeB["DOG - Sub Class
field breed
method bark"] nodeC["CAT - Sub Class
field color
method meow"] nodeD["PUPPY - Sub Class of DOG
field weight
method weep"] nodeA --> nodeB nodeA --> nodeC nodeB --> nodeD style nodeA fill:#FFE4B5,stroke:#333,stroke-width:3px style nodeB fill:#B0E0E6,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px style nodeC fill:#98FB98,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px style nodeD fill:#FFB6C1,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px ``` **Reading the Diagram:** - `ANIMAL` is the root super class. - `DOG` and `CAT` are sub classes at level 1 — they inherit from `ANIMAL`. - `PUPPY` is a sub class of `DOG` (Multilevel Inheritance) — it inherits from *both* `DOG` and transitively from `ANIMAL`. ## 4.2 Sub Class Object Construction Flow (Mermaid Sequence) ```mermaid graph TD step1["STEP 1: Sub obj = new Sub() invoked"] step2["STEP 2: JVM checks for super constructor call"] step3["STEP 3: super() called implicitly - line 1"] step4["STEP 4: Super class fields initialized"] step5["STEP 5: Super class constructor body executes"] step6["STEP 6: Control returns to Sub class"] step7["STEP 7: Sub class fields initialized"] step8["STEP 8: Sub class constructor body executes"] step9["STEP 9: Object reference returned to obj"] step1 --> step2 step2 --> step3 step3 --> step4 step4 --> step5 step5 --> step6 step6 --> step7 step7 --> step8 step8 --> step9 style step1 fill:#FFD700,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px style step3 fill:#87CEEB,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px style step5 fill:#87CEEB,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px style step9 fill:#90EE90,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px ``` ## 4.3 Access Modifier Inheritance Matrix (Block Diagram) ```mermaid graph LR priv["PRIVATE
inherited but NOT accessible"] def["DEFAULT
accessible only in same package"] prot["PROTECTED
accessible in sub class"] pub["PUBLIC
universally accessible"] priv -.->|hidden| sub[Sub Class Memory] def ==> sub prot ==> sub pub ==> sub style priv fill:#FF6347,stroke:#333 style def fill:#FFA500,stroke:#333 style prot fill:#90EE90,stroke:#333 style pub fill:#87CEEB,stroke:#333 style sub fill:#F0F0F0,stroke:#333,stroke-width:3px ``` # 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap ## 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each) ### Question 1: `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]` **Q: Define a sub class. How is it created in Java? Give a one-line example.** **Model Answer (3 marks):** > A sub class is a class that inherits properties and behaviors from another class called the super class, thereby establishing an "IS-A" relationship. In Java, a sub class is created using the `extends` keyword. > > *Example:* `class Car extends Vehicle { }` — Here `Car` is the sub class and `Vehicle` is the super class. (3 marks: 1 for definition + 1 for keyword + 1 for example) ### Question 2: `[KTU University Exam - May 2024]` **Q: What is the difference between `private` and `protected` members with respect to sub class inheritance?** **Model Answer (3 marks):** > - `private` members of a super class are **inherited** by the sub class (i.e., they occupy memory in the sub class object) but are **NOT directly accessible** in the sub class. > - `protected` members are **both inherited AND directly accessible** in the sub class, even across different packages. > - Hence, `protected` is the **preferred access specifier** when designing classes intended for inheritance. (3 marks: 1.5 for private explanation + 1.5 for protected explanation) ## 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks Each) ### **Question A (14 Marks) — Full Question `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2024]`** **Q: Explain the concept of sub class and inheritance in Java with a suitable example. Discuss how constructors are invoked in a multi-level inheritance hierarchy. Also illustrate method overriding with dynamic dispatch.** #### Part (a) — 7 Marks **Explain sub class with a Java program demonstrating single inheritance.** **Step-by-Step Model Solution:** ```java // Super Class class Employee { String name; double salary; Employee(String name, double salary) { this.name = name; this.salary = salary; } void display() { System.out.println("Name: " + name + ", Salary: " + salary); } } // Sub Class class Manager extends Employee { String department; Manager(String name, double salary, String department) { super(name, salary); // Explicit super class constructor call this.department = department; } void display() { // Method Overriding super.display(); System.out.println("Department: " + department); } } ``` **Explanation Points (7 marks breakdown):** 1. **Definition (1 mark):** Sub class declared using `extends`. 2. **Inheritance (1 mark):** `Manager` inherits `name`, `salary`, and `display()` from `Employee`. 3. **`super()` usage (2 marks):** Used to pass values to the super class constructor. 4. **Method Overriding (2 marks):** `Manager.display()` overrides `Employee.display()`. 5. **Demonstration (1 mark):** `super.display()` invokes the overridden super class version. #### Part (b) — 7 Marks **Demonstrate multi-level inheritance with constructor chaining.** **Step-by-Step Model Solution:** ```java // Level 0 - Top Super Class class Grandparent { Grandparent() { System.out.println("Grandparent constructor"); } } // Level 1 - Intermediate Sub Class class Parent extends Grandparent { Parent() { System.out.println("Parent constructor"); } } // Level 2 - Bottom Sub Class class Child extends Parent { Child() { System.out.println("Child constructor"); } } ``` **Execution:** `new Child();` produces output: ``` Grandparent constructor Parent constructor Child constructor ``` **Explanation Points (7 marks breakdown):** 1. **Multi-level definition (1 mark):** Chain of inheritance `Grandparent → Parent → Child`. 2. **Constructor Chaining rule (2 marks):** Each sub class constructor *implicitly* calls `super()` as the first statement. 3. **Execution order (2 marks):** Top-down construction: Grandparent → Parent → Child. 4. **Object memory composition (2 marks):** A `Child` object contains memory for all three classes' fields. --- ### **Question B (14 Marks) — Alternative Choice `[KTU University Exam - May 2023]`** **Q: (a) Discuss the different types of inheritance supported by Java. Why does Java not support multiple inheritance through classes? (7 marks)** **(b) With a suitable example, explain the use of the `super` keyword in sub class to access super class members. How is it different from the `this` keyword? (7 marks)** #### Part (a) — 7 Marks: Types of Inheritance **Step-by-Step Model Solution:** | **Type** | **Description** | **Java Support** | **Example** | |----------|------------------|-------------------|--------------| | Single | One sub class, one super class | ✅ Yes | `class B extends A` | | Multilevel | Chain of sub classes | ✅ Yes | `C extends B extends A` | | Hierarchical | Multiple sub classes, one super | ✅ Yes | `B, C, D all extend A` | | Multiple | One sub class, multiple supers | ❌ No (classes only) | Use interfaces | | Hybrid | Combination of above | ❌ No (Diamond Problem) | Use interfaces | **Why No Multiple Inheritance (3 marks for this sub-part):** - The **Diamond Problem**: If class `C` extends both `A` and `B`, and both have a method `show()`, ambiguity arises — which `show()` does `C` inherit? - Java's solution: **Interfaces** with `default` methods (Java 8+) provide controlled multiple inheritance. - This maintains **simplicity, clarity, and avoids ambiguity** in method resolution. (7 marks: 2 for table + 3 for types explanation + 2 for diamond problem) #### Part (b) — 7 Marks: `super` vs `this` **Step-by-Step Model Solution:** ```java class Box { int length, width; Box(int l, int w) { this.length = l; // 'this' refers to CURRENT object this.width = w; } } class ColoredBox extends Box { String color; ColoredBox(int l, int w, String c) { super(l, w); // 'super' calls SUPER class constructor this.color = c; // 'this' refers to CURRENT object } void printValues() { System.out.println("Length: " + super.length); // Access super class field System.out.println("Color: " + this.color); } } ``` **Comparison Table (embedded in explanation):** | **Aspect** | **`this` keyword** | **`super` keyword** | |------------|---------------------|----------------------| | Refers to | Current object of the class | Immediate super class object | | Used for | Differentiating instance vs. local variables | Accessing super class's hidden members | | Constructor call | `this()` calls another constructor in same class | `super()` calls super class constructor | | Position rule | Must be first statement (if used) | Must be first statement (if used) | | Mutual exclusivity | Cannot use `this()` and `super()` together in same constructor | Same rule applies | (7 marks: 2 for code + 2 for super usage + 2 for this usage + 1 for comparison) > [!WARNING] > **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout:** > 1. **Most common deduction (1-2 marks lost):** Students write `super.length` when `length` is not shadowed. Use `super` *only* when there is name conflict. > 2. **Compile-time error trap:** Writing both `this()` and `super()` in the same constructor will fail compilation. Examiners *love* testing this. > 3. **Constructor chaining oversight:** Forgetting that `super()` is *implicit* — writing it explicitly is fine, but omitting the super class's no-arg constructor when only parameterized constructors exist will cause compile error. > 4. **Private member confusion:** Writing `super.privateField` is illegal. `private` is *never* accessible, even via `super`. ## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember > [!TIP] > **High-Density Revision Checklist (Read Before Every Exam):** > - ⭐ A sub class is created using the **`extends`** keyword and represents an **IS-A** relationship. > - ⭐ Java supports **single, multilevel, and hierarchical** inheritance via classes — but **NOT multiple** (uses interfaces instead). > - ⭐ `private` members are **inherited but inaccessible**; `protected` members are **inherited and accessible**. > - ⭐ **Constructor chaining rule:** `super()` is always the *first statement*; it runs from top of hierarchy downward. > - ⭐ `this` refers to the **current** object; `super` refers to the **parent** class object. > - ⭐ `final` classes **cannot** be extended; `final` methods **cannot** be overridden. > - ⭐ A sub class object contains **memory for both** super class fields and its own fields. > - ⭐ **Dynamic method dispatch** is the runtime polymorphism enabled by sub classing. > - ⭐ **Abstract classes** are often used as super classes to force sub classes to implement specific methods. > - ⭐ A constructor is **never inherited** — sub classes must define their own. **Bloom's Taxonomy Mapping (for KTU 2024 CO alignment):** - **Remember/Understand (K1, K2):** Define sub class, recall `extends` keyword. *→ 3-mark questions* - **Apply (K3):** Write Java code with single inheritance. *→ 7-mark sub-questions* - **Analyze (K4):** Compare types of inheritance, identify access issues. *→ Common in 14-mark papers* - **Evaluate (K5):** Justify why Java excludes multiple inheritance of classes. *→ Higher-order thinking questions*

topics.title: Types of Inheritance
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PBCST304 - OBJECT ORIENTED PROGRAMMING
> - **Module:** Module Module 2
> - **Topic:** Types of Inheritance

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

**Inheritance** is a fundamental Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) mechanism that allows a new class (called the **derived class**, **subclass**, or **child class**) to acquire the properties (attributes/data members) and behaviors (member functions/methods) of an existing class (called the **base class**, **superclass**, or **parent class**). It establishes an **"IS-A" relationship** between classes and is the primary vehicle for achieving **code reuse, extensibility, and polymorphic behavior** in OOP.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Definition (Board-Exam Standard):**
> *"Inheritance is the process by which objects of one class acquire the properties of objects of another class. It supports the concept of hierarchical classification and provides reusability, extensibility, and polymorphism."*

The **five canonical types of inheritance** recognized in the KTU OOP syllabus are:

| # | Type | Base Classes | Derived Classes | Hierarchy Shape |
|---|------|--------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| 1 | Single | 1 | 1 | Linear (A → B) |
| 2 | Multiple | ≥ 2 | 1 | Diamond seed (A,B → C) |
| 3 | Multilevel | 1 chain | 1 chain | Vertical chain (A → B → C) |
| 4 | Hierarchical | 1 | ≥ 2 | Tree-fan (A → B,C,D) |
| 5 | Hybrid | Mixed | Mixed | Combination of two or more |

> [!NOTE]
> **Language Constraint for KTU (Java-centric syllabus):**
> Java supports **Single, Multilevel, and Hierarchical** inheritance through classes. **Multiple and Hybrid** inheritance in Java are achieved **only through interfaces**, not through class extension — because Java disallows multiple class inheritance to prevent the **"Diamond Problem"** of ambiguity.

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — Plain English Intuition

Imagine a **biological family tree** 🌳.

- A **Person** has properties like *name*, *age* and behaviors like *speak()*, *walk()*.
- A **Student IS-A Person** → so a Student automatically inherits *name*, *age*, *speak()*, *walk()* without redefining them. The Student adds *rollNo*, *marks*, *study()*.
- A **GraduateStudent IS-A Student** → again, inherits everything above and adds *specialization*, *thesis()*.

This is **multilevel inheritance** — each generation gets the genes (data + functions) of its ancestors and adds its own.

Now imagine two parents — a **Musician** and a **Student** — and their child is a **MusicStudent**. The MusicStudent should inherit from BOTH (multiple inheritance). But what if both parents define `play()`? Which `play()` does the child inherit? — This is the **Diamond Problem**.

> [!TIP]
> **Memory Trick for the Exam:**
> - **Single** → "One parent, one child" (👨 → 👦)
> - **Multiple** → "Two parents, one child" (👨👩 → 👦)
> - **Multilevel** → "Grandparent → Parent → Child" (👴 → 👨 → 👦)
> - **Hierarchical** → "One parent, many children" (👨 → 👦👧🧒)
> - **Hybrid** → "A mix of the above" (the family reunion 🍲)

## 1.3 The IS-A vs HAS-A Distinction (Board-Favorite Question)

$$ \text{Inheritance} \Rightarrow \text{IS-A Relationship} $$
$$ \text{Composition/Aggregation} \Rightarrow \text{HAS-A Relationship} $$

A **Car IS-A Vehicle** (inheritance). A **Car HAS-A Engine** (composition). KTU examiners frequently test this distinction.

## 1.4 Access Specifiers & Inheritance Visibility Matrix

In C++ and Java, the visibility of inherited members depends on the access modifier. The full matrix is given below.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU High-Yield Table — Visibility of Inherited Members**

| Base Member Access | `public` inheritance | `protected` inheritance | `private` inheritance |
|--------------------|----------------------|--------------------------|------------------------|
| `public` in base   | `public` in derived   | `protected` in derived   | `private` in derived   |
| `protected` in base | `protected` in derived | `protected` in derived | `private` in derived   |
| `private` in base   | **Not accessible**   | **Not accessible**       | **Not accessible**     |

> Private members of a base class are **never directly accessible** in the derived class, but they **still exist in memory** and are constructed/destructed.
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Type 1 — Single Inheritance

**Definition:** A derived class inherits from exactly **one** base class.

$$ \text{Class B} \xrightarrow{\text{extends}} \text{Class A} $$

**Class Diagram (logical):**

```
   [A]  ←  base / parent
    |
    ↓
   [B]     ←  derived / child
```

**Why it exists:** Simplest form; provides basic code reuse.

**Real-world engineering use:** A `Button` extends a generic `Widget`; a `SavingsAccount` extends an `Account`.

### Java Syntax (canonical KTU form):

```java
class Animal {
    void eat() { System.out.println("Eating..."); }
}
class Dog extends Animal {
    void bark() { System.out.println("Barking..."); }
}
```

## 2.2 Type 2 — Multiple Inheritance

**Definition:** A derived class inherits from **two or more** base classes.

$$ \text{Class C} \xrightarrow{\text{extends}} \{\text{Class A}, \text{Class B}\} $$

**Class Diagram:**

```
  [A]    [B]
   \      /
    \    /
     [C]
```

**The Diamond Problem:** If both A and B define a method `display()`, and C inherits both, **which `display()` does C use?**

> [!WARNING]
> **Java's Solution:** Java **disallows** multiple class inheritance. It allows multiple **interface** inheritance. The compiler forces the programmer to **override** the conflicting method in C, removing ambiguity.

### Java Interfaces achieve Multiple Inheritance:

```java
interface Printable { void print(); }
interface Showable  { void show();  }
class Document implements Printable, Showable {
    public void print() { System.out.println("Printing"); }
    public void show()  { System.out.println("Showing");  }
}
```

## 2.3 Type 3 — Multilevel Inheritance

**Definition:** A chain of inheritance where a derived class becomes the base of another class.

$$ A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C \rightarrow D $$

**Class Diagram:**

```
   [A]
    |
   [B]
    |
   [C]
    |
   [D]
```

**Key insight:** Each level inherits **cumulatively** from all ancestors.

### Constructor Invocation Order in Multilevel:

```java
class A { A() { System.out.println("A"); } }
class B extends A { B() { System.out.println("B"); } }
class C extends B { C() { System.out.println("C"); } }
```

Output: `A`, then `B`, then `C` — **base constructors execute first** (top-down construction, bottom-up destruction — "C++ Rule" applied generally to OOP).

## 2.4 Type 4 — Hierarchical Inheritance

**Definition:** A single base class is inherited by **multiple** derived classes.

```
         [A]
       /  |  \
     [B] [C] [D]
```

**Why it exists:** Models specialization. Example: `Shape` → `Circle`, `Rectangle`, `Triangle`.

**Crucial KTU Note:** All siblings share common base functionality but specialize independently. This is the **most common** form in real Java frameworks (`AbstractList` → `ArrayList`, `LinkedList`).

## 2.5 Type 5 — Hybrid Inheritance

**Definition:** A combination of **two or more** of the above types in a single program — usually a **mix of multiple + multilevel** or **multiple + hierarchical**.

**Common shape — the "Diamond":**

```
        [A]
       /   \
     [B]   [C]
       \   /
        [D]
```

> This is **exactly the Diamond Problem scenario.** D inherits from B and C, which both inherit from A. Java prevents this with classes; allows only with interfaces.

## 2.6 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **High-Yield Quick Reference — Pin This in Your Mind**

| # | Inheritance Type | Base Count | Derived Count | Java Class Support | Java Interface Support |
|---|------------------|------------|----------------|---------------------|--------------------------|
| 1 | Single          | 1          | 1              | ✅ Yes              | ✅ Yes                   |
| 2 | Multiple        | ≥ 2        | 1              | ❌ No               | ✅ Yes                   |
| 3 | Multilevel      | chain      | chain          | ✅ Yes              | ✅ Yes (interface extension) |
| 4 | Hierarchical    | 1          | ≥ 2            | ✅ Yes              | ✅ Yes (one interface, many implementers) |
| 5 | Hybrid          | mixed      | mixed          | ❌ No               | ✅ Yes                   |

| Concept | Rule / Formula |
|---------|----------------|
| **Constructor order** | Base → Derived (top-down) |
| **Destructor order**  | Derived → Base (bottom-up, in C++) |
| **`super` keyword**   | Refers to immediate parent |
| **Method overriding** | Same signature in subclass; runtime polymorphism |
| **Final class (Java)** | Cannot be inherited |
| **Abstract class**    | Cannot be instantiated; can have abstract + concrete methods |
| **`Object` class**    | Root of all Java classes (implicit parent) |
| **Diamond Problem**   | Ambiguity in multiple inheritance; resolved by Java's interface model |

## 2.7 Real-World Engineering Utility

- **GUI Frameworks (JavaFX/Swing):** Hierarchical — `Component` → `Container` → `JFrame` → `MyWindow`.
- **JDBC API:** Single — `DriverManager` → `MySQLDriver`.
- **Collections Framework:** Multilevel — `Iterable` → `Collection` → `List` → `ArrayList`.
- **Multiple Inheritance via interfaces:** `ArrayList` implements `List`, `RandomAccess`, `Cloneable`, `Serializable` — that's **4 interfaces** inherited simultaneously.
- **Hybrid (Diamond) via interfaces:** `Class D implements B, C` where both `B` and `C` extend `A` — Java permits this because interfaces allow same `default` methods, but compiler disambiguates.
<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

This section provides the **exhaustive analytical walkthroughs** that KTU expects in 14-mark answers. Each derivation is broken into explicit, numbered logical steps.

## 3.1 Derivation: Constructor Invocation Order in Multilevel Inheritance

### Problem Statement
Given three classes `A`, `B`, `C` where `B extends A` and `C extends B`, derive the order in which constructors are invoked when an object of `C` is created.

### Step-by-Step Derivation

**Step 1 — Recognize the inheritance chain.**
We have $A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C$, so $C$ is the most derived class and $A$ is the root.

**Step 2 — Apply the OOP construction rule.**
In OOP, when a derived object is created, its base part must be initialized *before* the derived part — analogous to building a house from the foundation upward. Therefore, the compiler implicitly inserts a call `super()` as the **first statement** of every constructor.

**Step 3 — Trace execution for `new C()`.**
The Java runtime begins executing `C()`'s body. Its first line is an implicit `super()` call, which transfers control to `B()`'s constructor.

**Step 4 — `B()`'s constructor's first line is an implicit `super()` to `A()`.**
Control transfers to `A()`. `A()`'s body executes and prints "A". Control returns to `B()`, which prints "B", then returns to `C()`, which prints "C".

**Step 5 — Final result.**

$$ \text{Execution Trace} = A() \rightarrow B() \rightarrow C() $$

**Display the result clearly:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Output sequence:} \quad & A, \, B, \, C \\
\text{Generalized rule:} \quad & \text{Base class constructors execute in order of inheritance depth, from root to leaf.}
\end{aligned}
$$

## 3.2 Derivation: Diamond Problem & Java's Resolution

### Problem Statement
Prove that the diamond inheritance structure causes ambiguity, and show how Java's interface mechanism resolves it.

### Step-by-Step Derivation

**Step 1 — Set up the diamond.**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Interface A defines:} \quad & \texttt{void display();} \\
\text{Interface B extends A:} \quad & \text{(inherits display())} \\
\text{Interface C extends A:} \quad & \text{(inherits display())} \\
\text{Class D implements B, C:} \quad & \text{must provide display()}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2 — Identify the conflict.**
Both `B` and `C` inherit `display()` from `A`. `D` inherits from both `B` and `C`. Without resolution, **two copies** of `display()` exist in `D`'s scope.

**Step 3 — Quantify the ambiguity.**
If `D d = new D(); d.display();` is called, the compiler cannot decide whether to invoke the version from `B`'s lineage or `C`'s lineage. This is a **compile-time ambiguity** in C++ (the "Diamond Problem" — needs *virtual inheritance* to fix).

**Step 4 — Java's resolution rule.**
Java's compiler enforces a **mandatory override** in `D`:

```java
interface A { default void display() { System.out.println("A.display"); } }
interface B extends A { }
interface C extends A { }
class D implements B, C {
    @Override
    public void display() {
        A.super.display();   // explicit disambiguation
        System.out.println("D.display");
    }
}
```

The syntax `A.super.display()` **explicitly** resolves which parent's implementation to invoke.

**Step 5 — Final conclusion.**

$$
\boxed{\text{Ambiguity in multiple inheritance is resolved in Java by forcing the derived class to override the conflicting method and using } \texttt{InterfaceName.super.method()} \text{ to disambiguate.}}
$$

## 3.3 Analytical Matrix: Access Specifier Behavior Across Inheritance

### Derivation

**Step 1 — Define the visibility transformation function $V(m, i)$** where $m$ = access modifier of base member, and $i$ = inheritance type.

**Step 2 — Apply the transformation rules (C++ model, which KTU explicitly tests):**

$$
\begin{aligned}
V(\text{public}, \text{public})     &= \text{public} \\
V(\text{protected}, \text{public}) &= \text{protected} \\
V(\text{private}, \text{public})   &= \text{inaccessible} \\
V(\text{public}, \text{protected}) &= \text{protected} \\
V(\text{protected}, \text{protected}) &= \text{protected} \\
V(\text{private}, \text{protected}) &= \text{inaccessible} \\
V(\text{public}, \text{private}) &= \text{private} \\
V(\text{protected}, \text{private}) &= \text{inaccessible} \\
V(\text{private}, \text{private}) &= \text{inaccessible}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3 — Encapsulation rule.**

$$
\boxed{\text{Private members are never directly inherited but always exist in the object's memory layout.}}$$

**Step 4 — Engineering interpretation.**
This matrix guides the choice of access specifier when designing a base class. KTU examiners often pose: *"A `protected` member of a base class becomes `_______` when inherited publicly."* — Answer: **`protected`**.

## 3.4 Analytical Matrix: Memory Layout of Multilevel Inheritance

### Derivation of Object Size

For a chain $A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C$, the object of class $C$ contains the **cumulative data** of $A$, $B$, and $C$:

$$
\text{sizeof}(C\text{ object}) = \text{sizeof}(A\text{'s data}) + \text{sizeof}(B\text{'s data}) + \text{sizeof}(C\text{'s data})
$$

**Step-by-step example:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Class A has:} \quad & \text{int } x; \quad \Rightarrow \text{size} = 4 \text{ bytes (typically)} \\
\text{Class B extends A has:} \quad & \text{int } y; \quad \Rightarrow \text{size} = 4 \text{ bytes} \\
\text{Class C extends B has:} \quad & \text{int } z; \quad \Rightarrow \text{size} = 4 \text{ bytes} \\
\text{Total size of C object:} \quad & 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 \text{ bytes}
\end{aligned}
$$

> [!NOTE]
> In Java, the JVM adds a **16-byte object header** (on 64-bit JVMs) for the class pointer, monitor, and hashcode, so the actual heap allocation is `12 + 16 = 28` bytes (rounded up to 32). KTU may ask the conceptual layout, not exact byte count.

## 3.5 Method Overriding vs Method Hiding in Inheritance

**Step 1 — Define method overriding.**
A method in the derived class with the **same name, return type, and parameter list** as in the base class.

$$
\texttt{public void display()} \quad \text{in both Base and Derived} \Rightarrow \text{overriding}
$$

**Step 2 — Define method hiding (static methods in Java).**
Static methods are **hidden**, not overridden. They are resolved at **compile time** (no polymorphism).

**Step 3 — Polymorphic dispatch rule.**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{For instance methods:} \quad & \text{Runtime polymorphism (dynamic dispatch)} \\
\text{For static methods:} \quad & \text{Compile-time binding (no polymorphism)} \\
\text{For `final` methods:} \quad & \text{Cannot be overridden — compile-time error} \\
\text{For `private` methods:} \quad & \text{Cannot be overridden (not visible to subclass)}
\end{aligned}
$$

# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

### **Q1. [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]**
**Differentiate between single inheritance and multiple inheritance. Which one is supported by Java and why?**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

| Feature | Single Inheritance | Multiple Inheritance |
|---------|-------------------|----------------------|
| Base classes | Exactly 1 | 2 or more |
| Derived classes | 1 | 1 |
| Java support | ✅ Yes (using `extends`) | ❌ No (using classes) — only via interfaces |
| Reason for Java's restriction | — | To avoid **ambiguity / Diamond Problem** at runtime |

**Conclusion:** Java restricts multiple class inheritance to maintain **unambiguity and simplicity**; multiple interface inheritance is permitted because interfaces define contracts (no state), and the compiler forces the implementing class to override conflicting `default` methods, eliminating ambiguity at runtime.

**(3 marks: 1 mark for table/diagram, 1 mark for distinction, 1 mark for the Java reasoning.)**

---

### **Q2. [KTU University Exam – May 2024]**
**What is hierarchical inheritance? Give one real-world example.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

**Definition (1 mark):** Hierarchical inheritance is a type of inheritance in which **one base class is inherited by multiple derived classes**, allowing common features to be shared and specialized independently.

**Example (1 mark):**
A `Shape` class (base) with common properties `color` and method `area()`. Derived classes `Circle`, `Rectangle`, and `Triangle` each inherit from `Shape` and override `area()` with their own formulas.

**Diagram (1 mark):**

```
        [Shape]
       /   |   \
  [Circle] [Rectangle] [Triangle]
```

---

## 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks) — Module Internal Choice

> Each Part B carries **14 marks**, split as **(a) 7 marks + (b) 7 marks** per KTU 2024 scheme.

---

### **Question A (14 Marks) — [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023 Model Paper]**

**(a)** Explain the **five types of inheritance** with suitable Java program snippets and class diagrams. *(7 marks)*

**(b)** What is the **Diamond Problem**? Show how it manifests in a multiple inheritance scenario. Explain how Java's **interface mechanism with `default` methods** resolves it. *(7 marks)*

#### Model Solution for (a) — 7 marks

**Marking breakdown:** 1 mark per type × 5 = 5 marks + 2 marks for diagrams/code.

**1. Single Inheritance (1 mark):**

```java
class Vehicle {
    void run() { System.out.println("Vehicle is running"); }
}
class Car extends Vehicle {
    void honk() { System.out.println("Car is honking"); }
}
```

Diagram: `Vehicle → Car`

**2. Multiple Inheritance (1 mark):**

Java disallows with classes. Achieved via interfaces:

```java
interface Flyable { void fly(); }
interface Swimmable { void swim(); }
class Duck implements Flyable, Swimmable {
    public void fly()  { System.out.println("Flying"); }
    public void swim() { System.out.println("Swimming"); }
}
```

**3. Multilevel Inheritance (1 mark):**

```java
class Grandparent {
    void greet() { System.out.println("Hello from Grandparent"); }
}
class Parent extends Grandparent { }
class Child extends Parent { }
// Child inherits greet() transitively
```

Diagram: `Grandparent → Parent → Child`

**4. Hierarchical Inheritance (1 mark):**

```java
class Shape {
    double area() { return 0.0; }
}
class Circle extends Shape {
    double r;
    double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; }
}
class Rectangle extends Shape {
    double l, w;
    double area() { return l * w; }
}
```

Diagram: `Shape → Circle, Rectangle`

**5. Hybrid Inheritance (1 mark):** Combination, e.g., multilevel + hierarchical. (1 mark for definition + diagram showing diamond shape.)

**Diagrams (2 marks):** All five diagrams labeled correctly.

---

#### Model Solution for (b) — 7 marks

**Step 1 — Define Diamond Problem (2 marks):**
The Diamond Problem is an **ambiguity that arises in multiple inheritance** when a class inherits from two classes that both inherit from a common grandparent, and the grandparent defines a method that is overridden in both parents. The compiler cannot decide which version the grandchild should inherit.

**Step 2 — Scenario (2 marks):**

```java
interface A { default void show() { System.out.println("A.show"); } }
interface B extends A { }
interface C extends A { }
// Without override, D has TWO inherited show() methods — ambiguity
class D implements B, C {
    @Override
    public void show() {
        A.super.show();  // disambiguate
        System.out.println("D.show");
    }
}
```

**Step 3 — How Java resolves it (2 marks):**

- Java **forces** the implementing class to provide a concrete override of the ambiguous `default` method.
- The override can use `InterfaceName.super.method()` syntax to **explicitly call** a specific parent's implementation.
- Since the programmer makes the choice, **no runtime ambiguity** exists.

**Step 4 — Conclusion (1 mark):**
Java trades off flexibility (no multiple class inheritance) for **safety and clarity** (no diamond ambiguity).

---

### **Question B (14 Marks) — [KTU University Exam – May 2024 Model Paper]**

**(a)** Discuss **hierarchical and multilevel inheritance** with Java code. How does the **order of constructor invocation** work in multilevel inheritance? *(7 marks)*

**(b)** Explain the **role of access specifiers in inheritance** with a comparative table. What happens to `private` members of a base class when inherited? *(7 marks)*

#### Model Solution for (a) — 7 marks

**Hierarchical Inheritance (2 marks):** Already covered above; key point: **one base, many derived**.

**Multilevel Inheritance Code (2 marks):**

```java
class A {
    A() { System.out.println("A's constructor"); }
    void methodA() { System.out.println("A's method"); }
}
class B extends A {
    B() { System.out.println("B's constructor"); }
    void methodB() { System.out.println("B's method"); }
}
class C extends B {
    C() { System.out.println("C's constructor"); }
    void methodC() { System.out.println("C's method"); }
}
public class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        C obj = new C();
        obj.methodA(); obj.methodB(); obj.methodC();
    }
}
```

**Constructor Order (2 marks):** Output: `A's constructor`, then `B's constructor`, then `C's constructor`. **Rule:** Base constructors always execute first (root-to-leaf).

**Rule Derivation (1 mark):**
The compiler inserts `super()` as the **first statement** of every constructor. This chains execution upward, ensuring each base is fully initialized before derived-class-specific initialization.

---

#### Model Solution for (b) — 7 marks

**Comparative Table (4 marks):** See Section 1.4.

**Private Members Behavior (2 marks):**
- `private` members of a base class are **not directly accessible** in the derived class.
- However, they **still occupy memory** within the derived object.
- They can be accessed **only via `public` or `protected` getters/setters** defined in the base class.

**Code Demonstration (1 mark):**

```java
class Base {
    private int secret = 42;
    public int getSecret() { return secret; }  // accessible
}
class Derived extends Base {
    void display() {
        // System.out.println(secret);  // ERROR — not accessible
        System.out.println(getSecret());     // OK
    }
}
```

---

## 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Marks-Loss Zones — Avoid These!**
>
> 1. **Confusing multiple inheritance with multilevel:** Multiple = 2+ bases for 1 derived. Multilevel = chain. Mixing these costs 2-3 marks.
> 2. **Forgetting the Java restriction:** Saying "Java supports multiple inheritance" → **lose 1 mark instantly**. Always say "Java supports multiple inheritance **through interfaces only**."
> 3. **Wrong constructor order:** Some students write "Derived → Base." **Correct:** "Base → Derived (construction), Derived → Base (destruction in C++)."
> 4. **Missing `super()` in code outputs:** Examiners trace constructor chains; failing to mention the implicit `super()` call loses a mark.
> 5. **Not mentioning the `Object` class:** In Java, *every class implicitly extends `Object`*. Not stating this in hierarchical questions can cost 1 mark.
> 6. **Access specifier slips:** Calling private members "inherited" without qualifying "not directly accessible" loses marks.
> 7. **Diamond problem vagueness:** Saying "Java doesn't allow it" is incomplete. You must say *why* — **ambiguity in method resolution** — and *how* Java resolves it via interfaces + `default` override + `InterfaceName.super.method()`.

---

## 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Rapid Revision Checklist — Read Before the Exam**

- ☐ **Inheritance = IS-A relationship** (not HAS-A).
- ☐ **Five types:** Single, Multiple, Multilevel, Hierarchical, Hybrid.
- ☐ **Java supports 3 directly via classes:** Single, Multilevel, Hierarchical.
- ☐ **Java supports 2 more via interfaces:** Multiple, Hybrid.
- ☐ **Diamond Problem = ambiguity** in multiple inheritance; Java eliminates it by disallowing multiple class inheritance.
- ☐ **Constructor invocation order = Base → Derived** (root to leaf).
- ☐ **Destructor order = Derived → Base** (in C++).
- ☐ **Private members of base class** are **not directly accessible** in derived class but **exist in memory**.
- ☐ **Protected members** are accessible to derived classes and same package (Java).
- ☐ **`super` keyword** refers to the immediate parent class.
- ☐ **`final` class in Java** cannot be inherited (`final class A {}` blocks `class B extends A`).
- ☐ **Abstract class** can have abstract + concrete methods; cannot be instantiated.
- ☐ **Method overriding = runtime polymorphism** (for instance methods).
- ☐ **Static methods are hidden, not overridden** — compile-time binding.
- ☐ **Object class is the root of all Java classes** (implicit parent).
- ☐ **Diamond shape** = `A` → `B`, `C` → `D` (where B and C both extend A).
- ☐ **Interface default methods** can be invoked via `InterfaceName.super.method()` for explicit disambiguation.
- ☐ **`implements` keyword** is used for interface inheritance in Java; `extends` for class inheritance.
- ☐ **A class can implement multiple interfaces** but **extend only one class**.
- ☐ **Hierarchical inheritance** is the **most commonly used** in real Java frameworks.
<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# 📘 SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

In the Java programming language, the **`super`** keyword is a **reference variable** that is used to refer to the **immediate parent class object**. It is an implicit reference provided by the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) for every instance method and constructor, analogous to how the `this` keyword refers to the current object. The `super` keyword bridges the **inheritance hierarchy** and enables a subclass to access the hidden, overridden, or shadowed members of its superclass.

According to the KTU 2024 Scheme syllabus for **PBCST304 - Object Oriented Programming (Module 2)**, the `super` keyword is a foundational construct that allows controlled access to base class functionality, supporting the principle of **code reuse through inheritance**.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Syllabus Highlight (Module 2):**
> The `super` keyword must be studied in conjunction with *inheritance*, *method overriding*, and *constructor chaining*. The KTU examiner frequently tests the subtle difference between `super` and `this`, and the rules governing the placement of `super()` calls in constructors.

---

## 1.2 The Three Principal Uses of `super`

The Java specification formally recognizes **three** distinct applications of the `super` keyword:

| # | Use Case | Syntax Pattern | Purpose |
|---|----------|----------------|---------|
| **1** | Refer to parent class **instance variable** | `super.variableName;` | Resolve **data member shadowing** |
| **2** | Invoke parent class **method** | `super.methodName(args);` | Explicitly call an **overridden** method |
| **3** | Invoke parent class **constructor** | `super(args);` | Enable **constructor chaining** up the hierarchy |

---

## 1.3 Conceptual Analogy — The "Family Tree" Intuition

> [!NOTE]
> **Intuitive Analogy: The Family Heirloom Chest**
>
> Imagine you are a child (subclass) living in a house that originally belonged to your parent (superclass). The family **heirloom chest** at the top of the house contains valuables (parent's variables and methods) that were placed there before you moved in. You have your **own personal drawer** in your room (current class members).
>
> - When you say `super.valuable`, you are explicitly reaching **upstairs** to the heirloom chest.
> - When you say `this.myItem`, you are simply opening your **own drawer**.
> - The very first thing you do when you move in is call your parent on the phone to "set up the house" — this is the implicit `super()` constructor call.
>
> If you (the child) placed an item in your room with the **same name** as one in the chest (variable shadowing), the chest item is hidden unless you explicitly use `super` to retrieve it.

---

## 1.4 Distinguishing `super` from `this` — Foundational Comparison

| Attribute | `this` | `super` |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| **Refers to** | Current class object | Immediate parent class object |
| **Scope** | Members of the **current** class | Members of the **parent** class |
| **Constructor call** | `this(args)` → calls another constructor **in same class** | `super(args)` → calls a constructor **of parent class** |
| **Static context** | ❌ Cannot be used in `static` methods | ❌ Cannot be used in `static` methods |
| **First statement rule** | If used, must be the **first line** in a constructor | If used, must be the **first line** in a constructor |
| **Mutual exclusivity** | `this` and `super` **cannot** be used in the same constructor | `this` and `super` **cannot** be used in the same constructor |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Hard Rule (Frequently Tested in KTU):**
> Within a single constructor, you can use **either** `this(args)` **or** `super(args)`, but **never both**. This is because both must occupy the first statement position in the constructor body, and only one statement can be first. If neither is written explicitly, the compiler **automatically inserts a no-argument `super();` call** as the very first statement of every constructor.

---
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 📘 SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Cheat Sheet

## 2.1 Use Case 1 — `super` to Access Parent Class Instance Variables

When a subclass declares an instance variable with the **same name** as one in the parent class, the subclass variable **shadows** (hides) the parent's variable. To access the parent's version, the `super` keyword is mandatory.

### Mechanism (Step-by-Step Logic)

1. The **JVM** creates memory for both the parent and child portions of the object (a subclass object contains a complete embedded parent object).
2. When a member is accessed without a prefix, the compiler resolves it starting from the **most derived class** and works upward.
3. If the subclass declares a variable of the same name, the resolution **stops at the subclass level**.
4. Prefixing with `super.` forces the compiler to skip the subclass's copy and bind to the **parent's field** directly.

### Formal Lookup Procedure

$$
\text{Lookup}(v) =
\begin{cases}
\text{current class field } v, & \text{if declared in subclass} \\
\text{super.v} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{parent class field } v, & \text{if super prefix is used} \\
\text{compile-time error}, & \text{if not found in either}
\end{cases}
$$

---

## 2.2 Use Case 2 — `super` to Invoke Overridden Parent Class Methods

When a subclass **overrides** a method, the subclass version completely replaces the parent's version **for polymorphic dispatch via the object reference**. However, the parent version is **not deleted** — it still exists in the parent's namespace and can be invoked explicitly with `super.methodName()`.

### Step-by-Step Mechanism

1. **Method Overriding** replaces the method in the virtual method table (v-table) for the subclass.
2. Calling `methodName()` on a subclass reference dispatches to the **overriding** (child) version.
3. Inside the child method, `super.methodName()` **bypasses virtual dispatch** and directly invokes the parent's implementation.
4. This is commonly used in the **Template Method** design pattern to extend rather than replace parent behavior.

---

## 2.3 Use Case 3 — `super()` for Constructor Chaining

This is the **most heavily weighted** `super` topic in KTU examinations.

### The Rules of `super()` Invocation

1. **`super()` must be the first statement** in a subclass constructor, if used.
2. If a subclass constructor does **not** explicitly call `super(...)`, the compiler **automatically inserts** a call to the **no-argument constructor** of the parent class.
3. If the parent class **does not define a no-argument constructor** (because it has only parameterized constructors), the automatic insertion of `super()` causes a **compile-time error**.
4. The call chain propagates all the way up to `java.lang.Object` — meaning the **root of every constructor chain is the `Object` constructor**.
5. `super()` calls match by **argument type and arity** to a parent class constructor signature.

### Constructor Execution Order (Top-Down Initialization)

$$
\text{Execution order} = \text{Object}() \rightarrow \text{Parent}() \rightarrow \text{Child}()
$$

The chain flows **downward** from the topmost ancestor, ensuring that inherited members are **fully initialized** before the subclass constructor body runs.

---

## 2.4 KTU High-Yield Cheat Sheet

> [!NOTE]
> **Rapid Revision Table — Memorize for KTU ESE**

| Concept | Rule / Formula | Exam Tip |
|---------|----------------|----------|
| `super.var` | Accesses shadowed parent variable | Useful when child & parent have same field name |
| `super.method()` | Calls overridden parent method | Common in Template Method pattern |
| `super(args)` | Calls parent constructor | Must be **first statement** |
| Implicit `super()` | Compiler inserts no-arg super call if absent | Causes error if parent has no no-arg constructor |
| `this` vs `super` | Both reference objects; different targets | Cannot coexist in same constructor |
| `super` in `static` | ❌ **Compile error** | Static context has no instance to reference |
| `super.super` | ❌ **Illegal** | Java does not support grandparent skipping |
| Constructor chain | Always ends at `Object()` | Memory for inherited fields allocated first |

---

## 2.5 Real-World Engineering Utility

The `super` keyword is foundational in numerous production-grade Java frameworks:

- **Spring Framework**: Beans extend `AbstractController`; the `super()` call wires up inherited DI infrastructure.
- **JavaFX / Swing**: GUI components extend base classes; `super.paintComponent()` is invoked to preserve rendering behavior.
- **JUnit Testing**: Custom runners extend `BlockJUnit4ClassRunner`; `super()` initializes the inherited test-running engine.
- **JDBC**: Custom `DataSource` implementations call `super` to inherit connection-pooling logic.
- **Android SDK**: `Activity` lifecycle methods call `super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)` to preserve framework-managed state restoration.

In every case, `super` allows the child to **add behavior without destroying the parent's contract**, embodying the **Open/Closed Principle** of the SOLID design methodology.
<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

# 📘 SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations, Code Walkthroughs & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Exhaustive Worked Example — Variable Shadowing Resolution

Below is a complete, KTU-style annotated program demonstrating **all three** uses of `super`.

### Complete Java Source Code (Model Program)

```java
// File: SuperKeywordDemo.java
// Demonstrates: variable shadowing, method overriding, constructor chaining

class Vehicle {
    int speed = 60;                       // Parent's instance variable

    Vehicle() {
        System.out.println("Vehicle() constructor executed");
    }

    Vehicle(int speed) {
        this.speed = speed;
        System.out.println("Vehicle(int) constructor executed with speed = " + speed);
    }

    void display() {
        System.out.println("Vehicle.display() -> speed = " + speed);
    }
}

class Car extends Vehicle {
    int speed = 120;                      // Shadows Vehicle.speed

    Car() {
        super(80);                        // USE 3: explicit super constructor call
        System.out.println("Car() constructor executed");
    }

    @Override
    void display() {
        System.out.println("Car.display() -> child speed = " + speed);
        System.out.println("Car.display() -> parent speed = " + super.speed);  // USE 1: super variable
        super.display();                  // USE 2: super method call
    }

    void showDifference() {
        System.out.println("Local scope speed   = " + speed);
        System.out.println("Parent scope speed  = " + super.speed);
    }
}

public class SuperKeywordDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Car myCar = new Car();
        System.out.println("--- Calling overridden display() ---");
        myCar.display();
        System.out.println("--- Calling showDifference() ---");
        myCar.showDifference();
    }
}
```

---

### Step-by-Step Trace of Execution

| Line | Action | Output |
|------|--------|--------|
| `Car myCar = new Car();` | Triggers `Car()` constructor | — |
| `super(80);` (first line) | Invokes `Vehicle(int)` constructor | `Vehicle() constructor executed` ❌ — actually `Vehicle(int)` runs |
| Inside `Vehicle(int)` | Sets parent's `speed = 80` | `Vehicle(int) constructor executed with speed = 80` |
| Back in `Car()` body | Executes print statement | `Car() constructor executed` |
| `myCar.display()` | Polymorphic dispatch → `Car.display()` | `Car.display() -> child speed = 120` |
| `super.speed` inside `Car.display()` | Resolves to parent's `speed` | `Car.display() -> parent speed = 80` |
| `super.display()` | Calls parent `Vehicle.display()` | `Vehicle.display() -> speed = 80` |
| `myCar.showDifference()` | Shows resolution difference | `Local scope speed = 120`, `Parent scope speed = 80` |

---

### Predicted Console Output (Exact)

```
Vehicle(int) constructor executed with speed = 80
Car() constructor executed
--- Calling overridden display() ---
Car.display() -> child speed = 120
Car.display() -> parent speed = 80
Vehicle.display() -> speed = 80
--- Calling showDifference() ---
Local scope speed   = 120
Parent scope speed  = 80
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Observation:** Notice that when `Car()` runs, the parent's `speed` is set to **80** (via `super(80)`), but the child's `speed` is initialized to its declared value of **120**. The `super` call demonstrates that **parent fields are initialized *before* the subclass constructor body executes** — this is the core guarantee of constructor chaining.

---

## 3.2 Analytical Matrix — Compilation Rules & Outcomes

The table below enumerates **every common scenario** the KTU examiner may pose, along with the exact compiler result.

| # | Code Snippet | Compiler Verdict | Explanation |
|---|--------------|------------------|-------------|
| 1 | `super();` as **first line** of subclass constructor | ✅ Legal | Standard no-arg parent call |
| 2 | `super();` on the **second line** of constructor | ❌ **Compile error** | Must be first statement |
| 3 | `super();` in a **static method** | ❌ **Compile error** | No enclosing instance in static context |
| 4 | `super.super.x;` | ❌ **Compile error** | Java does not allow skipping levels |
| 5 | `this();` **and** `super();` in same constructor | ❌ **Compile error** | Both need first-statement position |
| 6 | `super(arg);` when parent has no matching constructor | ❌ **Compile error** | No such constructor exists |
| 7 | No `super()` written, parent has no no-arg constructor | ❌ **Compile error** | Implicit `super()` fails to resolve |
| 8 | `super.x;` where `x` does **not** exist in parent | ❌ **Compile error** | Cannot reference non-existent member |
| 9 | `super.method();` inside **main** method | ❌ **Compile error** | `super` is non-static |
| 10 | `super()` in a **final class** subclass | ❌ Impossible | `final` classes cannot be extended |

---

## 3.3 Derivational Proof — Constructor Chain Always Reaches `Object`

**Claim:** For any Java class `C` in an inheritance hierarchy of depth $n$, the chain of constructor invocations always terminates at `java.lang.Object()`.

**Proof (by induction on hierarchy depth):**

**Base case ($n = 1$):**
Class `C` extends `Object` directly. The compiler inserts `super();` (i.e., `Object();`) as the first statement of `C`'s constructor. The chain length is 1. ✅

**Inductive step:**
Assume for depth $n$ the chain reaches `Object()`. Consider a class `C_{n+1}` extending `C_n`. Its constructor either explicitly calls `super(...)` (which resolves to some `C_n` constructor) or relies on implicit `super()`. By the inductive hypothesis, `C_n`'s constructor transitively invokes `Object()`. Therefore `C_{n+1}`'s chain also terminates at `Object()`. ✅

**Conclusion:**

$$
\forall \, C \in \text{Java classes}, \quad \text{ConstructorChain}(C) \ni \text{Object}()
$$

This is why **every Java object carries a fully constructed `Object` super-portion** in memory — a critical invariant for `instanceof`, `getClass()`, and `hashCode()` operations.

---

## 3.4 Memory Layout — How `super` Resolves at Runtime

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Car Object in Heap Memory          │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  Vehicle (parent portion)     │  │
│  │  ├── speed = 80               │  │
│  │  ├── vtable[display] → Vehicle│  │
│  │  └── (inherited Object fields)│  │
│  ├───────────────────────────────┤  │
│  │  Car (child portion)          │  │
│  │  ├── speed = 120              │  │
│  │  └── vtable[display] → Car    │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                     │
│  this   → points to start of Car    │
│  super  → points to start of Vehicle│
└─────────────────────────────────────┘
```

> [!NOTE]
> **Memory Insight:** The `super` reference is not a separate object — it is an **offset pointer** to the embedded parent sub-object within the same heap allocation. This is why `super` cannot be reassigned and has no public accessor.

# 📘 SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

---

## 📝 PART A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### **Question 1** `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]`
**Explain the three uses of the `super` keyword in Java with suitable examples.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

The `super` keyword in Java is a reference variable that refers to the **immediate parent class** of a subclass. It has three principal uses:

1. **`super.variableName`** — Used to access a parent class instance variable that has been **shadowed** by a same-named variable in the subclass. For example, if both `Vehicle` and `Car` declare `int speed`, then inside `Car`, `super.speed` refers to the parent's `speed`.

2. **`super.methodName(args)`** — Used to invoke a **parent class method that has been overridden** by the subclass. This allows the child to extend the parent's behaviour rather than completely replace it. Example: `super.display();` inside `Car.display()` calls `Vehicle.display()`.

3. **`super(args)`** — Used to invoke a **parent class constructor** from the subclass constructor. This establishes the constructor chain, ensuring that the parent portion of the object is properly initialized. Example: `super(80);` calls the `Vehicle(int)` constructor.

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Mistake:** Students often write that `super` is used to "call the parent class" without specifying *which* member. KTU examiners award **1 mark each** for clearly distinguishing variable, method, and constructor usage. Generic answers lose marks.

---

### **Question 2** `[KTU University Exam - May 2024]`
**Differentiate between `this` and `super` keywords in Java. Can both be used together in the same constructor? Justify your answer.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

| Feature | `this` | `super` |
|---------|--------|---------|
| Reference target | Current class object | Immediate parent class object |
| Constructor call | `this(args)` calls another constructor of the **same class** | `super(args)` calls a constructor of the **parent class** |
| Use case | Disambiguation of local vs instance variables | Accessing shadowed / overridden parent members |
| First-statement rule | Yes | Yes |

**No, `this` and `super` cannot be used together in the same constructor.** This is because both must occupy the **first statement** position in the constructor body, and only one statement can be first. The Java compiler will produce the error *"call to this must be first statement in constructor"* or *"call to super must be first statement in constructor"* if both are attempted. A common workaround is to have `this(args)` call another constructor in the same class, which in turn calls `super(args)`, thereby chaining the two calls across two constructors.

---

## 📝 PART B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each, with Internal Choice)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Pattern:** Part B questions carry **14 marks**, typically split as **Part (a) — 7 marks** and **Part (b) — 7 marks**. Students must answer **either** Option A **or** Option B in full.

---

### **Question A (14 Marks)** `[KTU University Exam - May 2023, Module 2]`

**(a)** Write a Java program to demonstrate how the `super` keyword can be used to invoke the **parent class constructor** and access a **shadowed instance variable** of the parent class. Explain the output with a step-by-step trace. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** Explain the **rules and restrictions** associated with the use of the `super` keyword in Java. What happens if the parent class does not have a no-argument constructor and the subclass does not explicitly invoke `super()`? Illustrate with a code example. **(7 marks)**

---

#### ✅ Model Solution — Part (a) (7 marks)

**Java Program:**

```java
class Animal {
    String name = "Generic Animal";   // Parent variable

    Animal() {
        System.out.println("Animal() constructor invoked");
    }

    Animal(String name) {
        this.name = name;
        System.out.println("Animal(String) constructor invoked with name = " + name);
    }

    void speak() {
        System.out.println("Animal speaks generically.");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    String name = "Buddy";   // Shadows parent variable

    Dog() {
        super("Bruno");      // Calls Animal(String)
        System.out.println("Dog() constructor invoked");
    }

    void printNames() {
        System.out.println("Child name   = " + name);
        System.out.println("Parent name  = " + super.name);
    }
}

public class SuperDemoA {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Dog d = new Dog();
        d.printNames();
    }
}
```

**Step-by-Step Execution Trace:**

| Step | Action | Resulting State |
|------|--------|-----------------|
| 1 | `new Dog()` triggers `Dog()` | Constructor begins |
| 2 | `super("Bruno")` (first line) calls `Animal(String)` | `Animal.name = "Bruno"` |
| 3 | Control returns to `Dog()` body | `Dog.name = "Buddy"` (from initializer) |
| 4 | `d.printNames()` called | Prints both names |
| 5 | `name` resolves to child's `"Buddy"` | Output: `Child name = Buddy` |
| 6 | `super.name` skips child, resolves to parent's `"Bruno"` | Output: `Parent name = Bruno` |

**Predicted Output:**

```
Animal(String) constructor invoked with name = Bruno
Dog() constructor invoked
Child name   = Buddy
Parent name  = Bruno
```

**Mark Distribution:**
- 2 marks: Correct class hierarchy and syntax
- 2 marks: Use of `super("Bruno")` to invoke parent constructor
- 2 marks: Use of `super.name` to access shadowed variable
- 1 mark: Correct output trace

---

#### ✅ Model Solution — Part (b) (7 marks)

**Rules and Restrictions of the `super` Keyword:**

1. **`super` cannot be used in a `static` method or static block**, because `super` refers to an instance and static context has no enclosing instance. *(1 mark)*

2. **`super()` or `super(args)` must be the first statement** in a subclass constructor if it is used. *(1 mark)*

3. **`this()` and `super()` cannot appear in the same constructor**, since both demand the first-statement position. *(1 mark)*

4. **Implicit `super()` insertion:** If a subclass constructor does not explicitly call `super(...)`, the compiler automatically inserts a no-argument `super();` call. *(1 mark)*

5. **`super.super` is illegal** — Java does not support skipping intermediate levels in the inheritance chain. *(1 mark)*

**Illustrative Code — Failure Scenario:**

```java
class Parent {
    Parent(int x) {                         // Only parameterized constructor
        System.out.println("Parent(int) called with " + x);
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    Child() {
        // No explicit super() call here
        // Compiler auto-inserts: super();
        // But Parent has NO no-arg constructor!
        // => COMPILE-TIME ERROR
        System.out.println("Child() called");
    }
}

public class SuperErrorDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Child();
    }
}
```

**Compiler Error Message:**

```
error: no suitable constructor found for Parent()
    Child() {
         ^
  constructor Parent.Parent(int) cannot be applied to given types
```

**Resolution:** The child must explicitly call `super(10);` as the first line.

**Mark Distribution:**
- 3 marks: Enumeration of rules
- 2 marks: Code example showing the error
- 2 marks: Correct resolution explanation

---

### **Question B (14 Marks)** `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2022, Module 2]`

**(a)** With a suitable Java program, demonstrate how the `super` keyword is used to call an **overridden method** of the parent class. Show the difference between calling the method normally and calling it with the `super` prefix. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** Discuss the **order of execution** of constructors in a multi-level inheritance hierarchy in Java. How does the `super()` call ensure that parent class members are initialized before the subclass members? Provide a three-level inheritance example. **(7 marks)**

---

#### ✅ Model Solution — Part (a) (7 marks)

**Java Program:**

```java
class Shape {
    void draw() {
        System.out.println("Drawing a generic Shape.");
    }
}

class Circle extends Shape {
    @Override
    void draw() {
        System.out.println("Drawing a Circle.");
        super.draw();    // Explicitly call parent version
        System.out.println("Circle drawing complete.");
    }
}

public class SuperMethodDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Circle c = new Circle();
        c.draw();
    }
}
```

**Execution Analysis:**

| Call Site | Resolved To | Reason |
|-----------|-------------|--------|
| `c.draw()` (external) | `Circle.draw()` | Polymorphic dispatch via v-table |
| `this.draw()` (inside Circle) | `Circle.draw()` | Normal binding, would cause infinite recursion |
| `super.draw()` (inside Circle) | `Shape.draw()` | Bypasses virtual dispatch, binds to parent |

**Predicted Output:**

```
Drawing a Circle.
Drawing a generic Shape.
Circle drawing complete.
```

**Significance:** This pattern is the essence of the **Template Method** design — the child extends behaviour by invoking the parent's logic at a controlled point rather than duplicating it.

**Mark Distribution:**
- 2 marks: Correct method overriding
- 2 marks: Correct use of `super.draw()`
- 2 marks: Output explanation
- 1 mark: Mention of Template Method / extension pattern

---

#### ✅ Model Solution — Part (b) (7 marks)

**Three-Level Hierarchy Example:**

```java
class Grandparent {
    Grandparent() {
        System.out.println("1. Grandparent() constructor");
    }
}

class Parent2 extends Grandparent {
    Parent2() {
        System.out.println("2. Parent2() constructor");
    }
}

class Child2 extends Parent2 {
    Child2() {
        System.out.println("3. Child2() constructor");
    }
}

public class ConstructorChainDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Child2 obj = new Child2();
    }
}
```

**Predicted Output (Top-Down Order):**

```
1. Grandparent() constructor
2. Parent2() constructor
3. Child2() constructor
```

**Conceptual Explanation:**

1. The JVM begins executing `Child2()`.
2. Its first statement is the implicit `super();` → calls `Parent2()`.
3. `Parent2()`'s first statement is the implicit `super();` → calls `Grandparent()`.
4. `Grandparent()`'s first statement is the implicit `super();` → calls `Object()`.
5. `Object()` runs to completion; control unwinds downward.
6. Only after `Grandparent()` finishes does `Parent2()`'s body run.
7. Only after `Parent2()` finishes does `Child2()`'s body run.

This guarantees that **all inherited members are fully initialized** before the child class uses them — preventing the use of uninitialized state.

**Mark Distribution:**
- 3 marks: Correct hierarchical code
- 2 marks: Accurate execution order explanation
- 2 marks: Justification of why this order is enforced

---

## 🚨 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning

> [!WARNING]
> **Top 5 Pitfalls Where KTU Students Lose Marks:**
>
> 1. **Forgetting that `super()` is implicit** — If the question shows a constructor with no explicit `super()` call, students often assume no parent constructor runs. **Marks lost: 2–3** for the missing trace step.
>
> 2. **Confusing `super.x` with `super()`** — The dot-suffix `super.x` is a *member access*; the parenthesis `super()` is a *constructor invocation*. Mixing them in code yields compile errors.
>
> 3. **Claiming `super` can be used in `static` methods** — This is a **hard compile error**. Examiners specifically test this misconception.
>
> 4. **Believing `super.super` is valid** — Java does not allow direct grandparent access. Students must traverse one level at a time.
>
> 5. **Writing `super()` after some other statement** — Java mandates that `super()` be the **first statement**. Any preceding print or assignment causes a compile error.
>
> **Pro Tip:** When asked to "explain the output," always trace **every constructor call** including the implicit `super()` insertions. The KTU answer key explicitly rewards step-by-step traces.

---

## 🎯 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Rapid-Revision Checklist (Print & Pin This!)**

- ✅ `super` is a **reference variable** to the immediate parent class object.
- ✅ Three uses: **variable access**, **method invocation**, **constructor chaining**.
- ✅ `super` **resolves shadowing** of same-named instance variables.
- ✅ `super.method()` calls the **overridden parent version**, bypassing virtual dispatch.
- ✅ `super(args)` calls a **parent constructor** and must be the **first statement**.
- ✅ If no `super()` is written, the compiler **auto-inserts** a no-argument `super();`.
- ✅ Auto-insertion **fails** if the parent lacks a no-arg constructor → compile error.
- ✅ `super` **cannot be used in `static` methods** or `static` blocks.
- ✅ `super.super.x` is **illegal** in Java.
- ✅ `this()` and `super()` **cannot coexist** in the same constructor.
- ✅ Constructor chain **always terminates at `Object()`**, regardless of hierarchy depth.
- ✅ Execution order is **top-down**: ancestors initialize before descendants.
- ✅ Memory-wise, `super` is an **offset pointer** to the embedded parent sub-object, not a separate allocation.
- ✅ Common in production: **Template Method pattern**, **framework extension** (Spring, JUnit, JavaFX), **lifecycle hooks** (Android `onCreate`).
- ✅ Frequently asked in KTU as 3-mark (definition) and 7-mark (code + trace) questions.

---
