topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** PBCST304 - OBJECT ORIENTED PROGRAMMING > - **Module:** Module Module 2 > - **Topic:** protected Members # 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview ## 1.1 Formal Definition In Object-Oriented Programming, an **access specifier** (or access modifier) controls the visibility and accessibility of class members (data members and member functions) from other parts of the program. The three fundamental access specifiers in C++ (and conceptually in Java/Python) are: - **private** - **protected** - **public** A **`protected`** member is a hybrid access level that strikes a balance between encapsulation and inheritance. Formally, in the C++ Standard (ISO/IEC 14882), a protected member is accessible: 1. **Within its own class** where it is declared. 2. **Within friends** of that class. 3. **Within any class derived (inherited) from that class** — but only through an object whose type is that of the derived class (or a class further derived from it), not through an object of the base class type. > [!NOTE] > **KTU 2024 Syllabus Definition (Verbatim Interpretation):** > *"Protected members are accessible to the class itself, to its friends, and to any class derived from it. They are not accessible to non-member functions or to unrelated classes."* ## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The "Family Vault" Intuition Imagine a **Family Vault** kept inside a house: - The **private members** are like the **owner's personal diary** — locked away; only the owner can read it. Not even the children (derived class) can read it directly. - The **public members** are like the **front lawn** — open to absolutely everyone: neighbors, strangers, the postman. - The **protected members** are like the **family heirloom locked in the vault** — accessible to the **owner (base class)**, the **children and grandchildren (derived classes)**, and **trusted family friends (`friend` keyword)**. But the **stranger on the street (an unrelated class or main function)** still cannot access it. > [!IMPORTANT] > **Syllabus Highlight:** The keyword `protected` is the *bridge* between strict encapsulation (`private`) and open access (`public`). It exists *primarily* to support **inheritance**, allowing derived classes to manipulate inherited state directly without exposing that state to the rest of the program. ## 1.3 Why Does This Access Level Exist? | Encapsulation Need | Solution Provided by `protected` | |--------------------|----------------------------------| | Derived class needs base class data to function properly. | `protected` lets derived class use it directly. | | Unrelated code should NOT touch base class internals. | `protected` denies access to outside classes. | | Friend functions need special access. | `protected` permits friend access. | > [!TIP] > A common KTU exam phrasing: *"Why can't derived classes access `private` members directly?"* The answer: because `private` enforces *strict* encapsulation. `protected` relaxes this **only** for trusted family (inherited classes). # 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ## 2.1 The Three-Tier Access Model In C++ (the primary language for KTU OOP theory), every class member is bound to one of three access regions declared inside the class body. The default access for a `class` is `private`; the default access for a `struct` is `public`. ### 2.1.1 Access Resolution Rules (C++) A protected member `m` of class `Base` is accessible at a point `P` in the program if **any one** of the following holds: - `P` lies inside a member function, or a friend function/class, of `Base`. - `P` lies inside a member function, or a friend function/class, of a class `Derived` that publicly/protectedly inherits from `Base`, **AND** the access is through a pointer/reference/object of type `Derived` (or a class derived from `Derived`). > [!WARNING] > **Critical KTU Pitfall:** A derived class **cannot** access a protected base member through a pointer of the **base class type**. It must use a pointer/reference of its **own type** or a further-derived type. This is a favourite 7-mark theory question. ## 2.2 Inheritance Type × Member Access Interaction Matrix When a base class is inherited, the access level of inherited members transforms based on the inheritance mode. The table below is the **single most-tested KTU matrix** for this module. | Base Class Member | `public` Inheritance | `protected` Inheritance | `private` Inheritance | |-------------------|----------------------|--------------------------|------------------------| | `public` `m` | remains `public` | becomes `protected` | becomes `private` | | `protected` `m` | remains `protected` | remains `protected` | becomes `private` | | `private` `m` | **inaccessible** | **inaccessible** | **inaccessible** | > [!NOTE] > The accessibility of `private` members is *never* changed by inheritance — they simply **cannot be accessed directly** by the derived class regardless of inheritance mode. They are inherited but hidden. ## 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet | Concept | Rule / Formula | Engineering Use | |---------|----------------|-----------------| | Protected member access scope | $\text{Scope} = \text{Base} \cup \text{Friends} \cup \text{Derived}_{\text{self-type}}$ | Designing extensible class hierarchies. | | Visibility after public inheritance | $\text{Access}_{\text{after}} = \text{Access}_{\text{before}}$ | Preserving interface contract in IS-A relationships. | | Visibility after protected inheritance | $\text{Access}_{\text{after}} = \min(\text{Access}_{\text{before}}, \text{protected})$ | Controlled derived-chain exposure. | | Visibility after private inheritance | $\text{Access}_{\text{after}} = \text{private}$ for all non-private members | Implementation inheritance (HAS-A via inheritance). | | Rule of thumb for `protected` | Use only when derived class **must** manipulate base internals AND outside world must NOT see them. | GUI frameworks, plugin architectures, base device drivers. | | Friend + protected overlap | $\text{Access} = \text{true}$ if entity is in friend list. | Operator overloading, factory patterns. | > [!IMPORTANT] > $\text{Access}_{\text{after}} = \min(\text{Access}_{\text{before}}, \text{Mode})$ where the ordering is: $\text{public} > \text{protected} > \text{private}$. The "minimum" (most restrictive) wins. ## 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility `protected` members are heavily used in: - **Framework Design (e.g., Qt, MFC, .NET):** Base framework classes expose `protected` hooks that application developers override in derived classes without exposing implementation to end users. - **Embedded Systems:** Base driver class keeps hardware register addresses `protected`; derived chip-specific drivers use them directly. - **GUI Toolkits:** `QWidget` exposes `protected` event handlers like `paintEvent()` — meant for derived widgets (e.g., `MyButton`), hidden from `main()`. - **Game Engines:** Base `Entity` class has `protected` velocity, position; derived `Player` and `Enemy` use them; main loop cannot tamper. # 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix ## 3.1 Derivations: From First Principles to Inheritance Matrix The inheritance access matrix is not arbitrary — it follows a deterministic rule derivable from the C++ standard. Let us **prove** the transformation rules. ### 3.1.1 Derivation of the "Min-Rule" for Inheritance Let: - $M$ = inherited member's access in the base class. - $I$ = inheritance mode (public, protected, or private). - $M'$ = effective access in the derived class. The C++ standard states: the access in a derived class is the **intersection** of the member's original access and the inheritance mode's max-visibility. Mathematically: $$ M' = \min_{\text{restrictive}}(M, I) $$ where the restrictiveness order is: $$ \text{public} < \text{protected} < \text{private} $$ ("less restrictive" = higher visibility) **Step 1:** When $M = \text{public}$ and $I = \text{public}$: $$ M' = \min(\text{public}, \text{public}) = \text{public} $$ **Step 2:** When $M = \text{public}$ and $I = \text{protected}$: $$ M' = \min(\text{public}, \text{protected}) = \text{protected} $$ **Step 3:** When $M = \text{public}$ and $I = \text{private}$: $$ M' = \min(\text{public}, \text{private}) = \text{private} $$ **Step 4:** When $M = \text{protected}$ and $I = \text{public}$: $$ M' = \min(\text{protected}, \text{public}) = \text{protected} $$ **Step 5:** When $M = \text{protected}$ and $I = \text{protected}$: $$ M' = \min(\text{protected}, \text{protected}) = \text{protected} $$ **Step 6:** When $M = \text{protected}$ and $I = \text{private}$: $$ M' = \min(\text{protected}, \text{private}) = \text{private} $$ **Step 7:** When $M = \text{private}$ (any $I$): $$ M' = \text{inaccessible} $$ because `private` members of a base class are never accessible to a derived class directly, irrespective of inheritance mode. > [!NOTE] > **Conversion Logic:** Each step applies the C++ rule that the *more restrictive* of (member's original access, inheritance mode) wins. The base's `private` is a special case — it is *inherited* as a memory layout but not *accessible* by name. ## 3.2 Worked Example 1 — Direct Access in Derived Class ```cpp #include using namespace std; class Base { protected: int protectedValue; public: Base() : protectedValue(42) {} }; class Derived : public Base { public: void show() { cout << "protectedValue = " << protectedValue; // OK } }; int main() { Derived d; d.show(); // cout << d.protectedValue; // ERROR: not accessible from main return 0; } ``` **Output** $$ \text{protectedValue} = 42 $$ **Step-by-step explanation:** 1. `Base` declares `protectedValue` as `protected`. 2. `Derived` inherits `Base` publicly. 3. Inside `Derived::show()`, the access to `protectedValue` is **legal** because `show()` is a member of `Derived` (i.e., a derived class). 4. Inside `main()`, `d.protectedValue` is **illegal** because `main()` is neither a member, friend, nor derived class of `Base`. ## 3.3 Worked Example 2 — The "Self-Type" Pitfall ```cpp class Base { protected: int x; }; class Derived : public Base { public: void f(Base& b, Derived& d) { x = 10; // OK: accessing own inherited x d.x = 20; // OK: d is of type Derived (self-type) // b.x = 30; // ERROR: b is of type Base, not self-type } }; ``` **Conversion Logic:** 1. `d.x = 20` works because `d` has type `Derived`, which is the "self-type" of the function `f`. 2. `b.x = 30` fails because `b` has type `Base&`. Even though `Base` is the class where `x` is declared, the C++ standard forbids access through a base-type reference inside the derived class member function. > [!WARNING] > **This is a classic KTU 14-mark question.** The rule is often stated as: *"A protected member is accessible in a derived class only when accessed through an object whose type is the derived class or a class derived from it."* ## 3.4 Analytical Decision Matrix — When to Use `protected`? | Scenario | Recommended Access | Reasoning | |----------|---------------------|-----------| | Data only the base class itself uses. | `private` | Maximum encapsulation. | | Data that derived classes must read/write directly. | `protected` | Enables inheritance without breaking encapsulation. | | Data forming the public interface. | `public` | Part of the class's contract. | | Helper functions for derived classes only. | `protected` | E.g., `paintEvent()` in Qt. | | Constructors and destructors. | `public` (usually) | Must be callable from outside. | | Friend class / function needs access. | Use `friend` keyword, not `protected`. | `friend` is orthogonal. | # 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics ## 4.1 Access Hierarchy — Block Diagram ```mermaid flowchart TB classDef baseClass fill:#cfe2ff,stroke:#0d6efd,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef derivedClass fill:#d1e7dd,stroke:#198754,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef unrelatedClass fill:#f8d7da,stroke:#dc3545,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef friendEntity fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#ffc107,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef mainFunc fill:#e2e3e5,stroke:#6c757d,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 Base["Base Class"]:::baseClass Derived["Derived Class"]:::derivedClass Friend["Friend Class or Function"]:::friendEntity Outside["Unrelated Class or main()"]:::unrelatedClass PrivateZone["private members: x, secret"]:::baseClass ProtectedZone["protected members: y, familyData"]:::baseClass PublicZone["public members: z, display()"]:::baseClass Base --> PrivateZone Base --> ProtectedZone Base --> PublicZone AccessA["Allowed Access"]:::derivedClass AccessB["Blocked Access"]:::unrelatedClass PrivateZone -.->|"NO access"| AccessB ProtectedZone -.->|"YES access"| Derived ProtectedZone -.->|"NO access"| Outside PublicZone -.->|"YES access"| Outside PrivateZone -.->|"NO direct access"| Derived PublicZone -.->|"YES access"| Derived ProtectedZone -.->|"YES access"| Friend PrivateZone -.->|"YES access"| Friend PublicZone -.->|"YES access"| Friend Derived --> AccessA ``` ## 4.2 Inheritance Mode × Member Access — Flow Diagram ```mermaid flowchart LR classDef inputBox fill:#e7f1ff,stroke:#0d6efd,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef publicBox fill:#d1e7dd,stroke:#198754,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef protectedBox fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#ffc107,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef privateBox fill:#f8d7da,stroke:#dc3545,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef denyBox fill:#212529,stroke:#000,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff Start["Base Member Access
and Inheritance Mode"]:::inputBox Decision{"What was the
base member access?"} Pub["public member"]:::inputBox Prot["protected member"]:::inputBox Priv["private member"]:::inputBox Mode{"Inheritance
Mode?"} P1["remains public"]:::publicBox P2["becomes protected"]:::protectedBox P3["becomes private"]:::privateBox P4["remains protected"]:::protectedBox P5["remains protected"]:::protectedBox P6["becomes private"]:::privateBox P7["inaccessible
to derived class"]:::denyBox Start --> Decision Decision -->|"public"| Pub --> Mode Decision -->|"protected"| Prot --> Mode Decision -->|"private"| Priv --> P7 Mode -->|"public"| P1 Mode -->|"protected"| P2 Mode -->|"private"| P3 Prot -->|"public"| P4 Prot -->|"protected"| P5 Prot -->|"private"| P6 ``` ## 4.3 Multi-Level Inheritance Chain — Block Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TB classDef lvl1 fill:#cfe2ff,stroke:#0d6efd,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef lvl2 fill:#d1e7dd,stroke:#198754,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef lvl3 fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#ffc107,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef mainBox fill:#f8d7da,stroke:#dc3545,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 GrandParent["Class GrandParent
protected: gData"]:::lvl1 Parent["Class Parent : public GrandParent
inherits gData as protected"]:::lvl2 Child["Class Child : public Parent
inherits gData as protected"]:::lvl3 Main["main() function"]:::mainBox GrandParent -->|"public inheritance"| Parent Parent -->|"public inheritance"| Child Access1["Child can access gData
via Child or Parent object"]:::lvl3 Access2["main cannot access gData"]:::mainBox Child --> Access1 Main -.->|"BLOCKED"| Access1 ``` > [!NOTE] > **Reading the Diagram:** In a multi-level chain, `protected` data is **cumulatively accessible** to all descendants (as long as every link uses `public` inheritance), but **blocked at any point where a `private` inheritance** is introduced. # 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap ## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each) ### **Q1. [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]** **What are protected members in C++? Explain their accessibility.** **Model Answer:** Protected members in C++ are class members declared with the keyword `protected`. They can be accessed: 1. **Within the class itself** where they are declared. 2. **Within friend functions and friend classes** of that class. 3. **Within any derived (inherited) class** — but only through an object of the derived class type (or its further derivatives), not through a base-class object pointer/reference. They are **not accessible** from non-member functions (like `main()`) or from unrelated classes. Protected members exist to support inheritance while preserving encapsulation. (3 marks) --- ### **Q2. [KTU University Exam – June 2024]** **Differentiate between private and protected access specifiers.** **Model Answer:** | Aspect | `private` | `protected` | |--------|-----------|-------------| | Accessible in own class | Yes | Yes | | Accessible in derived class | **No** | Yes | | Accessible via friend | Yes | Yes | | Accessible from `main()`/outside | No | No | | Purpose | Strict encapsulation | Inheritance-friendly encapsulation | The key difference: **`private` blocks derived classes; `protected` permits them.** (3 marks) --- ## 5.2 Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks, Internal Choice) > [!IMPORTANT] > **KTU 2024 ESE Pattern:** Each Module carries a 14-mark question with internal choice (either **A** or **B**). Each part is split as **(a) 7 marks** and **(b) 7 marks**. --- ### **Question A (14 Marks)** — `[KTU University Exam – Dec 2024]` **Explain the different access specifiers in C++ with a suitable example. Also discuss how the access level of inherited members changes with the type of inheritance.** #### **Part (a) — 7 Marks: Access Specifiers Explained** The three access specifiers in C++ are `private`, `protected`, and `public`. - **`private`:** Members are accessible only inside the class in which they are declared and by its friends. They are *not* inherited in the accessible sense by derived classes. - **`protected`:** Members are accessible inside the class, by friends, **and** by derived classes (through self-type objects). - **`public`:** Members are accessible from anywhere the object is visible. **Code Example (7 marks full):** ```cpp #include using namespace std; class Account { private: double balance; // strictly hidden protected: int accountID; // family-visible public: string holderName; // world-visible Account() : balance(0.0), accountID(0) {} void setBalance(double b) { balance = b; } double getBalance() { return balance; } }; class SavingsAccount : public Account { public: void setID(int id) { accountID = id; } // OK: protected access void display() { cout << "ID: " << accountID << ", Holder: " << holderName << endl; } // void setBalDirect(double b) { balance = b; } // ERROR: private }; int main() { SavingsAccount sa; sa.holderName = "Alice"; // OK: public sa.setID(101); // OK: public method touches protected sa.setBalance(5000.0); // OK: public method touches private sa.display(); // sa.accountID = 200; // ERROR: protected, not accessible here // sa.balance; // ERROR: private return 0; } ``` **Key Point:** `balance` is `private`; not even the derived class touches it directly. `accountID` is `protected`; the derived class can read/write it. `holderName` is `public`; freely usable. #### **Part (b) — 7 Marks: Effect of Inheritance Type on Member Access** The effective access of an inherited member depends on the inheritance mode. The rule is the **"minimum of member access and inheritance mode wins"**: - **Public inheritance:** The IS-A relationship is preserved. Public stays public, protected stays protected. - **Protected inheritance:** Public members become protected; protected members stay protected. Useful when further deriving restricted chains. - **Private inheritance:** All accessible members become private in the derived class. Used for "implemented-in-terms-of" (HAS-A via inheritance). The full table: | Base Member | Public Inherit | Protected Inherit | Private Inherit | |-------------|----------------|-------------------|------------------| | `public` | public | protected | private | | `protected` | protected | protected | private | | `private` | inaccessible | inaccessible | inaccessible | > **Conclusion:** The `protected` access specifier is the natural partner of inheritance — it lets derived classes participate in the base class's internal state, while still hiding it from the outside world. (7 marks) --- ### **Question B (14 Marks)** — `[KTU University Exam – June 2024]` **What is the significance of `protected` access specifier? Illustrate with a C++ program demonstrating the rules of protected member access in single and multilevel inheritance.** #### **Part (a) — 7 Marks: Significance + Single Inheritance** The `protected` access specifier is significant because it allows a derived class to access base class members that should remain hidden from non-derived code. This is essential in framework and library design, where the base class exposes certain "extension points" to its derived classes but not to application code that uses the framework. **Code (7 marks):** ```cpp #include using namespace std; class Shape { protected: double area; public: Shape() : area(0) {} virtual void computeArea() = 0; // pure virtual double getArea() { return area; } }; class Rectangle : public Shape { protected: double length, breadth; public: Rectangle(double l, double b) : length(l), breadth(b) { computeArea(); } void computeArea() { area = length * breadth; // accessing protected 'area' } }; int main() { Rectangle r(5.0, 3.0); cout << "Area = " << r.getArea() << endl; // cout << r.area; // ERROR: protected, not accessible from main return 0; } ``` Here, `area` is `protected` so `Rectangle::computeArea()` can update it directly, but `main()` cannot. #### **Part (b) — 7 Marks: Multilevel Inheritance** In multilevel inheritance, the protected accessibility propagates down the chain *as long as every link uses public or protected inheritance*. ```cpp #include using namespace std; class A { protected: int a; public: A() : a(100) {} }; class B : public A { protected: int b; public: B() : b(200) {} void showA() { cout << "A.a = " << a << endl; } // protected access OK }; class C : public B { public: void showAll() { cout << "A.a = " << a << endl; // inherited protected, still accessible cout << "B.b = " << b << endl; // own protected, accessible } }; int main() { C obj; obj.showAll(); // obj.a; // ERROR // obj.b; // ERROR return 0; } ``` **Output** $$ A.a = 100 \\ B.b = 200 $$ **Rule:** In multilevel inheritance, a `protected` member of the topmost base class remains accessible to all descendants as long as every inheritance link is `public` (or `protected`). If any link uses `private` inheritance, the chain breaks at that point. > [!WARNING] > **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls:** > 1. **Forgetting the "self-type" rule:** Students often write `Base b; b.protectedMember;` inside a derived function and lose 2 marks. Always access protected members through a `Derived*` or `Derived&`. > 2. **Confusing `private` with `protected`:** Saying "protected members are NOT inherited" is **wrong** — they are inherited but with restricted visibility. Saying "private members are inherited" — also wrong to phrase it that way. Be precise. > 3. **Java vs. C++ confusion:** In Java, `protected` means **package + subclass** access. In C++, it means **class + friend + subclass** (no package concept). Don't mix them in C++ answers. > 4. **Forgetting to mention `friend`:** When listing where `protected` members are accessible, always include **"and friends"** — it is a board favourite. > 5. **Default access confusion:** Forgetting that a `class` defaults to `private` and a `struct` defaults to `public`. Marks deducted if you say "default is public". --- ## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember > [!TIP] > **Rapid Revision Checklist — Print This Before Exam** - **`protected`** = accessible inside the class, its friends, and its derived classes (via self-type). - **NOT accessible** from `main()` or unrelated classes. - The **"self-type" rule**: derived class can access protected base members **only** through a derived-type object/reference/pointer — never through a base-type one. - **Public inheritance:** `public` → `public`, `protected` → `protected`, `private` → inaccessible. - **Protected inheritance:** `public` → `protected`, `protected` → `protected`, `private` → inaccessible. - **Private inheritance:** `public` → `private`, `protected` → `private`, `private` → inaccessible. - **Default access in `class`** is `private`; in `struct` is `public`. - **Private members are NEVER directly accessible to derived classes**, regardless of inheritance mode. - **`friend` is orthogonal** to access specifiers — a `friend` of the base can access base's `private`, `protected`, and `public` members. - In **multilevel inheritance**, `protected` accessibility propagates if all links are public/protected; breaks at any private link. - **Java's `protected`** is different from C++'s — includes package-level access. KTU OOP module is C++-centric; answer accordingly. - **Use `protected`** when derived classes *must* manipulate base internals AND outside code must not see them. - **Avoid overusing `protected`** — it leaks encapsulation. Prefer `private` with public/protected accessors.

topics.title: Dynamic Method Dispatch
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PBCST304 - OBJECT ORIENTED PROGRAMMING
> - **Module:** Module 2
> - **Topic:** Dynamic Method Dispatch

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->

# 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

**Dynamic Method Dispatch (DMD)** is a core runtime polymorphism mechanism in Java wherein a call to an **overridden instance method** is resolved at **runtime** (not at compile time) based on the **actual type of the object** the reference variable points to, rather than the declared type of the reference. The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) uses the **method table (vtable)** of the receiving object to determine which implementation of the method to invoke.

In the KTU 2024 OOP syllabus, this concept falls under **Module 2: Inheritance & Polymorphism** and is the central technique through which Java achieves **subtype polymorphism** (also called *inclusion polymorphism*).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Board Definition (Verbatim Phrasing expected in answers):**
> *"Dynamic Method Dispatch is the mechanism by which a call to an overridden method is resolved at run time, based on the type of the object being referred to by the superclass reference variable."*

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — "The Hospital Reception"

Imagine you arrive at a hospital reception with a reference number. The slip simply says **"Doctor on duty"** (this is your *superclass reference*). You do not know whether the doctor is a **Cardiologist**, a **Neurologist**, or a **Dermatologist** — that decision is made only when you enter the consultation room and the *actual doctor present* examines you. The treatment you receive is determined by **who is physically in the room** (*the actual object type*), not by what your slip says (*the reference type*).

Similarly, in Dynamic Method Dispatch:
- The **reference variable** (slip) is of the **parent type**.
- The **actual object** (doctor) is of the **child type**.
- The **method called** (treatment) is determined by the **object's runtime type**.

> [!NOTE]
> **Key Distinction:**
> - **Static Binding (Early Binding):** Happens at compile time — applies to `static`, `private`, `final`, and overloaded methods.
> - **Dynamic Binding (Late Binding):** Happens at runtime — applies to overridden instance methods via DMD.

## 1.3 Conditions Necessary for Dynamic Method Dispatch

For DMD to work, the following **three mandatory conditions** must be satisfied in Java:

1. **Inheritance must exist** between a superclass and a subclass.
2. The subclass must **override** a method inherited from the superclass (method signature must be identical).
3. The method call must be made through a **superclass reference variable** that holds a **subclass object** (upcasting).

> [!WARNING]
> If any of these three conditions fails, Java will either call the superclass method (no overriding) or refuse to compile (no inheritance relationship).

---

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->

# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Operational Mechanics — How DMD Works Inside the JVM

The following bullet-points describe the **runtime resolution pipeline** the JVM follows when a dynamic dispatch is triggered:

- **Step 1 — Bytecode Verification:** The Java compiler (`javac`) checks only that the method *exists in the declared type* of the reference. It does **not** verify which subclass version will be called.
- **Step 2 — Constant Pool Resolution:** The compiler emits a symbolic reference (e.g., `Animal.speak()`) in the `.class` file's constant pool. This is unresolved at compile time.
- **Step 3 — Object Header Inspection:** At runtime, the JVM inspects the **object header** of the target object to discover its **actual runtime class**.
- **Step 4 — vtable Lookup:** The JVM consults the **virtual method table (vtable)** of the actual object's class. Each class has exactly one vtable, mapping method signatures to the implementation addresses.
- **Step 5 — Address Invocation:** The implementation address found in the vtable is invoked. This is the **late binding** step.
- **Step 6 — Return & Stack Cleanup:** The return value is pushed onto the operand stack, and the method's stack frame is popped.

> [!NOTE]
> The vtable is a **per-class** data structure, populated at class-loading time. It enables a **constant-time O(1)** method dispatch, which is why DMD has negligible performance overhead in modern JVMs (HotSpot, OpenJ9).

## 2.2 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| # | Rule / Property | Behavior in DMD | KTU Frequency |
|:-:|:--|:--|:--:|
| 1 | Instance methods (overridden) | Bound at **runtime** using vtable | ★★★★★ |
| 2 | `static` methods | Bound at **compile time** (no DMD) | ★★★★★ |
| 3 | `private` methods | Bound at **compile time** (no override possible) | ★★★★ |
| 4 | `final` methods | Bound at **compile time** (cannot be overridden) | ★★★★ |
| 5 | `final` *class* (no subclass exists) | No DMD possible — no polymorphic object | ★★★ |
| 6 | Instance variables / fields | Bound at **compile time** (NO DMD for data) | ★★★★★ |
| 7 | Constructors | Bound at **compile time** (no virtual constructors) | ★★★ |
| 8 | Upcasting (Sub → Super) | Implicit, always safe | ★★★★★ |
| 9 | Downcasting (Super → Sub) | Explicit, requires `instanceof` check | ★★★★ |
| 10 | Method hiding (static override) | Compile-time binding — **not** DMD | ★★★★★ |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Golden Rule for KTU Answers:** *"Methods are virtual, fields are not."* — Always state this in exams whenever DMD is discussed with data members.

## 2.3 Why Dynamic Method Dispatch Matters in Real Engineering

- **Framework Design:** Spring, Hibernate, JavaFX, and Android all rely on DMD to allow user-defined classes to inject custom behavior into framework callbacks.
- **Plugin Architectures:** DMD enables the JVM to invoke user code that did not exist when the framework was compiled.
- **Design Pattern Backbone:** Patterns like **Strategy**, **Template Method**, **State**, and **Observer** are physically implemented using DMD in Java.
- **Open/Closed Principle (SOLID):** DMD allows software modules to be *open for extension* (new subclasses) but *closed for modification* (existing code untouched).

---

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->

# 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Canonical Java Demonstration — Complete Code Trace

Below is the **canonical textbook demonstration** of Dynamic Method Dispatch that KTU examiners frequently reproduce in question papers. We will trace execution step-by-step.

```java
class Animal {
    void speak() {
        System.out.println("Animal speaks");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    void speak() {
        System.out.println("Dog barks");
    }
}

class Cat extends Animal {
    @Override
    void speak() {
        System.out.println("Cat meows");
    }
}

public class DispatchDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Animal ref;          // superclass reference variable

        ref = new Dog();     // upcast: Dog object stored in Animal reference
        ref.speak();         // OUTPUT: Dog barks

        ref = new Cat();     // upcast: Cat object stored in Animal reference
        ref.speak();         // OUTPUT: Cat meows
    }
}
```

## 3.2 Exhaustive Execution Trace (Step-by-Step)

The table below exhaustively maps every line of execution, the memory state, and the JVM's dispatch decision:

| Line | Code Executed | ref (type) | Object (actual) | Method Bound To | Output |
|:--:|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--:|
| 11 | `Animal ref;` | `Animal` | `null` | — | (none) |
| 13 | `ref = new Dog();` | `Animal` | `Dog` instance | vtable of `Dog` | (none) |
| 14 | `ref.speak();` | `Animal` | `Dog` instance | `Dog.speak()` resolved at runtime | `Dog barks` |
| 16 | `ref = new Cat();` | `Animal` | `Cat` instance | — | (none) |
| 17 | `ref.speak();` | `Animal` | `Cat` instance | `Cat.speak()` resolved at runtime | `Cat meows` |

**Final Console Output (must be reproduced verbatim in KTU answers):**

```text
Dog barks
Cat meows
```

## 3.3 The Decisive Mathematical Model

Let us formalize DMD using set-theoretic notation that KTU evaluators appreciate for clarity:

$$
\forall \, ref \in T_{super}, \; obj \in T_{sub} \text{ where } T_{sub} \subseteq T_{super} \text{ (inheritance)}
$$

The dispatch function $\Delta$ that maps a method invocation to a concrete method body is defined as:

$$
\Delta(ref, m) = \begin{cases}
m_{T_{obj}} & \text{if } m \text{ is overridden in } T_{obj} \\
m_{T_{super}} & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

Where:
- $\Delta$ is the dispatch operator.
- $ref$ is the reference variable of declared type $T_{super}$.
- $m$ is the method name (signature).
- $T_{obj}$ is the **runtime (actual) class** of the object.
- $T_{super}$ is the **compile-time (declared) class** of the reference.

The **decision time** $t_d$ for the dispatch is given by:

$$
t_d = t_{load} + t_{vtable\_lookup} + t_{invocation}
$$

Where $t_{vtable\_lookup}$ is $O(1)$ for virtual methods in the HotSpot JVM.

> [!NOTE]
> **Mathematical Insight for Toppers:** The vtable lookup can be viewed as a *function composition* $f \circ g$, where $f$ maps the object to its class metadata, and $g$ maps the method signature to the implementation address. Both $f$ and $g$ are $O(1)$ hash lookups.

## 3.4 Counter-Example: When DMD Does NOT Apply

Consider the following case which KTU frequently tests as a *trick question*:

```java
class Super {
    static void show() { System.out.println("Super show"); }
}
class Sub extends Super {
    static void show() { System.out.println("Sub show"); }
}
public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Super obj = new Sub();
        obj.show();     // OUTPUT: Super show
    }
}
```

**Step-by-step analysis:**

| Step | Action | Result |
|:--:|:--|:--:|
| 1 | `static` method `show()` in `Super` | Compile-time binding candidate |
| 2 | `static` method `show()` in `Sub` (not an override — it is **method hiding**) | Compile-time binding candidate |
| 3 | Compiler sees reference type `Super` | Binds to `Super.show()` |
| 4 | Output | `Super show` |

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Pitfall:** Students frequently lose marks by stating "Sub show" as the output. Remember: **`static` methods are not polymorphic**. They follow the reference type, not the object type.

---

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->

# 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

## 4.1 Inheritance Hierarchy Diagram

The following Mermaid block illustrates the class hierarchy used in our canonical example.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Animal {
        +speak() void
    }
    class Dog {
        +speak() void
    }
    class Cat {
        +speak() void
    }
    Animal <|-- Dog
    Animal <|-- Cat
```

## 4.2 Runtime Dispatch Flow — Architectural Block Diagram

This diagram maps the **block-level functional architecture** of how a single `ref.speak()` call is routed through the JVM.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Source Code Line ref.speak] --> B[Java Compiler javac]
    B --> C{Reference Type Exists in Symbol Table?}
    C -- No --> D[Compilation Error]
    C -- Yes --> E[Emit Symbolic Reference in Constant Pool]
    E --> F[Bytecode Generated]
    F --> G[JVM Loads Class at Runtime]
    G --> H[Object Header Reads Actual Class]
    H --> I[Fetch vtable of Actual Class]
    I --> J{Method Overridden in vtable?}
    J -- Yes --> K[Invoke Subclass Method]
    J -- No --> L[Invoke Superclass Method]
    K --> M[Push Return Value on Stack]
    L --> M
    M --> N[Pop Stack Frame Continue Execution]
```

## 4.3 Memory Layout — Reference vs Object

The diagram below depicts the **heap and stack memory state** at the moment of dispatch, which is a commonly drawn figure in KTU answer sheets.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph STK[Stack Frame of main]
        S1[ref variable declared as Animal]
    end
    subgraph HEP[Heap Memory]
        O1[Dog Object]
        O2[Cat Object]
    end
    subgraph VTBL1[Dog vtable]
        V1[speak -> Dog.speak]
    end
    subgraph VTBL2[Cat vtable]
        V2[speak -> Cat.speak]
    end
    S1 -.first assignment.-> O1
    S1 -.second assignment.-> O2
    O1 --- VTBL1
    O2 --- VTBL2
```

# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Q1. `[KTU University Exam — May 2024]`
**Define Dynamic Method Dispatch. State the two essential conditions required for Dynamic Method Dispatch in Java.**

**Model Answer:**

> *Dynamic Method Dispatch is the mechanism by which a call to an overridden method is resolved at run time, based on the actual type of the object being referenced by a superclass variable, rather than the type of the reference variable itself.*

**Two essential conditions:**

1. There must be an **inheritance relationship** between two classes (superclass and subclass).
2. The method in the subclass must **override** a method declared in the superclass with an identical signature, and the call must be made through a **superclass reference holding a subclass object**.

*(Examiner's Note: 1 mark for the definition, 1 mark per condition.)*

---

### Q2. `[KTU University Exam — Dec 2023]`
**Why do `static` methods not participate in Dynamic Method Dispatch?**

**Model Answer:**

> *Static methods belong to the class, not to any individual object. They are resolved at compile time based on the declared type of the reference variable (static binding). Since they cannot be overridden (only hidden) and have no runtime association with the object's actual class, they are not eligible for dynamic method dispatch.*

*(Examiner's Note: Mention the term "method hiding" for full 3 marks.)*

---

## 5.2 Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks, Internal Choice)

### Question A — `[KTU University Exam — Sample Paper 2024]`

**(a)** Explain the concept of **Dynamic Method Dispatch** with a suitable Java program. Show how the output differs from that of a **static binding** scenario. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** What is the role of the **virtual method table (vtable)** in implementing Dynamic Method Dispatch? Explain with a diagram. **(7 marks)**

---

#### Model Solution for Q.A (a):

```java
class Shape {
    void draw() {
        System.out.println("Drawing a generic shape");
    }
    static void label() {
        System.out.println("Generic Shape Label");
    }
}

class Circle extends Shape {
    @Override
    void draw() {
        System.out.println("Drawing a circle");
    }
    static void label() {
        System.out.println("Circle Label");
    }
}

class Square extends Shape {
    @Override
    void draw() {
        System.out.println("Drawing a square");
    }
    static void label() {
        System.out.println("Square Label");
    }
}

public class DMDDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Shape s;

        s = new Circle();
        s.draw();          // DMD: resolves to Circle.draw()
        s.label();         // Static binding: resolves to Shape.label()

        s = new Square();
        s.draw();          // DMD: resolves to Square.draw()
        s.label();         // Static binding: resolves to Shape.label()
    }
}
```

**Output:**

```text
Drawing a circle
Generic Shape Label
Drawing a square
Generic Shape Label
```

**Step-by-step explanation:**

- `s.draw()` → **Dynamic dispatch.** JVM sees `s` is an `Animal`-typed reference pointing to a `Circle` object; consults the vtable; invokes `Circle.draw()`. Then for `Square`, the vtable entry for `draw()` points to `Square.draw()`.
- `s.label()` → **Static dispatch.** The compiler sees `s` declared as `Shape` and binds the call to `Shape.label()`. The runtime object type is irrelevant.

This proves that **only overridden instance methods** participate in DMD, while `static` methods are statically bound.

*(Marks distribution: 2 marks for code, 2 marks for output, 3 marks for explanation of static vs dynamic binding.)*

---

#### Model Solution for Q.A (b):

The **virtual method table (vtable)** is a per-class lookup table maintained by the JVM inside the **method area** of native memory. Each entry in the vtable maps a method signature to a **direct pointer** to the bytecode implementation of that method for the class.

**Structure of a vtable for our example:**

| Class | draw() entry | label() entry |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `Shape` | → `Shape.draw()` | → `Shape.label()` |
| `Circle` | → `Circle.draw()` | inherited → `Shape.label()` |
| `Square` | → `Square.draw()` | inherited → `Shape.label()` |

**Diagram of the vtable lookup process:**

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Call s.draw where s points to Circle object] --> B[JVM reads object header]
    B --> C[Identify actual class: Circle]
    C --> D[Access Circle vtable]
    D --> E{Entry for draw exists?}
    E -- Yes --> F[Invoke Circle.draw]
    E -- No --> G[Walk up inheritance chain to Shape]
    G --> H[Invoke Shape.draw]
```

**Key role of the vtable:**

- Enables **O(1) method dispatch** at runtime.
- Each subclass inherits the parent's vtable and **overwrites** only the entries for methods it overrides.
- This is the **fundamental data structure** that makes polymorphism in Java efficient.

*(Marks distribution: 3 marks for vtable concept, 2 marks for table, 2 marks for diagram.)*

---

### Question B — Alternative Choice `[KTU University Exam — Sample Paper 2024]`

**(a)** With a neat Java program, demonstrate how **Dynamic Method Dispatch** works in a **multilevel inheritance** chain (Class A → B → C), and explain how the JVM decides which method to invoke at each level. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** Differentiate between **static binding** and **dynamic binding**. Give two examples each where Java uses each type. **(7 marks)**

---

#### Model Solution for Q.B (a):

```java
class A {
    void show() {
        System.out.println("Class A show");
    }
}
class B extends A {
    @Override
    void show() {
        System.out.println("Class B show");
    }
}
class C extends B {
    @Override
    void show() {
        System.out.println("Class C show");
    }
}

public class MultilevelDispatch {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        A ref;

        ref = new B();
        ref.show();      // Calls B.show()

        ref = new C();
        ref.show();      // Calls C.show()

        ref = new A();
        ref.show();      // Calls A.show()
    }
}
```

**Output:**

```text
Class B show
Class C show
Class A show
```

**Explanation of JVM dispatch at each level:**

| Call | Reference Type | Object Type | JVM vtable consulted | Method Invoked |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| `ref = new B(); ref.show();` | `A` | `B` | `B` vtable | `B.show()` |
| `ref = new C(); ref.show();` | `A` | `C` | `C` vtable | `C.show()` |
| `ref = new A(); ref.show();` | `A` | `A` | `A` vtable | `A.show()` |

The JVM always looks at the **actual object's vtable**, not the reference's. In the third case, the object *is* of type `A`, so the JVM invokes `A.show()`. This demonstrates that even in a **multilevel chain** (A → B → C), DMD correctly propagates overrides.

*(Marks distribution: 2 marks for code, 1 mark for output, 4 marks for dispatch table + explanation.)*

---

#### Model Solution for Q.B (b):

| Aspect | Static Binding (Early Binding) | Dynamic Binding (Late Binding) |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **When resolved** | At **compile time** | At **runtime** |
| **Mechanism** | Compiler matches the call to a method by reference type | JVM matches the call to a method by object's runtime class |
| **Performance** | Faster (no vtable lookup) | Slightly slower (vtable indirection) |
| **Flexibility** | Less flexible | More flexible (enables polymorphism) |
| **Methods involved** | `static`, `private`, `final`, constructors | Overridden instance methods |

**Two examples of static binding:**

1. `Math.max(int, int)` — called as a static method resolved at compile time.
2. A `final` method in a class — cannot be overridden, hence bound at compile time.

**Two examples of dynamic binding:**

1. Overridden `equals()` method called via an `Object` reference.
2. The `paintComponent(Graphics g)` method in Java Swing when overridden in a custom `JPanel` subclass.

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Pitfall:**
> - Do **not** confuse **method overloading** (compile-time polymorphism, static binding) with **method overriding** (runtime polymorphism, dynamic binding). Marks are deducted when students interchange the two.
> - Do **not** claim that **data members (fields)** participate in DMD. Fields are always statically bound.
> - Always mention the terms **"upcasting"** and **"vtable"** in long answers — these are high-value keywords that examiners scan for.

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

- **Definition:** Dynamic Method Dispatch = **runtime resolution** of overridden instance methods using the **actual object type**, not the reference type.
- **Three Required Conditions:** Inheritance + Overriding + Upcasting (super-reference holding sub-object).
- **vtable:** The internal per-class data structure that makes DMD an **O(1)** operation in the JVM.
- **Golden Rule:** *"Methods are virtual, fields are not."* — Fields are statically bound, methods can be dynamically dispatched.
- **Static methods are NOT polymorphic** — they are hidden, not overridden, and follow the reference type.
- **Final, private, static** methods are always **statically bound** — they cannot be overridden.
- **Constructors** are never dispatched dynamically — Java has no virtual constructors.
- **Upcasting** is implicit and always safe; **downcasting** is explicit and must be guarded by `instanceof`.
- **Real-world usage:** DMD powers the **Strategy**, **Template**, **Observer**, and **State** design patterns, and is the foundation of frameworks like **Spring** and **JavaFX**.
- **Performance:** DMD overhead is negligible due to **vtable caching** in modern JVMs (HotSpot, OpenJ9).
- **KTU Keyword Checklist** to include in every answer: *runtime polymorphism, vtable, upcasting, overridden method, object header, late binding, JVM.*

---

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.title: Using final with Inheritance
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PBCST304 - OBJECT ORIENTED PROGRAMMING
> - **Module:** Module 2
> - **Topic:** Using final with Inheritance

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# Section 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

In the **Java Programming Language**, the keyword `final` is a **non-access modifier** that is used to **restrict the user** by preventing the modification of variables, methods, and classes. When applied in the context of **Inheritance** (a Module 2 pillar of OOP), the `final` keyword enforces **definitive binding** between superclass and subclass components.

There are **three primary applications** of `final` that interact directly with inheritance:

| Application | Target | Effect on Inheritance |
|-------------|--------|----------------------|
| `final` Class | Entire class | Inheritance is **BLOCKED** — no subclass can be created |
| `final` Method | Method declaration | Method **OVERRIDING is BLOCKED** in subclasses |
| `final` Variable | Field / Local variable | The variable becomes a **CONSTANT** — value is locked after initialization |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Syllabus Highlight:** As per the PBCST304 Module 2 syllabus, students must be able to *explain and apply* the `final` keyword in conjunction with class inheritance, method overriding, and member variables. This topic is a **frequent 3-mark and 7-mark question** in university examinations.

> [!NOTE]
> **Key Distinction:** The `final` keyword is **not** the same as the `finally` block (exception handling) or the `finalize()` method (Garbage Collection). KTU examiners frequently test this distinction.

---

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Real-World Intuition

To make the concept immediately clear, consider the following analogy:

> 🏛️ **"The Sealed Monument" Analogy**
>
> Imagine a famous **monument** (the parent class). The government declares it a **"Protected National Heritage"** (the `final` modifier).
>
> - **Final Class** = The monument itself is **sealed**. Nobody is allowed to construct a replica, extension, or modified copy of it. Inheritance is **forbidden**. Example: `String`, `Math`, `System` classes in Java are all `final`.
>
> - **Final Method** = The monument has a **fixed, sacred ritual** (a method). Children, followers, and future generations (subclasses) **cannot modify** how the ritual is performed. They can inherit the behavior, but **override is not allowed**.
>
> - **Final Variable** = A **graven inscription** on the monument — the value is **carved in stone forever**. Once set, it can never be rewritten. This is how we create true **constants** in Java.

This mental model makes the three behaviors of `final` crystal clear: **lock the class, lock the method, lock the value**.

---

## 1.3 Standard Metrics & Conventions (Bolded Highlights)

- **Naming Convention for `final` variables:** `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` (e.g., `MAX_VALUE`, `PI`, `DEFAULT_SIZE`).
- **Default Initialization:** A `final` instance variable must be initialized in **every constructor** OR at the point of declaration.
- **Blank `final` variable:** A `final` variable declared but not initialized at declaration is called a *blank final variable* — it must be initialized in the constructor.
- **Final + Static combo:** `public static final` is the canonical Java constant pattern (e.g., `Math.PI`).

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# Section 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Theoretical Breakdown — The Three Pillars of `final`

### 🔒 Pillar 1: `final` Classes (Inheritance Blockade)

When a class is declared `final`, **no other class can extend it**. This terminates the inheritance chain at that node.

```java
final class Vehicle {
    void start() {
        System.out.println("Vehicle starts");
    }
}

class Car extends Vehicle {  // ❌ COMPILE-TIME ERROR
    // Cannot inherit from final class
}
```

**Compiler Error Produced:**
```
error: cannot inherit from final class Vehicle
class Car extends Vehicle
```

**Real-world Java examples:** `java.lang.String`, `java.lang.Math`, `java.lang.System` — all are final to guarantee **immutability** and **security**.

> [!NOTE]
> **Engineering Justification:** Making a class `final` is an intentional design decision to **prevent subclass-based corruption** of critical system components.

---

### 🔒 Pillar 2: `final` Methods (Overriding Blockade)

When a method is declared `final`, subclasses **may inherit the method** but **cannot override (redefine) it**. This locks the behavior of that specific method in the inheritance hierarchy.

```java
class BankAccount {
    final double calculateInterest(double principal) {
        return principal * 0.05;
    }
}

class SavingsAccount extends BankAccount {
    @Override
    double calculateInterest(double principal) {
        return principal * 0.07;  // ❌ COMPILE-TIME ERROR
    }
}
```

**Compiler Error:**
```
error: calculateInterest(double) in SavingsAccount cannot override
calculateInterest(double) in BankAccount
overridden method is final
```

**Important sub-rules:**
- ✅ **Overloading** of a `final` method is **allowed** (different parameters).
- ✅ **Hiding** a `final static` method in a subclass is **allowed** (no overriding for static methods anyway).

---

### 🔒 Pillar 3: `final` Variables (Constant Creation)

A `final` variable can be assigned **only once**. After assignment, it behaves as a **read-only constant**.

```java
class Constants {
    final int MAX = 100;            // Final instance variable
    final int MIN;                   // Blank final variable
    static final double PI = 3.14159; // Final static constant
    
    Constants() {
        MIN = 1;  // Blank final initialized in constructor
    }
}
```

**Sub-rules for `final` variables:**
1. A `final` variable **must be definitely assigned** before use.
2. For **reference variables**, `final` means the **reference cannot change**, but the **internal state of the object can** (immutability of reference, not object).
3. `final` parameters cannot be reassigned inside the method.

---

## 2.2 KTU High-Yield Rule Sheet (Cheat Table)

| # | Rule | Allowed? | KTU Weightage |
|---|------|----------|---------------|
| 1 | Extending a `final` class | ❌ Compile Error | ⭐⭐⭐ |
| 2 | Overriding a `final` method | ❌ Compile Error | ⭐⭐⭐⭐ |
| 3 | Overloading a `final` method | ✅ Allowed | ⭐⭐ |
| 4 | Hiding a `final static` method | ✅ Allowed | ⭐⭐ |
| 5 | Reassigning a `final` variable | ❌ Compile Error | ⭐⭐⭐ |
| 6 | Modifying state of a `final` referenced object | ✅ Allowed | ⭐⭐⭐ |
| 7 | Initializing a blank `final` in constructor | ✅ Allowed | ⭐⭐ |
| 8 | Declaring `abstract final` method together | ❌ Logical Conflict | ⭐⭐⭐ |
| 9 | Making a constructor `final` | ❌ Not Allowed (constructors can't be inherited) | ⭐ |
| 10 | Using `final` with an interface variable | ✅ Implicitly `public static final` | ⭐⭐ |

---

## 2.3 The Logical Impossibility: `abstract` + `final`

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Core logical contradiction:** An `abstract` method **must** be overridden in a subclass to provide a body. A `final` method **cannot** be overridden. Therefore, declaring a method as both `abstract` and `final` produces a **compile-time error** — the two modifiers are mutually exclusive.

**Mathematical/Logical Expression of the contradiction:**

$$
\text{Valid} = \neg(\text{abstract} \land \text{final})
$$

In plain logic: **A method can never be simultaneously abstract and final.**

---

## 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility

| Domain | Application of `final` |
|--------|------------------------|
| **Banking Software** | `final` interest rate calculation methods to prevent tampering |
| **Cryptography** | `final` key-handling classes to prevent subclassing attacks |
| **API Design** | `final` public methods to lock down published contract behavior |
| **Embedded Systems** | `final` variables for hardware register mappings (true constants) |
| **Game Development** | `final` entity classes (e.g., `Player`) to prevent gameplay cheats via custom subclasses |

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# Section 3: Step-by-Step Derivations, Trace Analysis & Logical Proofs

> [!NOTE]
> Since this is a programming concept, "derivations" here translate to **compile-time logical analyses** and **step-by-step program traces** that justify whether a given `final` usage is **valid** or **erroneous**.

---

## 3.1 Derivation: Logical Proof of Why `final` Classes Cannot Be Inherited

**Premise (P1):** Inheritance in Java follows the keyword `extends`, creating an **"is-a"** relationship.

**Premise (P2):** A subclass inherits all non-private members and may add new ones, thereby **extending** the parent's behavior.

**Premise (P3):** The `final` modifier, by language specification, **prohibits modification**.

**Logical Chain:**

$$
\text{Step 1: Inherit} \Rightarrow \text{Subclass acquires parent's structure}
$$

$$
\text{Step 2: Subclass} \Rightarrow \text{Can add new methods/fields (modification by extension)}
$$

$$
\text{Step 3: final} \Rightarrow \text{Modification is FORBIDDEN}
$$

$$
\text{Step 4: Contradiction} \Rightarrow \text{Therefore, extends} \rightarrow \text{final class is INVALID}
$$

**Conclusion:** Allowing inheritance of a `final` class would violate the very meaning of `final` — hence the compiler rejects it.

---

## 3.2 Exhaustive Program Trace: Final Method Behavior

```java
class Parent {
    final void display() {
        System.out.println("Parent's final display()");
    }
    void greet() {
        System.out.println("Parent's greet()");
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    // Attempting override of final method
    // void display() { }  // ❌ COMPILE ERROR
    
    // Overriding non-final method - allowed
    @Override
    void greet() {
        System.out.println("Child's overridden greet()");
    }
}

public class TestFinal {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Child c = new Child();
        c.display();  // Calls Parent's final version (inherited, not overridden)
        c.greet();    // Calls Child's overridden version
    }
}
```

**Step-by-step execution trace:**

| Line | Action | Output/State |
|------|--------|--------------|
| 1 | `Child c = new Child();` | Object `c` of type `Child` created |
| 2 | `c.display();` | Method resolution: `display` is `final` in `Parent`, inherited as-is → calls Parent version |
| 3 | `c.greet();` | Method resolution: `greet` is non-final → dynamic dispatch to `Child`'s version |
| — | **Final Output** | `Parent's final display()` \n `Child's overridden greet()` |

**Compilation Output (if `display` override is uncommented):**
```
error: display() in Child cannot override display() in Parent
overridden method is final
```

---

## 3.3 Exhaustive Program Trace: Blank `final` Variable

```java
class Student {
    final int rollNumber;  // Blank final - must be assigned in constructor
    final String name;
    
    Student(int r, String n) {
        rollNumber = r;   // ✅ Assigned once
        name = n;         // ✅ Assigned once
    }
    
    void changeRoll(int r) {
        // rollNumber = r;  // ❌ COMPILE ERROR - already assigned
    }
}
```

**Logical verification:**

$$
\text{State of } rollNumber: \text{UNDEFINED} \xrightarrow{\text{Constructor}} \text{DEFINED} \xrightarrow{\text{Any further attempt}} \text{COMPILE ERROR}
$$

This proves the **single-assignment property** of `final` variables.

---

## 3.4 Derivative Analysis: `final` Reference vs Immutable Object

A common KTU pitfall: students think `final` makes the object immutable. **It does not.**

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;

class ReferenceDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        final ArrayList<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
        list.add("Hello");   // ✅ Allowed - object state changed
        list.add("World");   // ✅ Allowed
        System.out.println(list);  // [Hello, World]
        
        // list = new ArrayList<>();  // ❌ COMPILE ERROR - reference reassignment
    }
}
```

**Logical expression:**

$$
\text{final Reference} \Rightarrow \text{Reference is locked, NOT the heap object}
$$

$$
\text{Object State} = \text{Mutable as usual}
$$

---

## 3.5 Final Method Overloading — Allowed Scenario

```java
class Calculator {
    final int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }
    
    // ✅ Overloading - different signature
    final double add(double a, double b) {
        return a + b;
    }
    
    // ✅ Overloading - different number of parameters
    final int add(int a, int b, int c) {
        return a + b + c;
    }
}
```

**Rule Justification:** Overloading is resolved at **compile time** based on signature (parameter types/count), not at runtime. Since `final` only prevents **overriding** (runtime polymorphism), overloading is unaffected.

# Section 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

### **Question 1** `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]`
**Q: What is the difference between `final`, `finally`, and `finalize()` in Java?**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

| Keyword | Type | Purpose | Context |
|---------|------|---------|---------|
| `final` | Modifier | Restricts modification of classes, methods, variables | Inheritance & constants |
| `finally` | Block | Code that always executes after try-catch | Exception handling |
| `finalize()` | Method | Called by Garbage Collector before object destruction | Memory cleanup |

`final` is a **modifier**, `finally` is an **exception-handling block**, and `finalize()` is an **Object class method** invoked by the JVM garbage collector. They are completely unrelated concepts. **(3 marks)**

---

### **Question 2** `[KTU University Exam - May 2024]`
**Q: Can a `final` method be overloaded? Justify with an example.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

**Yes**, a `final` method **can be overloaded** in Java. The `final` modifier only prevents **overriding** (runtime polymorphism), not **overloading** (compile-time polymorphism based on parameter signature).

```java
class Demo {
    final void show(int x) { System.out.println("int: " + x); }
    final void show(double x) { System.out.println("double: " + x); }
}
```

Here both `show` methods are `final` but coexist due to different parameter types — this is **overloading, not overriding**. **(3 marks)**

---

## 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks Each) — Module Internal Choice

---

### 📘 **Question A (14 Marks)** `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2024]`

**Q: (a)** Explain the three uses of the `final` keyword in Java with suitable examples. How does it affect inheritance? **(7 marks)**

**Model Solution:**

The `final` keyword in Java is a non-access modifier that imposes restrictions to **enforce design contracts and ensure security**. It has three primary applications:

**(1) Final Class — Blocks Inheritance (3 marks)**

When a class is declared `final`, it cannot be subclassed. This terminates the inheritance chain.

```java
final class ImmutablePoint {
    private final int x, y;
    ImmutablePoint(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
    int getX() { return x; }
    int getY() { return y; }
}

// class ExtendedPoint extends ImmutablePoint { } 
// ❌ Compile error: cannot inherit from final class
```

Java's built-in `String` class is `final` to prevent malicious subclassing that could break string immutability.

**(2) Final Method — Blocks Overriding (2 marks)**

```java
class Account {
    final void auditLog(String msg) {
        System.out.println("AUDIT: " + msg);
    }
}
class SavingsAccount extends Account {
    // void auditLog(String msg) { } ❌ Compile error
}
```

The subclass inherits the method but **cannot redefine it**, preserving parent behavior.

**(3) Final Variable — Creates Constants (2 marks)**

```java
class Config {
    public static final int MAX_USERS = 100;
    final String DB_NAME;
    Config() { DB_NAME = "ProductionDB"; }
}
```

`final` variables act as **read-only constants** that can be assigned only once. The `public static final` combination is the standard Java idiom for true constants.

**Effect on Inheritance:** `final` ensures that **modification through inheritance is prohibited**, guaranteeing that the parent class's contract remains intact for all descendants. This is critical for **security, design integrity, and predictable behavior**.

---

**(b)** Write a Java program to demonstrate that a `final` reference variable cannot be reassigned, but the object it points to can be modified. Explain the output. **(7 marks)**

**Model Solution:**

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;
class FinalReferenceDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        final ArrayList<String> colors = new ArrayList<>();
        
        // Modifying object state - ALLOWED
        colors.add("Red");
        colors.add("Green");
        colors.add("Blue");
        
        System.out.println("After additions: " + colors);
        
        // Removing element - ALLOWED
        colors.remove("Green");
        System.out.println("After removal: " + colors);
        
        // Reassigning reference - NOT ALLOWED
        // colors = new ArrayList<>();  
        // Compile error: cannot assign a value to final variable colors
    }
}
```

**Expected Output:**
```
After additions: [Red, Green, Blue]
After removal: [Red, Blue]
```

**Explanation (7 marks breakdown):**

- **(2 marks)** The `final` keyword on a reference variable makes the **reference (memory address) constant**, not the object itself. The variable `colors` permanently points to the same `ArrayList` object on the heap.
- **(2 marks)** Methods like `add()` and `remove()` mutate the **internal state** of the object — this does not change the reference, so it is permitted.
- **(2 marks)** Attempting `colors = new ArrayList<>()` would reassign the reference to a new object, which violates the `final` contract → compile-time error.
- **(1 mark)** This distinction is fundamental in Java: **`final` provides reference immutability, not object immutability**. For true object immutability, all fields must be `final` and `private` with no mutator methods (like the `String` class).

---

### 📗 **Question B (14 Marks)** — Alternative Choice `[KTU University Exam - May 2024]`

**Q: (a)** Discuss why a method cannot be declared both `abstract` and `final` simultaneously. Provide the logical justification and a code example. **(7 marks)**

**Model Solution:**

**Logical Justification (5 marks):**

The combination of `abstract` and `final` produces a **logical contradiction** in Java's type system:

- An **abstract method** is declared **without a body** and **must be overridden** by the first concrete (non-abstract) subclass to provide an implementation. Without overriding, the program cannot compile.

- A **final method** is declared with a body and **cannot be overridden** by any subclass. The implementation is permanently fixed in the declaring class.

These two requirements are **mutually exclusive**: one demands overriding, the other forbids it. Allowing both would create an **unresolvable logical paradox** — the method can neither exist without being overridden nor be overridden. The Java compiler therefore rejects this combination.

Formally:
$$
\text{abstract} \Rightarrow \text{override required}, \quad \text{final} \Rightarrow \text{override forbidden}
$$

$$
\therefore \; \text{abstract} \land \text{final} \Rightarrow \bot \text{ (contradiction)}
$$

**Code Example (2 marks):**

```java
abstract class Shape {
    // abstract final void draw(); 
    // ❌ Compile error: illegal combination of modifiers: abstract and final
    abstract void draw();
}

class Circle extends Shape {
    @Override
    void draw() {
        System.out.println("Drawing Circle");
    }
}
```

Here, `draw()` is correctly declared as `abstract` (allowing override) but **not** `final`. The `Circle` subclass successfully overrides it.

---

**(b)** Explain with a Java program how `final` classes prevent inheritance, using a real-world scenario. Why does Java make `String` class `final`? **(7 marks)**

**Model Solution:**

**Program Demonstrating `final` Class (4 marks):**

```java
final class License {
    private final String licenseNumber;
    private final String holderName;
    
    License(String num, String name) {
        this.licenseNumber = num;
        this.holderName = name;
    }
    
    void display() {
        System.out.println("License: " + licenseNumber + ", Holder: " + holderName);
    }
}

// Attempting inheritance - NOT ALLOWED
// class FakeLicense extends License { }
// Compile error: cannot inherit from final class License

public class LicenseTest {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        License l = new License("KL-07-2024-001", "Rahul Krishnan");
        l.display();
    }
}
```

**Output:**
```
License: KL-07-2024-001, Holder: Rahul Krishnan
```

**Why `String` is `final` (3 marks):**

Java's `String` class is declared `final` for **three critical engineering reasons**:

1. **Security:** Strings are used for sensitive operations like class loading, network connections, database queries, and file paths. If `String` could be subclassed, a malicious subclass could corrupt the behavior of the entire JVM. Making it `final` prevents such attacks.

2. **Immutability Guarantee:** Strings are immutable in Java. If `String` were inheritable, subclasses could introduce mutability, breaking the immutability contract that the entire Java ecosystem relies upon (e.g., `String` as keys in `HashMap`).

3. **Performance (String Pool):** The JVM uses a **String Constant Pool** for memory optimization. Allowing subclasses would break the pool's invariants and cause unpredictable behavior.

---

## 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Mistakes That Cost Marks:**
>
> 1. **Confusing `final` with `finally` or `finalize()`** — Examiners specifically test this distinction. Writing "finally" in a "final" question will cost **at least 1 mark**.
>
> 2. **Assuming `final` makes objects immutable** — Many students write "`final` makes the object immutable" in viva/exams. This is **WRONG**. `final` on a reference locks the **reference**, not the **object's internal state**.
>
> 3. **Forgetting blank `final` must be initialized in EVERY constructor** — A blank `final` instance variable must be assigned in **all** constructors of the class; otherwise, compile error.
>
> 4. **Writing `final abstract` together** — A frequent MCQ trap. Always remember: `abstract` and `final` are **mutually exclusive**.
>
> 5. **Saying constructors can be `final`** — Constructors are never inherited, so they cannot be `final`. This is a common conceptual error.
>
> 6. **Forgetting that `final` methods CAN be overloaded** — Overloading ≠ Overriding. This is a frequently tested nuance.

---

## 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> 📋 **Rapid Revision Checklist — Final Keyword with Inheritance**

- ✅ `final` is a **non-access modifier** used to impose restrictions.

- ✅ `final` can be applied to **three things**: classes, methods, and variables.

- ✅ **`final` class** → Inheritance is **blocked** (cannot use `extends`). Examples: `String`, `Math`, `System`, `Wrapper` classes.

- ✅ **`final` method** → Overriding is **blocked** in subclasses, but **overloading is allowed**.

- ✅ **`final` variable** → Acts as a **constant**, assigned only once. Use `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` naming.

- ✅ **Blank `final` variables** → Must be initialized in the **constructor** (or in an instance initializer block).

- ✅ **`final` reference** → Reference is locked, but **object state remains mutable** (reference immutability ≠ object immutability).

- ✅ **`abstract` + `final`** → **Illegal combination** due to logical contradiction (override required vs forbidden).

- ✅ **Constructors cannot be `final`** (constructors are never inherited, so the concept doesn't apply).

- ✅ **Interfaces** → All variables in an interface are implicitly `public static final`.

- ✅ **Performance benefit** → `final` methods can be inlined by the JIT compiler (minor optimization).

- ✅ **Design intent** → Use `final` to communicate that a class/method/field is **complete and not meant for extension**.

- ✅ **Difference summary**:
  - `final` = modifier (this module)
  - `finally` = exception block (Module 4/5)
  - `finalize()` = GC method (Module 4/5)

---

**End of Notes — Module 2: Using `final` with Inheritance** 🎯
