topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PBCST304 - OBJECT ORIENTED PROGRAMMING
> - **Module:** Module 4
> - **Topic:** Swing Controls

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus)

**Swing** is a GUI (Graphical User Interface) toolkit in Java provided as part of the **Java Foundation Classes (JFC)**. It is housed under the `javax.swing` package and represents a set of **lightweight, platform-independent** components that are entirely written in Java, building upon the older, heavyweight AWT (`java.awt`) framework.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Syllabus Highlight:** The `javax.swing` package provides classes such as `JButton`, `JLabel`, `JTextField`, `JTextArea`, `JCheckBox`, `JRadioButton`, `JComboBox`, `JList`, `JTable`, `JMenu`, and `JMenuBar`. Every Swing component inherits from `java.awt.Container` (via `JComponent`), and unlike AWT, they do not depend on the underlying operating system's peer components.

**Swing Controls** are the interactive widgets (buttons, text fields, tables, menus, etc.) that the user manipulates to interact with a Java application. They are the **visual vocabulary** of any desktop application built using Java.

### Conceptual Analogy / Intuition

Imagine you are **building a physical dashboard for a car**:
- The **steering wheel, accelerator, and gear stick** are the *controls* — they let the driver give input.
- The **speedometer and fuel gauge** are the *display* — they show output.
- The **dashboard layout** is the *Layout Manager* — it arranges everything neatly.
- The **wiring that makes the speedometer needle move when you press the accelerator** is the *Event Handling* mechanism.

In Java Swing:
- `JButton`, `JTextField`, `JCheckBox` = the **steering wheel** (input controls)
- `JLabel` = the **speedometer** (output display)
- `BorderLayout`, `FlowLayout` = the **dashboard layout**
- `ActionListener`, `ItemListener` = the **wiring**

> [!NOTE]
> **Key Terminology for Exams:**
> - **Lightweight Component**: A component written entirely in Java that does *not* rely on a native OS peer. (e.g., `JButton`)
> - **Heavyweight Component**: A component that uses a native OS peer (e.g., `java.awt.Button`). Swing is mostly lightweight, with `JFrame`, `JDialog`, and `JApplet` being the exceptions.
> - **Pluggable Look and Feel (PLAF)**: The ability of Swing components to change appearance dynamically without changing code.
> - **MVC Architecture**: Swing components follow the Model-View-Controller design pattern.

### The Class Hierarchy of Swing Controls

The most critical knowledge to memorize is the inheritance chain. KTU frequently asks diagrams of this hierarchy.

```
java.lang.Object
    └── java.awt.Component
            └── java.awt.Container
                    └── javax.swing.JComponent  ← ROOT OF ALL SWING CONTROLS
                            ├── JLabel
                            ├── JButton (extends AbstractButton)
                            │       └── JToggleButton
                            │               ├── JCheckBox
                            │               └── JRadioButton
                            ├── JTextField (extends JTextComponent)
                            ├── JTextArea  (extends JTextComponent)
                            ├── JComboBox
                            ├── JList
                            ├── JTable
                            ├── JTree
                            ├── JMenuBar
                            ├── JMenu
                            ├── JMenuItem
                            └── JPanel
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Every Swing control ultimately extends `JComponent`**, which itself extends `java.awt.Container`. This means every Swing control can itself act as a container and hold other components.

### Key Standard Metrics (Bolded for Visibility)

- **Package**: `javax.swing`
- **Root Class**: `javax.swing.JComponent`
- **Top-Level Containers**: `JFrame`, `JDialog`, `JApplet`
- **Default Look & Feel**: Cross-platform (Metal) — platform-independent rendering
- **Thread Safety Rule**: All Swing components must be accessed only from the **Event Dispatch Thread (EDT)**, except a few specifically marked thread-safe methods like `repaint()`, `revalidate()`.
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & Swing Controls Master Reference

## 2.1 Classification of Swing Components

Swing components are broadly classified into **three architectural tiers**:

| Tier | Description | Examples | Exam Weight |
|------|-------------|----------|-------------|
| **Top-Level Containers** | Can be displayed standalone; have a `JRootPane` | `JFrame`, `JDialog`, `JApplet` | High |
| **Intermediate Containers** | Used to group and lay out components | `JPanel`, `JScrollPane`, `JSplitPane`, `JTabbedPane`, `JToolBar` | Medium |
| **Atomic Components (Leaves)** | Cannot contain other components; used for input/display | `JButton`, `JLabel`, `JTextField`, `JCheckBox`, etc. | Very High |

## 2.2 Detailed Analysis of Every Major Swing Control

### 2.2.1 JLabel — The Display Component

**Why it exists**: To display uneditable text, icons, or both. It is *passive* — it does not generate events on its own.

**Key Methods (must memorize)**:
- `JLabel()` — default constructor
- `JLabel(String text)` — constructor with text
- `JLabel(Icon image)` — constructor with icon
- `setText(String text)` / `getText()` — to change/read the displayed text
- `setIcon(Icon icon)` / `getIcon()` — to set/read the icon
- `setHorizontalAlignment(int alignment)` — `SwingConstants.CENTER`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`
- `setVerticalAlignment(int alignment)` — `SwingConstants.TOP`, `CENTER`, `BOTTOM`

**Engineering Utility**: Form field captions, status bar messages, image banners in CMS systems.

### 2.2.2 JButton — The Primary Action Trigger

**Why it exists**: A clickable button that fires an `ActionEvent` when pressed.

**Key Methods**:
- `JButton(String text)`
- `JButton(Icon icon)`
- `addActionListener(ActionListener l)` — registers a listener
- `setEnabled(boolean b)` — to enable/disable
- `setMnemonic(char mnemonic)` — keyboard shortcut (Alt + key)
- `setToolTipText(String text)` — hover hint

> [!NOTE]
> **Inheritance Note**: `JButton` extends `AbstractButton`, which is the abstract parent of `JToggleButton`, `JCheckBox`, `JRadioButton`, and `JMenuItem`. So the methods like `setText()`, `setIcon()`, `setEnabled()` are inherited from `AbstractButton`.

### 2.2.3 JTextField — Single-Line Input

**Why it exists**: To accept a single line of text input from the user (e.g., username, search box).

**Key Methods**:
- `JTextField(int columns)` — preferred constructor
- `JTextField(String text, int columns)`
- `getText()` / `setText(String)`
- `addActionListener(ActionListener l)` — fires when user presses Enter
- `setEditable(boolean)` — true by default
- `setHorizontalAlignment(int)` — for aligning displayed text

### 2.2.4 JTextArea — Multi-Line Input

**Why it exists**: To accept or display **multiple lines** of text (e.g., comments, descriptions).

**Key Methods**:
- `JTextArea(int rows, int columns)`
- `append(String str)` — adds text at the end
- `setLineWrap(boolean)` / `setWrapStyleWord(boolean)`
- `setEditable(boolean)`
- `insert(String str, int pos)`

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Exam Trap**: `JTextArea` does **not** support scrolling natively. You **must** wrap it inside a `JScrollPane` to get scrollbars:
> ```java
> JTextArea area = new JTextArea(5, 20);
> JScrollPane scroll = new JScrollPane(area);
> frame.add(scroll);
> ```

### 2.2.5 JCheckBox — Boolean Toggle

**Why it exists**: To represent a binary on/off choice. Multiple checkboxes can be selected **independently** (unlike radio buttons).

**Key Methods**:
- `JCheckBox(String label, boolean selected)`
- `isSelected()` — returns true if checked
- `setSelected(boolean b)`
- `addItemListener(ItemListener l)` — fires when state changes
- Inherits from `AbstractButton` via `JToggleButton`

### 2.2.6 JRadioButton — Mutually Exclusive Choice

**Why it exists**: To represent a choice where only **one** option in a group can be selected at a time (e.g., Male/Female/Other).

**Key Methods**:
- `JRadioButton(String label, boolean selected)`
- `isSelected()` / `setSelected(boolean)`
- `addItemListener(ItemListener l)`

> [!NOTE]
> **The `ButtonGroup` Class**: To make radio buttons mutually exclusive, you MUST add them to the same `ButtonGroup` object. A `ButtonGroup` is **not a visual component** — it is purely a *logical grouping*. The radio buttons are still added to the container (e.g., `JPanel`) for display.

```java
JRadioButton male = new JRadioButton("Male");
JRadioButton female = new JRadioButton("Female");
ButtonGroup group = new ButtonGroup();
group.add(male);     // logical grouping
group.add(female);   // logical grouping
panel.add(male);     // visual display
panel.add(female);   // visual display
```

### 2.2.7 JComboBox — Drop-Down List

**Why it exists**: To show a list of options that the user can select **one from**. Saves space when there are many options.

**Key Methods**:
- `JComboBox()` / `JComboBox(Object[] items)` / `JComboBox(Vector<?> items)`
- `getSelectedItem()` / `getSelectedIndex()`
- `addItem(Object item)` / `removeItem(Object)`
- `addItemListener(ItemListener l)` — fires when selection changes
- `setEditable(boolean)` — allows user to type their own value

### 2.2.8 JList — Multi/Single Selection List

**Why it exists**: To display a scrollable list of items from which the user can select one or more. Unlike `JComboBox`, **multiple items are visible at once**.

**Key Methods**:
- `JList(Object[] listData)` / `JList(Vector<?> listData)`
- `getSelectedValue()` / `getSelectedValuesList()`
- `getSelectedIndex()` / `getSelectedIndices()`
- `setSelectionMode(int mode)` — `ListSelectionModel.SINGLE_SELECTION`, `SINGLE_INTERVAL_SELECTION`, `MULTIPLE_INTERVAL_SELECTION`
- `addListSelectionListener(ListSelectionListener l)`

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Exam Trap**: `JList` **does not** provide scrollbars by default. You **must** wrap it in a `JScrollPane`.

### 2.2.9 JTable — Tabular Data Display

**Why it exists**: To display data in a row-column format (like a spreadsheet).

**Key Constructors & Concepts**:
- `JTable(Object[][] rowData, Object[] columnNames)`
- `JTable(TableModel dm)` — preferred for real applications
- The model is typically a `DefaultTableModel`
- Important related class: `JTableHeader` (for column headers)
- Default editors and renderers: `DefaultTableCellRenderer`, `DefaultCellEditor`

### 2.2.10 JMenu, JMenuBar, JMenuItem — Application Menus

**Why it exists**: To provide a standardized menu bar at the top of an application.

**Class Roles**:
- `JMenuBar` — the horizontal bar that holds menus. Set on a `JFrame` using `setJMenuBar(JMenuBar)`.
- `JMenu` — a dropdown menu (e.g., "File", "Edit"). Added to a `JMenuBar`.
- `JMenuItem` — an individual clickable item inside a `JMenu` (e.g., "Open", "Save").
- `JCheckBoxMenuItem` and `JRadioButtonMenuItem` — special menu items.

```java
JMenuBar menuBar = new JMenuBar();
JMenu fileMenu = new JMenu("File");
JMenuItem openItem = new JMenuItem("Open");
fileMenu.add(openItem);
menuBar.add(fileMenu);
frame.setJMenuBar(menuBar);
```

### 2.2.11 Intermediate Containers

| Container | Purpose |
|-----------|---------|
| `JPanel` | Generic grouping; uses its own layout manager |
| `JScrollPane` | Provides scrollbars for any component |
| `JSplitPane` | Two components separated by a movable divider |
| `JTabbedPane` | Tabbed interface (like browser tabs) |
| `JToolBar` | Movable toolbar of buttons |
| `JOptionPane` | Pop-up dialogs (showMessageDialog, showInputDialog, showConfirmDialog) |

## 2.3 Event Handling Model — The "Wiring" of Swing

**How it works (Why + How)**:

1. The user interacts with a control (e.g., clicks a button).
2. The control creates an **Event object** (e.g., `ActionEvent`).
3. The control sends the event to all **registered listeners**.
4. The listener's callback method is invoked, executing the response logic.

This is the **Delegation Event Model** — the source delegates the task of handling the event to a separate listener.

**Common Event Listeners (Memorize the Mapping)**:

| Event Class | Listener Interface | Callback Method | Triggered By |
|-------------|-------------------|-----------------|--------------|
| `ActionEvent` | `ActionListener` | `actionPerformed(ActionEvent)` | `JButton` click, Enter in `JTextField`, `JMenuItem` |
| `ItemEvent` | `ItemListener` | `itemStateChanged(ItemEvent)` | `JCheckBox`, `JRadioButton`, `JComboBox` selection change |
| `TextEvent` | `TextListener` | `textValueChanged(TextEvent)` | `JTextField`, `JTextArea` text changes |
| `MouseEvent` | `MouseListener` | 5 methods: `mouseClicked`, `mousePressed`, `mouseReleased`, `mouseEntered`, `mouseExited` | Any mouse interaction |
| `KeyEvent` | `KeyListener` | `keyTyped`, `keyPressed`, `keyReleased` | Keyboard input |
| `ListSelectionEvent` | `ListSelectionListener` | `valueChanged(ListSelectionEvent)` | `JList` selection change |

**Two Ways to Register a Listener (Both are exam-relevant)**:

**Method 1: Separate Listener Class** (preferred for OOP design)
```java
class MyFrame extends JFrame implements ActionListener {
    JButton b;
    MyFrame() {
        b = new JButton("Click");
        b.addActionListener(this); // 'this' implements ActionListener
    }
    public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
        // handle event
    }
}
```

**Method 2: Anonymous Inner Class** (concise, often used in examples)
```java
button.addActionListener(new ActionListener() {
    public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
        System.out.println("Clicked!");
    }
});
```

# 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Analytical Matrix — Which Component for Which Job?

The single most common KTU exam question is: *"Given a scenario, choose the appropriate Swing component and justify."* This matrix is your master tool.

| Scenario / Requirement | Best Component | Reason |
|-------------------------|----------------|--------|
| Display static text under a text field | `JLabel` | Non-editable, no event generation |
| Single-line text input (e.g., Name) | `JTextField` | Optimized for one line |
| Multi-line text input (e.g., Comments) | `JTextArea` inside `JScrollPane` | Multi-line support + scrollbars |
| Click to submit a form | `JButton` | Standard trigger for actions |
| Multiple independent choices (Hobbies) | `JCheckBox` | Each is independent; can select any/all |
| Choose one gender from M/F/Other | `JRadioButton` + `ButtonGroup` | Mutually exclusive |
| Choose one country from a long list | `JComboBox` | Saves space, dropdown UI |
| Display a list of 100 student names with multi-select | `JList` inside `JScrollPane` | Multiple visible items + scroll + multi-select |
| Display data in rows and columns | `JTable` | Tabular representation |
| Tree of folders | `JTree` | Hierarchical data |
| Top-of-window menu (File, Edit) | `JMenuBar` → `JMenu` → `JMenuItem` | Standard OS-like menu bar |
| Show a small pop-up message | `JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(...)` | Modal dialog utility |
| Display a status bar that can be re-styled | `JLabel` with custom border | Lightweight, no event cost |

## 3.2 Step-by-Step: Building a Swing Application (The "Five-Step" Method)

Every Swing program you write for KTU exams should follow this canonical pattern. I will derive it step-by-step.

### **Step 1: Import the Required Packages**

```java
import javax.swing.*;          // All Swing classes
import java.awt.*;             // AWT classes (Layouts, Color, Font)
import java.awt.event.*;       // Event classes and listeners
```

**Explanation**: The wildcard `*` imports all classes from these packages. This is acceptable in exam code for brevity.

### **Step 2: Choose the Top-Level Container**

```java
public class MyApp extends JFrame {
    MyApp() {
        setTitle("My Application");
        setSize(400, 300);
        setDefaultCloseOperation(JFrame.EXIT_ON_CLOSE);
        setLayout(new FlowLayout());  // default; can change
    }
}
```

**Explanation**:
- `extends JFrame` — inherits windowing behavior.
- `setSize(400, 300)` — width × height in pixels.
- `setDefaultCloseOperation(JFrame.EXIT_ON_CLOSE)` — closes the JVM on window close. Without this, the window closes but the program continues running. The four valid constants are:
  - `WindowConstants.DO_NOTHING_ON_CLOSE` (0)
  - `WindowConstants.HIDE_ON_CLOSE` (1)
  - `WindowConstants.DISPOSE_ON_CLOSE` (2)
  - `WindowConstants.EXIT_ON_CLOSE` (3)

### **Step 3: Create the Components**

```java
JLabel nameLabel = new JLabel("Name:");
JTextField nameField = new JTextField(15);
JButton submitBtn = new JButton("Submit");
```

**Explanation**: `JTextField(15)` sets the preferred width to 15 columns, which determines the field's pixel width roughly as `15 × averageCharWidth`.

### **Step 4: Add Components to a Container**

```java
JPanel panel = new JPanel();
panel.add(nameLabel);
panel.add(nameField);
panel.add(submitBtn);
add(panel); // adds panel to the JFrame's content pane
```

**Explanation**:
- We group components into a `JPanel` (which uses `FlowLayout` by default).
- The `JPanel` is then added to the `JFrame`.
- Adding the panel to the `JFrame` is equivalent to `getContentPane().add(panel)`. In Java 5+, this is automatic.

### **Step 5: Register Event Listeners and Make Visible**

```java
submitBtn.addActionListener(new ActionListener() {
    public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
        String name = nameField.getText();
        JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(null, "Hello, " + name);
    }
});

setVisible(true);
```

**Explanation**:
- `setVisible(true)` MUST be called at the end; otherwise, the window never appears.
- The anonymous inner class implements `ActionListener`. The `actionPerformed` method is the callback that runs when the button is clicked.

## 3.3 Complete Reference Program — A Login Form

Here is a complete, exam-ready program that synthesizes everything. Each line is annotated for KTU study purposes.

```java
import javax.swing.*;
import java.awt.*;
import java.awt.event.*;

public class LoginForm extends JFrame implements ActionListener {
    // 1. Declare all components
    JLabel userLabel, passLabel, msgLabel;
    JTextField userField;
    JPasswordField passField;  // Special: hides characters
    JButton loginBtn, resetBtn;
    JPanel panel;

    // 2. Constructor
    LoginForm() {
        setTitle("Login Form");
        setSize(350, 200);
        setDefaultCloseOperation(JFrame.EXIT_ON_CLOSE);

        // 3. Initialize components
        userLabel  = new JLabel("Username:");
        passLabel  = new JLabel("Password:");
        userField  = new JTextField(15);
        passField  = new JPasswordField(15);
        loginBtn   = new JButton("Login");
        resetBtn   = new JButton("Reset");
        msgLabel   = new JLabel("");

        // 4. Register listeners
        loginBtn.addActionListener(this);
        resetBtn.addActionListener(this);

        // 5. Layout
        panel = new JPanel(new GridLayout(4, 2, 5, 5));
        panel.add(userLabel);   panel.add(userField);
        panel.add(passLabel);   panel.add(passField);
        panel.add(loginBtn);    panel.add(resetBtn);
        panel.add(new JLabel("")); panel.add(msgLabel);

        add(panel);
        setLocationRelativeTo(null); // Center on screen
        setVisible(true);
    }

    // 6. Event handler
    public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
        if (e.getSource() == loginBtn) {
            String user = userField.getText();
            String pass = new String(passField.getPassword());
            if (user.equals("admin") && pass.equals("1234"))
                msgLabel.setText("Login Successful!");
            else
                msgLabel.setText("Invalid Credentials");
        } else if (e.getSource() == resetBtn) {
            userField.setText("");
            passField.setText("");
            msgLabel.setText("");
        }
    }

    // 7. Main method
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new LoginForm();
    }
}
```

### Step-by-Step Walkthrough of the Above Program

**Why we used `JPasswordField`**: A `JTextField` would display the password in plain text. `JPasswordField` masks it with `●` characters and stores it in a `char[]` (not `String`) for security.

**Why we used `GridLayout(4, 2, 5, 5)`**: This creates a 4-row, 2-column grid with 5px horizontal and 5px vertical gaps. Each cell is the same size — perfect for label/field pairs.

**Why we used `setLocationRelativeTo(null)`**: This centers the window on the screen. The `null` argument means "center relative to the screen" (the default toolkit screen).

**Why we convert `passField.getPassword()` to `String`**: `getPassword()` returns `char[]` (a security feature — `String` is immutable and can be snooped in the String pool). For our simple comparison, we wrap it in `new String(char[])`.

**Why we used `e.getSource()`**: When one listener handles events from multiple sources, we use `e.getSource()` to identify *which* component fired the event. It returns the source object, which we compare using `==`.

## 3.4 Analytical Comparison: AWT vs. Swing

KTU frequently asks: *"Differentiate between AWT and Swing."* Here is the master comparison:

| Feature | AWT (`java.awt`) | Swing (`javax.swing`) |
|---------|------------------|------------------------|
| Package | `java.awt` | `javax.swing` |
| Component type | Heavyweight (uses OS peers) | Lightweight (pure Java) |
| Look & Feel | Same as native OS | Pluggable; can mimic any OS or use Metal |
| Component count | Limited | Rich (more components like `JTable`, `JTree`) |
| Root class | `java.awt.Component` | `javax.swing.JComponent` (extends `Component`) |
| MVC | No | Yes |
| Buttons | `Button` | `JButton` (and many more) |
| Pluggable | No | Yes |
| Performance | Faster (native code) | Slightly slower (pure Java) |
| Modern recommendation | Legacy | Preferred |

## 3.5 Layout Manager Reference (Important)

A control's position is determined by the **layout manager** of its container. Choosing the right layout is half the battle in Swing exams.

| Layout | Class | Behavior | Best Used For |
|--------|-------|----------|---------------|
| Flow | `FlowLayout` | Components left-to-right, wrap to next line | Toolbars, button rows |
| Border | `BorderLayout` | Five regions: N, S, E, W, C | Main window structure |
| Grid | `GridLayout` | Equal-sized cells in rows × columns | Forms, calculators |
| Box | `BoxLayout` | Vertical or horizontal stacking | Side panels |
| GridBag | `GridBagLayout` | Complex, flexible grid with constraints | Professional UIs |
| Card | `CardLayout` | Stack of panels; show one at a time | Wizards, tab-like flows |
| Group | `GroupLayout` | Preferred by NetBeans GUI Builder | Designer-generated UIs |
| Spring | `SpringLayout` | Constraint-based | Advanced custom layouts |
| null | (no layout) | Absolute positioning with `setBounds(x,y,w,h)` | Quick demos only |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Exam Trap**: If you use `setLayout(null)`, you **must** also call `setBounds(x, y, width, height)` on every component. Otherwise, the component has size 0 and won't appear.

### **Question A2** [KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]
*Explain the role of `JScrollPane` with a suitable example.*

**Model Answer (3 marks)**:

`JScrollPane` is an intermediate Swing container that provides **horizontal and/or vertical scrollbars** to any component that is too large to fit in its allocated area. It is essential for components that display variable-length content, such as `JTextArea`, `JList`, `JTable`, and `JTree`.

**Example**:
```java
JTextArea area = new JTextArea(10, 30);
JScrollPane scroll = new JScrollPane(area);  // wrap area inside scroll
frame.add(scroll);
```
Without `JScrollPane`, the `JTextArea` would be fixed in size and overflow text would be invisible. With it, scrollbars appear automatically when content exceeds the visible area.

## 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks Each — Module Internal Choice)

### **Question A (14 Marks)** [KTU University Exam - May 2024]

**(a) (7 marks)** Explain the Delegation Event Model in Java Swing with a suitable diagram. List any four event listener interfaces from `java.awt.event`.

**(b) (7 marks)** Write a Java Swing program to create a form that accepts a student's name, age, and gender (using radio buttons). On clicking a "Display" button, show all entered details in a `JOptionPane` message dialog.

#### **Model Solution for (a):**

**Delegation Event Model** is the event-handling mechanism used by Swing (and modern AWT). It works on the principle that **the source of an event delegates the responsibility of handling it to a separate listener object**.

**Step-by-step flow**:
1. The user interacts with a Swing component (e.g., clicks a `JButton`).
2. The component (the **source**) constructs an `Event` object (e.g., `ActionEvent`) containing details such as the source, the command, and any modifiers.
3. The component fires the event by passing it to all **registered listeners**.
4. The listener's corresponding callback method (e.g., `actionPerformed`) is invoked, executing the response logic.

**Diagram**:
```
   User Action
       ↓
   Component (Source)  --fires-->  Event Object
       ↓
   Registered Listeners
       ↓
   Callback Method Executes
       ↓
   Response Logic
```

**Four Event Listener Interfaces from `java.awt.event`**:
1. **`ActionListener`** — interface with `actionPerformed(ActionEvent)` method. Used by `JButton`, `JMenuItem`, `JTextField` (on Enter).
2. **`ItemListener`** — interface with `itemStateChanged(ItemEvent)` method. Used by `JCheckBox`, `JRadioButton`, `JComboBox`.
3. **`MouseListener`** — interface with 5 methods: `mouseClicked`, `mousePressed`, `mouseReleased`, `mouseEntered`, `mouseExited`. Used by any component.
4. **`KeyListener`** — interface with 3 methods: `keyTyped`, `keyPressed`, `keyReleased`. Used for keyboard handling.

#### **Model Solution for (b):**

```java
import javax.swing.*;
import java.awt.*;
import java.awt.event.*;

public class StudentForm extends JFrame implements ActionListener {
    JLabel nameLbl, ageLbl, genderLbl;
    JTextField nameField, ageField;
    JRadioButton male, female, other;
    JButton displayBtn;
    JPanel panel;

    StudentForm() {
        setTitle("Student Form");
        setSize(350, 250);
        setDefaultCloseOperation(JFrame.EXIT_ON_CLOSE);
        setLayout(new FlowLayout());

        nameLbl  = new JLabel("Name:");
        nameField = new JTextField(15);
        ageLbl   = new JLabel("Age:");
        ageField = new JTextField(15);
        genderLbl = new JLabel("Gender:");

        male   = new JRadioButton("Male");
        female = new JRadioButton("Female");
        other  = new JRadioButton("Other");

        ButtonGroup bg = new ButtonGroup();
        bg.add(male); bg.add(female); bg.add(other);

        displayBtn = new JButton("Display");
        displayBtn.addActionListener(this);

        add(nameLbl);  add(nameField);
        add(ageLbl);   add(ageField);
        add(genderLbl);
        add(male);     add(female);  add(other);
        add(displayBtn);

        setVisible(true);
    }

    public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
        String name = nameField.getText();
        String age  = ageField.getText();
        String gender = male.isSelected() ? "Male" :
                        female.isSelected() ? "Female" :
                        other.isSelected() ? "Other" : "Not specified";
        JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(this,
            "Name: " + name + "\nAge: " + age + "\nGender: " + gender);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new StudentForm();
    }
}
```

**Key Points (worth 7 marks)**:
- `JFrame`, `JLabel`, `JTextField`, `JRadioButton`, `JButton`, `JOptionPane` correctly used.
- `ButtonGroup` correctly created to make radio buttons mutually exclusive.
- `addActionListener(this)` registers the form (which implements `ActionListener`) as the listener.
- The ternary operator correctly identifies which radio is selected.
- `JOptionPane.showMessageDialog` displays a modal dialog.

#### **Model Solution for (b):**

```java
import javax.swing.*;
import java.awt.*;
import java.awt.event.*;

public class LanguageInfo extends JFrame implements ItemListener {
    JComboBox<String> langBox;
    JLabel descLabel;

    LanguageInfo() {
        setTitle("Programming Language Info");
        setSize(400, 200);
        setDefaultCloseOperation(JFrame.EXIT_ON_CLOSE);
        setLayout(new FlowLayout());

        String[] langs = {"Java", "Python", "C++", "JavaScript", "Ruby"};
        langBox = new JComboBox<>(langs);
        langBox.addItemListener(this);

        descLabel = new JLabel("Select a language to see its description.");
        descLabel.setPreferredSize(new Dimension(380, 60));
        descLabel.setVerticalAlignment(SwingConstants.TOP);

        add(new JLabel("Choose Language:"));
        add(langBox);
        add(descLabel);

        setVisible(true);
    }

    public void itemStateChanged(ItemEvent e) {
        if (e.getStateChange() == ItemEvent.SELECTED) {
            String lang = (String) langBox.getSelectedItem();
            String desc;
            switch (lang) {
                case "Java":     desc = "Java: Object-oriented, platform-independent, used in enterprise."; break;
                case "Python":   desc = "Python: High-level, dynamic, used in AI/ML and scripting."; break;
                case "C++":      desc = "C++: High-performance, systems programming, OOP."; break;
                case "JavaScript": desc = "JavaScript: Web scripting, frontend and Node.js backend."; break;
                case "Ruby":     desc = "Ruby: Dynamic, elegant syntax, used in Rails web framework."; break;
                default:         desc = "No description available.";
            }
            descLabel.setText(desc);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new LanguageInfo();
    }
}
```

**Key Points (worth 7 marks)**:
- `JComboBox<String>` uses generics to specify the type of items.
- `ItemListener` is the correct listener for `JComboBox` selection change.
- The check `e.getStateChange() == ItemEvent.SELECTED` filters out `DESELECTED` events (which fire twice for each change in some swing versions).
- `getSelectedItem()` returns `Object` (cast to `String` here).
- The `switch` statement is Java 7+ syntax, fully supported in KTU 2024.

---

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls:**
> 
> 1. **Forgetting `setVisible(true)`**: If a student writes a complete program but forgets `setVisible(true)`, the window never shows. **Lose 1 mark**.
> 
> 2. **Not wrapping `JTextArea` in `JScrollPane`**: When asked for a multi-line input, students often add the `JTextArea` directly to the frame. The examiner expects scrollbars. **Lose 1 mark**.
> 
> 3. **Confusing `WindowListener` with `ActionListener`**: For a button click, the answer is `ActionListener` + `actionPerformed`, NOT `WindowListener` (which is for window-level events like open/close).
> 
> 4. **Confusing `JFrame`'s `add()` and `setJMenuBar()`**: Adding a `JMenu` to a `JFrame` using `add()` will not display the menu at the top — only `setJMenuBar(JMenuBar)` does. **Lose 2 marks** on menu questions.
> 
> 5. **Missing `ButtonGroup` for RadioButtons**: If you show radio buttons but no `ButtonGroup`, they will behave like checkboxes (multiple can be selected). **Lose 1.5 marks**.
> 
> 6. **Using `==` to compare strings**: A common bug. Use `.equals()` for `String` comparison. **Lose 1 mark**.
> 
> 7. **Confusing `getText()` from `JTextField` vs. `JPasswordField`**: For `JPasswordField`, you MUST use `getPassword()` (returns `char[]`), not `getText()`. The `getText()` method is deprecated for `JPasswordField` for security reasons.
> 
> 8. **Forgetting `setDefaultCloseOperation(JFrame.EXIT_ON_CLOSE)`**: Without this, clicking the close button hides the window but the JVM keeps running, and the program appears to hang.

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

### **Quick-Recall Bullet Checklist**

- **Package**: `javax.swing` — the package to import for all Swing components.
- **Root Class**: `JComponent` — all Swing controls (except `JFrame`, `JDialog`, `JApplet`) extend this.
- **Top-Level Containers**: `JFrame` (main window), `JDialog` (pop-up), `JApplet` (browser). Only these are heavyweight.
- **Lightweight vs. Heavyweight**: Swing is lightweight (pure Java); AWT is heavyweight (OS peers).
- **Pluggable Look and Feel (PLAF)**: A key advantage of Swing — change appearance without changing code.
- **JLabel**: For displaying text/icons; not editable; no events generated on its own.
- **JButton**: Clickable button; fires `ActionEvent`; `addActionListener()` to handle.
- **JTextField**: Single-line text input; `addActionListener` fires on Enter key.
- **JTextArea**: Multi-line text input; **MUST** be wrapped in `JScrollPane` for scrollbars.
- **JPasswordField**: Special text field that masks input; use `getPassword()` (returns `char[]`), not `getText()`.
- **JCheckBox**: Independent toggle; use `isSelected()` to check state; fires `ItemEvent`.
- **JRadioButton**: Mutually exclusive; **MUST** be added to a `ButtonGroup` for mutual exclusion.
- **ButtonGroup**: A *logical* (not visual) group; does not display; holds radio buttons for grouping.
- **JComboBox**: Drop-down list; saves space; fires `ItemEvent` on selection change.
- **JList**: Visible scrollable list; **MUST** be in `JScrollPane`; supports multi-select via `setSelectionMode()`.
- **JTable**: Tabular data display; use `DefaultTableModel` for real applications.
- **JMenuBar**: The top horizontal bar; set on a frame with `setJMenuBar(JMenuBar)`.
- **JMenu**: A dropdown menu inside a `JMenuBar` (e.g., "File", "Edit").
- **JMenuItem**: An individual clickable item inside a `JMenu` (e.g., "Open", "Save").
- **Delegation Event Model**: The source creates an event and delegates handling to a registered listener.
- **ActionListener**: `actionPerformed(ActionEvent)` — for buttons, menu items, Enter in text fields.
- **ItemListener**: `itemStateChanged(ItemEvent)` — for checkboxes, radio buttons, combo boxes.
- **Layout Managers**: `FlowLayout` (default for `JPanel`), `BorderLayout` (default for `JFrame`'s content pane), `GridLayout`, `BoxLayout`, `GridBagLayout`.
- **setLayout(null)**: Disables the layout manager; you must call `setBounds(x, y, width, height)` on every component.
- **setVisible(true)**: Must be called last in the constructor for the window to appear.
- **setDefaultCloseOperation(EXIT_ON_CLOSE)**: Closes the JVM on window close. Without it, the program hangs.
- **EDT (Event Dispatch Thread)**: All Swing GUI operations should occur on this thread for thread safety.
- **MVC**: Swing components follow Model-View-Controller; model holds data, view displays, controller handles input.
- **getContentPane()**: In Java < 5, you had to call this to add components to a `JFrame`. From Java 5+, `add()` on the frame is automatic.
- **addXxxListener(XxxListener l)**: The general pattern for registering any event listener in Swing.
- **Anonymous Inner Class**: A common, concise way to register a listener inline, e.g., `button.addActionListener(new ActionListener() { ... })`.
- **Lambda Expressions**: In Java 8+, `button.addActionListener(e -> { ... })` is the modern way; allowed in KTU 2024 scheme.
- **JOptionPane**: Static methods `showMessageDialog`, `showInputDialog`, `showConfirmDialog` for pop-up dialogs.
- **setLocationRelativeTo(null)**: Centers the window on the screen.
<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.title: Components and Containers
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PBCST304 - OBJECT ORIENTED PROGRAMMING
> - **Module:** Module 4
> - **Topic:** Components and Containers

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# 📘 SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology)

In the Java Abstract Window Toolkit (**AWT**) and **Swing** frameworks, every visual element that the user can see and interact with on a Graphical User Interface (GUI) is fundamentally built upon two cornerstone abstract classes: **`Component`** and **`Container`**.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Official KTU Definition:**
> - **Component:** An abstract class (`java.awt.Component`) that serves as the *superclass* for all GUI-related classes which can be displayed on the screen and can interact with the user. Examples include `Button`, `Label`, `TextField`, `Checkbox`, `List`, etc.
> - **Container:** A specialized subclass of `Component` that has the unique ability to *hold and organize other components* (including other containers). A container provides a spatial layout mechanism for the components added to it. Examples include `Frame`, `Dialog`, `Panel`, and `Applet`.

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Intuition 🎨

Think of building a GUI like assembling a **physical office desk**:

| Real-World Object | Java GUI Equivalent |
|------------------|---------------------|
| The desk itself | The **Frame** (top-level window) |
| Drawers, trays, folders on the desk | **Components** (Button, Label, TextField) |
| The desktop organizer holding pens, papers, etc. | **Container** (Panel) |
| The "how things are arranged" rule (rows, columns, grid) | **Layout Manager** (FlowLayout, GridLayout) |

Just as a desk has multiple compartments that hold objects, a **Container holds Components**. You cannot place a button directly onto the screen — you must place it inside a container (like a `Frame` or `Panel`), which itself is placed on the screen.

> [!NOTE]
> **Critical Hierarchy Insight:** A `Container` **IS-A** `Component` (it inherits from it). This means a container can be placed *inside* another container! This enables nested, hierarchical UI construction.

## 1.3 Key Physical/Conceptual Constants

- The base class is **`java.awt.Component`** in AWT (and `javax.swing.JComponent` in Swing).
- Every Java GUI program must inherit from either **`java.applet.Applet`** (deprecated) or top-level container classes like **`java.awt.Frame`** / **`javax.swing.JFrame`**.
- The `main()` method of a standalone GUI application typically ends with the standard exit code value of **0**.

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 📘 SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Cheat Sheet

## 2.1 The Component Class Hierarchy (AWT)

The `Component` class is the **root of all visual AWT classes**. Below is the structural breakdown:

### 📂 Class Hierarchy Breakdown

- **`java.awt.Component`** (Abstract Class)
  - **Container** (Abstract Subclass — can hold other components)
    - `Panel` (Generic container, no title bar)
      - `Applet` (Embedded in web/browser — deprecated)
    - `Window` (Top-level window, no title bar/borders)
      - `Frame` (Top-level window WITH title bar & borders)
        - `Dialog` (Pop-up window for messages)
    - `ScrollPane` (Container with scrollable region)
  - **Non-Container Components** (Visual elements, cannot hold others)
    - `Button`, `Label`, `TextField`, `TextArea`
    - `Checkbox`, `Choice`, `List`
    - `Canvas` (Custom drawing surface)

## 2.2 Container — The "Holder" of Components

A `Container` object has the exclusive ability to invoke the **`add()`** method to insert other components. The signature is:

$$ \text{Component add(\text{Component comp})} $$

The container is responsible for **layout management** — deciding the position and size of every added component based on the **LayoutManager** it is assigned.

## 2.3 Layout Managers — The Arrangement Rules

A Layout Manager is an object that implements the `java.awt.LayoutManager` interface and governs component placement.

| Layout Manager | Arrangement Strategy | Best Used For |
|---------------|---------------------|---------------|
| `FlowLayout` | Left-to-right, wraps to next line | Toolbars, button rows |
| `BorderLayout` | 5 regions: North, South, East, West, Center | App frames, dialogs |
| `GridLayout` | Equal-sized cells in a grid | Calculators, keypads |
| `GridBagLayout` | Flexible grid with varying cell sizes | Complex forms |
| `CardLayout` | Stacked cards, one visible at a time | Tabbed wizards, slideshows |
| `null` (Absolute) | Manual `setBounds(x, y, w, h)` | Pixel-perfect custom UIs |

## 2.4 KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet (Cheat Table)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Memorize the following **must-know** methods for KTU exams:

| Method | Purpose | Container/Component |
|--------|---------|---------------------|
| `add(Component c)` | Adds component to container | Container |
| `setLayout(LayoutManager m)` | Sets layout strategy | Container |
| `setSize(int w, int h)` | Sets dimensions in pixels | Component |
| `setBounds(int x, int y, int w, int h)` | Sets position & size | Component |
| `setTitle(String s)` | Sets window title | Frame |
| `setVisible(boolean b)` | Shows/hides component | Component |
| `setBackground(Color c)` | Sets background color | Component |
| `setForeground(Color c)` | Sets foreground (text) color | Component |
| `addWindowListener(WindowListener l)` | Handles window events | Window |
| `validate()` | Re-lays out container | Container |
| `getContentPane().add(...)` | Adds to frame's content area (Swing) | JFrame |

## 2.5 Real-World Engineering Utility

GUI components and containers are the **backbone of every desktop, web, and mobile application**. From the ATM machine you use, to the cockpit of an aircraft, to the SCADA dashboards in power plants — every interactive system is built upon this exact **Component–Container paradigm**. Mastering it equips you to design any visual interface.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# 📘 SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations, Examples & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 The "Why" Behind Container Composition — Analytical Breakdown

### Step 1: Why does `Container` extend `Component`?

**Reasoning:** Because a container itself *must be displayable* on the screen. Since a Frame is a Container and we want to *see* the Frame, the Frame must inherit all the display-related behavior (`setSize`, `setVisible`, `setBackground`) from `Component`. This enables **nested composition**: a `Panel` (a Container) can be added *into* a `Frame` (also a Container), forming a tree structure.

### Step 2: The "add() Method" Decision Logic

When you call `container.add(button)`, the following sequence executes internally:

1. The container **stores a reference** to the `button` in its internal data structure (a list/array of components).
2. The container's **current `LayoutManager`** is consulted.
3. The layout manager **calculates** the position and size of the button based on the container's current dimensions and the layout's rules.
4. The button is **rendered** on screen at the calculated coordinates.

### Step 3: The Layout Manager Equation (Generalized)

For a container of width $W$ and height $H$, with $n$ components, the position of the $i$-th component under different layouts is given by:

$$ \text{Position}_i = f(W, H, n, \text{layoutRule}) $$

#### Worked Example: FlowLayout Positioning

For a `FlowLayout` with horizontal gap $g_h$ and vertical gap $g_v$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_i &= x_0 + (i \cdot (w_i + g_h)) \mod W_{\text{row}} \\
y_i &= y_0 + (\text{rowIndex}_i \cdot (h_{\max} + g_v))
\end{aligned}
$$

Where:
- $x_0, y_0$ = origin offset (usually 5 pixels)
- $w_i$ = width of component $i$
- $h_{\max}$ = maximum height in the current row
- $\text{rowIndex}_i$ = row number of component $i$

#### Worked Example: GridLayout Cell Calculation

For a `GridLayout` with $R$ rows and $C$ columns inside a container of size $(W, H)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{cellWidth} &= \frac{W - (C-1) \cdot g_h}{C} \\
\text{cellHeight} &= \frac{H - (R-1) \cdot g_v}{R} \\
\text{cellRow}_i &= \left\lfloor \frac{i}{C} \right\rfloor \\
\text{cellCol}_i &= i \mod C
\end{aligned}
$$

This means for cell index $i = 0, 1, 2, \dots, n-1$, you can compute the exact pixel position of any component on the grid.

## 3.2 The Complete GUI Construction — Analytical Matrix

| Step | Action | Code | Why |
|------|--------|------|-----|
| 1 | Create the top-level container | `Frame f = new Frame("MyApp");` | Frame is a visible top-level Container |
| 2 | Set the layout manager | `f.setLayout(new FlowLayout());` | Defines how children will be arranged |
| 3 | Create child components | `Button b = new Button("OK");` | Components are the interactive elements |
| 4 | Add children to container | `f.add(b);` | Container holds and displays them |
| 5 | Set container size | `f.setSize(400, 300);` | Defines window dimensions in pixels |
| 6 | Make it visible | `f.setVisible(true);` | Renders it on screen |

## 3.3 The Swing Equivalent — Content Pane Concept

In **Swing**, a `JFrame` does not directly accept `add()`. Instead, you must use:

$$ \text{frame.getContentPane().add(\text{component})} $$

**Why?** A `JFrame` is composed of multiple layers (root pane, layered pane, glass pane, content pane). The **content pane** is the actual `Container` that holds your visual components. The reasoning: this layered architecture enables advanced features like menu bars, tool tips, and pop-up dialogs to be rendered on separate layers without interfering with your main UI.

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
# 📘 SECTION_4: Structural Diagrams & Schematics

## 4.1 Component-Class Hierarchy (AWT) — Visual Map

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[Object] --> B[Component]
    B --> C[Container]
    B --> D[Button]
    B --> E[Label]
    B --> F[TextField]
    B --> G[Checkbox]
    B --> H[List]
    B --> I[Choice]
    B --> J[Canvas]
    C --> K[Panel]
    C --> L[Window]
    C --> M[ScrollPane]

    L --> P[Dialog]
    O --> Q[MyApp]
    K --> R[MyPanel]
    Q --> R
    R --> S[Btn1]
    R --> T[Btn2]
    R --> U[Btn3]
```

## 4.2 Block-Level Functional Architecture: GUI Composition Flow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Screen] --> B[Frame Top-Level Container]
    B --> C{LayoutManager}
    C -->|FlowLayout| D[Left to Right Row]
    C -->|BorderLayout| E[5 Region Map]
    C -->|GridLayout| F[Equal Cell Grid]
    C -->|CardLayout| G[Stacked Cards]
    D --> H[Component 1]
    D --> I[Component 2]
    D --> J[Component 3]
    E --> K[North]
    E --> L[South]
    E --> M[East]
    E --> N[West]
    E --> O[Center]
    F --> P[Cell 1]
    F --> Q[Cell 2]
    F --> R[Cell 3]
    F --> S[Cell 4]
    G --> T[Card A]
    G --> U[Card B]
```

## 4.3 Container-Component Containment Model

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Frame] --> B[Panel North]
    A --> C[Panel Center]
    A --> D[Panel South]
    B --> E[Label Title]
    B --> F[TextField Input]
    C --> G[TextArea Output]
    C --> H[Button Submit]
    D --> I[Button Cancel]
    D --> J[Button Reset]
```

## 4.4 The `add()` Method Execution Pipeline

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as Developer
    participant Cont as Container
    participant LM as LayoutManager
    participant OS as Operating System
    Dev->>Cont: add(button)
    Cont->>Cont: store reference internally
    Cont->>LM: request layout calculation
    LM->>LM: compute x, y, width, height
    LM-->>Cont: return position data
    Cont->>OS: request redraw
    OS-->>Dev: visible on screen
```

<!-- SECTION_4_END -->

<!-- SECTION_5_START -->
# 📘 SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 📝 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Q1. [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]

**Define the terms Component and Container in Java AWT. How are they related?**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

> A **Component** is an abstract class in `java.awt` that is the superclass of all graphical user interface elements which can be displayed on the screen and can interact with the user. Examples include `Button`, `Label`, `TextField`, and `Checkbox`. **(1 mark)**
>
> A **Container** is a subclass of `Component` that has the unique capability of holding and organizing other components (including other containers) by providing a spatial layout. Examples include `Frame`, `Dialog`, and `Panel`. **(1 mark)**
>
> **Relationship:** A Container **IS-A** Component (it inherits from it), which means containers themselves can be displayed on the screen and can also contain other containers, enabling a nested, hierarchical UI tree. **(1 mark)**

---

### Q2. [KTU University Exam – June 2024]

**List any three LayoutManager classes in Java AWT and state the arrangement strategy of each.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

| Layout Manager | Strategy (1 mark each) |
|---------------|------------------------|
| `FlowLayout` | Arranges components left-to-right in rows, wrapping to the next row when the container width is exceeded. |
| `BorderLayout` | Divides the container into 5 regions: North, South, East, West, and Center. |
| `GridLayout` | Arranges components in a grid of equal-sized cells defined by rows and columns. |

---

## 📝 Part B Questions (14 Marks Each — Internal Choice)

### 🔹 Question A (14 Marks)

#### Q3a. [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023] (7 marks)

**Explain the AWT Component class hierarchy with a neat diagram. Differentiate between Panel and Frame.**

**Model Answer:**

The AWT Component class hierarchy is rooted at `java.awt.Component` (abstract class). The key branches are:

1. **`Container` (abstract)** – A subclass of Component that can hold other components.
2. **Non-container visual components** – `Button`, `Label`, `TextField`, etc.

The `Container` branch further splits into:
- `Panel` (a generic container without a title bar or border)
- `Window` (top-level window)
  - `Frame` (window with title bar and borders)
  - `Dialog` (pop-up window)
- `ScrollPane` (container with scrollable region)

**Diagram:**

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[Component] --> B[Container]
    A --> C[Button]
    A --> D[Label]
    B --> E[Panel]
    B --> F[Window]
    B --> G[ScrollPane]
    F --> H[Frame]
    F --> I[Dialog]
```

**Difference between Panel and Frame: (3 marks)**

| Feature | Panel | Frame |
|---------|-------|-------|
| Title bar | Does not have | Has a title bar |
| Borders/Menu | No native borders or menu support | Supports borders and menu bar |
| Top-level | Cannot be displayed standalone | Can be top-level window |
| Use case | Embedded inside Frame/Applet | Main application window |
| Inheritance | Extends Container directly | Extends Window |

#### Q3b. (7 marks)

**Write a Java AWT program to create a Frame with three Buttons (OK, Cancel, Submit) arranged using FlowLayout. Set the frame size to 400×300 and make it visible.**

**Model Answer:**

```java
import java.awt.*;

class AWTButtonDemo extends Frame {
    AWTButtonDemo() {
        // Step 1: Set the layout manager (1 mark)
        setLayout(new FlowLayout());
        
        // Step 2: Create components (1 mark)
        Button b1 = new Button("OK");
        Button b2 = new Button("Cancel");
        Button b3 = new Button("Submit");
        
        // Step 3: Add components to container (1 mark)
        add(b1);
        add(b2);
        add(b3);
        
        // Step 4: Set size and visibility (1 mark)
        setSize(400, 300);
        setTitle("Button Demo");
        setVisible(true);
    }
    
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        AWTButtonDemo f = new AWTButtonDemo();  // (3 marks)
    }
}
```

**Explanation:** The class `AWTButtonDemo` extends `Frame` (a top-level container). The constructor sets a `FlowLayout`, creates three `Button` components, adds them via `add()`, and configures the frame's size and visibility.

---

### 🔹 Question B (Alternative 14 Marks)

#### Q4a. [KTU University Exam – June 2024] (7 marks)

**Explain the BorderLayout with a diagram. How is it different from GridLayout?**

**Model Answer:**

**BorderLayout (4 marks):** It divides the container into **5 distinct regions**: `North` (top), `South` (bottom), `East` (right), `West` (left), and `Center` (middle). Each region can hold at most **one component** (or a container of components). The North and South regions span the full width horizontally; East and West occupy the remaining vertical space; Center fills the leftover space.

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[BorderLayout Container] --> B[North]
    A --> C[South]
    A --> D[East]
    A --> E[West]
    A --> F[Center]
```

**Difference from GridLayout (3 marks):**

| Feature | BorderLayout | GridLayout |
|---------|--------------|------------|
| Regions | 5 named regions | Equal grid of rows × columns |
| Component size | Variable per region | All cells are equal size |
| Components per area | 1 per region | 1 per cell |
| Default for Frame | Yes | No |

#### Q4b. (7 marks)

**Write a Java AWT program that uses a `Panel` inside a `Frame` to display a `Label` and a `TextField` using BorderLayout.**

**Model Answer:**

```java
import java.awt.*;

class PanelDemo extends Frame {
    PanelDemo() {
        // Frame uses BorderLayout by default (1 mark)
        setLayout(new BorderLayout());
        
        // Create a Panel (2 marks)
        Panel p = new Panel();
        p.setLayout(new FlowLayout());
        
        // Create components
        Label l = new Label("Name:");
        TextField tf = new TextField(20);
        
        // Add components to Panel
        p.add(l);
        p.add(tf);
        
        // Add Panel to Frame's center (2 marks)
        add(p, BorderLayout.CENTER);
        
        // Frame configuration
        setSize(400, 150);
        setTitle("Panel Demo");
        setVisible(true);  // (2 marks)
    }
    
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new PanelDemo();
    }
}
```

**Explanation:** A `Panel` (a generic Container) is created and populated with a `Label` and `TextField` using `FlowLayout`. This panel is then added to the center region of a `Frame` that uses `BorderLayout`. This demonstrates **nested container composition** — a container inside another container.

---

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls:**
> 1. **Forgetting `setVisible(true)`:** The most common mistake — your program compiles and runs but nothing appears. Always remember to call `setVisible(true)` as the LAST step.
> 2. **Confusing AWT vs Swing imports:** AWT uses `java.awt.*` (e.g., `Frame`, `Button`). Swing uses `javax.swing.*` (e.g., `JFrame`, `JButton`). Mixing them causes compilation errors.
> 3. **Swing content pane oversight:** In Swing, `frame.add(button)` will compile but **not display** the button. You must use `frame.getContentPane().add(button)`.
> 4. **Wrong BorderLayout region names:** Use **exact strings** `"North"`, `"South"`, `"East"`, `"West"`, `"Center"` (capitalized). Lowercase will throw a runtime error.
> 5. **Not extending `Frame`:** In a standalone Java GUI, the main class must extend `Frame` (AWT) or `JFrame` (Swing) for the window to be a valid top-level container.
> 6. **Missing `main()` method signature:** KTU strictly requires `public static void main(String[] args)`.

---

## 🧠 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!NOTE]
> **Rapid-Revision Checklist for Exam Day:**

- ✅ **`Component`** is the abstract superclass of all AWT visual elements; it defines display-related methods like `setSize`, `setVisible`, `setBackground`.
- ✅ **`Container`** is a subclass of `Component` that can hold other components via the `add()` method.
- ✅ A **Container IS-A Component** — this is what enables nested UI (containers inside containers).
- ✅ **`Frame`** is the most commonly used top-level container in standalone AWT applications; it has a title bar and border.
- ✅ **`Panel`** is a generic container without a title bar — used to group components inside a Frame.
- ✅ **Default Layouts:** `Frame` → `BorderLayout`; `Panel` → `FlowLayout`.
- ✅ **5 BorderLayout regions:** `North`, `South`, `East`, `West`, `Center` — exactly one component per region.
- ✅ **GridLayout** divides the container into equal-sized cells in a rows × columns grid.
- ✅ **FlowLayout** arranges components left-to-right, wrapping to the next line.
- ✅ **For Swing:** Use `JFrame`, `JButton`, etc. and always use `getContentPane().add()`.
- ✅ The execution order in any AWT program: **Create Container → Set Layout → Create Components → Add Components → setSize → setVisible(true)**.
- ✅ **The `add()` method signature:** `Component add(Component comp)` — returns the added component.
- ✅ `Applet` is **deprecated** since Java 9; KTU may still ask conceptually, but avoid in practical code.

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

# Swing Layout Managers — Foundational Overview

## 1.1 Formal Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology)

> [!NOTE]
> **Layout Manager (Java AWT/Swing):** A `java.awt.LayoutManager` (or its sub-interface `LayoutManager2`) is a **strategy object** that governs the **size, position, and arrangement** of `Component` objects (widgets) inside a `Container`. It implements the **Strategy Design Pattern** from the Gang-of-Four catalog, decoupling *what* is placed in a container from *how* it is visually arranged.

In the **KTU 2024 Scheme** (Course Outcome: **CO4** — *Apply event-driven programming concepts to develop GUI-based applications using Java Swing*), Layout Managers form the **non-visual backbone** of any desktop application. Without a layout manager, components either overlap, get clipped, or fail to resize correctly when the user stretches the window.

**Hierarchy in the Java Class Library:**

$$ \text{LayoutManager (interface)} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{LayoutManager2 (sub-interface)} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{Concrete classes} $$

All concrete layout managers (`BorderLayout`, `FlowLayout`, `GridLayout`, `BoxLayout`, `GridBagLayout`, `CardLayout`, `GroupLayout`, `SpringLayout`) implement one of these two interfaces and are part of the **`java.awt`** package, even when used inside Swing (`javax.swing`) components.

## 1.2 The Intuition — A Real-World Analogy

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Analogy — The Interior Designer of Your Window**
>
> Imagine you are moving into a **new apartment room** (your `JFrame` / `JPanel`). You have furniture (your buttons, labels, text fields — the `Component` objects). You could drop the furniture randomly on the floor, but the room will look chaotic, and if you re-shape the room, furniture will sit on top of the carpet edges.
>
> Hiring a **Layout Manager** is like hiring an **interior designer** who follows specific rules:
> - A **FlowLayout** designer lines furniture up in a row, wrapping to the next row when the line is full.
> - A **GridLayout** designer places furniture in a strict N × M matrix, like egg cartons.
> - A **BorderLayout** designer divides the room into five zones — North wall, South wall, East wall, West wall, and the Center — placing the most important piece in the Center.
> - A **BoxLayout** designer stacks furniture either vertically (bookshelf) or horizontally (shelf).
> - A **GridBagLayout** designer is the most flexible — a perfectionist who uses a spreadsheet of constraints to place every piece exactly where you want it, even if pieces are different sizes.

**Why is this important to KTU examiners?** Because the examiner is not testing whether you can *memorize* a constructor — they are testing whether you can **choose the correct layout** for a problem, **justify** the choice, and **predict** what happens when the window is resized.

## 1.3 Key Constants & Metrics

- **Pixel (px)** — the standard unit of measurement; default font in `MetalLookAndFeel` is typically the **Dialog 12 pt** font (~ **12 pixels** tall).
- **Container insets** — measured in **pixels**, default top/left/bottom/right = **11, 11, 11, 11** for `JFrame` content pane, **0** for `JPanel`.
- **`setPreferredSize(Dimension)`** — the **layout-hint size** in **pixels**; the layout manager respects this *only* when there is room to honour it.
- **Reasonable upper bound for component count in a single panel** — typically **≤ 30** before usability degrades (usability guideline, not a Java constant).

---

## 1.4 Why Layout Managers Exist — The Problem They Solve

If you set absolute coordinates via `setBounds(x, y, width, height)`, three problems appear:

1. **Platform dependency** — fonts and widget sizes differ across Windows, macOS, Linux.
2. **Resizing failure** — the layout freezes when the user resizes the window.
3. **Locale dependency** — translated text (e.g., German "Abbrechen" vs English "Cancel") overflows fixed-width components.

Layout Managers solve all three by treating the container as a **rectangular contract** and re-computing child geometry every time the container is invalidated (`validate()` / `revalidate()`).

# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Reference Sheet

## 2.1 The LayoutManager Contract — Operational Logic

Every `LayoutManager` must implement **five** methods. A `LayoutManager2` extends this with two more:

**Core contract (LayoutManager):**

1. `addLayoutComponent(String name, Component comp)` — called when a component is added with a *string constraint* (used by `BorderLayout` to assign "North", "South", etc.).
2. `removeLayoutComponent(Component comp)` — called when a component is removed.
3. `preferredLayoutSize(Container parent)` — returns the **ideal** size of the container that will display all children comfortably.
4. `minimumLayoutSize(Container parent)` — returns the **smallest** acceptable size (usually smaller than preferred).
5. `layoutContainer(Container parent)` — the **drawing call**: actually positions and sizes every child. Called automatically by the AWT/Swing rendering thread.

**Extended contract (LayoutManager2):**

6. `addLayoutComponent(Component comp, Object constraints)` — the **modern, type-safe** way to attach a constraint object (e.g., a `GridBagConstraints` instance).
7. `maximumLayoutSize(Container parent)` — the **largest** acceptable size, used by scrolling containers.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Favourite Question Pattern:** *"Explain the role of the `layoutContainer()` method. When is it invoked?"* — The answer must mention that the AWT event-dispatch thread calls it **after** `validate()` (or `revalidate()`) and that the layout manager is responsible for calling `component.setBounds(...)` on every child.

---

## 2.2 The "Big Five" Layout Managers — KTU Reference Sheet

| # | Manager | Default for | Arrangement Rule | Constructor Variants | Key Methods |
|---|---------|-------------|------------------|----------------------|-------------|
| 1 | **FlowLayout** | `JPanel` | Left-to-right, top-to-bottom wrapping | `()`, `(int align)`, `(int align, int hgap, int vgap)` | align ∈ {LEFT, CENTER, RIGHT} |
| 2 | **BorderLayout** | `JFrame` content pane, `JDialog` | 5 zones: NORTH, SOUTH, EAST, WEST, CENTER | `()`, `(int hgap, int vgap)` | `add(comp, BorderLayout.NORTH)` etc. |
| 3 | **GridLayout** | none (opt-in) | Rigid N × M grid, equal cells | `(rows, cols)`, `(rows, cols, hgap, vgap)` | cells expand to fill container |
| 4 | **BoxLayout** | Boxes (`Box.createXxxBox()`) | Single row OR single column | `new BoxLayout(target, axis)` | axis ∈ {X\_AXIS, Y\_AXIS, LINE\_AXIS, PAGE\_AXIS} |
| 5 | **GridBagLayout** | none (opt-in) | Flexible grid with per-cell constraints | `new GridBagLayout()` | paired with `GridBagConstraints` |

### Supplementary Layout Managers (often asked as 3-mark questions)

| Manager | Use Case |
|---------|----------|
| **CardLayout** | Tab-like UIs, wizards (step 1 → step 2 → step 3) — `next()`, `previous()`, `show(cardName)` |
| **GroupLayout** | Auto-generated by NetBeans GUI Builder; horizontal + vertical parallel/sequential groups |
| **SpringLayout** | Precise constraint-based positioning via `Spring` objects |
| **GridLayout(rows, cols, hgap, vgap)** | When *hgap* or *vgap* is 0, cells touch — useful for calculator-style button panels |

---

## 2.3 The Chain of Method Calls — How Layout Works at Runtime

When a `JFrame` is first shown, the AWT rendering pipeline executes the following sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{1. } & \texttt{setVisible(true)} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{Peer created, native window opens} \\
\text{2. } & \texttt{addNotify()} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{Component attached to native resource} \\
\text{3. } & \texttt{validate()} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{Tree validated top-down} \\
\text{4. } & \texttt{layoutContainer(parent)} \;\text{ called on each container's layout manager} \\
\text{5. } & \text{Each child receives } \texttt{setBounds(x, y, w, h)} \\
\text{6. } & \texttt{paint()} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{Components actually drawn on screen}
\end{aligned}
$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Engineering Utility:** The same contract is used in **embedded systems GUI toolkits** (e.g., Qt's QLayout, Android's ConstraintLayout, JavaFX's Pane) — the Strategy Pattern transcends languages.

---

## 2.4 Decision Matrix — "Which Layout Should I Use?"

| Scenario | Recommended Layout | Reasoning |
|----------|-------------------|-----------|
| A login form (2 labels + 2 fields + 1 button) | `GridBagLayout` or nested `JPanel`s with `BoxLayout` | Need aligned columns, mixed sizes |
| A toolbar with 4 buttons in a row | `FlowLayout(LEFT)` or `BoxLayout(X\_AXIS)` | Single horizontal row, natural wrap if window shrinks |
| A main app window with menu, status bar, central canvas | `BorderLayout` | The textbook 5-zone pattern |
| A calculator button pad (4×4 = 16 equal buttons) | `GridLayout(4, 4, 2, 2)` | Equal cells, 2px gaps |
| A multi-step form (Page 1 → Page 2 → Page 3) | `CardLayout` | Show one "card" at a time |
| A complex form with labels, fields, checkboxes, radio buttons | **Nested panels**, each with its own layout | Most real-world GUIs use this pattern |

## 3.1 Example 1 — `BorderLayout` (Default of `JFrame`)

**Step 1 — Conceptual goal:** Place a header at the top, a status bar at the bottom, a navigation panel on the left, a settings panel on the right, and a main canvas in the center.

**Step 2 — Java code with exhaustive annotation:**

```java
import javax.swing.*;
import java.awt.*;

public class BorderLayoutDemo extends JFrame {
    public BorderLayoutDemo() {
        setTitle("BorderLayout Demo");
        setSize(500, 400);
        setDefaultCloseOperation(JFrame.EXIT_ON_CLOSE);

        // Step 3: Get the content pane. In Swing, you do NOT add
        // directly to the JFrame; you add to its content pane.
        Container cp = getContentPane();

        // Step 4: Set the layout manager explicitly.
        // (It is ALREADY BorderLayout by default — shown for clarity.)
        cp.setLayout(new BorderLayout(5, 5));   // 5px gaps

        // Step 5: Add components with region constraints.
        cp.add(new JButton("North Menu"),  BorderLayout.NORTH);
        cp.add(new JButton("South Status"), BorderLayout.SOUTH);
        cp.add(new JButton("West Nav"),     BorderLayout.WEST);
        cp.add(new JButton("East Settings"),BorderLayout.EAST);
        cp.add(new JTextArea("Center Work Area"), BorderLayout.CENTER);

        // Step 6: Make the window visible — triggers validate() internally.
        setVisible(true);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SwingUtilities.invokeLater(BorderLayoutDemo::new);
    }
}
```

**Step-by-step reasoning:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Line } \texttt{cp.setLayout(new BorderLayout(5, 5))} \;&\Rightarrow\; \text{hgap = vgap = 5 pixels} \\
\text{Line } \texttt{cp.add(..., BorderLayout.NORTH)} \;&\Rightarrow\; \text{LayoutManager2.addLayoutComponent stores (button, "North")} \\
\text{Line } \texttt{setVisible(true)} \;&\Rightarrow\; \text{Invokes} \; \texttt{validate()} \;\Rightarrow\; \texttt{layoutContainer()} \\
\text{Inside } \texttt{layoutContainer()} \;&\Rightarrow\; \text{NORTH and SOUTH take preferred height, full width} \\
                                  \;&\Rightarrow\; \text{WEST and EAST take preferred width, remaining height} \\
                                  \;&\Rightarrow\; \text{CENTER takes ALL remaining space}
\end{aligned}
$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Critical KTU pitfall:** If you call `frame.add(button)` **without** a region, the button is silently assigned to `CENTER`. If you then add a second component without a region, it **replaces** the first one. Many students lose marks for not knowing this.

## 3.2 Example 2 — `GridLayout` (Calculator Pad)

**Step 1 — Conceptual goal:** Build a 4 × 4 calculator button pad with 16 equal-sized buttons and 3-pixel gaps.

**Step 2 — Java code with annotation:**

```java
import javax.swing.*;
import java.awt.*;

public class GridLayoutDemo extends JFrame {
    public GridLayoutDemo() {
        setTitle("GridLayout Demo — Calculator Pad");
        setSize(300, 300);
        setDefaultCloseOperation(JFrame.EXIT_ON_CLOSE);

        Container cp = getContentPane();

        // Step 3: rows = 4, cols = 4, hgap = 3, vgap = 3
        cp.setLayout(new GridLayout(4, 4, 3, 3));

        // Step 4: The order of add() = left-to-right, top-to-bottom.
        String[] labels = {
            "7", "8", "9", "/",
            "4", "5", "6", "*",
            "1", "2", "3", "-",
            "0", ".", "=", "+"
        };
        for (String s : labels) {
            cp.add(new JButton(s));
        }

        setVisible(true);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SwingUtilities.invokeLater(GridLayoutDemo::new);
    }
}
```

**Step-by-step reasoning:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Grid cell width} \;&=\; \frac{\texttt{containerWidth} - 4 \times \texttt{hgap}}{4} \\
\text{Grid cell height} \;&=\; \frac{\texttt{containerHeight} - 4 \times \texttt{vgap}}{4} \\
\text{All cells} \;&=\; \text{exactly that size — the layout IGNORES component preferred size} \\
\text{Component count} \;&>\; \texttt{rows} \times \texttt{cols} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{extra cells ignored} \\
\text{Component count} \;&<\; \texttt{rows} \times \texttt{cols} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{rows is forced to fit}
\end{aligned}
$$

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner Trap:** Many students write `new GridLayout(0, 4)` thinking *"any number of rows"*. Java's behavior is the opposite: setting `rows = 0` means **any number of rows**, but the **columns are fixed at 4**. Confusing the two will cost marks.

## 3.3 Example 3 — `BoxLayout` (Vertical Form)

**Step 1 — Conceptual goal:** Stack 4 form rows vertically, each row a label + text field.

**Step 2 — Java code with annotation:**

```java
import javax.swing.*;
import java.awt.*;

public class BoxLayoutDemo extends JFrame {
    public BoxLayoutDemo() {
        setTitle("BoxLayout Demo — Vertical Form");
        setSize(350, 200);
        setDefaultCloseOperation(JFrame.EXIT_ON_CLOSE);

        JPanel form = new JPanel();
        // Step 3: BoxLayout is constructor-injected with the target
        // container as the FIRST argument and axis as the second.
        form.setLayout(new BoxLayout(form, BoxLayout.Y_AXIS));

        // Step 4: Add label-field rows.
        for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) {
            form.add(new JLabel("Field " + i + ":"));
            form.add(new JTextField(15));
        }

        add(form);
        setVisible(true);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SwingUtilities.invokeLater(BoxLayoutDemo::new);
    }
}
```

**Step-by-step reasoning:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{BoxLayout} \;&\Rightarrow\; \text{components arranged along ONE axis only} \\
\text{Y\_AXIS} \;&\Rightarrow\; \text{top-to-bottom stack} \\
\text{X\_AXIS} \;&\Rightarrow\; \text{left-to-right row} \\
\text{Alignment} \;&\Rightarrow\; \text{default is CENTER; can override per-component with } \texttt{setAlignmentX(float)} \\
\text{Fillers} \;&\Rightarrow\; \texttt{Box.createVerticalGlue()} \text{ pushes components apart}
\end{aligned}
$$

## 3.4 Example 4 — `GridBagLayout` (The Power Tool)

**Step 1 — Conceptual goal:** A login form with two labels, two fields, a "Remember me" checkbox, and a "Login" button — all aligned in two columns.

**Step 2 — Java code with annotation:**

```java
import javax.swing.*;
import java.awt.*;

public class GridBagLayoutDemo extends JFrame {

    private void addComponent(Container cp, Component c,
                              int row, int col, int width, int height,
                              int anchor, int fill) {
        GridBagConstraints g = new GridBagConstraints();
        g.gridx = col;        g.gridy = row;
        g.gridwidth = width;  g.gridheight = height;
        g.anchor = anchor;    g.fill = fill;
        g.insets = new Insets(4, 4, 4, 4);  // 4px padding around each cell
        g.weightx = (width > 1) ? 1.0 : 0.5;
        g.weighty = (height > 1) ? 1.0 : 0.0;
        cp.add(c, g);
    }

    public GridBagLayoutDemo() {
        setTitle("GridBagLayout Demo — Login");
        setSize(400, 200);
        setDefaultCloseOperation(JFrame.EXIT_ON_CLOSE);

        Container cp = getContentPane();
        cp.setLayout(new GridBagLayout());

        addComponent(cp, new JLabel("Username:"), 0, 0, 1, 1,
                     GridBagConstraints.WEST, GridBagConstraints.NONE);
        addComponent(cp, new JTextField(15),       0, 1, 1, 1,
                     GridBagConstraints.WEST, GridBagConstraints.HORIZONTAL);
        addComponent(cp, new JLabel("Password:"),  1, 0, 1, 1,
                     GridBagConstraints.WEST, GridBagConstraints.NONE);
        addComponent(cp, new JPasswordField(15),   1, 1, 1, 1,
                     GridBagConstraints.WEST, GridBagConstraints.HORIZONTAL);
        addComponent(cp, new JCheckBox("Remember me"), 2, 0, 2, 1,
                     GridBagConstraints.WEST, GridBagConstraints.NONE);
        addComponent(cp, new JButton("Login"),     3, 1, 1, 1,
                     GridBagConstraints.EAST, GridBagConstraints.NONE);

        setVisible(true);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SwingUtilities.invokeLater(GridBagLayoutDemo::new);
    }
}
```

**Step-by-step reasoning:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\texttt{gridx}, \texttt{gridy} \;&\Rightarrow\; \text{cell coordinates (top-left = 0,0)} \\
\texttt{gridwidth}, \texttt{gridheight} \;&\Rightarrow\; \text{how many cells this component spans} \\
\texttt{fill} \;&\Rightarrow\; \text{NONE, HORIZONTAL, VERTICAL, BOTH} \\
\texttt{anchor} \;&\Rightarrow\; \text{CENTER, NORTH, NORTHWEST, etc.} \\
\texttt{weightx}, \texttt{weighty} \;&\Rightarrow\; \text{how extra space is distributed (0 = don't grow)} \\
\texttt{insets} \;&\Rightarrow\; \text{per-component padding in pixels}
\end{aligned}
$$

> [!WARNING]
> **High-loss-of-marks area:** Students often set `fill = BOTH` on a `JLabel` — the label then stretches to fill the entire cell, and text appears in the top-left corner with vast empty space. The KTU correct answer: use `fill = NONE` with an appropriate `anchor`.

## 3.5 Example 5 — `CardLayout` (Tab-like Wizard)

**Step 1 — Conceptual goal:** A 3-step registration wizard with "Next" and "Previous" buttons.

**Step 2 — Java code with annotation:**

```java
import javax.swing.*;
import java.awt.*;
import java.awt.event.*;

public class CardLayoutDemo extends JFrame {
    private CardLayout cards = new CardLayout();
    private JPanel cardPanel = new JPanel(cards);

    public CardLayoutDemo() {
        setTitle("CardLayout Demo — Wizard");
        setSize(400, 250);
        setDefaultCloseOperation(JFrame.EXIT_ON_CLOSE);

        // Step 3: Build the three "cards"
        JPanel p1 = new JPanel(); p1.add(new JLabel("Step 1: Name"));   p1.add(new JTextField(12));
        JPanel p2 = new JPanel(); p2.add(new JLabel("Step 2: Email"));  p2.add(new JTextField(12));
        JPanel p3 = new JPanel(); p3.add(new JLabel("Step 3: Submit"));

        // Step 4: Register each card with a string name
        cardPanel.add(p1, "step1");
        cardPanel.add(p2, "step2");
        cardPanel.add(p3, "step3");

        // Step 5: Navigation buttons
        JButton prev = new JButton("< Prev");
        JButton next = new JButton("Next >");
        prev.addActionListener(e -> cards.previous(cardPanel));
        next.addActionListener(e -> cards.next(cardPanel));

        JPanel nav = new JPanel();
        nav.add(prev);  nav.add(next);

        // Step 6: Outer layout — BorderLayout so cards fill the center
        setLayout(new BorderLayout());
        add(cardPanel, BorderLayout.CENTER);
        add(nav,      BorderLayout.SOUTH);

        cards.show(cardPanel, "step1");
        setVisible(true);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SwingUtilities.invokeLater(CardLayoutDemo::new);
    }
}
```

**Step-by-step reasoning:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{All "cards" are added to the SAME container} \;&\Rightarrow\; \text{but only one is visible at a time} \\
\texttt{cards.next(container)} \;&\Rightarrow\; \text{advance to the next registered card} \\
\texttt{cards.previous(container)} \;&\Rightarrow\; \text{go back one} \\
\texttt{cards.show(container, "name")} \;&\Rightarrow\; \text{jump directly to a named card} \\
\text{Use case} \;&\Rightarrow\; \text{wizards, tabbed views without a } \texttt{JTabbedPane}
\end{aligned}
$$

---

## 3.6 Analytical Comparison Matrix — "What happens when I resize the window?"

| Layout Manager | Resize Behaviour | Honours Preferred Size? | Best For |
|----------------|------------------|-------------------------|----------|
| `FlowLayout` | Components wrap to next row/column | ✅ Yes | Toolbars, button bars |
| `BorderLayout` | NORTH/SOUTH stay at preferred height; CENTER stretches | ⚠️ Partially | Main app windows |
| `GridLayout` | All cells resize equally; preferred size ignored | ❌ No | Calculator pads |
| `BoxLayout` | Components keep preferred size; glue/filler absorbs extra | ✅ Yes | Vertical/horizontal stacks |
| `GridBagLayout` | Components grow proportionally based on `weightx`/`weighty` | ⚠️ Configurable | Complex forms |
| `CardLayout` | All cards fill the entire container | ❌ No | Wizards |
| `null` (no manager) | **Nothing** — components freeze at `setBounds()` | N/A | Never (anti-pattern) |
