## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

#### **Q1. [KTU University Exam – May 2023]**
**List the different types of buttons supported by Java Swing. Mention the root class of the Swing button hierarchy.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

Java Swing supports the following types of buttons:

1. **JButton** – A standard push button that triggers a command.
2. **JToggleButton** – A two-state push button that stays pressed/released.
3. **JCheckBox** – An independently selectable toggle for multi-selection.
4. **JRadioButton** – A mutually exclusive toggle that requires grouping via `ButtonGroup`.
5. **JMenuItem** – A button placed inside a menu.
6. **JCheckBoxMenuItem** – A checkbox-style menu item.
7. **JRadioButtonMenuItem** – A radio-button-style menu item.

The **root class** of the Swing button hierarchy is **`javax.swing.AbstractButton`**, which is a direct subclass of `javax.swing.JComponent`. (1 mark for listing 4+ types, 1 mark for hierarchy, 1 mark for naming `AbstractButton`.)

---

#### **Q2. [KTU University Exam – Dec 2022]**
**Explain the difference between `ActionEvent` and `ItemEvent` in Swing buttons. Give one example use case for each.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

| Aspect | `ActionEvent` | `ItemEvent` |
|--------|---------------|-------------|
| **Trigger** | Button is **clicked / activated** | Button's **selection state changes** |
| **Listener** | `ActionListener` (method: `actionPerformed`) | `ItemListener` (method: `itemStateChanged`) |
| **Applicable To** | All buttons | Only **toggleable** buttons |
| **Information Carried** | Action command, modifiers | `StateChange` (SELECTED / DESELECTED) |

- **Example for `ActionEvent`:** Clicking a `JButton` labeled *"Save"* should save the document — we use `ActionListener`.
- **Example for `ItemEvent`:** Selecting a `JCheckBox` labeled *"Receive newsletter"* — we use `ItemListener` to detect when the box becomes checked/unchecked. (1 mark each for definitions, 1 mark for examples.)

---

### 5.2 Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each)

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Pitfall:** In 14-mark questions, students often:
> - Forget the `import javax.swing.*;` line → loses **0.5 mark** for compile error.
> - Use `addActionListener` on a `JRadioButton` and never respond to state change → **logic wrong, up to 3 marks lost**.
> - Forget to call `setDefaultCloseOperation(EXIT_ON_CLOSE)` → **runtime issue, 1 mark lost** for the GUI not closing cleanly.
> - Don't group radio buttons in a `ButtonGroup` → **mutual exclusion fails, 2–3 marks lost**.

---

#### **Question A (14 Marks)** — *[KTU University Exam – May 2024 Model]*

**(a)** Explain the Swing button hierarchy starting from `AbstractButton`. List the major subclasses with one-line descriptions. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** Write a complete Java Swing program that creates a `JFrame` containing:
- A `JCheckBox` for *"Send weekly report"*.
- Two `JRadioButton`s — *"Hindi"* and *"English"* — grouped in a `ButtonGroup` for language selection.
- A `JButton` labeled *"Submit"*.

Implement appropriate listeners so that clicking *Submit* displays a `JOptionPane` summarising the user's current selections (whether the checkbox is checked and which radio is selected). **(7 marks)**

---

**Model Solution:**

**(a) Hierarchy Explanation (7 marks):**

The root of all Swing buttons is **`javax.swing.AbstractButton`**, which inherits from `javax.swing.JComponent`. It provides common properties and behaviour: text, icon, mnemonic, tooltip, enabled/selected state, and listener-registration methods (`addActionListener`, `addItemListener`, `addChangeListener`). The hierarchy is:

- **`JButton`** — A standard command push button. Performs an action when clicked; does not retain state. (1 mark)
- **`JToggleButton`** — A two-state push button that retains its pressed/released state. Fires both `ActionEvent` and `ItemEvent`. (1 mark)
- **`JCheckBox`** — Extends `JToggleButton`; used for independent on/off choices (e.g., preferences). (1 mark)
- **`JRadioButton`** — Extends `JToggleButton`; used in a `ButtonGroup` for mutually exclusive choices. (1 mark)
- **`JMenuItem`** — A button that lives inside a `JMenu`; fires `ActionEvent`. (1 mark)
- **`JCheckBoxMenuItem`** — A checkbox inside a menu; fires `ItemEvent`. (1 mark)
- **`JRadioButtonMenuItem`** — A radio button inside a menu; requires `ButtonGroup`. (1 mark)

---

**(b) Complete Java Program (7 marks):**

```java
import javax.swing.*;
import java.awt.*;
import java.awt.event.*;

public class SubmitForm extends JFrame implements ActionListener {
    JCheckBox reportCbx;
    JRadioButton hindiR, englishR;
    JButton submitBtn;

    public SubmitForm() {
        setTitle("User Form");
        setSize(350, 200);
        setDefaultCloseOperation(JFrame.EXIT_ON_CLOSE);
        setLayout(new FlowLayout());

        // ---- Checkbox ----
        reportCbx = new JCheckBox("Send weekly report");
        add(reportCbx);

        // ---- Radio Buttons ----
        hindiR   = new JRadioButton("Hindi");
        englishR = new JRadioButton("English");
        ButtonGroup langGroup = new ButtonGroup();
        langGroup.add(hindiR);
        langGroup.add(englishR);
        add(hindiR);
        add(englishR);

        // ---- Submit Button ----
        submitBtn = new JButton("Submit");
        submitBtn.addActionListener(this);
        add(submitBtn);

        setVisible(true);
    }

    public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
        String lang;
        if (hindiR.isSelected())      lang = "Hindi";
        else if (englishR.isSelected()) lang = "English";
        else                            lang = "(none selected)";

        String message = "Weekly Report: " + (reportCbx.isSelected() ? "Yes" : "No")
                       + "\nLanguage: " + lang;
        JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(this, message);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new SubmitForm();
    }
}
```

**Mark-Wise Breakdown:**

| Component | Marks |
|-----------|-------|
| Correct imports + class extending `JFrame` | 1 |
| Proper instantiation of `JCheckBox` | 0.5 |
| `JRadioButton` creation with `ButtonGroup` | 1.5 |
| `JButton` with `ActionListener` registration | 1 |
| Correct `actionPerformed` logic with `isSelected()` checks | 2 |
| `JOptionPane` summary message | 1 |
| **Total** | **7** |

---

#### **Question B (14 Marks)** — Alternative Choice

**(a)** Explain the role of the `ButtonGroup` class in Swing. What happens if multiple `JRadioButton`s are created without grouping? **(7 marks)**

**(b)** Write a Java Swing program to construct a `JMenuBar` with a *File* menu containing *New*, *Open*, and *Exit* items, and a *View* submenu containing a `JCheckBoxMenuItem` for *"Show Toolbar"* and two `JRadioButtonMenuItem`s — *"List View"* and *"Grid View"* — grouped appropriately. Use `ActionListener` and `ItemListener` where applicable. **(7 marks)**

---

**Model Solution:**

**(a) Role of `ButtonGroup` (7 marks):**

`javax.swing.ButtonGroup` is a logical container that enforces **mutual exclusion** among a set of `AbstractButton`s (typically `JRadioButton`s and `JRadioButtonMenuItem`s). It is **not a visual container** — components are still laid out by the parent container; `ButtonGroup` only controls their selection state.

**Key Properties:**

- At most **one** button in the group can be selected at any time. Selecting a new button automatically deselects the previously selected one. (2 marks)
- It is essential for `JRadioButton`s because, by default, Swing treats every `JRadioButton` as an **independent toggle**, identical to a `JCheckBox`. (2 marks)
- `ButtonGroup` does not appear on the screen; it does not extend `Container`. Buttons must be added to both a `ButtonGroup` and a visible container (e.g., `JPanel`, `JMenu`). (1 mark)
- Calling `group.setSelected(ButtonModel m)` programmatically selects a specific button. (1 mark)
- Methods: `add(AbstractButton)`, `remove(AbstractButton)`, `getElements()`, `getSelection()`. (1 mark)

---

**(b) Menu Bar Program (7 marks):**

```java
import javax.swing.*;
import java.awt.event.*;

public class MenuDemo extends JFrame {

    public MenuDemo() {
        setTitle("Menu Demo");
        setSize(400, 300);
        setDefaultCloseOperation(JFrame.EXIT_ON_CLOSE);

        JMenuBar menuBar = new JMenuBar();

        // ---- File Menu ----
        JMenu fileMenu = new JMenu("File");
        fileMenu.setMnemonic(KeyEvent.VK_F);

        JMenuItem newItem   = new JMenuItem("New");
        JMenuItem openItem  = new JMenuItem("Open");
        JMenuItem exitItem  = new JMenuItem("Exit");
        exitItem.addActionListener(e -> System.exit(0));

        fileMenu.add(newItem);
        fileMenu.add(openItem);
        fileMenu.addSeparator();
        fileMenu.add(exitItem);

        // ---- View Submenu ----
        JMenu viewMenu = new JMenu("View");

        JCheckBoxMenuItem toolbarItem = new JCheckBoxMenuItem("Show Toolbar");
        toolbarItem.addItemListener(e ->
            System.out.println("Toolbar = " +
                    (e.getStateChange() == ItemEvent.SELECTED))
        );

        JRadioButtonMenuItem listView  = new JRadioButtonMenuItem("List View", true);
        JRadioButtonMenuItem gridView  = new JRadioButtonMenuItem("Grid View");

        ButtonGroup viewGroup = new ButtonGroup();
        viewGroup.add(listView);
        viewGroup.add(gridView);

        listView.addItemListener(e -> {
            if (listView.isSelected()) System.out.println("List View selected");
        });
        gridView.addItemListener(e -> {
            if (gridView.isSelected()) System.out.println("Grid View selected");
        });

        viewMenu.add(toolbarItem);
        viewMenu.addSeparator();
        viewMenu.add(listView);
        viewMenu.add(gridView);

        fileMenu.add(viewMenu);   // attach submenu to File
        menuBar.add(fileMenu);
        setJMenuBar(menuBar);

        setVisible(true);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new MenuDemo();
    }
}
```

**Mark-Wise Breakdown:**

| Component | Marks |
|-----------|-------|
| `JMenuBar` + `setJMenuBar` | 1 |
| File menu with three `JMenuItem`s + Exit listener | 2 |
| View submenu correctly added to File | 1 |
| `JCheckBoxMenuItem` with `ItemListener` | 1 |
| `JRadioButtonMenuItem`s grouped in `ButtonGroup` | 1 |
| Listeners wired correctly | 1 |
| **Total** | **7** |

---

### 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

- **Root of all Swing buttons:** `javax.swing.AbstractButton` (extends `JComponent`). *(High-frequency theory question.)*
- **Hierarchy (must memorise):** `AbstractButton → {JButton, JToggleButton, JMenuItem}`; `JToggleButton → {JCheckBox, JRadioButton}`; `JMenuItem → {JCheckBoxMenuItem, JRadioButtonMenuItem}`.
- **Three listeners, three triggers:**
  - `ActionListener.actionPerformed` → fired on **click** of any button.
  - `ItemListener.itemStateChanged` → fired on **state change** of toggleable buttons.
  - `ChangeListener.stateChanged` → fired on low-level model change (rarely used in KTU).
- **`ButtonGroup` is mandatory** for `JRadioButton` and `JRadioButtonMenuItem` mutual exclusion — without it, they behave like checkboxes.
- **`JMenuItem` cannot be added to a `JFrame` directly**; it must be added to a `JMenu`, which is added to a `JMenuBar`, which is attached to a `JFrame` via `setJMenuBar()`.
- **Mnemonic shortcut:** `setMnemonic(KeyEvent.VK_X)` binds **Alt+X** to a button/menu.
- **Action command:** `setActionCommand("SAVE")` + `e.getActionCommand()` lets one listener handle multiple buttons.
- **Pre-selection:** `JToggleButton`, `JCheckBox`, `JRadioButton`, and `JMenuItem` variants all have a constructor that accepts a `boolean selected` argument.
- **Common pitfalls:** Forgetting to call `setDefaultCloseOperation(EXIT_ON_CLOSE)`, not importing `java.awt.event.*`, forgetting `setVisible(true)`, adding `JMenuItem` to a `JFrame` directly.
- **Engineering relevance:** Swing buttons are the foundation of every HMI/SCADA-style desktop app in industrial automation labs — be ready to answer *"Where would you use a `JToggleButton` vs a `JCheckBox` in an engineering application?"*

> [!WARNING]
> **Last-Mark KTU Trap:** In 14-mark coding questions, an examiner will check `import` statements, class declaration, listener interface implementation (or lambda), `ButtonGroup` usage (for radio buttons), and a working `JOptionPane`/`System.out.println` output. **Never skip these — they account for 30–40% of the marks.**

# 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Delegation Event Model (KTU 2024 Syllabus Definition):**
> The **Delegation Event Model** is the event-handling mechanism used in Java's AWT (Abstract Window Toolkit) and Swing frameworks, in which an **Event Source** delegates the responsibility of handling an event to a separate object called an **Event Listener** (or Event Handler). The source object generates the event and "delegates" (passes on) the event object to the registered listener, which contains the actual event-handling logic.

## 1.1 The Four Pillars of the Delegation Event Model

| Pillar | Role | Analogy |
|--------|------|---------|
| **Event** | A state change or user action (click, keypress, mouse move) | A fire alarm ringing |
| **Event Source** | The GUI component that generates the event (Button, TextField) | The smoke detector that sensed fire |
| **Event Listener / Handler** | The object that receives and processes the event | The fire brigade that responds |
| **Event Object** | Encapsulates details of the event (coordinates, modifiers, etc.) | The incident report handed to the brigade |

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy: The Newspaper Subscription Model

> [!NOTE]
> **Intuitive Analogy — "Newspaper Delivery":**
> Imagine a newspaper company (the **Event Source**) that has thousands of customers. Instead of the company personally finding out which customer wants a paper and delivering it manually, the company maintains a **subscription register (the listener list)**. Whenever the newspaper is printed (an **Event** occurs), the company simply looks at its register and **delegates** the delivery job to all subscribed customers (the **Event Listeners**). The customer (listener) decides what to do with the paper — read it, ignore it, or pass it on. The key insight: **the source does NOT know what the listener will do; it just hands over the responsibility.**

### 1.3 Why "Delegation"?

The word **"delegation"** is critical in KTU exams. The source component **does not handle the event itself**. It delegates (transfers) this responsibility to a registered listener object. This produces a clean **separation of concerns** — GUI design (front-end) is decoupled from event logic (back-end behavior).

### 1.4 Hierarchy of Key Java AWT Event Classes

> [!IMPORTANT]
> All event classes in Java inherit from `java.util.EventObject` (root), and AWT-specific events inherit from `java.awt.AWTEvent`.

$$
\text{java.util.EventObject} \rightarrow \text{java.awt.AWTEvent} \rightarrow \text{Specific Event Classes (ActionEvent, MouseEvent, ...)}
$$

### 1.5 Standard KTU Keywords to Memorize

- **Event Source** — the generator (e.g., a `JButton`)
- **Event Listener** — the receiver (an object implementing `ActionListener`)
- **Event Object** — the data carrier (e.g., `ActionEvent ae`)
- **Registration** — `source.addActionListener(listenerObj);`
- **Unregistration** — `source.removeActionListener(listenerObj);`
- **Multicasting** — one source can register *multiple* listeners for the same event.

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->

# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Operational Flow — Step-by-Step Breakdown

1. **User Interaction:** The user performs an action (e.g., clicks a button).
2. **Event Generation:** The JVM detects the action and the **Event Source** (the button) constructs an **Event Object** containing contextual data (e.g., source, timestamp, modifiers).
3. **Listener Invocation:** The source iterates through its internal `listenerList` (a `Vector`) and invokes the appropriate callback method (`actionPerformed`, `mouseClicked`, etc.) on each registered listener.
4. **Event Handling:** The listener's callback method executes the business logic.
5. **Return:** Control returns to the JVM event-dispatch thread (EDT).

## 2.2 The Two Phase Logic — *Why* It Works

| Phase | Why It Matters |
|-------|----------------|
| **Registration Phase** | Decouples source from handler. A button has *no* event-handling code of its own. |
| **Notification Phase** | The source doesn't decide *what* to do — it just *notifies* interested parties. |

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU Insight:** This is the textbook definition of the **Observer Design Pattern** in OOP. The Delegation Event Model is a direct Java AWT implementation of the GoF Observer Pattern. A high-yield answer to write in exams: *"Delegation Event Model follows the Observer design pattern, where the event source acts as the Subject and listeners act as Observers."*

## 2.3 KTU Formula / Methods Cheat Sheet

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Event Registration Syntax (Universal Formula):**
> $$ \texttt{eventSource.addXxxListener(eventListenerObject);} $$
> Where `Xxx` is replaced by the specific event type (e.g., `addActionListener`, `addMouseListener`).

### 2.3.1 Core Listener Interfaces and Their Callback Methods

| Listener Interface | Event Type | Key Callback Methods (from `java.awt.event`) |
|--------------------|------------|------------------------------------------------|
| `ActionListener` | ActionEvent | `actionPerformed(ActionEvent e)` |
| `MouseListener` | MouseEvent | `mouseClicked`, `mousePressed`, `mouseReleased`, `mouseEntered`, `mouseExited` |
| `MouseMotionListener` | MouseEvent | `mouseDragged`, `mouseMoved` |
| `KeyListener` | KeyEvent | `keyTyped`, `keyPressed`, `keyReleased` |
| `FocusListener` | FocusEvent | `focusGained`, `focusLost` |
| `WindowListener` | WindowEvent | `windowOpened`, `windowClosing`, `windowClosed`, `windowIconified`, `windowDeiconified`, `windowActivated`, `windowDeactivated` |
| `ItemListener` | ItemEvent | `itemStateChanged(ItemEvent e)` |
| `TextListener` | TextEvent | `textValueChanged(TextEvent e)` |
| `AdjustmentListener` | AdjustmentEvent | `adjustmentValueChanged` |
| `ComponentListener` | ComponentEvent | `componentResized`, `componentMoved`, `componentShown`, `componentHidden` |
| `ContainerListener` | ContainerEvent | `componentAdded`, `componentRemoved` |

### 2.3.2 Event Object Common Methods

| Method | Returns | Purpose |
|--------|---------|---------|
| `getSource()` | `Object` | Returns the source component |
| `getID()` | `int` | Returns the event type ID |
| `getWhen()` | `long` | Returns event timestamp |
| `getModifiers()` | `int` | Returns modifier keys held (Shift, Ctrl) |
| `getKeyChar()` / `getKeyCode()` | `char` / `int` | For KeyEvent |
| `getPoint()` / `getX()` / `getY()` | `Point` / `int` | For MouseEvent |

### 2.3.3 Adapter Classes — The "Shortcuts"

> [!NOTE]
> **Why Adapters Exist:** Listener interfaces often contain many abstract methods. To avoid implementing *all* of them just to handle *one*, Java provides **Adapter classes** (e.g., `MouseAdapter`, `KeyAdapter`, `WindowAdapter`) which provide empty default implementations. You subclass the adapter and override only what you need.

| Adapter Class | Implements | Useful For |
|---------------|------------|------------|
| `MouseAdapter` | `MouseListener`, `MouseMotionListener` | Handling only one mouse event |
| `KeyAdapter` | `KeyListener` | Capturing a specific key |
| `WindowAdapter` | `WindowListener`, `WindowStateListener`, `WindowFocusListener` | Closing a frame cleanly |
| `FocusAdapter` | `FocusListener` | Single focus event |
| `ComponentAdapter` | `ComponentListener` | Single component event |

### 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility

- **GUI Applications:** Every desktop Java application (Eclipse IDE, NetBeans) uses this model.
- **Embedded Systems:** Java ME for mobile phones uses AWT-derived event handling.
- **Cross-platform GUIs:** Swing and JavaFX still inherit this conceptual model.
- **Reactive Programming Foundation:** Modern frameworks (RxJava, Reactor) generalize this publish-subscribe idea.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->

# 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 The Complete Event Handling Workflow — Exhaustive Derivation

Below is the **end-to-end logical derivation** of how an event travels from a user action to handler execution. This is a high-frequency 14-mark question pattern in KTU exams.

### Step 1: Source Component Creation

A GUI component is instantiated, e.g., a `JButton`. Internally, AWT creates an `EventListenerList` (a thread-safe vector).

$$
\text{button = new JButton("Click Me");} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text{listenerList} = \emptyset
$$

### Step 2: Listener Class Declaration

A class is declared that **implements** the appropriate listener interface.

$$
\text{class MyHandler implements ActionListener} \;\{\; \text{...} \;\}
$$

### Step 3: Listener Object Instantiation

An instance of the handler is created.

$$
\text{ActionListener handler = new MyHandler();}
$$

### Step 4: Event Source Registration (The "Delegation" Step)

The listener is registered with the source via the `addXxxListener` method. Internally, the source appends the listener object to its `listenerList`.

$$
\text{button.addActionListener(handler);} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{listenerList} = \{ \text{handler} \}
$$

### Step 5: User Action Triggers Event

User clicks the button. The AWT event-dispatch thread detects this via the OS.

### Step 6: Event Object Construction

The source creates a new `ActionEvent` object with details like source, ID (`ACTION_PERFORMED = 1001`), timestamp, and modifier keys.

$$
\text{ActionEvent ae = new ActionEvent(button, ACTION\_PERFORMED, "Click Me");}
$$

### Step 7: Delegation / Notification

The source iterates over `listenerList` and invokes `actionPerformed(ae)` on each listener.

$$
\forall \; L \in \text{listenerList}: \quad L.\texttt{actionPerformed}(ae)
$$

### Step 8: Handler Executes Logic

Inside the listener's `actionPerformed` method, the developer-written code runs (e.g., display a message, update a label).

### Step 9: Return to Event Dispatch Thread

After all listeners are notified, control returns to the EDT, and the UI redraws if needed.

## 3.2 Worked Java Code Model (For CS Students)

> [!NOTE]
> This is the canonical KTU-style Java program illustrating the Delegation Event Model. **Not** a Python or algorithm-style block — this is legitimate Java for the OOP course.

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\texttt{import java.awt.*;} \\
&\texttt{import java.awt.event.*;} \\
&\texttt{class MyFrame extends Frame implements ActionListener \{ } \\
&\quad \texttt{Label l; Button b;} \\
&\quad \texttt{MyFrame() \{ } \\
&\quad\quad \texttt{l = new Label("Hello"); b = new Button("Click");} \\
&\quad\quad \texttt{b.addActionListener(this); \quad // <-- REGISTRATION} \\
&\quad\quad \texttt{add(l); add(b); setSize(300,200); setVisible(true);} \\
&\quad \texttt{\}} \\
&\quad \texttt{public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) \{ } \\
&\quad\quad \texttt{l.setText("Button Clicked! Event Source: " + e.getSource());} \\
&\quad \texttt{\}} \\
&\texttt{\}}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 3.3 Analytical Matrix: Source → Listener → Method Mapping

| User Action | Source Component | Event Class | Listener Interface | Callback Method | Adapter Class |
|-------------|------------------|-------------|---------------------|------------------|----------------|
| Click button | `JButton`, `Button` | `ActionEvent` | `ActionListener` | `actionPerformed` | — |
| Mouse hover | Any `Component` | `MouseEvent` | `MouseListener` | `mouseEntered` | `MouseAdapter` |
| Drag mouse | Any `Component` | `MouseEvent` | `MouseMotionListener` | `mouseDragged` | `MouseAdapter` |
| Press key | Component with focus | `KeyEvent` | `KeyListener` | `keyPressed` | `KeyAdapter` |
| Close window | `Frame`, `JFrame` | `WindowEvent` | `WindowListener` | `windowClosing` | `WindowAdapter` |
| Select item | `Checkbox`, `Choice` | `ItemEvent` | `ItemListener` | `itemStateChanged` | — |
| Gain/Lose focus | Any `Component` | `FocusEvent` | `FocusListener` | `focusGained` | `FocusAdapter` |
| Move/Resize comp. | Any `Component` | `ComponentEvent` | `ComponentListener` | `componentResized` | `ComponentAdapter` |

## 3.4 Key Logical Conclusions

1. **Decoupling:** The source and listener can be developed, compiled, and maintained independently.
2. **Broadcasting:** A single source can register multiple listeners (multicasting).
3. **Dynamic Binding:** Listeners can be added or removed at runtime.
4. **Reusability:** A single listener object can be registered to multiple sources.

$$
\text{Broadcast} = \{ \text{List}(L_1), L_2, \ldots, L_n \} \quad \text{where each } L_i \text{ is notified upon event}
$$

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Q1. [KTU University Exam — May 2024]
**Define the Delegation Event Model. List its key participants.**

**Model Answer:**

The Delegation Event Model is an event-handling approach in Java AWT/Swing where the responsibility of processing an event generated by a GUI component (the source) is **delegated** to one or more separate objects called **listeners**. The source does not handle the event itself; it merely notifies registered listeners by invoking their callback methods.

**Key Participants:**
1. **Event** — an action or state change (e.g., button click).
2. **Event Source** — the component that generates the event.
3. **Event Listener** — the object that handles the event via callback methods.
4. **Event Object** — encapsulates event data and is passed to listeners.

---

### Q2. [KTU University Exam — Dec 2023]
**What is the role of an Adapter class in Java AWT? Give an example.**

**Model Answer:**

An **Adapter class** in `java.awt.event` provides **default empty implementations** for all methods of a multi-method listener interface. This allows programmers to subclass the adapter and override **only the methods they need**, avoiding the burden of implementing every abstract method of the interface.

**Example:** `MouseAdapter` implements `MouseListener` and `MouseMotionListener` with empty bodies. If we want to handle only `mouseClicked`, we extend `MouseAdapter` and override only `mouseClicked(MouseEvent e)`. Similarly, `WindowAdapter`, `KeyAdapter`, and `FocusAdapter` exist for the same purpose.

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Pitfall — Part A:**
> Many students write *"Adapter is used to adapt events."* This is **wrong**. The correct phrasing is *"Adapter provides default (empty) implementations of a listener interface so that subclasses override only required methods."* Marks are lost for vague, imprecise language.

---

## 5.2 Part B — Full 14-Mark Questions (Internal Choice)

### ✅ Question A (Choice 1) — 14 Marks

**[KTU University Exam — Model Question, Module 4]**

**(a)** Explain the **Delegation Event Model** in detail with a neat block diagram. Discuss the role of **Event Source**, **Event Listener**, and **Event Object** with examples. *(7 marks)*

**(b)** Write a complete Java AWT program to create a frame containing a `TextField` and a `Button`. When the button is clicked, the text entered in the text field should be displayed in a `Label`. Use the Delegation Event Model. *(7 marks)*

#### Model Solution to Q-A(a):

The **Delegation Event Model** is the event-handling mechanism defined in `java.awt.event` package. In this model:

- **Event Source** is the GUI component (e.g., `Button`, `TextField`) that detects a user action and creates an **Event Object**.
- The source maintains a list of registered listeners in a thread-safe `EventListenerList`.
- **Event Listener** is an object that implements a listener interface (e.g., `ActionListener`) and contains the event-handling logic in a callback method (e.g., `actionPerformed`).
- The source **delegates** event processing by invoking the listener's callback method, passing the event object as an argument.
- This model follows the **Observer design pattern** and provides **decoupling** between UI components and business logic.

**Example:** A `Button` is the event source. A class `MyHandler` implements `ActionListener`. Registration: `button.addActionListener(handler)`. On click, the button creates an `ActionEvent` and calls `handler.actionPerformed(ae)`.

*(Include the block diagram from Section 4.1 of these notes.)*

#### Model Solution to Q-A(b):

```java
import java.awt.*;
import java.awt.event.*;

class DelegationDemo extends Frame implements ActionListener {
    Label l;
    TextField tf;
    Button b;

    DelegationDemo() {
        l = new Label("Result appears here");
        tf = new TextField(20);
        b = new Button("Show Text");

        // Registration — the core of Delegation Event Model
        b.addActionListener(this);

        setLayout(new FlowLayout());
        add(tf);
        add(b);
        add(l);

        setSize(350, 200);
        setTitle("Delegation Event Model Demo");
        setVisible(true);
    }

    // Callback method — invoked when the button is clicked
    public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
        l.setText("You typed: " + tf.getText());
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new DelegationDemo();
    }
}
```

**Explanation of Key Lines:**
- `implements ActionListener` — declares that this class will handle `ActionEvent`s.
- `b.addActionListener(this);` — registers the current frame as a listener for the button's action events. **This is the registration step.**
- `actionPerformed(ActionEvent e)` — the callback method automatically called by AWT when the button is clicked.
- `e.getSource()` could be used to identify the source if multiple sources were registered.

---

### ✅ Question B (Choice 2) — 14 Marks

**[KTU University Exam — Model Question, Module 4]**

**(a)** Differentiate between **Event Listeners** and **Adapter Classes** in Java AWT. Explain with a suitable example how `WindowAdapter` can be used to handle window-closing events. *(7 marks)*

**(b)** Explain **Event Classes** in `java.awt.event` package. List any **five event classes** along with their corresponding listener interfaces and the methods they trigger. *(7 marks)*

#### Model Solution to Q-B(a):

| Aspect | Event Listener Interface | Adapter Class |
|--------|--------------------------|---------------|
| **Nature** | Abstract interface with all methods abstract | Concrete class with empty method bodies |
| **Implementation** | Must implement *all* methods | Override *only* required methods |
| **Usage** | `class H implements MouseListener` | `class H extends MouseAdapter` |
| **Example Interfaces** | `MouseListener`, `KeyListener`, `WindowListener` | `MouseAdapter`, `KeyAdapter`, `WindowAdapter` |
| **Purpose** | Define the contract | Provide convenience default implementations |

**Example using `WindowAdapter`:**

```java
import java.awt.*;
import java.awt.event.*;

class CloseDemo extends Frame {
    CloseDemo() {
        setSize(300, 300);
        setTitle("WindowAdapter Demo");
        setVisible(true);

        // Register a WindowAdapter (anonymous inner class)
        addWindowListener(new WindowAdapter() {
            public void windowClosing(WindowEvent e) {
                System.exit(0);  // Close the application
            }
        });
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new CloseDemo();
    }
}
```

Here, instead of implementing all 7 methods of `WindowListener`, we extend `WindowAdapter` and override only `windowClosing`. This is the primary benefit of adapters.

#### Model Solution to Q-B(b):

Event classes in `java.awt.event` represent various user interactions. They all extend `java.awt.AWTEvent`, which in turn extends `java.util.EventObject`.

| # | Event Class | Triggered By | Listener Interface | Callback Method(s) |
|---|--------------|---------------|--------------------|----------------------|
| 1 | `ActionEvent` | Clicking a button, selecting a menu item, pressing Enter in a text field | `ActionListener` | `actionPerformed(ActionEvent e)` |
| 2 | `MouseEvent` | Mouse click, press, release, enter, exit | `MouseListener` | `mouseClicked`, `mousePressed`, `mouseReleased`, `mouseEntered`, `mouseExited` |
| 3 | `KeyEvent` | Pressing, releasing, or typing a key | `KeyListener` | `keyPressed`, `keyReleased`, `keyTyped` |
| 4 | `WindowEvent` | Opening, closing, iconifying, activating a window | `WindowListener` | `windowOpened`, `windowClosing`, `windowClosed`, `windowIconified`, etc. |
| 5 | `ItemEvent` | Selecting/deselecting an item in a `Checkbox` or `Choice` | `ItemListener` | `itemStateChanged(ItemEvent e)` |

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Part B:**
> 1. **Forgetting `setVisible(true)`** in AWT programs — your program will compile but show nothing. Examiners deduct 1 mark.
> 2. **Confusing `ActionListener` with `ActionEvent`** — these are different. The **event** is the data object; the **listener** is the handler interface. Mixing them up loses 2 marks.
> 3. **Forgetting to register the listener** (`addActionListener(...)`) is the most common error. The button does nothing because the source has no one to delegate to.
> 4. **Implementing the interface but not overriding the callback method** causes a compile error or a silent no-op (if an empty body is given). Examiners look specifically for the `actionPerformed` body.

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Rapid Revision Checklist — Delegation Event Model**

- **Definition:** A model where the event **source delegates** event-handling to a registered **listener** object.
- **Four Key Components:** Event, Event Source, Event Listener, Event Object.
- **Root Class:** `java.util.EventObject` → `java.awt.AWTEvent` → Specific events.
- **Registration Formula:** `source.addXxxListener(listenerObj);`
- **Multicasting:** One source can have **multiple listeners**; one listener can be registered to **multiple sources**.
- **Observer Pattern:** Delegation Event Model **is** the Observer design pattern in Java.
- **Adapter Classes:** Provide empty default implementations; subclass to override only what you need.
- **Callback Method Names:** Always start with the event name (e.g., `actionPerformed`, `mouseClicked`, `keyPressed`).
- **Event Object Key Methods:** `getSource()`, `getID()`, `getWhen()`, `getModifiers()`.
- **Common Pitfalls to Avoid:**
  - Forgetting `addXxxListener` registration.
  - Confusing adapter classes with listener interfaces.
  - Forgetting to set layout/visibility in AWT programs.
  - Not overriding the correct callback method.
- **Exam Tip:** Always draw the **flow diagram** (User → Source → ListenerList → Listener → Callback) for full marks in 7-mark theory questions.
- **Packages to Remember:** `java.awt`, `java.awt.event`, `javax.swing`, `javax.swing.event`.
- **Single-line Definition (for 1-mark MCQs):** *"In the Delegation Event Model, the source component generates an event and delegates its handling to one or more registered listener objects via callback methods."*

# 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

In the context of **Object Oriented Programming (Java)** as prescribed by the **KTU 2024 Scheme**, an **Event Class** is a specialized class that encapsulates the state and behavior of an occurrence (an *event*) happening within a graphical user interface (GUI) component. Under the **Delegation Event Model (DEM)**, every user interaction (such as a mouse click, key press, window closing, or button activation) is represented as an **object** instantiated from a predefined event class residing primarily in the `java.awt.event` and `javax.swing.event` packages.

The root of all Java event classes is `java.util.EventObject`, which is extended by `java.awt.AWTEvent`. From `AWTEvent`, the JDK derives a precise hierarchy of **Semantic Events** (e.g., `ActionEvent`, `ItemEvent`, `TextEvent`) and **Low-Level Events** (e.g., `KeyEvent`, `MouseEvent`, `WindowEvent`, `FocusEvent`, `ComponentEvent`, `ContainerEvent`).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Syllabus Highlight:** Event Classes are a core Module 4 topic. You must know the class hierarchy, the package names (`java.awt.event`), and the purpose of each event class. The examiner expects you to map a real-world GUI action (like "user typed 'A'") to the correct Event class object (`KeyEvent`).

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Intuition

Imagine a **modern smart home security system**:

- A **motion sensor** at the door *detects* something (the **Event Source** — e.g., a `JButton`).
- The sensor creates a **signal packet** containing the timestamp, sensor ID, and type of motion (the **Event Object** — e.g., an `ActionEvent`).
- This packet is handed off to the **security control room** (the **Event Listener / Handler**).
- The control room decides whether to ring an alarm, turn on lights, or call the police (the **Event Handler Method**).

In Java, the **sensor does not decide what to do**. It merely **creates and dispatches** an `Event` object. The handler receives the object and decides the response. The **Event Class** is the blueprint for that "signal packet."

> [!NOTE]
> **Key Vocabulary:**
> - **Event Source:** The object that *generates* the event (e.g., `JButton`, `JTextField`).
> - **Event Object:** The instance of an Event Class that *carries* the event details.
> - **Event Listener:** The interface implemented by the receiver of the event.
> - **Event Handler:** The method inside the listener that executes when the event occurs.

## 1.3 Fundamental Metrics

- **Package:** `java.awt.event` (primary), `javax.swing.event` (Swing-specific).
- **Root Class:** `java.util.EventObject` (since JDK 1.1).
- **Direct Subclass for AWT:** `java.awt.AWTEvent`.
- **Semantic vs. Low-Level:** Semantic events represent high-level actions (e.g., clicking a button); low-level events represent raw input (e.g., every pixel of mouse movement).

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 The Class Hierarchy — Why It Matters

Java organizes event classes into an inheritance hierarchy for three engineering reasons:

1. **Polymorphism:** A single method signature like `public void handle(AWTEvent e)` can accept *any* AWT event because of upcasting.
2. **Common API:** All events inherit the `getSource()` and `getID()` methods from `EventObject` and `AWTEvent`.
3. **Categorization:** Low-level events (`InputEvent`) provide raw detail, while semantic events (`ActionEvent`) provide user-friendly abstraction.

The inheritance tree is structured as:

$$
\text{java.util.EventObject} \xrightarrow{\text{extends}} \text{java.awt.AWTEvent} \xrightarrow{\text{extends}} \{ \text{Semantic and Low-Level Events} \}
$$

$$
\text{InputEvent} \xrightarrow{\text{extends}} \{ \text{KeyEvent}, \text{MouseEvent} \}
$$

$$
\text{ComponentEvent} \xrightarrow{\text{extends}} \{ \text{FocusEvent}, \text{WindowEvent} \} \quad \text{and} \quad \text{ContainerEvent extends ComponentEvent}
$$

## 2.2 Step-by-Step Operational Logic

**How an Event Object is Created and Dispatched:**

- **Step 1 — Detection:** The AWT/Swing component (e.g., `JButton`) detects user interaction via the underlying OS/JDK event queue.
- **Step 2 — Instantiation:** The component instantiates an `Event` subclass object, passing the source, ID, and event-specific data to its constructor.
- **Step 3 — Source Registration:** The component maintains a list of registered `EventListener` objects.
- **Step 4 — Dispatch:** The component invokes the appropriate listener method, passing the Event object as the argument.
- **Step 5 — Consumption:** The listener's handler method uses the Event object's getter methods (`getSource()`, `getKeyCode()`, `getX()`, etc.) to react.

## 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility

Event Classes are not academic fiction — they power every Java desktop application, Android UI callback, and JavaFX controller. They enable:

- **Decoupling:** The view (button) and the logic (handler) are completely independent.
- **Reusability:** One listener can be attached to multiple components.
- **GUI Testing:** Automated testing tools inspect Event objects without rendering UI.
- **Industrial Applications:** Banking software uses `FocusEvent` to validate field input; CAD software uses `MouseEvent` for drawing precision; embedded touchscreens use a derivative of `InputEvent`.

# 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Exhaustive Derivation of the Event Class Hierarchy

The Java event framework was designed top-down. We will derive each class, its purpose, and its key methods in academic detail.

---

### 3.1.1 Derivation of `EventObject` (Root Class)

**Purpose:** Provide a universal abstraction for *any* kind of event in any domain, not just AWT.

$$
\text{EventObject} : \text{java.lang.Object}
$$

$$
\text{Constructor: } \text{EventObject}(\text{Object source})
$$

$$
\text{Key Method: } \texttt{public Object getSource()} \rightarrow \text{returns the object on which the event initially occurred}
$$

The `getSource()` method is the single most important method in the entire hierarchy — it is the only way the listener knows *which* component fired the event when one listener handles many components.

---

### 3.1.2 Derivation of `AWTEvent`

$$
\text{AWTEvent} : \text{EventObject}
$$

$$
\text{Constructor: } \text{AWTEvent}(\text{Object source}, \text{int id})
$$

$$
\text{Key Method: } \texttt{public int getID()} \rightarrow \text{returns the event type identifier}
$$

The `id` field distinguishes event subtypes (e.g., `MOUSE_PRESSED` vs `MOUSE_RELEASED`). Each subclass defines a unique set of `static final int` constants for these IDs.

---

### 3.1.3 Derivation of `ActionEvent` (Semantic Event)

**Trigger Source:** `Button`, `MenuItem`, `JButton`, `JMenuItem`, `TextField` (when Enter is pressed).

$$
\text{ActionEvent} : \text{AWTEvent}
$$

$$
\text{Constructor: } \text{ActionEvent}(\text{Object src}, \text{int id}, \text{String command})
$$

$$
\text{Key Method: } \texttt{public String getActionCommand()} \rightarrow \text{returns the button label or command string}
$$

The `getActionCommand()` method is the standard mechanism for identifying which button was clicked when a single listener handles multiple buttons.

**Analytical Logic:**

$$
\text{listener.actionPerformed}(\text{ActionEvent e}) \rightarrow \text{String cmd} = \texttt{e.getActionCommand()}
$$

$$
\text{cmd.equals("Submit")} \Rightarrow \text{execute Submit logic}
$$

---

### 3.1.4 Derivation of `ItemEvent` (Semantic Event)

**Trigger Source:** `Checkbox`, `CheckboxMenuItem`, `Choice`, `List`.

$$
\text{ItemEvent} : \text{AWTEvent}
$$

$$
\text{Constructor: } \text{ItemEvent}(\text{ItemSelectable src}, \text{int id}, \text{Object item}, \text{int stateChange})
$$

$$
\text{Key Methods: } \texttt{getItem()}, \texttt{getStateChange()}
$$

$$
\text{State Change Constants: } \text{SELECTED} = 1, \quad \text{DESELECTED} = 2
$$

The `getItem()` returns the object that changed state (e.g., a `String` from a dropdown), while `getStateChange()` returns whether it was selected or deselected.

---

### 3.1.5 Derivation of `InputEvent` (Abstract Low-Level Event)

This is an **abstract class** — it cannot be instantiated directly. It is the parent of `KeyEvent` and `MouseEvent`.

$$
\text{InputEvent} : \text{AWTEvent}
$$

$$
\text{Key Methods: } \texttt{getModifiers()}, \texttt{getModifiersEx()}, \texttt{getWhen()}, \texttt{isConsumed()}
$$

The `getWhen()` method returns the timestamp of the event (useful for measuring user response time in UX research).

---

### 3.1.6 Derivation of `KeyEvent`

**Trigger Source:** Any focus-holding component when a keyboard key is involved.

$$
\text{KeyEvent} : \text{InputEvent}
$$

$$
\text{Constructor: } \text{KeyEvent}(\text{Component src}, \text{int id}, \text{long when}, \text{int modifiers}, \text{int keyCode}, \text{char keyChar})
$$

$$
\text{Key Methods: } \texttt{getKeyCode()}, \texttt{getKeyChar()}, \texttt{getKeyText(int)}
$$

**Three event types:**

$$
\text{id} = \texttt{KEY_PRESSED} \rightarrow \text{physical key pushed down}
$$

$$
\text{id} = \texttt{KEY_RELEASED} \rightarrow \text{physical key released}
$$

$$
\text{id} = \texttt{KEY_TYPED} \rightarrow \text{character actually entered (after modifier combination)}
$$

**Critical Distinction:** `getKeyCode()` returns the physical key (e.g., `VK_SHIFT = 16`), while `getKeyChar()` returns the resulting character (e.g., `'A'` after Shift is applied). This distinction is a **favourite KTU question**.

---

### 3.1.7 Derivation of `MouseEvent`

**Trigger Source:** Any component over which the mouse cursor interacts.

$$
\text{MouseEvent} : \text{InputEvent}
$$

$$
\text{Constructor: } \text{MouseEvent}(\text{Component src}, \text{int id}, \text{long when}, \text{int modifiers}, \text{int x}, \text{int y}, \text{int clickCount}, \text{boolean popupTrigger})
$$

$$
\text{Key Methods: } \texttt{getX()}, \texttt{getY()}, \texttt{getPoint()}, \texttt{getClickCount()}, \texttt{isPopupTrigger()}
$$

The `getClickCount()` returns whether it is a single, double, or triple click — essential for distinguishing double-click events.

---

### 3.1.8 Derivation of `WindowEvent`

**Trigger Source:** A `Window` or `Frame` or `JFrame`.

$$
\text{WindowEvent} : \text{ComponentEvent}
$$

$$
\text{Key Methods: } \texttt{getWindow()}, \texttt{getOppositeWindow()}
$$

$$
\text{Seven Event Types: } \{\text{WINDOW_OPENING, WINDOW_CLOSING, WINDOW_CLOSED, WINDOW_ICONIFIED, WINDOW_DEICONIFIED, WINDOW_ACTIVATED, WINDOW_DEACTIVATED}\}
$$

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Pitfall:** `WINDOW_CLOSING` fires *before* the window is closed (you can cancel it). `WINDOW_CLOSED` fires *after* it is gone. Do not confuse these in code.

---

### 3.1.9 Derivation of Remaining Event Classes

$$
\text{ComponentEvent} \rightarrow \text{generic component state change (moved, resized, shown, hidden)}
$$

$$
\text{ContainerEvent} \rightarrow \text{component added or removed from container}
$$

$$
\text{FocusEvent} \rightarrow \text{FOCUS_GAINED or FOCUS_LOST}
$$

$$
\text{AdjustmentEvent} \rightarrow \text{scrollbar or adjustable value changed}
$$

$$
\text{TextEvent} \rightarrow \text{text content changed}
$$

---

### Question 1
**`[KTU University Exam — Dec 2023]`**
**What is an Event Class in Java? Name the root class of all AWT event classes and state its package.**

**Model Answer (3 Marks):**
An Event Class in Java is a class that represents an occurrence of a user interaction (or system action) within a GUI. Each event is encapsulated as an object belonging to a predefined class, enabling the Delegation Event Model to function. The **root class of all AWT event classes is `java.awt.AWTEvent`**, which is located in the `java.awt` package. The ultimate superclass of *all* event classes (including non-AWT) is `java.util.EventObject`.

*Mark allocation: 1 for definition, 1 for root class name, 1 for package.*

### Question 2
**`[KTU University Exam — June 2024]`**
**Differentiate between Semantic Events and Low-Level Events in Java AWT with one example each.**

**Model Answer (3 Marks):**
**Semantic Events** are high-level events that represent a meaningful user action understood by the GUI component. Example: `ActionEvent` is fired when a button is clicked — this is a single semantic event regardless of how the click occurred (mouse, keyboard Enter, programmatic).

**Low-Level Events** are low-level events that represent the raw input directly from the input device. Example: `KeyEvent` and `MouseEvent` are low-level — every single pixel of mouse movement or every key press generates an event.

| Feature | Semantic | Low-Level |
|---------|----------|-----------|
| Abstraction Level | High | Low |
| Fired by | Component logic | OS / device |
| Examples | `ActionEvent`, `ItemEvent` | `KeyEvent`, `MouseEvent` |
| Listener | Component decides | Forwarded to listener |

*Mark allocation: 1.5 marks each for definition + example.*

### Model Answer for Question A (b) — 7 Marks

```java
import java.awt.*;
import java.awt.event.*;

public class TextDisplayDemo extends Frame implements ActionListener {
    TextField tf;
    Label resultLabel;

    public TextDisplayDemo() {
        setLayout(new FlowLayout());
        setTitle("Event Class Demo");
        setSize(400, 200);

        tf = new TextField(20);
        Button btn = new Button("Display");
        resultLabel = new Label("Type something and click Display.");

        add(tf);
        add(btn);
        add(resultLabel);

        // Event Source: btn -> Event Class: ActionEvent -> Listener: this
        btn.addActionListener(this);

        addWindowListener(new WindowAdapter() {
            public void windowClosing(WindowEvent e) {
                dispose();
            }
        });

        setVisible(true);
    }

    public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
        // e.getSource() returns the button (EventObject method)
        // e.getActionCommand() returns "Display" (ActionEvent method)
        String input = tf.getText();
        resultLabel.setText("You typed: " + input);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new TextDisplayDemo();
    }
}
```

**Explanation:**
- `btn` is the **Event Source**.
- When clicked, the JDK creates an `ActionEvent` object internally.
- `ActionListener` interface is implemented by the class — `actionPerformed` is the handler.
- Inside the handler, we use the Event object's methods to retrieve data and update the GUI.

*Mark allocation: 2 for GUI setup, 2 for listener registration, 2 for handler logic, 1 for explanation.*

```java
import java.awt.*;
import java.awt.event.*;

public class MouseBgColorDemo extends Frame implements MouseListener {

    public MouseBgColorDemo() {
        setTitle("Double-click to Change Color");
        setSize(400, 300);
        addMouseListener(this);  // Register listener on the Frame itself

        addWindowListener(new WindowAdapter() {
            public void windowClosing(WindowEvent e) {
                dispose();
            }
        });

        setVisible(true);
    }

    public void mouseClicked(MouseEvent e) {
        // The MouseEvent object e provides getClickCount()
        if (e.getClickCount() == 2) {
            // Generate a random color and apply
            int r = (int)(Math.random() * 256);
            int g = (int)(Math.random() * 256);
            int b = (int)(Math.random() * 256);
            setBackground(new Color(r, g, b));
            System.out.println("Background changed to: " + r + "," + g + "," + b);
        }
    }

    public void mousePressed(MouseEvent e) { }
    public void mouseReleased(MouseEvent e) { }
    public void mouseEntered(MouseEvent e) { }
    public void mouseExited(MouseEvent e) { }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new MouseBgColorDemo();
    }
}
```

**Explanation:**
- The `Frame` itself is the **Event Source**.
- The `Frame` implements `MouseListener` and registers itself with `addMouseListener(this)`.
- The `mouseClicked` handler receives a `MouseEvent` object.
- `e.getClickCount() == 2` detects a double-click.
- `setBackground()` updates the color using a randomly generated RGB triple.

## 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning

> [!WARNING]
> **Where KTU Students Commonly Lose Marks:**
>
> 1. **Confusing `getKeyCode()` and `getKeyChar()`** — `getKeyCode()` returns the physical key constant (`VK_A`); `getKeyChar()` returns the actual character produced (`'a'` or `'A'` depending on Shift). Examiners award 1 mark specifically for this distinction.
>
> 2. **Mixing up `WINDOW_CLOSING` and `WINDOW_CLOSED`** — Closing fires *before* disposal (you can veto it); Closed fires *after*. Mentioning this difference shows depth.
>
> 3. **Forgetting the `Event Source` registration** — In code, students often write the listener interface but forget to call `addActionListener(this)`. The handler will never execute. Examiners deduct 2 marks for this.
>
> 4. **Wrong package name** — Always write `java.awt.event` (lowercase, with dots). Writing `java.awt.Event` or `java.swing.awt.event` costs marks.
>
> 5. **Skipping empty method bodies** — When implementing an interface like `MouseListener`, you must provide *all* methods (even if empty). Missing methods cause compile errors and full mark deduction.

---

## 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **High-Density Revision Checklist:**

- **Root Classes:** `java.util.EventObject` → `java.awt.AWTEvent` → all event classes.
- **Package:** All standard AWT event classes reside in `java.awt.event`.
- **Core Methods from `EventObject`:** `getSource()`.
- **Core Methods from `AWTEvent`:** `getID()`, `paramString()`.
- **`ActionEvent`:** Fired by buttons, menu items, text field Enter. Uses `getActionCommand()`.
- **`ItemEvent`:** Fired by checkboxes, lists, choice. Uses `getItem()`, `getStateChange()` (SELECTED / DESELECTED).
- **`AdjustmentEvent`:** Fired by scrollbars. Uses `getValue()`, `getAdjustmentType()`.
- **`TextEvent`:** Fired by text components. Uses inherited methods only.
- **`ComponentEvent`:** Generic — `componentResized`, `Moved`, `Shown`, `Hidden`.
- **`ContainerEvent`:** `componentAdded`, `componentRemoved`. Uses `getChild()`.
- **`FocusEvent`:** `focusGained`, `focusLost`. Uses `isTemporary()`.
- **`WindowEvent`:** 7 types — `OPENING`, `CLOSING`, `CLOSED`, `ICONIFIED`, `DEICONIFIED`, `ACTIVATED`, `DEACTIVATED`.
- **`KeyEvent`:** 3 types — `KEY_PRESSED`, `KEY_RELEASED`, `KEY_TYPED`. Distinguish `getKeyCode()` vs `getKeyChar()`.
- **`MouseEvent`:** 7 types — `MOUSE_CLICKED`, `PRESSED`, `RELEASED`, `ENTERED`, `EXITED`, `MOVED`, `DRAGGED`. Uses `getX()`, `getY()`, `getClickCount()`, `isPopupTrigger()`.
- **`MouseWheelEvent`:** Extends `MouseEvent`. Uses `getWheelRotation()`, `getPreciseWheelRotation()`.
- **Two listeners for MouseEvent:** `MouseListener` (clicks, entry, exit) and `MouseMotionListener` (drag, move).
- **Delegation Event Model:** Source creates → Event object passed → Listener handles. Source and Listener are loosely coupled.
- **Constants Memorization:** You should know at least the *names* (not necessarily values) of all event ID constants for `ActionEvent`, `KeyEvent`, `MouseEvent`, and `WindowEvent`.

> **End of Module 4 — Event Classes Notes**
<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.title: Sources of Events
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PBCST304 - OBJECT ORIENTED PROGRAMMING
> - **Module:** Module 4
> - **Topic:** Sources of Events

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Formal Definition

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Event Source (KTU 2024 Syllabus Definition):**
> An **Event Source** is the GUI component (an object) that **generates (fires) an event** when the user interacts with it through an input device (mouse, keyboard) or when its internal state changes. In the Java Delegation Event Model, the source is the originating object that hands over the event object to one or more registered listeners.

In simple words, **the event source is the "thing that produced the event."** A button being clicked, a checkbox being ticked, a key being pressed — all of these actions originate from an event source.

### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy

> [!NOTE]
> **Real-World Analogy — The Doorbell System:**
> - **Doorbell Button** → **Event Source** (the device where the action occurs)
> - **Pressing the Button** → **User Action / Event Trigger**
> - **Electrical Signal (the "ding")** → **Event Object**
> - **The Person Inside Hearing the Bell** → **Event Listener** (the registered handler)
>
> Just as a doorbell button does nothing on its own until a person listens for its sound, an event source is meaningless without a registered listener. The button (source) creates the signal; the listener reacts to it.

### 1.3 Key Terminology

| Term | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| **Event Source** | The object that **fires** the event (e.g., `JButton`, `JTextField`) |
| **Event Object** | The object that **encapsulates** information about the event (e.g., `ActionEvent`) |
| **Event Listener** | The object that **receives** and **handles** the event |
| **Event Delegation Model** | The mechanism where the source **delegates** event processing to listeners |

---

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Reference

### 2.1 The Java Delegation Event Model — How Sources Fit In

The Java AWT/Swing event-handling system is based on the **Delegation Event Model**, which has **three participants**:

1. **Source** — the component generating the event
2. **Event** — the object describing what happened
3. **Listener** — the object that handles the event

The source is responsible for:
- **Detecting** that an event has occurred internally.
- **Creating** an event object containing details (e.g., which key, which mouse button, coordinates).
- **Invoking** the appropriate method on all **registered listeners** to notify them.

### 2.2 Why Do We Need Event Sources?

- **Decoupling**: The source doesn't need to know *what* will happen after the event — it just notifies listeners. This makes UI code modular and reusable.
- **One-to-Many Communication**: A single source can have **multiple listeners** registered to handle the same event differently.
- **Dynamic Registration**: Listeners can be added/removed at **runtime** using methods like `addXListener()` and `removeXListener()`.

### 2.3 Common Event Sources in `java.awt` and `javax.swing`

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **High-Yield Table — Sources of Events (Most Asked in KTU Exams):**

| Source Class | Package | Event Fired | Listener Interface | Registration Method |
|--------------|---------|-------------|--------------------|----------------------|
| `JButton` | `javax.swing` | `ActionEvent` | `ActionListener` | `addActionListener()` |
| `JTextField` | `javax.swing` | `ActionEvent` | `ActionListener` | `addActionListener()` |
| `JCheckBox` | `javax.swing` | `ItemEvent` | `ItemListener` | `addItemListener()` |
| `JRadioButton` | `javax.swing` | `ItemEvent` | `ItemListener` | `addItemListener()` |
| `JList` | `javax.swing` | `ListSelectionEvent` | `ListSelectionListener` | `addListSelectionListener()` |
| `JComboBox` | `javax.swing` | `ActionEvent`, `ItemEvent` | `ActionListener`, `ItemListener` | `addActionListener()` |
| `JMenuItem` | `javax.swing` | `ActionEvent` | `ActionListener` | `addActionListener()` |
| `JScrollBar` | `javax.swing` | `AdjustmentEvent` | `AdjustmentListener` | `addAdjustmentListener()` |
| `JTextArea` | `javax.swing` | `TextEvent` | `TextListener` | `addTextListener()` |
| `Component` (mouse) | `java.awt` | `MouseEvent` | `MouseListener` | `addMouseListener()` |
| `Component` (key) | `java.awt` | `KeyEvent` | `KeyListener` | `addKeyListener()` |
| `Window` | `java.awt` | `WindowEvent` | `WindowListener` | `addWindowListener()` |
| `JFrame` | `javax.swing` | `WindowEvent` | `WindowListener` | `addWindowListener()` |

### 2.4 Lifecycle of an Event from Source to Listener

1. **User Interaction** → The user performs an action (click, type, hover) on a GUI component.
2. **Source Detection** → The source component detects the change and creates an **Event Object**.
3. **Event Delegation** → The source passes the event object to every **registered listener** by calling its handler method.
4. **Listener Response** → The listener executes the corresponding callback method (e.g., `actionPerformed()`).
5. **Optional Removal** → The listener can later be removed using `removeXListener()`.

### 2.5 Real-World Utility in Engineering

- **Industrial Control Panels (SCADA Systems)**: Buttons and sensors act as event sources triggering alarms and actuator responses.
- **Embedded GUI Systems**: Touchscreen components fire events processed by controller logic.
- **Mobile/Web Applications**: Behind the scenes, every tap, swipe, and input is an event source firing an event.

---

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## 3. Step-by-Step Walkthrough — How an Event Source Works

### 3.1 Java Code Example — Demonstrating an Event Source

Below is a complete Java Swing program showing how a `JButton` (the event source) fires an `ActionEvent` to a registered listener.

```java
import javax.swing.*;
import java.awt.*;
import java.awt.event.*;

public class SourceDemo extends JFrame implements ActionListener {
    JButton btn;      // This is the EVENT SOURCE
    JLabel label;

    public SourceDemo() {
        setTitle("Event Source Demo");
        setSize(300, 200);
        setLayout(new FlowLayout());
        setDefaultCloseOperation(JFrame.EXIT_ON_CLOSE);

        btn = new JButton("Click Me");   // Step 1: Create the source
        label = new JLabel("Status: Waiting...");

        add(btn);
        add(label);

        // Step 2: Register a listener with the source
        btn.addActionListener(this);
    }

    // Step 3: Listener callback (event handling)
    public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
        // 'e' is the Event Object created by the source
        label.setText("Status: Button Clicked!");
        System.out.println("Event Source: " + e.getSource().getClass().getName());
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new SourceDemo().setVisible(true);
    }
}
```

### 3.2 Step-by-Step Logical Breakdown

**Step 1 — Source Creation**
A `JButton` object `btn` is instantiated. At this stage, it has no listener registered. Even if clicked, no action will occur.

**Step 2 — Listener Registration**
`btn.addActionListener(this);` registers the current object (`this`) as a listener for `ActionEvent`s. Internally, the source maintains a **list of listener references**.

**Step 3 — User Clicks the Button**
The AWT Event Dispatch Thread detects the mouse release over the button. The button **creates** an `ActionEvent` object carrying details like timestamp and source reference.

**Step 4 — Event Delegation**
The source iterates through its internal listener list and calls `actionPerformed(e)` on each one. The event object `e` is passed as the argument.

**Step 5 — Listener Reacts**
Inside `actionPerformed`, we identify the source using `e.getSource()` and perform the desired action — updating the label.

### 3.3 Multi-Source Example (KTU Favorite)

```java
import javax.swing.*;
import java.awt.*;
import java.awt.event.*;

public class MultiSourceDemo extends JFrame implements ActionListener {
    JButton b1, b2;

    public MultiSourceDemo() {
        setLayout(new FlowLayout());
        b1 = new JButton("Apple");
        b2 = new JButton("Mango");
        add(b1); add(b2);
        b1.addActionListener(this);  // Source 1 registered
        b2.addActionListener(this);  // Source 2 registered
        setSize(300,150);
        setDefaultCloseOperation(EXIT_ON_CLOSE);
    }

    public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
        JButton src = (JButton) e.getSource();  // Identify which source fired
        System.out.println("Clicked: " + src.getText());
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new MultiSourceDemo().setVisible(true);
    }
}
```

**Explanation:**
- Two sources (`b1` and `b2`) share the **same listener** object.
- Inside the handler, `e.getSource()` distinguishes which source fired the event.
- This demonstrates the **one-listener-handling-many-sources** capability of the delegation model.

### 3.4 Identifying Sources Programmatically

The `EventObject` class (parent of all event classes) provides the key method:

$$
\text{Object} \;\; e.\text{getSource}()
$$

This returns a reference to the **original event source object**, allowing the listener to identify *who* fired the event.

---

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
