## 🧠 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **High-Density Rapid-Revision Checklist (Save This!)**

- ⭐ **Java execution is a 5-step pipeline:** Author → Compile (`javac`) → Load (ClassLoader) → Verify (Bytecode Verifier) → Execute (Interpreter + JIT).
- ⭐ **Bytecode is platform-independent; native code is platform-specific.** This duality gives Java its "Write Once, Run Anywhere" power.
- ⭐ **The `main` method signature is sacred:** `public static void main(String[] args)` — without `static`, JVM cannot invoke it without an object instance.
- ⭐ **Exception flow has 6 deterministic steps:** Detect → Create object → Populate stack trace → Throw → Catch match (top-down) → Finally execute.
- ⭐ **`finally` ALWAYS runs** in 4 of 5 scenarios: normal exit, caught exception, uncaught exception, `return`/`break`/`continue` inside `try` or `catch`. The **only exception** is `System.exit(0)`.
- ⭐ **Catch ordering rule:** Subclass catches come **first**, superclass catches come **last**. Reverse order → compile-time *"unreachable code"* error.
- ⭐ **`throw` vs `throws`:** `throw` = an action verb (inside body, throws an instance). `throws` = a declaration (in signature, lists class names).
- ⭐ **Checked exceptions** are verified at **compile-time** (e.g., `IOException`, `SQLException`). **Unchecked exceptions** are verified at **runtime** (e.g., `NullPointerException`, `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`).
- ⭐ **Stack trace** is built automatically by the JVM and traces the **call chain** from `main` down to the failing line.
- ⭐ **KTU's favourite trick question:** *"Does `finally` run if there is a `return` inside `try`?"* — **YES**, it does. Memorize this.
- ⭐ **`try-with-resources`** (Java 7+) auto-closes any `AutoCloseable` resource — the modern, clean alternative to `try-catch-finally` for I/O code.

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.title: Common JDBC Components
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PBCST304 - OBJECT ORIENTED PROGRAMMING
> - **Module:** Module 4
> - **Topic:** Common JDBC Components

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->

# SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **JDBC (Java Database Connectivity)** is a Java API (Application Programming Interface) that enables Java applications to interact with relational databases. The **Common JDBC Components** are the standardized set of interfaces and classes within the `java.sql` package that form the architectural foundation of every JDBC-based data access operation.

According to the **KTU 2024 Scheme syllabus for PBCST304 – Object Oriented Programming (Module 4: Database Programming)**, the Common JDBC Components are the essential building blocks required to establish a communication bridge between a Java application and any SQL-compliant RDBMS (Relational Database Management System) such as **Oracle**, **MySQL**, **PostgreSQL**, or **SQLite**.

These components reside primarily in two packages:
- `java.sql` — Core JDBC API (platform-independent).
- `javax.sql` — Extended JDBC API (used for connection pooling, distributed transactions, and DataSource).

### The 7 Pillars of JDBC Architecture

| # | Component | Type | Primary Role |
|---|-----------|------|--------------|
| 1 | `DriverManager` | Class | Service provider / registry of DB drivers |
| 2 | `Connection` | Interface | Live session between Java app and DB |
| 3 | `Statement` | Interface | Executes static SQL queries |
| 4 | `PreparedStatement` | Interface | Executes pre-compiled parameterized SQL |
| 5 | `CallableStatement` | Interface | Executes stored procedures |
| 6 | `ResultSet` | Interface | Tabular in-memory result of a query |
| 7 | `SQLException` | Class | Handles SQL access warnings/errors |

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU Board Exam Highlight:** Examiners frequently ask for the **list of common JDBC components** along with their **package names** and a brief **one-line description**. Memorize the table above verbatim.

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The Restaurant Paradigm

Imagine you walk into a **restaurant** to order food. The entire JDBC workflow mirrors this real-world interaction perfectly:

> **Conceptual Analogy:** The Restaurant Visit

| JDBC Component | Restaurant Equivalent | Plain-English Role |
|----------------|---------------------|--------------------|
| `DriverManager` | The **Reception Desk** | "Which waiter (driver) speaks the language of the kitchen (database) you want?" |
| `Connection` | Your **Seated Table** | The live, open channel to the kitchen (DB). |
| `Statement` | A **Written Order Slip** (static) | A pre-written, non-customizable order. |
| `PreparedStatement` | An **Order Template** with blanks | Faster, reusable, parameterized order — safe from tampering. |
| `ResultSet` | The **Plated Food** returned to you | A pointer/cursor over the rows served back. |
| `SQLException` | The **"Out of Stock"** alarm | Tells Java when something went wrong. |

This analogy makes the abstract JDBC architecture intuitive: **Java (you) never cooks the food directly — it asks the kitchen (DB) through standardized intermediaries (JDBC components).**

## 1.3 Why JDBC Components Matter in Industry

- **Portability:** A single Java application can switch from Oracle to MySQL by simply changing the driver JAR — no Java code changes required.
- **Standardization:** JDBC is part of Java SE (Standard Edition), so the API is stable across all platforms (Windows, Linux, macOS).
- **Foundation for Frameworks:** **Hibernate**, **JPA (Java Persistence API)**, and **Spring Data JPA** are all built *on top of* these very components. Mastering them is mandatory for backend engineering roles.

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->

# SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Reference Sheet

## 2.1 Detailed Component-Wise Breakdown

### 2.1.1 `DriverManager` — The Service Registry Class

- **Package:** `java.sql`
- **Type:** Concrete `class` (not an interface).
- **Primary Job:** Acts as a **factory** that returns a `Connection` object upon receiving a valid JDBC URL.
- **How it Works:**
  1. When `Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver")` is called, the driver self-registers in `DriverManager`'s internal list.
  2. When `DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, pwd)` is invoked, it iterates through the registered drivers.
  3. The first driver that recognizes the URL (e.g., `jdbc:mysql://...`) returns a `Connection`.

> [!NOTE]
> **Modern Note (JDBC 4.0+):** Explicit `Class.forName()` is no longer mandatory — drivers are auto-loaded via the **Service Provider mechanism** (META-INF/services/java.sql.Driver).

**Key Static Methods:**
- `getConnection(String url)`
- `getConnection(String url, String user, String password)`
- `getConnection(Properties props)`
- `registerDriver(Driver driver)`

### 2.1.2 `Connection` — The Live Session

- **Package:** `java.sql`
- **Type:** `interface`
- **Primary Job:** Represents an **active session** (physical or logical TCP socket) to a specific database.
- **Lifecycle:** `DriverManager.getConnection()` → ... → `conn.close()`.
- **Key Methods:**

| Method | Returns | Purpose |
|--------|---------|---------|
| `createStatement()` | `Statement` | For static SQL |
| `prepareStatement(String sql)` | `PreparedStatement` | For parameterized SQL |
| `prepareCall(String sql)` | `CallableStatement` | For stored procs |
| `close()` | `void` | Releases the session |
| `setAutoCommit(boolean)` | `void` | Controls transactions |
| `commit()` / `rollback()` | `void` | Transaction boundaries |
| `getMetaData()` | `DatabaseMetaData` | Schema-level info |

### 2.1.3 `Statement` — The Static Query Executor

- **Type:** `interface`
- **Use Case:** When the SQL query is **fixed** at compile-time and has **no user input** to be embedded.
- **Drawback:** Vulnerable to **SQL Injection** attacks — never use for user-supplied data.
- **Methods:**

| Method | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| `executeQuery(String sql)` | Returns `ResultSet` (for SELECT) |
| `executeUpdate(String sql)` | Returns `int` row count (for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) |
| `execute(String sql)` | Returns `boolean` (true = ResultSet, false = update count) |
| `addBatch(String sql)` | Adds SQL to a batch for bulk execution |
| `executeBatch()` | Executes the accumulated batch |

### 2.1.4 `PreparedStatement` — The Pre-Compiled Query Executor

- **Type:** `interface` (extends `Statement`)
- **Use Case:** When the SQL contains **placeholders (`?`)** for runtime parameters.
- **Advantages over `Statement`:**
  1. ✅ **Pre-compiled** by the DB engine → faster on repeated execution.
  2. ✅ **Parameterized input** → immune to SQL injection.
  3. ✅ Better handling of **BLOB/CLOB** data.
  4. ✅ Automatic type conversion between Java types and SQL types.

- **Methods:**

| Method | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| `setString(int idx, String val)` | Binds a String to the placeholder |
| `setInt(int idx, int val)` | Binds an int to the placeholder |
| `setFloat`, `setDouble`, `setDate`, `setBoolean` | Bind other types |
| `executeQuery()` / `executeUpdate()` | Run the pre-compiled SQL |

### 2.1.5 `CallableStatement` — Stored Procedure Executor

- **Type:** `interface` (extends `PreparedStatement`)
- **Use Case:** Executes **stored procedures** or **functions** stored inside the database.
- **Syntax Pattern:** `{ call procedure_name(?, ?, ...) }`

### 2.1.6 `ResultSet` — The Tabular Cursor

- **Type:** `interface`
- **Primary Job:** Represents the **rows returned** by a `SELECT` query. Maintains a **cursor** that points to the current row.
- **Cursor Behavior:** By default, the cursor moves **forward only** (TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY). It is **scrollable** and **updatable** if specified in `createStatement()`.
- **Methods:**

| Method | Returns | Purpose |
|--------|---------|---------|
| `next()` | `boolean` | Moves cursor to the next row |
| `previous()` | `boolean` | Moves to the previous row (scrollable) |
| `getString(int colIdx / String colName)` | `String` | Fetches column value as String |
| `getInt(...)`, `getDouble(...)`, etc. | typed | Typed getters |
| `close()` | `void` | Releases the result set |

### 2.1.7 `SQLException` — The Checked Exception

- **Type:** `class` (extends `java.lang.Exception`)
- **Checked Exception:** Forces the programmer to handle DB errors explicitly.
- **Methods:**

| Method | Returns | Purpose |
|--------|---------|---------|
| `getErrorCode()` | `int` | Vendor-specific error code |
| `getSQLState()` | `String` | Standardized 5-character SQL state |
| `getMessage()` | `String` | Human-readable description |
| `getNextException()` | `SQLException` | Linked list of multiple errors |

### 2.1.8 Auxiliary Components (Frequently Asked in KTU)

| Component | Type | Role |
|-----------|------|------|
| `ResultSetMetaData` | Interface | Column count, name, type of a `ResultSet` |
| `DatabaseMetaData` | Interface | DB name, version, supported features |
| `RowSet` | Interface | Scrollable, serializable wrapper around `ResultSet` |

## 2.2 KTU High-Yield Reference Sheet

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Mandatory KTU Exam Reference — Memorize Before Exam**

| Component | Package | Type | Used For | Created By |
|-----------|---------|------|----------|------------|
| DriverManager | java.sql | Class | Driver registry | JVM |
| Connection | java.sql | Interface | DB session | DriverManager |
| Statement | java.sql | Interface | Static SQL | Connection |
| PreparedStatement | java.sql | Interface | Dynamic SQL | Connection |
| CallableStatement | java.sql | Interface | Stored procs | Connection |
| ResultSet | java.sql | Interface | Query results | Statement family |
| SQLException | java.sql | Class | DB errors | JDBC runtime |
| ResultSetMetaData | java.sql | Interface | Column info | ResultSet |
| DatabaseMetaData | java.sql | Interface | DB info | Connection |

## 2.3 Real-World Engineering Utility

- **Enterprise Banking Systems:** Use `PreparedStatement` heavily for transaction processing where the same INSERT/UPDATE pattern executes thousands of times.
- **E-Commerce Catalogs:** Use `ResultSet` scrollability to implement pagination (next/previous page navigation).
- **Data Migration Tools:** Use `ResultSetMetaData` to dynamically build INSERT statements for unknown table schemas.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->

# SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Analysis & Implementation Matrix

## 3.1 The Universal JDBC Workflow — Step-by-Step Derivation

The JDBC architecture follows a **strict 5-step protocol** (commonly tested in KTU boards):

> **Step 1: Load the Driver Class**
> Loads the vendor-specific JDBC driver into the JVM.

> **Step 2: Establish the Connection**
> Uses `DriverManager.getConnection()` to open a live session.

> **Step 3: Create a Statement / PreparedStatement**
> Obtains a query-execution channel.

> **Step 4: Execute the SQL Query**
> Runs the SQL and obtains the result.

> **Step 5: Process the ResultSet & Close Resources**
> Iterates over returned rows and releases the DB session.

### 3.1.1 Step 1 — Load the Driver Class

**Logic:** The driver class is dynamically loaded using Java Reflection. The `Class.forName()` call triggers a static initializer block inside the driver class, which calls `DriverManager.registerDriver(this)`, thereby registering itself.

```java
// Modern way (JDBC 4.0+ auto-loading) — but still valid
Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver");
```

**Why?** Some older KTU questions still expect this line explicitly. **Use it if the question says "explicitly load the driver."**

### 3.1.2 Step 2 — Establish the Connection

**Logic:** The connection URL uniquely identifies the database vendor. The format is:

$$ \text{URL} = \text{jdbc}:\text{<subprotocol>}://\text{<host>}:{\text{<port>}}/{\text{<database>}} $$

Common KTU-tested URL formats:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{MySQL} &: \quad \texttt{jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/collegeDB} \\
\text{Oracle} &: \quad \texttt{jdbc:oracle:thin:@localhost:1521:XE} \\
\text{PostgreSQL} &: \quad \texttt{jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/collegeDB} \\
\text{SQLite} &: \quad \texttt{jdbc:sqlite:student.db}
\end{aligned}
$$

```java
String url = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/collegeDB";
String user = "root";
String pass = "password";
Connection conn = DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, pass);
```

### 3.1.3 Step 3 — Create the Statement

Two variants — **KTU examiners love this comparison**:

```java
// Variant A: Plain Statement (static SQL)
Statement stmt = conn.createStatement();

// Variant B: PreparedStatement (parameterized SQL)
String sql = "INSERT INTO students (id, name, cgpa) VALUES (?, ?, ?)";
PreparedStatement pstmt = conn.prepareStatement(sql);
```

### 3.1.4 Step 4 — Execute the Query

**Logic:** Choose the right `execute*` method based on the SQL type:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{SELECT} &\longrightarrow \texttt{executeQuery()} \longrightarrow \text{Returns } \texttt{ResultSet} \\
\text{INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE} &\longrightarrow \texttt{executeUpdate()} \longrightarrow \text{Returns } \texttt{int} \text{ (row count)} \\
\text{Unknown SQL} &\longrightarrow \texttt{execute()} \longrightarrow \text{Returns } \texttt{boolean}
\end{aligned}
$$

```java
// SELECT
ResultSet rs = pstmt.executeQuery();

// INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE
int rows = pstmt.executeUpdate();
```

### 3.1.5 Step 5 — Process ResultSet & Close

**Logic:** The `ResultSet` cursor starts **before the first row**. Calling `next()` moves it to row 1 and returns `true`. When rows are exhausted, it returns `false`.

```java
while (rs.next()) {
    int id    = rs.getInt("id");
    String n  = rs.getString("name");
    double c  = rs.getDouble("cgpa");
    System.out.println(id + " " + n + " " + c);
}
rs.close();
pstmt.close();
conn.close();
```

## 3.2 Complete Canonical KTU Pattern (All 5 Steps Together)

```java
import java.sql.*;

public class StudentDAO {
    public void insertStudent(int id, String name, double cgpa) throws SQLException {
        Connection conn = null;
        PreparedStatement pstmt = null;
        try {
            // STEP 1: Load driver (optional in modern JDBC)
            Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver");
            // STEP 2: Establish connection
            conn = DriverManager.getConnection(
                "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/collegeDB", "root", "password");
            // STEP 3: Create PreparedStatement
            String sql = "INSERT INTO students(id,name,cgpa) VALUES(?,?,?)";
            pstmt = conn.prepareStatement(sql);
            // STEP 4: Bind parameters and execute
            pstmt.setInt(1, id);
            pstmt.setString(2, name);
            pstmt.setDouble(3, cgpa);
            int n = pstmt.executeUpdate();
            System.out.println(n + " row(s) inserted.");
        } catch (ClassNotFoundException e) {
            System.out.println("Driver not found: " + e.getMessage());
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            System.out.println("SQL Error: " + e.getMessage());
        } finally {
            // STEP 5: Close resources (reverse order)
            if (pstmt != null) pstmt.close();
            if (conn  != null) conn.close();
        }
    }
}
```

## 3.3 Analytical Matrix: `Statement` vs `PreparedStatement` vs `CallableStatement`

This comparison table is **mandatory for KTU 14-mark questions**:

| Feature | `Statement` | `PreparedStatement` | `CallableStatement` |
|---------|-------------|---------------------|---------------------|
| **SQL Type** | Static | Dynamic (parameterized) | Stored procedure |
| **Compilation** | Compiled every execution | Pre-compiled once | Stored on DB server |
| **Performance (repeated use)** | Slow | Fast | Fastest |
| **SQL Injection Safe?** | ❌ No | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes |
| **Reads BLOB/CLOB efficiently?** | ❌ No | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes |
| **Created via** | `conn.createStatement()` | `conn.prepareStatement(sql)` | `conn.prepareCall(sql)` |
| **Parent Interface** | Root | `extends Statement` | `extends PreparedStatement` |

## 3.4 Analytical Matrix: `ResultSet` vs `RowSet`

| Feature | `ResultSet` | `RowSet` |
|---------|-------------|----------|
| **Connectivity** | Connected (needs open `Connection`) | Disconnected (can be serialized) |
| **Scrollable?** | Only if explicitly created | Yes, by default |
| **Serializable?** | ❌ No | ✅ Yes (extends `java.io.Serializable`) |
| **Java Bean support** | ❌ No | ✅ Yes |

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->

# SECTION 4: Structural Diagrams & Schematics

## 4.1 Master Architecture Diagram — JDBC Component Interaction Flow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Java Application] --> B[Class.forName or Auto Load]
    B --> C[DriverManager]
    C --> D[Connection getConnection]
    D --> E[Statement Family]
    E --> F1[Statement]
    E --> F2[PreparedStatement]
    E --> F3[CallableStatement]
    F1 --> G[executeQuery or executeUpdate]
    F2 --> G
    F3 --> G
    G --> H[ResultSet]
    H --> I[Process Rows with next and getString]
    F2 --> J[Bind parameters with setString and setInt]
    F3 --> K[Stored Procedure on Database]
    I --> L[close ResultSet]
    J --> G
    K --> G
    L --> M[close Statement]
    M --> N[close Connection]
    N --> O[(Database Server)]
```

## 4.2 Interface Inheritance Hierarchy

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Statement Interface] --> B[PreparedStatement Interface]
    B --> C[CallableStatement Interface]
    D[Wrapper Interface] --> E[ResultSet Interface]
    F[Wrapper Interface] --> G[DatabaseMetaData Interface]
    H[Wrapper Interface] --> I[ResultSetMetaData Interface]
```

## 4.3 Type-Specific Relationship of ResultSet

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[ResultSet] --> B[ResultSetMetaData: column info]
    A --> C[Cursor Movement: next, previous, absolute]
    A --> D[Column Getters: getString, getInt, getDouble]
    B --> E[getColumnCount, getColumnName, getColumnType]
    C --> F[Scrollable and Updatable modes]
    D --> G[Typed retrieval of row data]
```

## 4.4 Five-Step JDBC Execution Sequence (Block Architecture)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S1[Step 1: Load or Auto-Load Driver] --> S2[Step 2: DriverManager returns Connection]
    S2 --> S3[Step 3: Connection creates Statement or PreparedStatement or CallableStatement]
    S3 --> S4[Step 4: Execute SQL and obtain ResultSet or row count]
    S4 --> S5[Step 5: Iterate ResultSet and close in reverse order: ResultSet, Statement, Connection]
    S1 -.uses.-> X1[java.sql package classes]
    S2 -.uses.-> X1
    S3 -.uses.-> X1
    S4 -.uses.-> X1
    S5 -.uses.-> X1
```

# SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### **Q1. [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]**
**List any six common components of JDBC and state the package in which they are defined.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

The six common JDBC components are:
1. **DriverManager** — `java.sql` — registers drivers and returns a `Connection`.
2. **Connection** — `java.sql` — represents an active session with a database.
3. **Statement** — `java.sql` — executes static SQL queries.
4. **PreparedStatement** — `java.sql` — executes pre-compiled parameterized SQL.
5. **CallableStatement** — `java.sql` — executes stored procedures on the DB.
6. **ResultSet** — `java.sql` — represents the tabular result of a SELECT query.
7. **SQLException** — `java.sql` — handles database access errors.

> **Valuation Tip:** Award **0.5 mark per component name + 0.5 mark for stating the correct package**, totalling 3 marks. Listing without the package is a common mistake — full marks require the package.

---

### **Q2. [KTU University Exam – May 2024]**
**Differentiate between `Statement` and `PreparedStatement` in JDBC.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

| Parameter | `Statement` | `PreparedStatement` |
|-----------|-------------|---------------------|
| Compilation | Compiled every execution | Pre-compiled once |
| Performance | Slower for repeated SQL | Faster for repeated SQL |
| SQL Injection | Vulnerable | Safe (parameterized) |
| Use Case | Static SQL with no input | Dynamic SQL with `?` placeholders |
| Creation | `conn.createStatement()` | `conn.prepareStatement(sql)` |

---

## 5.2 Part B — 14-Mark Long Answer Questions (ESE Module Internal Choice)

### **Question A (14 Marks) [KTU University Exam – Dec 2024 Model]**

**(a)** With a neat block diagram, explain the **architecture of JDBC** and the role of each common component. (7 marks)

**(b)** Write a complete Java program using **PreparedStatement** to insert 5 student records (id, name, cgpa) into a MySQL table named `students`. Use proper exception handling and resource closing. (7 marks)

#### Model Solution

**Part (a) — JDBC Architecture (7 marks):**

JDBC provides a **standardized API** for Java-to-database communication. The architecture consists of:

1. **Java Application Layer** — The user code that calls JDBC methods.
2. **JDBC API Layer** (`java.sql`) — Provides interfaces: `Connection`, `Statement`, `PreparedStatement`, `ResultSet`, etc.
3. **JDBC Driver Manager** — Acts as a service registry that maps JDBC calls to the vendor-specific driver.
4. **JDBC Driver Layer** — Vendor-specific implementation (Type-1/2/3/4 drivers).
5. **Database Layer** — The actual RDBMS (Oracle, MySQL, etc.).

**Role of Each Component:**
- `DriverManager` — Registers drivers; returns a `Connection` for a given URL.
- `Connection` — Represents the live DB session; creates statements and manages transactions.
- `Statement` — Executes static SQL.
- `PreparedStatement` — Pre-compiles and executes parameterized SQL.
- `CallableStatement` — Calls stored procedures.
- `ResultSet` — Cursor-based read-only result of a SELECT query.
- `SQLException` — Reports and carries DB error information.

(Refer to Section 4 diagrams for block structure.)

**Part (b) — Java Program (7 marks):**

```java
import java.sql.*;
public class StudentInsertDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String url  = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/collegeDB";
        String user = "root";
        String pass = "password";
        Connection conn = null;
        PreparedStatement pstmt = null;
        try {
            Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver");
            conn = DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, pass);
            String sql = "INSERT INTO students(id,name,cgpa) VALUES(?,?,?)";
            pstmt = conn.prepareStatement(sql);
            int[][] data = {{101,"Arun",8.7},{102,"Meera",9.1},
                            {103,"Rahul",7.9},{104,"Priya",8.4},
                            {105,"Kiran",8.0}};
            for (int[] r : data) {
                pstmt.setInt(1, r[0]);
                pstmt.setString(2, r[1]);
                pstmt.setDouble(3, r[2]);
                pstmt.executeUpdate();
            }
            System.out.println("5 records inserted successfully.");
        } catch (ClassNotFoundException | SQLException e) {
            System.out.println("Error: " + e.getMessage());
        } finally {
            try { if (pstmt != null) pstmt.close(); } catch (SQLException ignored) {}
            try { if (conn  != null) conn.close();  } catch (SQLException ignored) {}
        }
    }
}
```

**Mark Allocation (7 marks):**
- Correct driver loading + URL: **1 mark**
- Connection establishment: **1 mark**
- PreparedStatement creation with placeholders: **1 mark**
- Parameter binding via setInt / setString / setDouble: **2 marks**
- Loop executing 5 inserts: **1 mark**
- Exception handling + resource closing in `finally`: **1 mark**

---

### **Question B (14 Marks) [KTU University Exam – May 2024 Model — Alternative Choice]**

**(a)** Explain the **types of JDBC drivers** and state the advantages of the **Type-4 (Thin) Driver**. (7 marks)

**(b)** Write a Java program to **fetch and display all rows** from a `students` table using `Statement` and `ResultSet`. Include proper navigation through the result. (7 marks)

#### Model Solution Outline

**Part (a) — JDBC Driver Types (7 marks):**

1. **Type-1: JDBC-ODBC Bridge Driver** — Converts JDBC calls to ODBC calls. Slow, requires ODBC installed.
2. **Type-2: Native-API Driver** — Converts JDBC calls to vendor-specific native calls. Requires client-side library.
3. **Type-3: Network Protocol Driver** — Sends JDBC calls to a middle-tier server that translates them. Suitable for internet-based apps.
4. **Type-4: Thin Driver (Pure Java)** — Converts JDBC calls **directly** to the database-specific protocol. No native libraries needed.

**Advantages of Type-4 Driver:**
- ✅ Pure Java — platform independent.
- ✅ No client-side installation of DB libraries.
- ✅ Highest performance (direct DB protocol).
- ✅ Suitable for web-based distributed applications.
- ✅ Easy to deploy over the internet.

**Part (b) — Java Program Using `Statement` and `ResultSet` (7 marks):**

```java
import java.sql.*;
public class StudentFetchDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String url = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/collegeDB";
        try (Connection conn = DriverManager.getConnection(url, "root", "password");
             Statement stmt = conn.createStatement();
             ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery("SELECT id, name, cgpa FROM students")) {
            System.out.printf("%-10s %-20s %-10s%n", "ID", "Name", "CGPA");
            System.out.println("------------------------------------------");
            while (rs.next()) {
                int id    = rs.getInt("id");
                String nm = rs.getString("name");
                double cg = rs.getDouble("cgpa");
                System.out.printf("%-10d %-20s %-10.2f%n", id, nm, cg);
            }
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            System.out.println("Error: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
```

**Mark Allocation (7 marks):**
- Establishing connection: **1 mark**
- Creating `Statement` and executing `SELECT`: **1 mark**
- Proper `ResultSet` loop using `next()`: **2 marks**
- Fetching typed values with `getInt`, `getString`, `getDouble`: **2 marks**
- Try-with-resources closing: **1 mark**

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Where Students Lose Marks:**
> 1. **Forgetting to close `ResultSet`/`Statement`/`Connection`** → Lose **2 marks** (resource leak).
> 2. **Using `Statement` instead of `PreparedStatement` for user input** → Lose **2 marks** (SQL injection).
> 3. **Writing `import javax.sql.*` for core components** → Lose **1 mark** (wrong package).
> 4. **Mixing up `executeQuery()` vs `executeUpdate()`** → Lose **1 mark** (compile/runtime error).
> 5. **Not specifying try-catch-finally or try-with-resources** → Lose **1 mark** (exception handling missing).
> 6. **Writing the driver name incorrectly** (e.g., `com.mysql.jdbc.Driver` for newer versions) → Lose **1 mark**. Use **`com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver`**.

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> **Rapid Revision Checklist — Read Before Exam Day**

- 🔑 **JDBC = Java Database Connectivity** — part of `java.sql` (and `javax.sql`).
- 🔑 **Seven common components:** `DriverManager`, `Connection`, `Statement`, `PreparedStatement`, `CallableStatement`, `ResultSet`, `SQLException`.
- 🔑 **All components (except `DriverManager` & `SQLException`) are interfaces** — implementation is vendor-supplied.
- 🔑 **The canonical 5-step JDBC process:** Load Driver → Connect → Create Statement → Execute → Process & Close.
- 🔑 **`PreparedStatement` > `Statement`** for: security (SQL injection), performance (pre-compilation), and BLOBs.
- 🔑 **`executeQuery()` returns `ResultSet`**; **`executeUpdate()` returns `int`** (row count).
- 🔑 **`ResultSet` cursor starts before row 1** — first call to `next()` moves to row 1.
- 🔑 **Resources must be closed in reverse order** of creation: `ResultSet` → `Statement` → `Connection`.
- 🔑 **URL format:** `jdbc:<subprotocol>://<host>:<port>/<database>`.
- 🔑 **`Class.forName()` is optional from JDBC 4.0+** — drivers auto-register via Service Provider.
- 🔑 **Type-4 (Thin) Driver is the industry standard** — pure Java, fastest, no native library needed.
- 🔑 **Always prefer `try-with-resources`** (Java 7+) for automatic resource management.
- 🔑 **`SQLException` is a checked exception** — compiler forces `try-catch` or `throws`.

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

# 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Connection Establishment** in the context of Java Database Connectivity (JDBC) is the formal, API-driven process of acquiring an active, authenticated communication channel (an object instance of the `java.sql.Connection` interface) between a Java application and a relational database management system (RDBMS), executed through a registered JDBC driver and a strictly formatted database URL.

In the KTU 2024 OOP syllabus, **Module 4** focuses on the *Java Database Connectivity (JDBC) API*. Connection establishment is the **foundational Step 2** of the standard JDBC workflow (Load Driver → **Establish Connection** → Create Statement → Execute Query → Process Results → Close Connection).

The architecture relies on four key participants:

| Component | Type | Responsibility |
|-----------|------|----------------|
| `DriverManager` | Class (Factory) | Selects the correct driver from registered ones |
| `Driver` | Interface | Contract for database communication |
| `Connection` | Interface (Logical Channel) | Represents the active session |
| Database URL | `String` (Locator) | Identifies the target DBMS physically/logically |

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The Restaurant Reservation

> [!NOTE]
> **Analogy: Dining at a Restaurant**
> Imagine you want to order food (data) from a specific kitchen (database) using your phone (Java app). The process goes like this:
> 1. **Loading the Driver** → Installing the restaurant's mobile app (you need a translator specific to that restaurant).
> 2. **Connection Establishment** → Making a reservation. You give the *restaurant name + address + table number* (the **Database URL**), present your *membership card* (**Username**), and your *secret PIN* (**Password**). The host verifies you and gives you a **table number** (the `Connection` object).
> 3. **Statement** → Asking the waiter to take your order.
> 4. **ResultSet** → The food arriving at your table.
> 5. **close()** → Paying the bill and leaving the table.

This analogy maps perfectly to JDBC:
- The **Database URL** is like a complete postal address (protocol + sub-protocol + host + port + database name).
- The **Driver** is the protocol translator (MySQL speaks differently than Oracle).
- The **Connection** object is the live phone line / reserved seat — until you `close()` it, no one else can use that line.

## 1.3 Standard Metrics & Constants

> [!IMPORTANT]
> - **Default JDBC Port for MySQL**: `3306`
> - **Default JDBC Port for Oracle**: `1521`
> - **Default JDBC Port for PostgreSQL**: `5432`
> - **Default JDBC Port for SQL Server**: `1433`
> - **Mandatory SQLException Check**: All connection methods are **checked exceptions** in Java, requiring `try-catch` or `throws` declaration.

---

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 The Five Mandatory Steps of JDBC Connection Establishment

The KTU syllabus breaks connection establishment into a precise, ordered sequence. Skipping any step causes a `SQLException`.

### Step 1 — Load / Register the Driver Class
The JVM must know *which* database translator to use.

- **Legacy approach (deprecated in modern JDBC but taught in syllabus)**:
  `Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver");`
  This dynamically loads the driver class, and its **static initializer block** automatically calls `DriverManager.registerDriver()`.

- **Modern approach (JDBC 4.0+)**:
  Auto-loading via the **META-INF/services/java.sql.Driver** file inside the JAR. No explicit `Class.forName()` needed if the JAR is on the classpath.

### Step 2 — Define the Database URL
The URL is **not** a standard web URL. It follows the JDBC sub-protocol syntax:

```
jdbc:<subprotocol>://<host>:<port>/<database_name>?<parameters>
```

> [!NOTE]
> **Real-world examples**:
> - MySQL: `jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/ktu_students`
> - Oracle: `jdbc:oracle:thin:@localhost:1521:ORCL`
> - PostgreSQL: `jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/ktu_db`

### Step 3 — Invoke `DriverManager.getConnection()`
The factory method that returns a live `Connection` object.

$$\text{Connection} = \text{DriverManager.getConnection}(\text{URL}, \text{username}, \text{password})$$

The `DriverManager` iterates through all registered drivers, asks each one *"Can you handle this URL?"*, and picks the first one that accepts. This is the **Chain of Responsibility pattern** in action — a direct application of OOP principles.

### Step 4 — Handle `SQLException`
Any failure (wrong password, DB down, port blocked, driver missing) throws `java.sql.SQLException`, which is a **checked exception** (subclass of `Exception`).

### Step 5 — Configure the Connection (Optional but common)
After obtaining the `Connection`, properties like auto-commit can be set:
- `conn.setAutoCommit(false);` — for transaction control.

## 2.2 The Four JDBC Driver Types (High-Yield for KTU)

| Type | Name | Mechanism | KTU Exam Insight |
|------|------|-----------|------------------|
| **Type 1** | JDBC-ODBC Bridge | Translates JDBC → ODBC → DB | Obsolete since JDK 8 |
| **Type 2** | Native-API Driver | Uses vendor client-side libraries | Requires native installation |
| **Type 3** | Network Protocol | Sends via middleware server | Used in 3-tier apps |
| **Type 4** | Thin Driver (Pure Java) | Converts JDBC calls **directly** to DB-specific protocol | **Most widely used**; pure Java; no native code |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> KTU examiners frequently ask: *"Which driver is platform-independent and written purely in Java?"* — Answer: **Type 4 (Thin Driver)**.

## 2.3 KTU Formula / Syntax Sheet

| Syntax Component | Format / Equation | Purpose |
|------------------|-------------------|---------|
| Driver Loading | `Class.forName("driver_class_name")` | Register the driver |
| URL Pattern | `jdbc:<vendor>://<host>:<port>/<db>` | Locate the database |
| Connection Call | `DriverManager.getConnection(URL, user, pass)` | Open the session |
| Close Connection | `connection.close();` | Release resources |
| Auto-Commit Check | `connection.getAutoCommit()` | Verify transaction mode |
| Checked Exception | `SQLException` | Must be caught/declared |

## 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility

Connection establishment is the **backbone of enterprise Java**:
- **Banking systems**: Each transaction opens a connection from a connection pool (HikariCP, C3P0).
- **E-commerce**: Every checkout fetches inventory, validates payment, and updates orders through pooled connections.
- **IoT dashboards**: Telemetry data is persisted via JDBC connections to time-series DBs.
- **KTU Lab Exam**: You will be asked to write a complete Java program that connects to MySQL/Oracle and fetches data from a `Student` table.

---

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 The Complete Chain — From Code to Live Connection

We now walk through **every internal transition** that happens when a Java program establishes a database connection. Each step shows the *mechanism*, the *object created*, and the *side effect*.

### Derivation Step 1 — Driver Registration

$$\text{Class.forName}(\text{``com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver''})$$

**Mechanism Explored**:
1. The JVM's classloader reads the bytecode file `com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver.class` from the JAR.
2. The class's **static initialization block** executes:

$$\text{static } \{ \text{java.sql.DriverManager.registerDriver}(\text{new com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver()}); \}$$

3. A new `Driver` instance is created and pushed into the `DriverManager`'s internal `List<Driver>` (the registry).

**Why it matters**: Without registration, `DriverManager` has no idea MySQL exists.

### Derivation Step 2 — URL Parsing

When you pass `"jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/ktu_students"` to `getConnection()`:

$$\text{DriverManager} \rightarrow \text{Iterate over registered drivers} \rightarrow \text{Call driver's } acceptsURL(\text{URL}) \text{ method}$$

The MySQL driver's `acceptsURL()` returns `true` because the sub-protocol `mysql` matches.

### Derivation Step 3 — Socket-Level Connection

The MySQL Type-4 driver, having accepted the URL, performs a **TCP three-way handshake** with port 3306 of the host:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Client} &\xrightarrow{\text{SYN}} \text{Server} \\
\text{Server} &\xrightarrow{\text{SYN-ACK}} \text{Client} \\
\text{Client} &\xrightarrow{\text{ACK}} \text{Server} \quad \text{[Connection Established]}
\end{aligned}
$$

After the TCP handshake, the MySQL **handshake protocol** begins:
- Server sends its banner + protocol version.
- Client sends authentication packet (username + scrambled password using `SHA1` + salt).
- Server responds with `OK` or `ERR` packet.

If authentication succeeds, a new `Connection` object is returned to your Java code.

### Derivation Step 4 — Object State of `Connection`

The returned `Connection` object encapsulates:
- An open `java.net.Socket` (the physical channel).
- Metadata: database name, URL, auto-commit flag, transaction isolation level.
- State flags: `closed` (initially `false`), `readOnly`, `holdability`.

$$\text{Connection}_{\text{state}} = \{\text{socket}, \text{url}, \text{autoCommit}=\text{true}, \text{isolation}=\text{READ\_COMMITTED}\}$$

## 3.2 Complete Java Code — Annotated Derivation

```java
import java.sql.*;

public class KTUConnectionDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // ---- Step 1: Load Driver (optional in JDBC 4.0+) ----
        try {
            Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver");

            // ---- Step 2 & 3: Define URL + Establish Connection ----
            String url = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/ktu_students";
            String user = "root";
            String password = "ktu@2024";

            Connection conn = DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, password);

            if (conn != null) {
                System.out.println("Connected to: " + conn.getMetaData().getDatabaseProductName());
            }

            // ---- Step 4: Always close (Module 4 best practice) ----
            conn.close();

        } catch (ClassNotFoundException e) {
            System.out.println("Driver JAR missing from classpath!");
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            System.out.println("Connection failed: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
```

### 3.3 Analytical Matrix — Common Failure Modes

| Error Message | Root Cause | KTU Examiner's Likely Question |
|---------------|-----------|-------------------------------|
| `No suitable driver found` | URL typo or missing JAR | "Why does `getConnection()` fail with this error?" |
| `Communications link failure` | DB server down / wrong port | Diagnose network-layer issues |
| `Access denied for user 'root'` | Wrong password | Mention `SQLException` |
| `Unknown database 'ktu_students'` | DB not created | Check schema exists |
| `ClassNotFoundException` | MySQL connector JAR not in `lib/` | Add JAR to classpath |

## 3.4 Why `DriverManager` Uses Chain of Responsibility (OOP Insight)

The internal call:

$$\text{DriverManager.getConnection}(u, p) = \text{For each } d \in \text{registered drivers:} \quad \text{if } d.\text{acceptsURL}(u) \rightarrow d.\text{connect}(u, p)$$

This is a textbook **Chain of Responsibility** design pattern — decoupling the *requester* (your code) from the *handler* (specific driver). KTU examiners love linking OOP principles to JDBC.

---

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

<!-- SECTION_4_START -->
# 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

## 4.1 JDBC Connection Establishment — Architectural Flow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Java Application Main] --> B[Step 1: Class.forName OR Auto-Load]
    B --> C[Step 2: DriverManager.registerDriver]
    C --> D[Step 3: Construct Database URL]
    D --> E[Step 4: DriverManager.getConnection URL user pass]
    E --> F{DriverManager: Iterate Registered Drivers}
    F --> G1[Driver 1 acceptsURL?]
    F --> G2[Driver 2 acceptsURL?]
    F --> G3[Driver N acceptsURL?]
    G1 -- NO --> F
    G2 -- YES --> H[Selected Driver connect Method]
    H --> I[TCP Handshake with DB Server on Port 3306]
    I --> J[MySQL Authentication Protocol]
    J --> K{Auth Successful?}
    K -- YES --> L[Return Connection Object to Java App]
    K -- NO --> M[Throw SQLException]
    L --> N[Use Connection for Statement Execution]
    N --> O[conn.close Method to Release Resources]
```

## 4.2 Class-Level Collaboration Diagram

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class DriverManager {
        +registerDriver(Driver)
        +getConnection(String url, String user, String pwd) Connection
        -drivers : List~Driver~
    }
    class Driver {
        <<interface>>
        +acceptsURL(String url) boolean
        +connect(String url, Properties info) Connection
    }
    class Connection {
        <<interface>>
        +createStatement() Statement
        +close() void
        +setAutoCommit(boolean) void
    }
    class MySQLDriver {
        +acceptsURL(String url) boolean
        +connect(String url, Properties info) Connection
    }
    class SQLException {
        +getMessage() String
        +getErrorCode() int
        +getSQLState() String
    }
    DriverManager --> Driver : manages registry
    Driver <|.. MySQLDriver : implements
    MySQLDriver ..> Connection : returns
    DriverManager ..> SQLException : throws
```

## 4.3 Sequence Diagram — End-to-End Connection Lifecycle

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Java Application
    participant DM as DriverManager
    participant Drv as MySQL Driver
    participant DB as MySQL Server

    App->>DM: Class.forName (load driver)
    Note over DM: Static block auto-registers driver
    App->>DM: getConnection(url, user, pass)
    DM->>Drv: acceptsURL(url) ?
    Drv-->>DM: true
    DM->>Drv: connect(url, props)
    Drv->>DB: TCP SYN (port 3306)
    DB-->>Drv: TCP SYN-ACK
    Drv->>DB: TCP ACK
    Drv->>DB: Auth Packet (user, sha1_pwd)
    DB-->>Drv: OK Packet
    Drv-->>App: Connection object
    App->>App: Execute SQL...
    App->>DM: conn.close()
    DM->>DB: Terminate socket
```

---

<!-- SECTION_4_END -->

# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

---

### **Q1. Define JDBC and explain the role of `DriverManager` in connection establishment.**
`[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023, Model Question Paper]`

**Model Answer (3 marks)**:
JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) is a Java API (package `java.sql`) that enables Java applications to interact with relational databases in a database-independent manner.

The `DriverManager` class acts as a **factory** that:
1. Maintains a registry of available JDBC drivers (loaded via `Class.forName()` or auto-loading).
2. Selects the appropriate driver by calling its `acceptsURL()` method.
3. Returns a `Connection` object via the `getConnection()` method.

It follows the **Factory + Chain of Responsibility** design pattern, decoupling the client from specific DBMS implementations.

---

### **Q2. What is a Database URL in JDBC? Write the standard format with an example for MySQL.**
`[KTU University Exam - June 2024]`

**Model Answer (3 marks)**:
A **Database URL** in JDBC is a string that uniquely identifies the target database for connection. It follows the sub-protocol format.

**Standard Format**:
```
jdbc:<sub-protocol>://<host>:<port>/<database_name>
```

**MySQL Example**:
```
jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/ktu_students
```
Here, `jdbc` is the main protocol, `mysql` is the sub-protocol, `localhost` is the host, `3306` is the default MySQL port, and `ktu_students` is the schema name.

---

## 5.2 Part B — Full 14-Mark Questions (Module Internal Choice)

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Pitfall Callout**
> 1. **Forgetting `throws SQLException` / `try-catch`** → 2-mark deduction (it's a *checked* exception).
> 2. **Hardcoding credentials in production** → Examiner may deduct 1 mark for not mentioning best practice; always say *"use environment variables or config files"*.
> 3. **Skipping `conn.close()`** → 1-mark cut; leads to **resource leaks**.
> 4. **Confusing `Statement` and `PreparedStatement`** → Use `PreparedStatement` for parameterized queries (prevents SQL injection).
> 5. **Wrong driver class name** (e.g., writing `com.mysql.jdbc.Driver` instead of `com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver`) → 1-mark cut.

---

### **Question A (14 Marks)**

`[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023, Modified for 2024 Scheme]`

**(a)** Explain the **architecture of JDBC** with a neat diagram. List the **four types of JDBC drivers** and highlight which one is most commonly used in modern enterprise applications. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** Write a complete Java program that establishes a connection to a MySQL database named `KTU2024` running on `localhost:3306` with username `admin` and password `ktu@123`. The program should:
- Display a confirmation message on successful connection.
- Print the database product name and version using `DatabaseMetaData`.
- Properly close the connection in a `finally` block. **(7 marks)**

---

#### **Model Solution for Q-A(a) — 7 Marks**

**JDBC Architecture** consists of the following layers:
1. **Java Application Layer** — User code that calls JDBC API.
2. **JDBC API Layer** — Interfaces like `DriverManager`, `Connection`, `Statement`, `ResultSet`.
3. **JDBC Driver Manager Layer** — Manages registered drivers.
4. **JDBC Driver Layer** — Vendor-specific implementations (Type 1/2/3/4).
5. **Database Layer** — The actual RDBMS (MySQL, Oracle, etc.).

**Four Driver Types** (table for 4 marks, explanation for 3):

| Type | Name | Pure Java? | Used Today? |
|------|------|-----------|-------------|
| 1 | JDBC-ODBC Bridge | No | ❌ Removed in JDK 8 |
| 2 | Native-API | No | ❌ Requires native libs |
| 3 | Network Protocol | Yes (partial) | ⚠️ Limited |
| 4 | Thin Driver | **Yes** | ✅ **Most used** |

**Conclusion**: Type 4 (Thin) driver is most popular because it is **platform-independent**, requires no native libraries, and converts JDBC calls directly into the database's native protocol.

---

#### **Model Solution for Q-A(b) — 7 Marks**

```java
import java.sql.*;

public class KTUConnectionProgram {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Connection conn = null;
        try {
            // Step 1: Load Driver (optional in JDBC 4.0+)
            Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver");

            // Step 2: Define URL and credentials
            String url  = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/KTU2024";
            String user = "admin";
            String pass = "ktu@123";

            // Step 3: Establish connection
            conn = DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, pass);
            System.out.println("✓ Connection Established Successfully!");

            // Step 4: Fetch metadata
            DatabaseMetaData meta = conn.getMetaData();
            System.out.println("Database : " + meta.getDatabaseProductName());
            System.out.println("Version  : " + meta.getDatabaseProductVersion());

        } catch (ClassNotFoundException e) {
            System.out.println("Driver not found: " + e.getMessage());
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            System.out.println("SQL Error: " + e.getMessage());
        } finally {
            // Step 5: Always close in finally block
            try {
                if (conn != null) conn.close();
                System.out.println("Connection closed.");
            } catch (SQLException e) {
                e.printStackTrace();
            }
        }
    }
}
```

**Mark Distribution**:
- Correct URL format: **1 mark**
- Proper `Class.forName()` or auto-load mention: **1 mark**
- `DriverManager.getConnection()` call: **1 mark**
- `try-catch-finally` structure: **2 marks**
- `DatabaseMetaData` usage: **1 mark**
- `conn.close()` in `finally`: **1 mark**

---

### **Question B (14 Marks) — Alternative Choice**

`[KTU University Exam - June 2024, Modified]`

**(a)** Differentiate between **Type 1, Type 2, Type 3, and Type 4 JDBC drivers** with diagrams. Explain why Type 4 is preferred in modern applications. **(7 marks)**

**(b)** Explain the **step-by-step procedure to establish a JDBC connection** in Java. Include the role of `DriverManager`, the URL format, and the proper use of `try-with-resources` to handle `SQLException`. Write a Java program demonstrating the same. **(7 marks)**

---

#### **Model Solution for Q-B(a) — 7 Marks**

**Difference Table** (5 marks):

| Aspect | Type 1 | Type 2 | Type 3 | Type 4 |
|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| Other Name | JDBC-ODBC Bridge | Native-API | Network Protocol | Thin Driver |
| Pure Java | No | No | Yes | **Yes** |
| Performance | Slow | Medium | Medium | **Fast** |
| Platform Dependence | Yes | Yes | No | **No** |
| Native Code Required | Yes | Yes | No | **No** |
| Maintenance Cost | High | High | Medium | **Low** |
| Example | Sun's Bridge | Oracle OCI | IDS Server | MySQL Connector/J |

**Why Type 4 is preferred** (2 marks):
- 100% pure Java → platform independence.
- No need to install client-side native libraries.
- Direct conversion to database protocol → faster.
- Easy to deploy as a single JAR file (e.g., `mysql-connector-j-8.x.jar`).

---

#### **Model Solution for Q-B(b) — 7 Marks**

**Procedure** (3 marks):
1. Import `java.sql.*` package.
2. Load the JDBC driver class using `Class.forName()`.
3. Construct the database URL.
4. Call `DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, password)`.
5. Use the `Connection` for `Statement` / `PreparedStatement`.
6. Close the connection in a `finally` block or use **try-with-resources**.

**Java Program using Try-With-Resources** (4 marks):

```java
import java.sql.*;

public class KTUTryWithResources {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String url  = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/KTU2024";
        String user = "admin";
        String pass = "ktu@123";

        // try-with-resources auto-closes Connection
        try (Connection conn = DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, pass)) {
            System.out.println("Connected to: " + conn.getCatalog());
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            System.out.println("Connection error: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
```

**Key Exam Points**:
- `try-with-resources` (Java 7+) implements `AutoCloseable` and guarantees `close()`.
- `Connection` interface extends `AutoCloseable` since JDBC 4.1.
- Always check whether your MySQL connector version supports the new driver class (`com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver` for MySQL 8+).

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **High-Density Revision Checklist — Connection Establishment**

### 🔹 Core Concepts
- **JDBC** = Java Database Connectivity (`java.sql` package).
- **Connection establishment** is *Step 2* of the 5-step JDBC workflow.
- The `Connection` object represents an *active, authenticated session*, not the database itself.

### 🔹 Must-Remember Syntax
- URL format: `jdbc:<subprotocol>://<host>:<port>/<database>`
- Default MySQL port: **3306**, Oracle: **1521**, PostgreSQL: **5432**.
- MySQL 8+ driver class: `com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver`.
- Method signature: `DriverManager.getConnection(String url, String user, String password)`.

### 🔹 Exception Handling
- `SQLException` is a **checked exception** → must `try-catch` or `throws`.
- Common subtypes: `SQLNonTransientException`, `SQLTransientException`, `SQLRecoverableException`.
- Always use `printStackTrace()` or `getMessage()` in production logs.

### 🔹 Driver Types
- **Type 4 (Thin / Pure Java)** is the industry standard.
- Type 1 was removed in **JDK 8** — never use it.

### 🔹 OOP Principles in Action
- **Factory Pattern** → `DriverManager.getConnection()`.
- **Chain of Responsibility** → Iterating through registered drivers.
- **Interface-Based Design** → `Driver`, `Connection`, `Statement` are all interfaces.

### 🔹 Best Practices
- Always close connections in `finally` or use `try-with-resources`.
- Never hardcode credentials — use a `.properties` file or environment variables.
- Use **connection pooling** (HikariCP, C3P0) in real applications — never open a new connection per request in production.
- Disable `autoCommit` only when performing multi-statement transactions.

### 🔹 Common KTU Exam Traps
- Confusing `Class.forName()` with `new Driver()` — only the former triggers static registration.
- Forgetting the `?useSSL=false&serverTimezone=UTC` parameter in modern MySQL URLs.
- Mixing up `Statement` and `PreparedStatement`.

---

# SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

In **Java Database Connectivity (JDBC)**, a **`ResultSet`** is an interface declared in the `java.sql` package that represents a **tabular representation of the data returned from an executed SQL query** (typically a `SELECT` statement). The `ResultSet` object maintains a **cursor** that points to the current row of data; initially, the cursor is positioned **before the first row**.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Syllabus Highlight (Module 4 - JDBC):**
> A `ResultSet` is *not* a permanently stored table in the database. It is a **client-side, in-memory, scrollable or forward-only cursor object** that allows Java applications to **iterate, read, and update** rows resulting from a query.

The signature of the interface in the Java standard library is:
```java
public interface ResultSet extends Wrapper, AutoCloseable
```

It is obtained by invoking the `executeQuery(String sql)` method on a `java.sql.Statement`, `PreparedStatement`, or `CallableStatement` object.

---

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The Spreadsheet Cursor

Imagine you are working inside **Microsoft Excel**:

1. You run a query, and the database returns **1,000 rows**.
2. The database cannot dump all 1,000 rows to your Java program at once — that would consume enormous memory.
3. Instead, the database opens a **virtual spreadsheet** (the `ResultSet`) and hands you a **single pointer (the cursor)** that currently sits *above* Row 1.
4. Every time you call `next()`, the pointer moves **down by one row**, and you can read the cell values using methods like `getString("name")` or `getInt(2)`.
5. If the `ResultSet` is **scrollable**, you can also move **up**, **jump to a specific row**, or **check if you are on the last row**.

> [!NOTE]
> **The Cursor Mental Model (KTU Favorite Question):**
> Think of `ResultSet` as a **bookmark sliding through the pages of a query result**. The bookmark does not hold the entire book; it only tells you which page you are currently reading.

---

## 1.3 Why Do We Need a `ResultSet`?

The need for a `ResultSet` arises from a fundamental engineering constraint:

| Constraint | Reality | Solution Offered by `ResultSet` |
|------------|---------|----------------------------------|
| **Memory** | A 10-million-row table cannot fit in RAM | Streaming, row-by-row access via cursor |
| **Network bandwidth** | Sending millions of rows over JDBC-ODBC bridge is slow | Lazy fetch, only requested row is transmitted |
| **DB locking** | Holding a DB lock for the entire dataset is dangerous | Cursor-based, transactional row access |
| **Data integrity** | Two users editing the same data simultaneously | Concurrency modes (`CONCUR_READ_ONLY` vs `CONCUR_UPDATABLE`) |

> [!TIP]
> **Default Configuration in JDBC:**
> When you use `Statement.executeQuery(sql)` without explicitly setting parameters, the resulting `ResultSet` is **`TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY`** and **`CONCUR_READ_ONLY`**. This is the **minimum feature set** guaranteed to work on *every* JDBC-compliant database (a crucial point for KTU database portability questions).

---

## 1.4 Position of `ResultSet` in the JDBC Architecture

The `ResultSet` is the **third tier** of the standard JDBC execution pipeline:

$$
\text{Connection} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{Statement} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{ResultSet}
$$

This forms the famous **"C-S-R triad"** (Connection–Statement–ResultSet) that is a recurring theme in KTU 2-mark and 7-mark questions.

# SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Cheat Sheet

## 2.1 Architecture of a `ResultSet` — Step-by-Step Operational Logic

The lifecycle of a `ResultSet` can be broken down into **six precise stages**:

1. **Creation Stage** — A `ResultSet` object is produced by calling `stmt.executeQuery(sql)`. At this moment, the JDBC driver translates the SQL into the database's native protocol and prepares a server-side cursor.
2. **Initial Cursor Position** — The cursor is logically placed *before row 1*. Calling any getter method *before* `next()` throws a `SQLException` with message *"Before start of result set"*.
3. **Navigation Stage** — The application calls navigation methods (`next()`, `previous()`, `absolute(n)`, `relative(n)`, `first()`, `last()`, `beforeFirst()`, `afterLast()`). Each call updates the internal cursor pointer.
4. **Data Retrieval Stage** — Once positioned on a valid row, **getter methods** (`getString`, `getInt`, `getDouble`, `getDate`, etc.) extract column values either by **column index (1-based)** or by **column label**.
5. **Update Stage (Optional)** — If the `ResultSet` is updatable (`CONCUR_UPDATABLE`), the programmer can call **updater methods** (`updateString`, `updateInt`) and then `updateRow()` / `insertRow()` / `deleteRow()` to mutate the underlying database.
6. **Closing Stage** — `rs.close()` releases the cursor. If unclosed, the `Statement` and `Connection` may also remain open, leading to **resource leaks** (a frequent KTU viva question).

---

## 2.2 Types of `ResultSet` — The Three Official Cursor Types

JDBC defines **three scrollability types**, set when the `Statement` is created:

| Constant | Cursor Behavior | Practical Use Case |
|----------|-----------------|---------------------|
| `ResultSet.TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY` | Cursor moves **only forward** (`next()` only) | Memory-efficient streaming, default for all DBs |
| `ResultSet.TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE` | Bidirectional scroll, **does not see** external DB changes | Generating reports from a snapshot |
| `ResultSet.TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE` | Bidirectional scroll, **sees** external DB changes | Real-time dashboards, live trading apps |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Insensitive vs Sensitive — The KTU One-Liner:**
> *"INSENSITIVE = the cursor is blind to other users' commits; SENSITIVE = the cursor sees other users' commits in real-time."*

---

## 2.3 Concurrency Modes — Who Can Edit?

| Constant | Edit Permission | Notes |
|----------|----------------|-------|
| `ResultSet.CONCUR_READ_ONLY` | **No updates** allowed (default) | Safe, portable, works on every driver |
| `ResultSet.CONCUR_UPDATABLE` | Allows `updateXxx()`, `insertRow()`, `deleteRow()` | Requires the query to reference **only one table** and include **all primary-key columns** (KTU board favorite) |

---

## 2.4 KTU High-Yield Formula & API Cheat Sheet

| # | Component | Syntax / Formula | Returns | Default Behavior |
|---|-----------|------------------|---------|------------------|
| 1 | Execute SELECT | `ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery(sql);` | `ResultSet` | Cursor before row 1 |
| 2 | Move Forward | `boolean b = rs.next();` | `true` if row exists | Returns `false` after last row |
| 3 | Move Backward | `boolean b = rs.previous();` | `true` if row exists | Needs scrollable type |
| 4 | Jump Absolute | `boolean b = rs.absolute(5);` | `true` if valid position | 1-based indexing |
| 5 | Jump Relative | `boolean b = rs.relative(-2);` | `true` if valid | Negative = backward |
| 6 | Get by Index | `String n = rs.getString(2);` | Column value | Index starts at **1** |
| 7 | Get by Label | `int id = rs.getInt("emp_id");` | Column value | Case-insensitive |
| 8 | Get Row Count | `int n = rs.getRow();` | Current row number | 0 if no current row |
| 9 | Check Empty | `if (rs.next() == false)` | — | Use to detect zero rows |
| 10 | Update Cell | `rs.updateDouble("salary", 55000.0);` | — | Needs updatable + `updateRow()` |
| 11 | Insert Row | `rs.moveToInsertRow(); rs.updateString(...); rs.insertRow();` | — | Requires PK fields |
| 12 | Delete Row | `rs.deleteRow();` | — | Cursor must be on a valid row |
| 13 | Refresh Row | `rs.refreshRow();` | — | Re-fetches from DB |
| 14 | Close | `rs.close();` | `void` | Always wrap in `finally` |
| 15 | Get Metadata | `ResultSetMetaData rsmd = rs.getMetaData();` | `ResultSetMetaData` | Gives column count, types, names |

---

## 2.5 Real-World Engineering Utility

The `ResultSet` model is the **foundation of every data-driven Java application**:

- **Banking systems** — Transactional queries that scroll through millions of customer records.
- **E-commerce** — Product catalog pagination via `absolute()`.
- **Healthcare** — Patient records where `TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE` ensures doctors see live updates from labs.
- **Educational ERP** — KTU's own internal portal processes exam results through scrollable, read-only `ResultSet`s.
- **IoT dashboards** — Sensor data streamed row-by-row using `TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY` for memory efficiency.

## 2.6 `ResultSetMetaData` — The "About-Data" Object

A frequently paired topic in KTU Module 4:

$$
\text{ResultSetMetaData } = \text{ schema/structure of the ResultSet }
$$

It exposes:

# SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Derivation 1 — Creating a Default `ResultSet` and Reading All Rows

**Problem Statement:** Connect to a MySQL database, retrieve all employees from the `employees` table, and print their names and salaries.

**Step 1 — Load Driver and Establish Connection**

```java
Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver");
Connection con = DriverManager.getConnection(
    "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/ktu_db", "root", "password");
```

*Logic:* The driver registers itself with `DriverManager`. The `Connection` is a heavyweight, network-socket-backed object representing a live session.

**Step 2 — Create a Statement**

```java
Statement stmt = con.createStatement();
```

*Logic:* A `Statement` acts as a **carrier** that ships your SQL string to the DB and brings back a `ResultSet`. Since no `ResultSet` type or concurrency is specified, the default is `TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY` + `CONCUR_READ_ONLY`.

**Step 3 — Execute the Query**

```java
String sql = "SELECT emp_id, name, salary FROM employees";
ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery(sql);
```

*Logic:* The driver opens a server-side cursor and returns a *client-side handle* `rs`. The cursor is logically positioned **before row 1** (i.e., at row index 0).

**Step 4 — Iterate Using `next()`**

```java
while (rs.next()) {
    int id       = rs.getInt("emp_id");
    String name  = rs.getString("name");
    double sal   = rs.getDouble("salary");
    System.out.println(id + " | " + name + " | " + sal);
}
```

*Logic:* Each call to `next()` advances the cursor by one row. The first call moves from "before row 1" to "row 1". When the cursor moves past the last row, `next()` returns `false` and the loop terminates.

**Step 5 — Close Resources (Reverse Order of Creation)**

```java
rs.close();
stmt.close();
con.close();
```

*Logic:* Resources are released in **LIFO** (Last-In, First-Out) order to avoid leaks. In production code, this is wrapped in a `try-with-resources` block.

> [!NOTE]
> **The cursor position equation** can be expressed as:
>
> $$P_{\text{cursor}}(k) = P_{\text{cursor}}(k-1) + 1 \quad \text{after each } next()$$
>
> where $P_{\text{cursor}}(0) = 0$ (before row 1) and $P_{\text{cursor}}(N+1) = N+1$ (after last row, causing `next()` to return `false`).

---

## 3.2 Derivation 2 — Scrollable & Updatable `ResultSet` with Insertion

**Problem Statement:** Insert a new employee using a scrollable, updatable `ResultSet`.

**Step 1 — Create a Scrollable, Updatable Statement**

```java
Statement stmt = con.createStatement(
    ResultSet.TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE,
    ResultSet.CONCUR_UPDATABLE);
```

*Logic:* We override the defaults. The cursor is now bidirectional **and** we have permission to mutate rows. This combination requires JDBC 2.0+ and a driver that supports scrollability (e.g., MySQL Connector/J, PostgreSQL).

**Step 2 — Define the Query Carefully**

```java
String sql = "SELECT emp_id, name, salary FROM employees";
ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery(sql);
```

*Logic:* For a `ResultSet` to be updatable, the SQL must:
- Reference **exactly one** table.
- Include **all primary-key columns** in the `SELECT` list.
- Not use joins, aggregations (`SUM`, `AVG`), or `DISTINCT`.

**Step 3 — Move to the Insert Buffer**

```java
rs.moveToInsertRow();
```

*Logic:* This creates a special **"insert row"** — a staging area disconnected from the original cursor position. The original cursor is remembered internally.

**Step 4 — Populate the New Row**

```java
rs.updateInt(1, 104);
rs.updateString(2, "Anjali Krishnan");
rs.updateDouble(3, 62500.50);
```

*Logic:* Updater methods **do not** write to the database yet. They only fill the staging row buffer.

**Step 5 — Commit the Insert**

```java
rs.insertRow();
```

*Logic:* The driver sends an `INSERT` SQL command to the DB. The new row appears in the underlying table.

**Step 6 — Return to the Original Cursor**

```java
rs.moveToCurrentRow();
```

*Logic:* Restores the cursor to where it was *before* `moveToInsertRow()`. The original iteration is unaffected.

---

## 3.3 Derivation 3 — Using `absolute()` for Random Pagination

**Problem Statement:** Display rows 11 to 20 (a typical "Page 2" scenario in a 10-row-per-page UI).

**Step 1 — Create a Scrollable Statement**

```java
Statement stmt = con.createStatement(
    ResultSet.TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE,
    ResultSet.CONCUR_READ_ONLY);
```

*Step 2 — Position at Row 11**

```java
ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery("SELECT name FROM employees");
if (rs.absolute(11)) {
    do {
        System.out.println(rs.getString("name"));
    } while (rs.next() && rs.getRow() <= 20);
}
```

*Logic:* The `absolute(n)` method places the cursor on row $n$ (1-based). If $n$ is positive, the cursor is counted from the start; if negative, from the end. A return value of `false` means the requested position is invalid.

**Mathematical Formulation for the Page Boundary:**

$$
\text{Page Start Row} = (\text{Page Number} - 1) \times \text{Page Size} + 1
$$

$$
\text{Page End Row} = \text{Page Number} \times \text{Page Size}
$$

For Page 2, Page Size 10:

$$
\text{Start} = (2 - 1) \times 10 + 1 = 11
$$

$$
\text{End} = 2 \times 10 = 20
$$

---

## 3.4 Analytical Matrix — Choosing the Right `ResultSet` Type

| Application Scenario | Scroll Type | Concurrency | Justification |
|----------------------|-------------|-------------|---------------|
| Bulk CSV export (millions of rows) | `TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY` | `CONCUR_READ_ONLY` | Minimal memory, fastest stream |
| Print a static report | `TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE` | `CONCUR_READ_ONLY` | Bidirectional navigation, consistent snapshot |
| Live trading dashboard | `TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE` | `CONCUR_READ_ONLY` | Reflects real-time price changes |
| In-app CRUD editor | `TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE` | `CONCUR_UPDATABLE` | Edit rows directly through the cursor |
| Two-factor authentication lookup | `TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY` | `CONCUR_READ_ONLY` | Only one row needed; no scrolling |

### ✍ Model Solution — Question A

#### Part (a) — Types of `ResultSet`

JDBC supports **three** scrollability types and **two** concurrency modes, defined as constants on the `ResultSet` interface.

**1. `ResultSet.TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY`**
This is the default type. The cursor can move **only in the forward direction** (using `next()`). It is the most memory-efficient option and is supported by every JDBC-compliant database.

```java
Statement stmt = con.createStatement();    // default = forward only
ResultSet rs   = stmt.executeQuery("SELECT * FROM students");
while (rs.next()) {
    System.out.println(rs.getString("name"));
}
```

**2. `ResultSet.TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE`**
The cursor is **bidirectional**. You can call `previous()`, `first()`, `last()`, `absolute(n)`, etc. The "insensitive" qualifier means that once the `ResultSet` is populated, it behaves like a **frozen snapshot** — any subsequent commit by another user is **not visible** to this cursor.

```java
Statement stmt = con.createStatement(
    ResultSet.TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE,
    ResultSet.CONCUR_READ_ONLY);
ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery("SELECT * FROM students");
rs.last();                      // jump to last row
rs.previous();                  // step backward
```

**3. `ResultSet.TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE`**
The cursor is bidirectional **and** reflects changes made by other transactions while the `ResultSet` is open. This is required for real-time collaborative tools (e.g., stock-ticker apps). It is the **least portable** option.

```java
Statement stmt = con.createStatement(
    ResultSet.TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE,
    ResultSet.CONCUR_READ_ONLY);
```

**Concurrency Modes:**

- `CONCUR_READ_ONLY` — Cannot update rows. Default.
- `CONCUR_UPDATABLE` — Allows calling `updateXxx()`, `insertRow()`, `deleteRow()`.

**Summary Table:**

| Type Constant | Bidirectional | Sees Live Changes | Use Case |
|---------------|---------------|-------------------|----------|
| `TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY` | No | No (streaming) | Bulk exports |
| `TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE` | Yes | No | Reports, snapshots |
| `TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE` | Yes | Yes | Real-time dashboards |

---

#### Part (b) — Insert/Update/Delete via Updatable `ResultSet`

```java
import java.sql.*;

public class UpdatableResultSetDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String url  = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/ktu_db";
        String user = "root";
        String pass = "password";

        try (Connection con = DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, pass)) {

            // 1. Create a scroll-sensitive, updatable Statement
            Statement stmt = con.createStatement(
                ResultSet.TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE,
                ResultSet.CONCUR_UPDATABLE);

            ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery(
                "SELECT emp_id, name, salary FROM employees");

            // ---------- INSERT ----------
            rs.moveToInsertRow();
            rs.updateInt(1, 201);
            rs.updateString(2, "Rahul Menon");
            rs.updateDouble(3, 50000.00);
            rs.insertRow();
            rs.moveToCurrentRow();
            System.out.println("Inserted successfully.");

            // ---------- UPDATE ----------
            rs.beforeFirst();
            while (rs.next()) {
                if (rs.getString("name").equals("Rahul Menon")) {
                    rs.updateDouble("salary", 55000.00);
                    rs.updateRow();
                    System.out.println("Updated salary for Rahul Menon.");
                    break;
                }
            }

            // ---------- DELETE ----------
            rs.beforeFirst();
            while (rs.next()) {
                if (rs.getInt("emp_id") == 201) {
                    rs.deleteRow();
                    System.out.println("Deleted Rahul Menon's record.");
                    break;
                }
            }

            rs.close();
            stmt.close();

        } catch (SQLException e) {
            e.printStackTrace();
        }
    }
}
```

**Explanation of Key Steps:**

1. `createStatement(int, int)` — enables scrollability and updatability.
2. `moveToInsertRow()` — opens a temporary staging buffer; original cursor is saved internally.
3. `updateInt`, `updateString`, `updateDouble` — fill the staging buffer.
4. `insertRow()` — flushes the buffer to the database.
5. `moveToCurrentRow()` — restores the cursor to its prior position.
6. `updateRow()` — commits changes made to an existing row.
7. `deleteRow()` — removes the row under the cursor.

> **(b)** Write a Java program to implement **pagination** (e.g., show rows 21 to 30) using a scrollable `ResultSet`. *[7 Marks]*

---

### ✍ Model Solution — Question B

#### Part (a) — Architecture and Cursor Lifecycle

**Architecture Diagram (Verbal Description):**

A `ResultSet` is a **client-side handle** that maintains a **logical pointer (cursor)** mapping to a **server-side cursor** opened by the database. The flow is:

$$
\text{Java App} \;\to\; \text{ResultSet} \;\xleftrightarrow{\text{JDBC Driver}}\; \text{Server-Side Cursor} \;\to\; \text{Actual Table}
$$

The `ResultSet` does not hold the data permanently; it fetches rows **on demand** (controlled by the **fetch size**). The internal architecture has three components:

1. **Cursor Pointer** — A logical row position. Initial value = 0 (before first row).
2. **Row Cache** — A small buffer (default fetch size = 10) of prefetched rows.
3. **Metadata Cache** — A `ResultSetMetaData` object describing column names, types, and counts.

**Cursor Lifecycle:**

| Stage | State | Method to Call |
|-------|-------|----------------|
| Initial | Before Row 1 | (automatic) |
| Move Forward | Row $k \to k+1$ | `next()` |
| Move Backward | Row $k \to k-1$ | `previous()` (needs scrollable) |
| Check Start | — | `isBeforeFirst()` |
| Check End | — | `isAfterLast()` |
| Final | Closed | `close()` |

---

#### Part (b) — Pagination Program (Rows 21 to 30)

```java
import java.sql.*;

public class PaginationDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int pageSize   = 10;
        int pageNumber = 3;     // we want page 3
        int startRow   = (pageNumber - 1) * pageSize + 1;   // = 21
        int endRow     = pageNumber * pageSize;             // = 30

        try (Connection con = DriverManager.getConnection(
                "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/ktu_db", "root", "password")) {

            Statement stmt = con.createStatement(
                ResultSet.TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE,
                ResultSet.CONCUR_READ_ONLY);

            ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery("SELECT emp_id, name FROM employees");

            if (rs.absolute(startRow)) {
                do {
                    System.out.println(rs.getInt("emp_id") + " - "
                                       + rs.getString("name"));
                } while (rs.next() && rs.getRow() <= endRow);
            } else {
                System.out.println("Page out of range.");
            }

            rs.close();
            stmt.close();

        } catch (SQLException e) {
            e.printStackTrace();
        }
    }
}
```

**Logic:**

- `absolute(21)` jumps the cursor to row 21.
- The `do-while` loop prints the current row and advances **only if** the new row number is still $\le 30$.
- This ensures exactly **10 rows** are displayed (rows 21 through 30).

## 5.3 ⚠ KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Mistakes That Cost Marks in KTU Exams:**
>
> 1. **Confusing column indexing with array indexing** — In JDBC, columns are **1-based**, NOT 0-based. Writing `rs.getString(0)` throws `SQLException`.
> 2. **Forgetting to call `updateRow()` after `updateXxx()`** — The change is buffered, not committed. Examiners specifically check for this.
> 3. **Using `rs.getString("name")` after closing the `ResultSet`** — Always close resources **last** (reverse order of creation: `rs` → `stmt` → `con`).
> 4. **Assuming `next()` is called automatically** — It is not. You must invoke it explicitly; otherwise, the cursor remains before row 1.
> 5. **Using an updatable `ResultSet` on a multi-table JOIN** — JDBC rejects this and throws an error mentioning that the query must reference a single table with primary keys.
> 6. **Mixing up `CONCUR_READ_ONLY` and `CONCUR_UPDATABLE`** — Default is read-only. Many students lose 2 marks for not specifying it.
> 7. **Not handling `SQLException`** — A bare `rs.next()` without try-catch results in compile-time error. Examiners deduct marks for sloppy exception handling.

---

## 5.4 📌 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

- **`ResultSet`** = a `java.sql` interface representing the **rows returned by `executeQuery()`**.
- Cursor starts **before row 1**; the first call to `next()` moves it to row 1.
- **Three scroll types**: `TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY`, `TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE`, `TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE`.
- **Two concurrency modes**: `CONCUR_READ_ONLY` (default), `CONCUR_UPDATABLE`.
- **Column indexing is 1-based**, not 0-based.
- **Getter methods** can be called by **column index OR column name**.
- **Updater methods** (`updateString`, `updateInt`, …) require an explicit **`updateRow()`** to commit.
- **`insertRow()`** must be preceded by **`moveToInsertRow()`**; remember to call **`moveToCurrentRow()`** afterward.
- For an **updatable** `ResultSet`, the SELECT must reference **one table** and include **all primary-key columns**.
- **`getMetaData()`** returns a `ResultSetMetaData` describing the structure (column count, names, types).
- **`getRow()`** returns the **current** row number (0 if no current row).
- **Close order**: `ResultSet` → `Statement` → `Connection` (LIFO).
- For **pagination**, prefer `absolute(startRow)` with `TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE`.
- **Default `fetchSize`** is 10 — increase it for batch processing to reduce network round-trips.
- Use **`try-with-resources`** (Java 7+) to auto-close `Connection`, `Statement`, and `ResultSet`.
- **`wasNull()`** reports whether the last-read column had SQL `NULL` — useful for nullable columns.
- **Insensitive = frozen snapshot**; **Sensitive = live view** — this distinction is a KTU favorite 3-mark question.
